title: A Light for Revelation
body: Planning Worship Focus text: Luke 2:22-40 Have you seen those pictures on Instagram where an older family member is surrounded by other generations, often including a baby, and each person is labeled based on generation or age? It’s usually a celebration of having four, five, or even six generations all in one place. When I think of the tableau of today’s scripture, I imagine a picture just like that of Joseph standing next to Mary as she holds baby Jesus, who is squeezing Simeon’s finger. Three generations, not all related by blood, yet bound together by a promise. Except, of course, the label over Jesus’ head reads “8 days/exists beyond time.” 😊 But truly, this story is an intergenerational masterpiece. The newness of an infant, the wisdom and waiting of one close to death, and new parents squeezed in between. Young adults, who are learning how to parent and make their way in a difficult world with a vulnerable baby who happens to be the Messiah, encounter an older man who affirms the identity of their son and the reality of what their lives will be like moving forward. And then, of course, we have Anna, who breaks into praise and celebration, which I am sure was welcomed by the couple who needed the encouragement, yet also distressing if they were in the middle of one of Jesus’ nap times. So, whether you are having church in pajamas, a Christmas carol sing, or a simple worship service following the grandeur of Christmas Eve, find ways for intergenerational connection in worship today. Put out pipe cleaners and ask people to make something together during the sermon. Have a child and an older adult read the scripture together. Have an extended passing of the peace and invite everyone to find someone older or younger to greet. Infuse worship with a sense of fun and togetherness that brings generations together. This is a day to share in the light and joy revealed to us in Jesus Christ that makes us family with and for one another and sustains us as a community to support one another through all the seasons of our lives. Author bio: Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, holds a Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology and a PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: Luke 2:22-40 So, now what? That is always my favorite question after a big event, after Christmas, Easter, or even Pentecost. Maybe even after more secular events: Mother’s or Father’s Day, the Fourth of July, graduation, wedding, or the birth or adoption of a new baby. So, now what? What has changed around me or around us that makes us take the next step into a new world? What has changed within me that makes everything I could do or think from now on evidence that I am not the same person as before, and that we are not the same community as before? So, now what? Simeon approaches this question a little differently. Luke says that he was righteous and devout and that he was waiting, or anticipating, or looking for … something. My favorite translation says he was looking forward to the consolation of Israel. I love that. I’m not sure what it means, but it sounds really nice. We would all like a little consolation. We’d like to be consoled. Not a consolation prize that says nice try, but you didn’t quite make it. But the very thing you have been aching for, longing for, hoping for, praying for has come to be. Other translations talk about restoration, rescue, or comfort. We are wrestling with what exactly Simeon was looking for. But that he was leaning into what God had in store for his people was clear. So, when the young couple stagger into the Temple with the ritual sacrifice for the first-born son and pay with the provision for the poor, two birds, Simeon gets an urge; maybe it’s an itch, an inclination, a compulsion, just something that catches his eye. He thinks that he needs to be part of the hospitality team for a moment. He rushes to the side of this somehow holy family, and he says … Well, what does he say? Here again, we can scan around the different translations and not be certain. In some, he seems to be asking for something; in others, he is acknowledging that something is happening. The traditional language of the “Nunc Dimittis” is “now let your servant depart in peace.” But our translation says, “you are dismissing your servant in peace.” “It’s already done,” or “Let it be done.” Does it matter? Maybe not, probably not. But there is something about agency here that seems significant. That God is at work in this is clear, but Simeon has a part to play. And that part is pointing to the light. Simeon isn’t even speaking to increasingly uncomfortable new parents. His opening words are a prayer to God, a prayer of thanks for God’s faithfulness. It is a celebration and confirmation of all that has been guiding his heart and his hopes for all these years. It is a naming of what had been revealed to him in the secret places of his own worship life. Maybe he talked about it before, but it seems more likely that it was his secret, his burden and joy to carry within his soul the hopes and fears of all the years for his people. But now, he sees with his eyes what has been an intangible vision and an indescribable dream within his being. And he is able to put into words, to name this longing that had motivated him for so long: salvation for all people. That’s an incredible statement, don’t you think? For all people. He goes further. “A light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel” (2:32). Glory, not as somehow better than everyone else; Not as setting up a hierarchy of nations. But glory as affirmation, or inspiration to continue to live as a sign of God’s presence in the world. Glory to the people who will continue to be your people. Glory for those who have known obedience and worship, who have lived ritual and community. Glory for God’s people, which has always been with them because God was with them, and the glory is God’s. But now doors are opening. Paths are being broken, trails are being blazed—by this infant, this sign of the presence, this hope in flesh. The unknown is now known because there is a light, the light of revelation. A light is now shining, Simeon prays, and Anna proclaims. A light of access, a light of invitation. This is a candle in the window, inviting the world to come home, drawing us all home. Then Simeon’s prayer ends, and he looks deep into the eyes of the young mother and sighs. He says, echoing cousin Elizabeth, blessed are you among women. But then, with the wisdom of age and sadness at the state of the world, he says that it won’t be easy. There are many things that do not like the light that shines into the whole world. There are those who want to be exclusive, who want only a few to hold power, to have agency. There are those who subscribe to the necessity of walls and the hierarchy of peoples. This person of light will be opposed, attacked, and seen as a threat to the status quo. It will not be easy to stand with him, to follow him, to mother him. A sword will pierce your own soul. Again and again. This is the life you fell into, the life you said yes to. But you are blessed. Even in the piercing, you are blessed because God is with you. Hope is with you. Light is with you. Embrace and follow that light. So, now what? Now, walk in the blessedness of a light of revelation. Walk through open doors and be the hospitality team that welcomes the world into this light. Walk in the light.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Christmas people, today we join Simeon as he greets Jesus, a baby in his mother’s arms, with a sense of wonder and promise. We welcome the Christ Child, the Light who reveals God’s glory in unexpected places. Today, we join Anna as she greets Jesus, God Incarnate, with joy and celebration. We rejoice in the arrival of the Christ Child, the Light who reveals God’s glory in unexpected places. Today, we join with Mary and Joseph, two poor parents of a young infant, who receive the witness of Simeon and Anna that this baby is, indeed, the Messiah. We open our hearts to the Christ Child, the Light who reveals God’s glory in unexpected places. Today, we join in the story once again as witnesses for and with one another that the Savior of the world, God Incarnate, has come among us in the vulnerability of an infant. We gather today in praise and thanksgiving for the coming of the Christ Child, the Light who reveals God’s glory in unexpected places. Thanks be to God! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, August 2026. Opening Prayer Emmanuel, God with us, Simeon saw your salvation in a little child, A light for revelation to the Gentiles And for glory to the people Israel. We too long to see your salvation: healing for broken spirits, hope for broken lives, light for those in the darkness of war, warmth for those in the chill of fear. We long to see the glory of angels Peace on earth, good news for all Harbingers of joy, glimpses of grace On earth as it is in heaven. Simeon saw your salvation in a little child Radiant light, glory streaming down Stretching across the centuries to us today. We can see your salvation too: healing for broken bodies, hope for broken lives, light for those in the darkness of war, warmth for those in the chill of fear. Open our hearts to receive the good news of peace today. Open our minds to notice glimpses of your grace in enemy and friend. Open our lips to sing with joy. Open our lives to bear fruit for your reign, on earth as it is in heaven. Like Simeon, we have seen your salvation And his name is Jesus. Amen. Adapted from Dr. Sheila Klassen-Wiebe, Associate Professor of New Testament at Canadian Mennonite University in Winnipeg, Manitoba. Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2016/12/litany-luke-2-25-32.html . Prayer of Confession On this third day of Christmas, as another year draws to a close, we come together before God and with one another, confessing the ways in which we have been caught up in the frenzied spirit of the holidays and turned away from Your Spirit of Peace; the times we have focused so much on our own lives and desires, that we have neglected the voices of your children who cry out for Justice; in our focus on making the season perfect, we have turned away from the hurting people and broken places in our world in need of Healing; in the times we have dismissed Christmas as a time only for children, and we have stubbornly closed our hearts to your amazing gift of Love. O Holy Child of Bethlehem, Word Become Flesh, our Savior and King, receive our humble prayer, Cast out our sin and enter in; be born in us today. Amen. Assurance of Pardon Receive the good news of Christmas: In the Christ Child, God reveals to us the wonders of divine love. For unto us a Child is born; unto us a Son is given. His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Glory to God! Amen. Adapted from Rev. Nancy J, on her blog, wonderings through life and other such nonsense . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/11/prayer-of-confession-after-christmas.html . Benediction May God bless you with the patience to watch and listen, so that, in the spirit of Simeon and Anna, we might pay attention and be ready to witness to the Light revealing God’s glory among us wherever we go. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, August 2026.

title: The Glory Shone
body: Planning Worship Focus text: Luke 2:1-14, (15-20) “And suddenly…” Two words that signal a wondrous, glorious surprise for the shepherds watching their flocks, a surprise we remember and re-encounter every year as we gather for worship on Christmas Eve. I wonder, after reading Luke 2 year after year, do the angels seem like such a surprise anymore? Does the story, though still wondrous, seem a bit routine? Surprises pervade the Christmas season. From little daily surprises in our Advent calendars to the surprise of a large present under the Christmas tree, there’s anticipation and excitement around the possibility that something unexpected might happen. But big surprises don’t leave much room for reflection and wondering. In the moment, they flood the senses with stimuli, and only after the fact can we stop and reflect. Perhaps it’s good that the story of Christ’s birth, the angelic announcement to the shepherds, and the impromptu gathering in the stable to celebrate Jesus’ arrival is no longer a source of surprise, so that it can become a source of wonder. As you prepare for Christmas Eve worship, leave room for wonder. Make space to encounter the glory of the story once again, not by hyping up the surprise but by inviting those gathered to reflect on the glory of God among us—the glory we encounter again and again when we love our neighbors, gather in worship, lift our voices in song, and notice the beauty of God’s creation. We all have our traditions for Christmas Eve, and this is not the time to remove traditions that continue to serve us. Instead, consider how a well-placed question or prayer can help us experience the routine in a new way. If you sing “O Come All Ye Faithful,” consider using the final phrase of the sixth verse—“Word of the Father, now in flesh appearing”—as part of a spoken prayer response. When you read Luke 2, consider reading it in dialogue with a storybook version of the Nativity story, such as N.T. Wright’s The First Christmas or the version in Archbishop Desmond Tutu’s Children of God Storybook Bible . If you celebrate Holy Communion, invite congregants to focus on the tactile reality of the bread and the juice, a physical reminder that Jesus came among us as a vulnerable baby, an embodiment of God’s love and glory. When it comes time to light candles in the darkness, take a moment and invite everyone to bask in the glory of God that shines all around us when we gather to worship and remember the coming of our Savior. Author bio: Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, holds a Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology and a PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: Luke 2:1-14, (15-20) “It’s always darkest before the dawn.” We’ve all heard that cliché. It is supposed to be a word of encouragement. Lord knows, we need as much of that as we can get. But it isn’t true. At least in a natural, cosmological sense. Before dawn, light begins to grow. It is almost too subtle to notice. Slowly, what was invisible begins to become detectible. What was imperceptible becomes obvious. The light grows, we say. Little by little, we see, and we understand, and we accept. It’s a process. We grow in faith; we walk the discipleship path; we’re on the way. And there is the glory. Except that isn’t how we expect glory to shine—for us or in us or, by the grace of God, from us. We expect a moment. A flash. The angel appeared, and the glory shone around them, Luke says (2:9). Suddenly – not gradually like dawn – suddenly, there was a multitude of the heavenly host singing “glory!” That’s how glory works, we believe. That bursting in, that interruption, that serendipity. And there are those moments aplenty. Maybe you’ve been a part of a meeting or retreat where the exercise was to share “glory sightings.” What are those? Often, they are a sudden realization, a breakthrough of some sort, a breath-catching moment, perhaps. We love those. We live for those. We live by those. That’s part of what the exercise is about – opening our eyes to the activity of the Spirit or the presence of God in our midst. There were shepherds keeping watch, Luke tells us. But he doesn’t tell us what they were watching. It’s self-evident, we assume. They were watching the flock. They were watching for predators. They were watching one another, most likely. They were watching the hours pass. What they weren’t watching for was what happened. They weren’t watching for an explosion of angels. They weren’t watching for an incursion from the other side of eternity. They weren’t watching for the glory that shone all around them. It just happened. Suddenly. Surprisingly. Frighteningly. Glory can shock us, startle us. Glory can shake us to our core. But even so, afterward, they wanted more. Or they wanted to do something to acknowledge it was real. “Let’s go,” they said to one another, “to see this thing; this thing we are somehow a part of; this thing that spilled out all over us and our flock and the fields and the stars still seem to vibrate somehow. Let’s go.” So, they went. Luke doesn’t say how far they went. “In the region,” he said. It could have been a field next to the town, the little town of Bethlehem. Or it might have been a hike. “What happened to the sheep?” we wonder. Did the shepherds draw straws, and some poor soul of a shepherd had to stay behind? They didn’t think about that. They were still awed by the glory. Their eyes were still vibrating; their hearts were still pounding. They were hip-deep in glory. So, they went. And they found Mary and Joseph and the babe – this thing that was made known to them – was lying in the manger. They ran all the way from the field, scruffy, sweaty, tired, and now here it was, right before them. They didn’t know what to do. How could they? Did they kneel? Did they stand in awe? Did they move closer or shy away? We don’t know. All Luke tells us is that they talked about what they heard and what they saw. They talked about the glory that burst upon them. They amazed everyone who had gathered, and they planted deep things in the heart of the young mother, who also knew glory. What was Mary’s experience of glory? It appears to be another instance of the sudden bursting in of this light. An angel in the living room seems sudden. A birth is a moment. One second, there is no baby, and then, there is. Sudden glory. So, yes, she had moments of glory. But it really seems as though her experience of glory was more like dawn. There was a moment with an angel, but then there was the slow realization of what that visitation had in store for her. Then, there was the long conversation with her fiancé. We don’t know much about that discussion, that revelation, here in Luke. Even Matthew skips over much of what must have happened. But there are hints that it was not sudden. It took more than a moment. Then there was the gestation. In our Advent observance, we read the story of the Annunciation. Then, days later, there was a birth. But this was human biology, however divinely instigated. There was growth; there was discomfort; there was blood and pain. I’m sure there were moments when it didn’t feel all that glorious. And yet. Something grew in Mary. In Joseph, too, no doubt. (Or rather, wrapped in doubt. Surrounded by, buried by, almost choked out by doubt.) But something grew. Some light began to dawn. It was hard to see at first, but it kept growing. Glory refused to be overlooked. Glory refused to stay in the shadows. Then it was time. The glory had to cross the horizon. It had to emerge into the darkness and be born. In water and blood, glory was born. And it was seen by a tired, scared, and wounded couple kneeling next to a manger; by a group of shepherds running in from the countryside, chased by a vision they could barely believe; by the passersby who somehow got caught up in this moment, heard an impossible story, and were somehow changed in ways they would begin to grasp only in time. Or they wouldn’t at all. A dawning of glory. Then, some thirty years later, in water and blood, the glory would be lifted up again. For the whole world. Christmas comes suddenly at times, gradually at times. But it comes. And it offers a glimpse of glory. It offers an experience, a shared experience of glory. That’s why we surround ourselves with light, even in the dark of the night. We want to capture, to re-live, to proclaim that glory is born tonight. Thanks be to God.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Christmas people, look around you—the glory of God is here among us! The glory of God is here among us! In the closeness of family and the greetings of strangers… The glory of God is here among us! In the lifting of our voices and the whispers of our prayers… The glory of God is here among us! In the surprising awe of the angels and the quiet wonder of a mother’s heart… The glory of God is here among us! Come, let us worship Christ, the newborn king! Come, let us welcome the Christ Child whose glory shines among us! Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, August 2026. Opening Prayer Holy God of Love, There is light in our lives because of the abundance of your steadfast love. A love so vast, so deep, so real, that you became one of us. May we live within the power of this love. And may we share its light with a world where too many dwell in darkness. Amen. Written by Joanna Harader and posted on Spacious Faith, http://spaciousfaith.com/ . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2016/12/call-to-worship-prayer-christmas.html . Prayer of Confession God of Light, we confess that we have gone astray and have left Your light. We follow the dim lights of the world of success and fortune. We follow the dim lights that call us to be more religious by following rules. We follow the fading light of personal salvation. Forgive us for not seeking the true Light of Your love for all the world. Forgive us for not following the ways of Jesus, who commanded us to love one another. Call us to be light-bearers of love, compassion, and justice, in which the Mystery of Your Love is revealed. In the name of Jesus the Messiah, we pray. Amen . Written by Rev. Mindi and posted on her Rev-o-lution website, http://rev-o-lution.org/ . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2016/12/prayer-of-confession-seeking-light.html . Benediction Christmas people, may Emmanuel, God with us, bless you today and every day with glimpses of glory to light our way as we work for peace and goodwill to reign throughout all of God’s glorious creation. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, August 2026.

liturgical: Christmas Eve, Year B

title: Music Notes
body: Music Notes This holy and precious season begins in the dark. We gather on Christmas Eve at night, but we bring the light with us. We celebrate the light that comes in quiet, yet significant ways. We’ve come at night to await the dawn. And it comes. Even in times of great darkness, a presence of glory remains; a light shines and shows us the way. We give thanks and remember together that “Dawn Breaks.” Abbreviations UMH =United Methodist Hymnal TFWS =The Faith We Sing W&S =Worship and Song Christmas comes suddenly at times, gradually at times. But it comes, and it offers a glimpse of glory. It offers a shared experience of glory. That’s why we surround ourselves with light, even in the dark of the night. We want to capture, to re-live, to proclaim that glory is born tonight. Thanks be to God. title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “When have you had a meaningful experience in worship or with your family that included at least three generations, even if the three generations were not related by blood or adoption?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. The focus text today is the story of Jesus being presented for circumcision as an eight-day- old, and a sacrifice was made for him, as was customary for Jews in those days. Read Luke 2:22-40 . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: What do you notice about Simeon from this passage? If this was the only passage on which you could draw, what does this passage indicate about the Holy Spirit? What do you think “the consolation of Israel” means? (v. 2:25) Imagine the response of Mary and Joseph to Simeon’s prayer and the blessing given to Mary (v. 2:34-35). Name some of the competing thoughts, emotions, or convictions that Mary could have been holding in that experience. What do you find compelling about Anna’s faithfulness from this text? The Preaching Notes for December 27 say: “[N]ow doors are opening. Paths are being broken, trails are being blazed—by this infant, this sign of the presence, this hope in flesh. The unknown is now known because there is a light, the light of revelation. A light is now shining, Simeon prays, and Anna proclaims. A light of access, a light of invitation. This is a candle in the window, inviting the world to come home, drawing us all home. How does this observation focus your thinking about the presence of Jesus in the world? The prayer that Simeon prays (Luke 2:29-32) is often referred to as the Nunc Dimittis, which are the first two words of this prayer in Latin that are commonly included in bedtime or evening worship or prayer. How does Simeon’s prayer point to something being completed? What does the completion open the possibility for? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or a phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one thing you want to do because of the discussion today? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [ Isaiah 61:10-62:3 , Psalm 148 , Galatians 4:4-7 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Lord, you now have set your servant free to go in peace as you have promised; For these eyes of mine have seen the Savior, whom you have prepared for all the world to see: a Light to enlighten the nations, and the glory of your people, Israel. Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit: as it was in the beginning, is now, and will be forever. Amen. (Nunc Dmittis) Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.
liturgical: Christmas Eve, Year B

title: Faithfulness as Firm as the Heavens
body: Worship Planning Notes Focus text: Luke 1:46b-55 or Psalm 89:1-4, 19-26 “I declare that your steadfast love is established forever; your faithfulness is as firm as the heavens” (Psalm 89:2). What an odd turn of phrase. As firm as the heavens? Perhaps from an ancient perspective, the heavens—or the sky—did seem rather firm or fixed, though ancient civilizations studied the movements of the stars, so at the very least, the stellar inhabitants of “the heavens” were not firm or fixed in place. But for us today, what does it mean to declare that God’s faithfulness is as firm as the heavens? Did Artemis II just demonstrate how thin and porous the boundary between Earth and space truly is? Surely, climate change is demonstrating just how volatile the atmosphere can become when we humans don’t tend creation well. None of this sounds like a good description of God’s faithfulness. But perhaps the comparison still works today. Because, for all the variability, volatility, and vulnerability of our atmosphere, it surrounds us still, holding us together as we travel through the heavens. And that…that sounds like God’s faithfulness to me. That seems appropriate, too, for the Sunday before Christmas Eve, the night we remember that Jesus came in our variability, volatility, and vulnerability as a small baby to show us how we can live in community held together by God’s love and faithfulness. Whether you choose to focus on Luke 1 or Psalm 89 or both, our song today is a song about love and faithfulness, about how God turns things upside down so they will be right side up, about how God keeps God’s promises even when we struggle to be faithful. What are the signs of God’s steadfast love and faithfulness in your community? Maybe you play a game of “I Spy” with the children to look for signs of love during the children’s message. (Maybe you play with the whole congregation!) Perhaps you ask people to take pictures of God sightings throughout the week, and you show them in a slide show during part of the sermon. Maybe you turn a few of the pictures upside down to see what you might discover. If God’s love is an anchor in the midst of the storm, the atmosphere holding us together in the vacuum of space, then we have to be able to find it for and with one another. So, tell stories of God’s faithfulness; pray and listen for how God is calling your congregation to love their neighborhood; sing the hymns that celebrate and remember God’s faithful love. Prepare your congregation to go into Christmas ready to encounter Love Incarnate once again, because lying in the manger is the beginning and end and beginning again of God’s restoration song. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies degrees from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.
liturgical: Fourth Sunday of Advent, Year B

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Texts: Luke 1:46b-55 or Psalm 89:1-4, 19-26 There is an “or” in the Psalm category for this Sunday. And we figured, why not make it an “and.” We want to lay the two texts side by side and see what sparks in that correlation. You are, of course, free to choose one or the other and still stay true to the theme for the week. If we continue to follow the tradition for this fourth Sunday of Advent, the word would be love . We chose “faithfulness” in our heading this week. In the end, however, you can see considerable overlap between love and faithfulness. Psalm 89 is a long psalm and worth spending some time over the whole. Yes, the lectionary helps by chopping it down to size and also manages to skip over some of the more uncomfortable moments—verse 38 and following, for example, where the psalmist begins to accuse God of not living up to the covenant. God isn’t acting God-like lately—at least that is how it seems to the writer. Maybe it is better that we leave that one alone, except we have been there. Any of us, all of us, have been wanting to accuse God of not holding up the divine end of the bargain, at least as we understand it. So here, we have permission for even those emotions to be heard in worship. We are allowed, according to the psalm, to feel abandoned, left out, short-changed. In the context of the whole psalm, however, there is scope for climbing out of that pit of despair and abandonment. The psalm begins by acknowledging God’s steadfast love and faithfulness and ends with a call to bless the God who loves and is faithful؅—even when it follows an expression of lack of faithfulness or the experience of a lack of love. How is such a thing possible? Returning to the assigned section, it is obvious why it was chosen for this fourth Sunday of Advent. There is a promise here, of David as a chosen one and one who lives in the blessing, in the steadfast love and faithfulness of God. And not just David, but David’s line as well. And so to our Christian eyes, we see a promise fulfilled in a way that even the psalmist couldn’t have imagined without divine inspiration. We see the son of David and the Son of God, standing in the gap, living out the covenant in transformative ways, embodying steadfast love and faithfulness in word and deed, in living and in dying and in being raised. Yet even we who claim this Jesus, son of David, as Lord, can sometimes feel abandoned. We can sometimes feel cut off from the steadfast love of God and the faithfulness of the covenant that promises an eternal relationship and a constant presence. We feel as though God is hiding from us. That is the blessing of the life of Christ. He walked where we walk; he lived as we live. He knows the distance we experience and the despair we sometimes feel. His very presence in the world is a sign of the constant presence and steadfast love of God. His birth, the Incarnation, blessed this life we live. This invites us to turn to the second “psalm” of this Sunday: the Magnificat, we call it. It is named by the beginning of the song, “My soul magnifies the Lord.” To really grasp the depth of this restoration song, we must ask a question we don’t usually ask of biblical texts: “How did this song that Mary sang to Elizabeth and all of us really sound?” Did it come bubbling out of her, like a mountain stream rushing down from the heights? Did it burst forth in a sudden explosion of passion and power and presence? Maybe. It surely could have. It might have built with every quickening step from her house to Elizabeth’s. And when Elizabeth greeted her, or rather when Elizabeth and her baby greeted Mary, because Luke says there was a leap, an internal leap when Mary said hello, Elizabeth was staggered by the enthusiasm of the child quickening inside of her and spoke to Mary with breathless wonder and surprise. Maybe that unleashed Mary’s own sense of amazement and excitement, and her song rings from the rafters of the parsonage there in the hill country. “My soul magnifies the Lord!” It starts with the high notes. It starts with the proclamation. “My spirit rejoices in God my savior.” Bam! Somehow, though, it feels different to me. It feels ... slower ... gentler ... more reflective. It is almost as if Mary is surprising herself with all that is coming to life within her: the baby surely, but something else too; something that will stay within her even when the child emerges. Something that will sustain her when that child grows and claims a ministry that takes him away from her. Something that will define her even when this miracle, this quickening inside suffers and dies in a particularly horrible way. And that something is hope. Hope. Real hope. Hope born of the steadfast love and faithfulness of God, not the shallow and fleeting hope that we espouse all too often: “I hope it doesn’t rain!” “I hope they get here soon.” “I hope I get my wish for Christmas.” There are hopes, and there is Hope. These hopes aren’t bad, but they aren’t sustaining; they aren’t transforming. Hope, on the other hand, makes us see differently and hear differently. Mary sings a song that is not real but is True. She is blessed to be a part, she says, of God’s turning the world right side up. The grand reversal has already happened. Look at the tenses - He has scattered the proud…he has brought down the powerful, and he has lifted up the lowly. Has he? The powerful still seem enthroned. The proud still seem to be in the center. And the lowly? Well, they’re scattered, pushed down, pushed out, refugees and the feared and hated. The world still seems unfinished, still seems upside down. Yet, Mary chooses to rejoice—not as a Pollyanna, rose-colored-glasses kind of approach that ignores the harsh realities. But she chooses instead to believe that we don’t have to accept the upside-down world as it is. We don’t have to listen to the rich and powerful who tell us how to think, whom to fear, whom to exclude. We don’t have to imagine a prideful world of celebrity and privilege, of entitlement, of rights that bring destruction to relationships and communities. We can choose to see differently. We can choose to lift up the lowly because they are being lifted up already—the lowly love of neighbor and welcome of the stranger; the lowly service to the outcast and the value of listening instead of making pronouncements. We choose how we feel. We can live in anger, as our society seems determined to do. Or we can rejoice in our spirits because we get to be a part of something bigger than ourselves, something healing, something loving, something that will last into eternity. We can be a part of the quickening of the kingdom. Maybe it doesn’t really work as an imperative. Maybe we can get the world to sing with us, to rejoice with us in spirit and in truth, when we start with testimony. “My soul magnifies the Lord, my spirit rejoices with God my savior.” Tell how you feel, and others might come feel with you. Of course, we’ve got to feel something first. Rejoice. Let it come to life within you this Christmas season. Let it come to life, born of the steadfast love of the Lord and the faithfulness that is as firm as the heavens. That’s the gift we celebrate this season. That’s the hope by which we live. We wrap ourselves in hope, in peace, in joy, and in love, in Advent and the rest of the year as well. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years. title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Focus Texts: Luke 1:46b-55 or Psalm 89:1-4, 19-26 Call to Worship Today, we join our voices with Mary to sing the truth of God’s love that meets us in our upside-down world and dares to turn us right side up. God, we will sing of your steadfast love forever! We come to listen for the good news that God is already at work, filling up the hungry and turning away the rich, lifting up the lowly and removing the powerful from their thrones. God, we will sing of your steadfast love forever! We come to encounter God’s faithfulness once again, trusting that God persists in setting the world to rights even when everything feels so wrong. God, we will sing of your steadfast love forever! Come, let us worship God, who has restored and is restoring us to live as followers of the Christ Child, whose birth we eagerly anticipate and whose life, death, and resurrection make our restoration possible. God, we will sing of your steadfast love forever! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026. Opening Prayer O God, you broke down the barriers when you crept in beside us. In Jesus, your hands touched all and touched us. You opened our minds to recognize how the hands of the rich were empty, and the hearts of the poor were full. You took the widow’s mite and the child’s loaves and used them to show us the Kingdom. Here in the company of the neighbor whom we know and the stranger in our midst, and the self from whom we turn, we ask to love as Jesus loved. Make this the place and time, good Lord, when heaven and earth become one, and we in word and flesh know ourselves beloved. Amen. Adapted from “ Opening Prayer: Loving as Jesus Loved ” on the website of Old South Church in Boston, http://www.oldsouth.org. Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2015/11/opening-prayer-loving-as-jesus-loved.html . Prayer of Confession We sing “O Come All Ye Faithful,” God, but we confess that we are not always faithful. We could have shown love this past week, but we kept ourselves busy with other things. We spoke without thinking and hurt someone. We treated the gifts and greetings and meals as chores, leaving out the most important ingredient—caring. We are sorry. Please forgive us and accept our worship. Amid the bright colors that surround us this season—the red, the green, the gold—send the light of your Christ, that all that is good may be revealed more clearly and all that is wrong may be exposed and changed. We pray in the name of Jesus, who was born in Bethlehem, who lived and died for our sakes, and who lives and reigns forever. Amen. Words of Assurance God chooses us, forgives us; lights our paths with the serenity of starlight, and sends us as messengers of hope, peace, joy, and love. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Glory to God! Amen. Written by Ruth C. Duck and Maren C. Tirabassi in Touch Holiness: Resources for Worship, Updated, ed. Ruth C. Duck and Maren C. Tirabassi (Cleveland: The Pilgrim Press, 2012), 7-8. For use in worship services, include the following permissions statement: Reprinted by permission of the publisher from Touch Holiness, ed. Ruth C. Duck and Maren C. Tirabassi. Copyright © 1990 by The Pilgrim Press. Benediction Beloved, the birth of Christ is near. May God, who is Love, bless you as you watch, wait, and notice Love Incarnate moving into the neighborhood, the embodiment of God’s steadfast love nurtured in a womb and born as a vulnerable infant. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026.
liturgical: Fourth Sunday of Advent, Year B

title: Candle Lighting Liturgy
body: Candle Lighting Liturgy Reader One: With Love Incarnate growing in her womb, Mary broke out into prophetic song, “[God] has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. He has brought down the powerful from their thrones and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty. He has come to the aid of his child Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever" (Luke 1:51-55 NRSV). Today, we too join in God’s restoration song, believing in the power of God’s love to transform the world. Congregation: We lift our voices to God, believing that in an uncertain and unstable world, we are not alone. God is with us. God’s steadfast love works in and among us, forming us as agents of life-giving, world-transforming Love that came to us in the vulnerability of a womb and a manger. Reader Two: We light this candle as a sign of God’s never-ending, never-failing Love—Love that sings over us a song of restoration and hope that cannot be silenced, Love that persists in fulfilling God’s promise of salvation and flourishing for all creation. Light the fourth candle of the Advent wreath.

body: Music Notes Hope. Real hope. Hope born of the steadfast love and faithfulness of God, not the shallow and fleeting hope that we espouse all too often: “I hope it doesn’t rain!” “I hope they get here soon.” “I hope I get my wish for Christmas.” There are hopes, and there is Hope. title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Faithful and Ever-Present God, your steadfast love endures even when we struggle to see it, and your promises stand firm across every generation. As Mary sang of your great reversal, we bring these gifts in hope, trusting that you are still lifting the lowly, filling the hungry, and turning the world toward your grace. When we feel forgotten, remind us of your covenant. When the world seems unchanged, help us live as witnesses to your transforming love. Use these offerings—and our lives—to magnify your name, to embody your faithfulness, and to join your work of renewal in the world. With grateful hearts, we rejoice in you. Amen. ( Luke 1:46b-55 or Psalm 89:1-4, 19-26 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). Invite participants to discuss the following in pairs or groups of three: “Has a song ever inspired you or come to mind in a way that oriented you to the ‘task at hand’? Share with one another how a song has encouraged you in your spirit.” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You likely won’t get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Psalm 89:1-4, 19-26 . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: In the first part of Psalm 89, the psalmist is rehearsing declarations of God’s faithfulness, saying it is as “firm as the heavens.” What do you think that means? Why is that a compelling affirmation of God’s faithfulness? The psalm points to the important role of David in the life of Israel. What does the psalmist say about David throughout verses 1-4 and 19-26? Based on just this section of scripture, what do you know about David? We have a second scripture text this week, which is a familiar part of the Advent scriptures. A pregnant Mary is visiting Elizabeth, also miraculously with child. After Elizabeth’s baby leaped for joy in her womb (Luke 1:44), Mary responds with what has come to be known as the Magnificat. Read Luke 1:46b-55 . How does the song that Mary sings show a turning upside down (or rather, right side up) of the typical ways of the world? How is this restoration? While not noted in this text, Mary is a descendant of King David. How does Mary’s song reflect what you learned about David from the previous discussion? The Preaching Notes for December 13 say: “Mary chooses to rejoice—not as a Pollyanna, rose-colored-glasses kind of approach that ignores the harsh realities. But she chooses instead to believe that we don’t have to accept the upside-down world as it is…We can live in anger, as our society seems determined to do. Or we can rejoice in our spirits because we get to be a part of something bigger than ourselves, something healing, something loving, something that will last into eternity. We can be a part of the quickening of the kingdom… Maybe we can get the world to sing with us, to rejoice with us in spirit and in truth, when we start with testimony. ‘My soul magnifies the Lord, my spirit rejoices with God my savior.’ Tell how you feel, and others might come feel with you…Rejoice….Let it come to life [in this Christmas season], born of the steadfast love of the Lord and the faithfulness that is as firm as the heavens. That’s the gift we celebrate this season. That’s the hope by which we live. We wrap ourselves in hope, in peace, in joy, and in love, in Advent and the rest of the year as well.” How does the season of Advent teach you about the restoration of the world? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one learning that you’ve had in this Advent season? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [ 2 Samuel 7:1-11, 16 , Romans 16:25-27 , Luke 1:26-38 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: We will sing of your steadfast love, O Lord! We celebrate your faithfulness through all generations as we remember the promise kept to your servant David. We thank you for the faithfulness we see in Mary as she bore witness to the new call you gave her. May we receive anew the gift of your Son, Jesus Christ, in this Advent season, so that we may be restored. May the love demonstrated through his life (and death, and resurrection) plant seeds of hope, peace, joy, and covenant faithfulness in each of our lives today. In the name of Jesus, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries. title: With Shouts of Joy
body: Worship Planning Notes Focus text: Psalm 126 One of the challenges of focusing on the Psalms for a whole series is that we lose the element of story or narrative. The gospels and many of our Old Testament texts are full of stories that invite us to explore different characters, settings, and meanings. Even when we struggle with a story, there is something inviting and familiar about a narrative with a beginning, middle, and end. But in the Psalms, sometimes it feels like being dropped in and pulled out right in the middle of a story. In Psalm 126, we don’t know much about the beginning of the story, and we don’t know for sure how the story ends. All we really have is the song the people sing during an inciting incident or other critical moment in the story. It’s the song of a people remembering a time when a crisis was over, and they were crying out for God to restore them again. Think about your congregation’s story over the last year. What has God been doing? When did you experience joy together? Are you experiencing joy now, or does it feel like you are waiting for joy to come again? How is God restoring joy among you right now? I love when the third Sunday of Advent in Year B comes around, because it means I have the perfect excuse to sing one of my favorite hymns, “When God Restored Our Common Life” ( The Faith We Sing 2182). Written by Ruth Duck, this hymn is a retelling of Psalm 126 that takes the singers through it as if we are singing the story of our community—past, present, and future—the way the ancient Israelites would have understood this psalm in their own context. One of the beautiful things Ruth Duck did in this hymn was to note that joy was present in past experiences with God, but also that laughter can go hand in hand with the toil we experience now, all in the context of God’s restorative grace. Whether you sing this hymn or simply go to it for inspiration, I encourage you to consider how Duck’s setting of Psalm 126 might inform the way you plan worship for this third Sunday in Advent. Consider, too, how the story of your community might be a text, of sorts, you bring into conversation with Psalm 126. In other words, the psalm might not be a story, but it may very well illuminate the story your people are living now or have lived in the recent past. Use witness, stories, pictures, and more to enliven this text and to create connections between the ancient and contemporary peoples who remember God’s work with joy and seek to faithfully discover joy through and in God once again. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies degrees from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Psalm 126 Professor Samantha Gilmore of Wartburg Theological Seminary in Iowa advances a fascinating theory about Psalm 126. Her question is, “What if it isn’t a metaphor?” “What metaphor?” you might be asking. Read the psalm again. It is a remembering psalm. It is a cry from a difficult moment, looking back to a better one. Remember when we often ask ourselves. But what does the psalmist want us to remember? It might be difficult to determine the specifics. Many argue that the reference is the return from exile. When the people of God came back to the land they considered their home and God’s home, there was unbridled joy, even though there was much work to be done. The rebuilding was not immediate; the restoration took time and effort. Perhaps that is why the psalmist described this joy as “being like those who dream.” When reality doesn’t match what is hoped for, it takes dreamers to see the potential. Driven by this dream, joy breaks out. Laughter and joy become possible even in desperate situations because the dream is powerful and real. Remember that? The psalmist asks the singers to recall those days, even if it is a historical remembrance. Family stories tell of the return and the joy that was found in rebuilding the community, both the infrastructure and relationships. The dream was strong and sustaining. But now? “Restore our fortunes,” cries the psalmist and the singers. So quickly, we turn from a glorious, remembered past to a desperate present. What happened? Who knows? Most likely, it was the return to the burden of daily living. Or it was the sense that instead of relying on the community, we are now on our own. Each one has the resources – it was assumed – to lead their own lives. Or perhaps instead of being enriched by neighbors, they began to be concerned about how others were living their lives. The neighbor became “other.” Instead of widening the circle, they shrank it. Instead of a sense of “we the people,” it became more of an “us-and-them,” an adversarial approach to those around them. This polarization did not satisfy, however. The people realized that something was wrong. Something was missing. Thus, the song of Psalm 126. “Remember those days,” they said in their own hearts and then maybe to those around them. Remember how real laughter was, how profound joy was? Do you remember that? We shouted, they said to one another, actually shouted our joy. When was the last time you shouted for joy? We need to get that back. We need to be those people again. Luckily, they were wise enough to know the source of the joy. Restore us, Lord. Restore our fortunes. Wait a minute. What is the request, really? Fortunes. How do we understand fortunes? Is this about material wealth? Of course, desperate people are seeking the resources they need to survive, perhaps even to thrive. There isn’t anything shameful about seeking restoration that involves financial stability. Yet, when the opening verse remembered restoration as freedom, nation-building, and community gathering, surely the new dream is more than simply financial. It is about well-being and turning tears into shouts of joy. It is about coming home with hope, living in peace and knowing a joy so profound it cannot be kept inside. It leaks out in shouts and in laughter. So, let’s go back to Professor Gilmore’s question. “What if Psalm 126 is not a metaphor, but a reality?” She is helping us answer the question of where this joy comes from. The psalm presents this joy as passive. We don’t generate this joy; it is given to us. Our mouths were filled … by someone from somewhere. But what would this look like today? What if this is not a metaphor for something less intense, which is often an assumption in 21st-century United States, thinking-over-feeling contexts, but something that God really does? This language does not suggest a few stifled giggles in an otherwise serious gathering but uncontrolled, tear-inducing, knee-slapping, belly-aching guffaws spreading through the crowd! What kind of events might bring this about? -- Samantha Gilmore, Working Preacher, https://www.workingpreacher.org/commentaries/revised-common-lectionary/third-sunday-of-advent-2/commentary-on-psalm-126-16 . Can we even imagine such a thing? Here we are in Advent, remembering the promise of eternity, but also remembering the inbreaking of the kingdom in a birth in a manger on a star-filled night. Who around you is filled with joy this season? Who among us knows what it is to be unable to keep joy contained? Maybe this is part of what Jesus meant when he told us we need to become like little children. Maybe he was suggesting that we need to be filled with joy, to let our mouths be filled with laughter, and to let it out every chance we get in shouts that serve as a reminder that something wonderful is happening, has happened, will happen, and therefore is happening . Psalm 126 wants us to let joy spill out like water in the desert. Our liturgical obligation this Advent season is to give space in worship and in work for shouts of joy. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Focus Text: Psalm 126 Call to Worship In the dry and arid places of our lives, God, come and bring new life. God, fill our mouths with laughter and our tongues with shouts of joy! In the lonely and isolated places of our lives, God, come and bring connection. God, fill our mouths with laughter and our tongues with shouts of joy! When we forget all you have done for us, God, come and help us tell the stories of your acts among us. God, fill our mouths with laughter and our tongues with shouts of joy! Beloved, come and let us worship God who saved and sustained us in the past and saves and sustains us now to be an Advent people of joy. God, fill our mouths with laughter and our tongues with shouts of joy that we may live as messengers of hope, peace, joy, and love in a hurting world. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026. Opening Prayer Come to this sanctuary, this house, this home, Holy Christ, And let us receive you with lavish welcome. You are the Restorer of our fortunes,The Promise of new life – We pour out our praise to you. Fill this room with your Spirit: The sound of wind, the warmth of flame, the scent of perfume And fill our hearts with your compassion, Not just in this time and place, But in all times and in all places, So that as we celebrate the great things you have done for us, We may also embody the love you give to all. Amen. Posted on the United Church of Christ’s Worship Ways Archive , http://www.ucc.org/ . Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2013/02/opening-prayer-psalm-126.html . Prayer of Confession Lord, you know that the time we’ve spent away from you has been filled with turmoil, disappointment, frustration, heartache, and despair. We have forgotten all about being blameless and turning the other cheek. We gave in to urges to be petty, spiteful, and hurtful. And while “telling it like it is” sure felt good at the time, we now find ourselves empty, confused, and ashamed. Today, we come here for Sabbath, for rest, refreshment, and renewal. Lord, we want to be sanctified and holy; we do. We want to be kind, to hold on to the good and encourage and greet each other in love, but you’re going to have to help us—a lot. Fill our mouths with praise and laughter, our hearts with joy and peace, and our souls with quiet satisfaction. This is our prayer. Amen. Words of assurance The grace of our Lord is all over us, no matter what comes or what goes. Whether there are floods, earthquakes, overdue bills, disease, hardheaded children, unresponsive parents, betrayal, unfaithfulness—it doesn’t matter because God is bigger than all the things that perplex us. May our hearts and minds be filled with confidence and peace. Amen. Written by Cynthia A. Bond Hopson in The Africana Worship Book, Year B (Nashville: Discipleship Resources, 2007), 148. Benediction May God bless you with joy that surpasses all understanding, rooted not in what goes right or wrong but in God’s faithful, steadfast love that even now is at work, in-breaking the kingdom of God among us and inviting us to join in with laughter and delight. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026.

title: Candle Lighting Liturgy
body: Candle Lighting Liturgy Reader One: In a world full of conflict, uncertainty, and suffering, joy is an act of resistance. Joy is an act of hope born out of our belief that God can and will restore us. God is, in fact, already restoring us into a future where God’s people “shall build up the ancient ruins; they shall raise up the former devastations; they shall repair the ruined cities, the devastations of many generations,” and God “will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations” (Isaiah 61:4, 11 NRSV). Today, we wait and work in joy for God’s restoration among us. Congregation: Faced with the distress and anxieties of the world, we choose joy. May this joy empower us to pay attention to the pain and hurt of others, inspire us to imagine a world where peace reigns, and enliven us to cooperate with God to restore abundant life and flourishing in our neighborhood, our community, and our world. Reader Two: We light this candle of joy as a sign of God’s restoring work that turns our weeping into rejoicing and our tears into shouts of joy. May we be witnesses of God’s life-giving, peace-making joy to all creation. Light the third (pink/rose) candle of the Advent wreath.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Joy-giving God, you restore us beyond what we can imagine, filling our mouths with laughter and our lives with hope. Receive these gifts as signs of our trust that you are still at work, turning tears into joy and scarcity into abundance. When we forget, remind us. When we grow weary, renew us. When we shrink the circle, widen our hearts again. Use what we offer to plant seeds of joy in dry places, so that communities may be rebuilt, relationships restored, and your people once again shout with gladness. In gratitude for what you have done, are doing, and will do, we give ourselves to you. Amen. ( Psalm 126 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). Invite participants to discuss the following questions in pairs or groups of three: “When is the last time you laughed out loud? What contributed to your laughter?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You likely won’t get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. This psalm, with restoration as a key theme, is divided into two parts: a previous restoration (or a dream of one) and a need for another restoration. Read Psalm 126 . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: How would you describe the first part (verses 1-3)? What attributes of restoration are described here? Metaphors in the second part (verses 4-6) of the passage are used to describe the anticipated restoration. What do you notice about the picture the psalmist paints of restoration? Count how many times “joy” or “rejoice” is used in Psalm 126. How have you seen joy and restoration go together in your life or in the life of a loved one? The Preaching Notes for December 13 say: “Here we are in Advent, remembering the promise of eternity, but also remembering the inbreaking of the kingdom in a birth in a manger on a star-filled night. Who around you is filled with joy this season? Who among us knows what it is to be unable to keep joy contained? Maybe this is part of what Jesus meant when he told us we need to become like little children. Maybe he was suggesting that we need to be filled with joy, to let our mouths be filled with laughter, and to let it out every chance we get in shouts that serve as a reminder that something wonderful is happening, has happened, will happen, and therefore is happening . Psalm 126 wants us to let joy spill out like water in the desert. Our liturgical obligation this Advent season is to give space in worship and in work for shouts of joy.” How easy is it for you to give yourself over to joy? What prevents you from being able to allow laughter to bubble up? How can you “give space” for shouts of joy in your life? Verse 6 connects weeping with shouts of joy. Weeping bears the seeds for sowing, and the “sheaves” of the harvest are accompanied by shouts of joy. What do you make of the connection between weeping and joy? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one thing that you can do to be present to both the seeds of weeping and the harvest of joy in the week ahead? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [ Isaiah 61:1-4, 8-11 , 1 Thessalonians 5:16-24 , John 1:6-8, 19-28 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Dear God of Restoration, you specialize in showing up in places of pain and grief, bringing renewal. Would you give us the courage to weep the tears of sorrow and give us eyes to see where you are bringing a harvest of joy? In this Advent season, as we await your restoration, may laughter slip between the cracks of control and judgment, breaking loose the places where joy can grow. Thank you for adding the gift of joy to your hope and peace. May we receive it with gladness! In the name of the one whose very presence is restoration, we pray, amen. title: Speak Peace to the People
body: Worship Planning Notes Focus text: Psalm 85:1-2, 8-13 Peace. As I sit here, writing worship planning notes almost seven months before Advent, I wonder if I, if we, will be longing for peace in December the way I long for it now. I feel the ache behind the psalmist’s will statements—God will speak, the Lord will give, righteousness will go before him… We say—or we sing— the will statements because we know they aren’t true of our world right now, but we hope they will be true in the future. So, why not this psalm for the first week of Advent, the hope week? Well, other than the fact that the lectionary assigned Psalm 85 for this particular week, I also wonder if real, true, life-giving peace isn’t possible without hope. Maybe peace and righteousness can’t meet without hope to guide them. Where is hope directing your community toward peace? I think if we can answer this question, we are well on our way to infusing worship with opportunities to listen for God speaking peace among us and calling us to speak peace to our world. Don’t be surprised if your answers point you to sing hymns of rejoicing in God’s work. Note: Psalm 85 begins with remembering the good things God has done. Remembering and rejoicing in God’s history among us bolsters our hope and our work for peace. At the same time, don’t despair if your answers point to the need for contemplation and rest in worship. For some of us, hope feels far away, and peace feels impossible. In those seasons, one of the best things we can do for our community is offer space to be gentle with one another, to name our pain and suffering, and to experience God’s faithfulness and solidarity with us. This, too, is a way God speaks peace to us. Either way, as you explore hope and peace in worship, consider what God’s hope and peace call us to do. It is very easy to read the end of Psalm 85 through a prosperity-gospel lens; i.e., do what God asks, and God will make you successful/wealthy/fruitful. However, remembering that these psalms were written in an agrarian culture, I’m struck by all the creation imagery. Perhaps it is not that we make God happy and God makes us prosperous, but rather that by living in God’s peace, we live in right relationship with all creation—the land, the skies, the creatures, and our fellow humans. So, whether you encounter peace by rejoicing in God’s goodness or sitting in God’s never-failing presence, how will worship today call people into right and peaceful relationship with God, self, neighbor, and all creation? Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies degrees from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: Psalm 85:1-2, 8-13 The traditional Advent theme sequence – hope, peace, joy, and love - isn’t carved in stone. It is not a theological or historical requirement. Yet, like so many traditions in this season, there is weight in maintaining the system. Surprisingly, attention to the psalms chosen for this liturgical year reveals these common themes. Or maybe it is the lens through which we have come to approach Advent, and so we see them everywhere. Last week, hope hovered underneath the call to restoration. And this week, peace is grounded in the song that is sung. It is there in the song that is heard, or that we long to hear – “Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his faithful, to those who turn to him in their hearts” (Ps. 85:8 NRSV). We want to hear peace spoken. If it isn’t spoken by the leaders of our nation or by the leaders of our churches, maybe we can hear it from God, if we listen carefully enough. Maybe we don’t deserve it. Plug back in the verses the lectionary leaves out. They speak of forgiveness and restoration. But that was in the past; we need to hear it again, the psalmist pleads. We need God to come back and speak to us again. Maybe God has wandered off, or maybe we did. Maybe we stopped listening. We got distracted by getting by and thinking we didn’t need to listen to the voice of God speaking peace into our lives anymore. We were doing okay, we thought. But now we are sagging; now we are hurting and afraid, and we wonder who will speak for us or to us in a difficult time. The superscription to this psalm is interesting Preaching from the superscription is not really advised. But there is something odd about this one. It is one of those that doesn’t say, “Of David.” Most scholars don’t believe that David wrote all the psalms that say “of David” on them anyway, and that “of David” really came to mean “in the style of David,” or “kinda like the ones David used to write,” or they were done by the King David Tribute band or something. But Psalm 85 says something different. It has three different statements: “To the leader.” “Of the Korahites.” “A Psalm.” You’d think that “A Psalm” would be a bit unnecessary, but then I guess some folks need to be reminded. “To the leader” might mean that this psalm was a commissioned work, that it was dedicated to a leader who had served well or who exemplified the kind of faithfulness that Psalm 85 calls for. The truth is, we don’t know. But it is the middle statement that is the most interesting: “Of the Korahites.” We could spend a lot of time tracing the biblical history of this family, but it wouldn’t really help us wrap our arms around Psalm 85. Suffice it to say that the Korahites have a checkered history in the Old Testament. Korah was from the line of Levites, servants of the priests and of the holy, but was among those who decided they could do better. He was among those who rebelled against Moses and his leadership. (See Numbers 26 for more.) Yet somehow his children survived, escaping the punishment that befell Korah. They became known as warriors, fighting alongside David when he was swept to power as Israel’s greatest king. These Korahites, or Sons of Korah as they became known, were not remembered because of their skill with swords or bows, however. They were like David in another way, not just able fighting men. They were also musicians of the highest caliber. David appointed them as leaders of worship for the people of God. They were singers, instrumentalists, and truth-tellers. A psalm, you see—not just music, not just words, but a psalm, an act of praise but also a declaration of faith, a claim to the traditions of the people, but also, a pointer into the future, a word of hope in dark times. That may mean that the first superscription - To the leader - might not be a dedication to the leader but an instruction to the singers, to the congregation. Maybe it means, “Look to the leaders!” Look to those who go before; look to those whose history might not be perfect, who had to climb out of some difficult times. Look to those who might have known the anger of the Lord they served and who might have known what it was like to feel abandoned. Look to those who know what it is to be revived. Look to those who lead the singing. That’s our story, isn’t it? That’s the song we sing: of being restored and then losing it, of being revived and full of life and then being drained and dead on our feet. That’s our pattern too, not just the people of the Old Testament, but us, right here, right now. Don’t we cry out for restoration again and again? Don’t we bump up against the walls of our own making, the walls of our own doubting, our own wandering? Don’t we get lost in the maze of trying to walk each day and satisfy all the hungers within us? So, how do we climb out of those pits? How do we turn around from the wrong paths? From the desperation of the everyday? By remembering. That’s why we follow the leader; that’s why we sing the songs of faith. “Morning by morning, new mercies I see, all I have needed thy hand hath provided, great is thy faithfulness, Lord unto me.” We sing those songs because they were true, because they are true, and because they will be true. And the great joy of Psalm 85 is that because they were true and because they will be true, they are true. Compare English translations of Psalm 85. You’ll find that the NRSV says “will” – He will speak peace ... Steadfast love and faithfulness will meet ... righteousness and peace will kiss each other ... Faithfulness will spring up from the ground ... righteousness will look down from the sky ... The LORD will give ... our land will yield ... Righteousness will go before ... and will make a path. It is a hope, a promise, a not yet in a world of striving and often failing, a world of conflict and brokenness, a world of division and hatred. Kissing seems out of the question. Singing seems out of the question. And yet, I’ve been kissed before. I have sung the songs of faith. You have too. There is connection already. Other translations make use the present tense. From the NIV [1] : “Love and faithfulness meet together; righteousness and peace kiss each other. Faithfulness springs forth from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven.” From the New King James Version [2] : “Mercy and truth have met together; Righteousness and peace have kissed.” From the New Living Translation [3] : “Unfailing love and truth have met together. Righteousness and peace have kissed!” Why the confusion? Because we can’t always tell. Because, even though it seems absent, this righteousness and faithfulness of God also seem really present. It is in the air around us, coming up from the ground beneath us—if we look; if we pay attention; if we live in hope and confidence; if we attempt to be as faithful as the one who shows us faithfulness every single day, every morning, then we will be restored; then we will be alive, even as we walk in darkness. Even when we feel that we have failed the one who loves us more than we can imagine. The very essence of God - steadfast love and faithfulness, righteousness and peace - will seep into our bones and become the aspects of love that can define us. It will become a song on our lips and in our hearts. Look to the leaders, the singers of songs, and be revived; be restored. And we who are broken can get up and walk along the path of righteousness. Because in listening to the leaders, in listening for the voice of God, peace is spoken into our lives once more. That is our earnest desire. That is our strong hope. We live for the day. Sing it again. Once more with feeling. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.
