title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Focus Text: Psalm 85:1-2, 8-13 Call to Worship Advent people, pulled in all directions by competing bids for our attention, time, and resources, what do you seek today? Let us hear what God will say, for God speaks peace to God’s people. Advent people, carrying heavy loads of grief, responsibility, and worry, what are you listening for today? Let us hear what God will say, for God speaks peace to God’s people. Advent people, noticing the suffering of the world but not knowing what to do, what are you watching for today? Let us hear what God will say, for God speaks peace to God’s people. Advent people, God is here, speaking peace to us. As we worship, may we receive God’s message of peace anew. We come to worship seeking, listening, and watching for God’s message of peace, that we may be messengers of peace in a hurting world. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026. Opening Prayer Loving God, As we come into this worship service, reveal to us what is righteous and good. We invite you, O God, to give us your love and your peace on this struggling journey. O God, our comforter, we invite you to help us in seeking life in you. Come, now, and fill our sanctuaries and our sacred temples. Lord, as we gather, we acknowledge your power. God of comfort, we willingly welcome you into this place. Amen. Adapted from Darlene A. Moore in The Africana Worship Book, Year B (Nashville: Discipleship Resources, 2007), 129. Prayer of Confession Silent Word, Creative Act, Hidden Truth, Revealed Love: we wait for you. To be precise, we are impatient for you to come and set things right. We are insecure with our world, fearful of crime in the streets, and anxious about ourselves. We refuse your guidance, but we often wish you would act according to our plans. We seldom pause to consider that you are waiting for us: waiting for some genuine act of contrition; waiting for us to repent and change; waiting for us to listen and respond with a burning passion to your truth, your justice, and your mercy. Furnish us with humble hearts and willing spirits to receive you as you come to us through all the experiences of our lives. Amen. Words of Assurance The Light shines in the darkness; and the darkness has never been able to overcome it. Good news of great joy—we are forgiven! Amen. Written by Allen P. Happe and Maren C. Tirabassi in Touch Holiness: Resources for Worship, Updated, ed. Ruth C. Duck and Maren C. Tirabassi (Cleveland: The Pilgrim Press, 2012), 6 and 8. For use in worship services, include the following permissions statement: Reprinted by permission of the publisher from Touch Holiness, ed. Ruth C. Duck and Maren C. Tirabassi. Copyright © 1990 by The Pilgrim Press. Benediction The psalmist writes that when salvation comes, and God’s glory dwells in the land, “Steadfast love and faithfulness will meet; righteousness and peace will kiss each other.” Beloved, may God bless you with courage to make peace and with ready hearts to notice steadfast love, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace as signs of God’s inbreaking kingdom all around you. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026.

title: Candle Lighting Liturgy
body: Candle Lighting Liturgy Reader One: The prophet Isaiah calls us to speak comfort to God’s people, because even now God is at work making peace among us, so that “Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain. Then the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken" (Isaiah 40:4-5 NRSV). Today, we wait and work for God’s peace, for a world marked by welcome, belonging, and access for all. Congregation: Because of God’s goodness to us in the past, we can imagine a future shaped by God’s peace, and we can cooperate with God and one another to speak peace, build peace, and flourish in peace right here and right now. Reader Two: We light this candle of peace as a sign of God’s peace-making among us, saving us and forming us to build a world where “faithfulness will spring up from the ground, and righteousness will look down from the sky” (Psalm 85:11 NRSV). Light the second candle of the Advent wreath.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Peace-speaking God, we come longing to hear your voice again—your word of mercy, your promise of restoration. Receive these gifts as signs of our trust that your steadfast love and faithfulness are already at work among us. Where we have wandered, guide us back. Where we have grown weary, revive us. Where division has taken hold, let righteousness and peace meet again through us. Use what we offer to help your church sing the old songs of faith with new conviction and to live as people through whom your peace is spoken into the world. In hope and gratitude, we give ourselves and these gifts to you. Amen. ( Psalm 85:1-2, 8-13)

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). Invite participants to discuss this statement in pairs or groups of three: “Metaphors are often used in scripture to describe complex spiritual truths in understandable ways. What metaphor could you use to describe 'peace' to someone who is experiencing distraction, disintegration, or disease?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Psalm 85:1-2, 8-13 . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: What do you learn about God’s past actions in this psalm? Repentance and confession are described starting in verse 8 of this psalm. What do you see as humans’ actions in turning to God? What are God’s actions? How do you see “land” described throughout this psalm? What do you think that means? The Preaching Notes for December 6 say, “Compare English translations of Psalm 85. You’ll find that the NRSV says ‘will’ –‘He will speak peace ... Steadfast love and faithfulness will meet ... righteousness and peace will kiss each other ... Faithfulness will spring up from the ground.’ It is a hope, a promise, a not-yet in a world of striving and often failing, a world of conflict and brokenness, a world of division and hatred…Other translations use the present tense. From the NIV [1] : ‘Love and faithfulness meet together; righteousness and peace kiss each other. Faithfulness springs forth from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven.’ From the New King James Version [2] [and New Living Translation [3] ]: ‘Mercy and truth have met together; Righteousness and peace have kissed.’ Why the confusion? Because we can’t always tell. Because, even though it seems absent, this righteousness and faithfulness of God also seem really present.” How does the meaning of this text change depending on whether the past, present, or future tense is used? “Peace” is the Advent theme for this week. After our discussion today, how do you think God does speak or will speak “peace to his people”? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or a phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one action you might take because of our conversation/study today? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the selected text [ Isaiah 40:1-11 , 2 Peter 3:8-15a , Mark 1:1-8 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: God of Creation and of the New Creation, you have restored your people and your land before, and we ask for you to restore us again. We confess that our hearts and our actions, or non-actions, have contributed to the need for restoration. Forgive us, we pray, and make us steadfast and faithful. Thank you for speaking words of peace to us, your people. May we receive your peace and extend it to others. In the name of the Prince of Peace, we pray, Amen. title: Restore Us, O God
body: Worship Planning Notes Focus text : Psalm 80:1-7, 17-19 Methodists are a singing people. The hymns of Charles Wesley did as much or more to teach and edify the early Methodists as John’s sermons and treatises. So, it is fitting that we return to the season of Advent—the beginning of the liturgical year—with singing. I’m always struck by all the words we use to try to explain the meaning and significance of Advent and how much they fall short. In Advent, we remember the waiting of our ancestors while sitting in our own waiting for the fulfillment of God’s kingdom on earth as it is in heaven. In some ways, we know the end of the story—the birth, life, death, and resurrection of Christ. At the same time, we are waiting for the fulfillment of our shared, millennia-long story. There is so much doctrine wrapped up in Advent, much less emotion and spirituality. So, while it may seem odd to focus on the Psalms for Advent, I wonder why we don’t do it more. What better way to capture the complexity of our Advent experiences than through the songbook that has accompanied untold generations of God-followers?! As you plan for Advent, consider what experiences and feelings your congregation may be carrying into this season. What griefs are they holding? What uncertainties and anxieties dominate conversations? What difficulties has your community faced this year? What moments of rejoicing have marked the past twelve months? What hopes are you carrying into the new year? Then, consider: how might the psalms of Advent meet your congregation and neighborhood where they are? Let the answers to these questions guide how the community sings, prays, proclaims, and responds during Advent. This series offers a wonderful opportunity for congregations to weave singing into the proclamation of scripture. For instance, you might consider weaving the hymn “Savior Like a Shepherd, Lead Us” ( United Methodist Hymnal 381) into the reading of Psalm 80, repeating verse 1 after every few verses of the psalm to create a call-and-response between the reader and the congregation. Or you might use the psalter at the back of the United Methodist Hymnal to read and/or sing Psalm 80 responsively ( United Methodist Hymnal 801). Finally, consider how the themes of each week in this series might enliven and deepen your congregation’s sense of God’s restorative work among us. How might you pray for restoration? How might you sing restoration? Is there a hymn or song you can weave into worship in different ways for the next four weeks to draw attention to God’s presence in our Advent waiting? That song may not even be Advent-specific. For instance, Over the Rhine has a simple but powerful song called “ New Redemption Song ” that could be used as an offertory, a meditative response to the sermon, and/or a congregational prayer response throughout Advent. Or you might find that a repetitive Taizé chorus like “Wait for the Lord” ( Worship and Song 3049) offers your congregation space to sit, reflect, and pray amid their Advent waiting. Above all, we want to offer congregants the space to communally experience the solidarity God and, through God, we all have with one another in the midst of this complex and beautiful season of the liturgical year. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies degrees from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Psalm 80:1-7, 17-19 Wait. An Advent series based on Psalms? That seems a bit … odd. Where are the prophetic utterances thundering from the mountain tops, bringing both hope and consternation? Where are the gospel stories of John the Baptist and Jesus talking about the kingdom for which we wait? This just doesn’t seem right. We understand. But go with us for a while and see if you can’t hear the prophetic call through the words of the psalms chosen by the lectionary for this season. See if you can’t hear the longing for the kingdom that Jesus came to proclaim and for which John paved the way. We can hear the ache for the fullness of God’s presence in these words. Psalm 80 is a perfect way to begin the season of anticipation and hope. God is absent, according to the psalmist. We haven’t heard a word from the Lord in so long. People are left to their own devices, and some of the devices have gone wildly astray. God seems angry with our prayers, staying silent as we beg for relief, for righting the ship of state that seems to have gone astray. We are scorned on the world stage; enemies laugh at us. Sorry, does that sound like political commentary? It is a historical reflection of the emotional state of the people of God from thousands of years ago. It is the struggle of the people to feel like God’s chosen, given all that was happening to them at the time. The psalmist gives voice to that despair. The psalmist allows the people to lament. Perhaps even better, the psalmist gives hurting people a song to sing. “Singing Resistance” was launched in Minneapolis at the beginning of this year to respond to the government's immigration siege. But they didn’t invent it. Singing has been part of resistance from the beginning, as the psalms repeatedly point out. Singing gives voice to pain, strengthens resolve, and unites people to stand against oppression. The people sang as they marched to Selma. They sang in concentration camps and detention centers. They sang as they made their march and died on the Trail of Tears. They sang as their children were ripped away and punished if they spoke the language of their families. They sang as they were driven from their homes at the order of the Tsar. They sang as they worked in the fields under the lash and the hot southern sun. They sang as they made bricks out of mud and straw, building monuments to the pharaohs. They sang. We sang. Singing songs of resistance with pleas for restoration is part of human history. Singing tells the truth of what is going on, with the effect of helping the singers and the hearers face the reality in which they live. The song of Psalm 80 is a lament. It is telling the truth about how it feels to be seemingly abandoned by God. The psalmist gives voice to the people’s despair, doubt, and brokenness. This is followed by a time of remembering. The lectionary leaves out the verses of how God has husbanded the fragile vine that was Israel, transplanting them from the sandy soil of Egypt into the lush lands of Palestine. You can decide if these verses are worth reading in the hearing of the people, or whether reference to the time of remembering is enough. When life is bad, it can be healing to remember when times were better. It can be sustaining to recall that it hasn’t always been like this. Suffering swells to fill our whole perception of our lives. By remembering different times, we can be sustained and encouraged to call for a return, not to those times, but to that relationship, that way of living bound up in the grace and provision of God— living in the tender mercies of a God who cares for us. That’s the Advent invitation. Let us live in partnership with God again. Let us walk, aware of grace, hospitality, and reconciliation again. Let us be the people who have hope of restoration into a new reality, a new kingdom, a new kin-dom. Let us watch and wait for what God has in store for all of creation, as we lean with eager longing into the promise. Let us live hope in its most powerful form: new life, new strength, new possibility. We begin this Advent season, as we often do, longing for hope. Restore us, O God. Psalm 80 has an interesting clue hidden in the final verses. The psalmist writes: “But let your hand be upon the one at your right hand, the one whom you made strong for yourself” (Ps. 80:17 NRSV). No doubt in the mind of the writer, this was the king or a prophet, maybe even a whole nation. who desired to be obedient to God and represent God’s law and mercy in all that was done. Through this “right-hand” man or woman, all people have an example of how to walk with God, how to hope in the silence, how to sing praises even in difficult times. No doubt, the psalmist imagined someone on the world stage then. But we hear something different this Advent season. We hear the promise of one who would live at the right hand of God and show us how to live there too. We hear of the one who brought God to us and us to God. We, this Advent season and always, look for the face to shine on us and then through us as we seek salvation. Restore us, O God, in the name of the one who sits at your right hand, Jesus the Christ. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Focus Text : Psalm 80:1-7, 17-19 Call to Worship Like generations upon generations before us, we enter Advent with longing for hope to reign where despair feels entrenched, for peace to rule where conflict and destruction overwhelm. Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved. We gather, wondering whether joy will return when we have experienced so much heartbreak, whether love can make a difference when hate and apathy seem so widespread. Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved. We gather to join our voices with the psalmists and musicians, the travelers, and the faithful from long ago, who also longed for restoration and salvation, who felt God was far away or perhaps felt how far they had wandered away from God. Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved. Come, you who wait and watch for the coming Messiah, to worship God who invites us to join in the Spirit’s restoration song until the day when earth and heaven both reflect the fullness of the kingdom of God. Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026. Opening Prayer God of justice and peace, from the heavens you rain down mercy and kindness, that all on earth may rise in awe and wonder before your marvelous deeds. Raise our heads in expectation, that we may yearn for the coming day of the Lord and come without blame before your Son, Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen. Adapted from Revised Common Lectionary Prayers copyright © 2002 Consultation on Common Texts admin. Augsburg Fortress. Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/11/collect-for-advent-1-year-b.html . Prayer of Confession Restore us, Lord. Once we prayed, knowing our help came from you. Once we defied injustice, knowing that you were on our side. Once, we prayed all night “’til our help came.” Once, we apologized for calling someone a fool. Once, we believed it was important to please you. Restore us as people who follow God even when no one is looking. Restore us, Lord. Silent prayers of confession Words of Assurance Jesus Christ, who loved us enough to leave heaven and live among us, hears our prayers and forgives heartfelt confession. Live now as people restored by the Lord, empowered to live as children of God. Amen. Written by Kwasi I. Kena in The Africana Worship Book, Year B (Nashville: Discipleship Resources, 2007), 147, 166. Benediction May God bless you with hope that cuts through despair, that we may join our voices with God’s restoration song and live in partnership with God and one another as we work for the flourishing of all God’s creation. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026.

title: Candle Lighting Liturgy
body: Candle Lighting Liturgy Reader One: The prophet Isaiah declares, “From ages past no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides you, who works for those who wait for him” (Isaiah 64:4 NRSV). Today, we continue to wait and call out in hope for God’s restoration to meet us here, believing that God knows our struggles and works even now for the fulfillment of our salvation. Congregation: When God feels far away, and our lament feels too heavy to bear, we remember God’s steadfast love. May this love empower us to wait and watch in hope for the day when God’s kingdom comes on earth as it is in heaven. Reader Two: We light this candle of hope as a sign of God’s promises, that we might persevere in hope, a hope grounded not in wishes and whims but in the trustworthy and persistent love of God already at work among us to save and restore all creation. Light the first candle of the Advent wreath.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Restoring God, in seasons when your presence feels distant, you still hear the cries of your people. We come with longing hearts, bringing these gifts as signs of hope in your renewing grace. Receive what we offer and use it to restore what is broken, to strengthen what is weary, and to shine your light in places of despair. As we wait for your coming, shape us into a people who remember your faithfulness, who sing even in difficult days, and who live as witnesses to your promise. Restore us again, O God, that your salvation may be seen through us. Amen. ( Psalm 80:1-7, 17-19 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “How can a song bring people together in the context of worship?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Frame the scripture reading by saying, “Today’s focus text is a psalm, the hymnbook of God’s people. While we don’t often focus on the psalms during Advent, this year we will pay attention to how the psalms focus our attention on God’s restoring work.” Then, read Psalm 80:1-7, 17-19 aloud, inviting participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Ask group members the following questions: What are some different ways that you interpret the tone of verses 1 and 2? What might the psalmist be saying to God here? What do you make of the language about “shining” throughout the psalm? What could that mean? What images related to God “shining forth” emerge for you in this Advent season? Re-read verses 4-7. This is an emotionally fraught passage. What questions does it bring forth for you about God or the people? Where do you see the Advent themes of waiting and hope in this passage? The Preaching Notes for November 29 say: “Psalm 80 has an interesting clue hidden in the final verses. The psalmist writes: ‘But let your hand be upon the one at your right hand, the one whom you made strong for yourself’ (Ps. 80:17 NRSV). No doubt in the mind of the writer, this was the king or a prophet, maybe even a whole nation, who desired to be obedient to God and represent God’s law and mercy in all that was done. Through this “right-hand” man or woman, all people have an example of how to walk with God, how to hope in the silence, how to sing praises even in difficult times…But we hear something different this Advent season. We hear the promise of one who would live at the right hand of God and show us how to live there too. We hear of the one who brought God to us and us to God. We—this Advent season and always—look for the face to shine on us and then through us as we seek salvation. Restore us, O God, in the name of the one who sits at your right hand, Jesus the Christ.” How does this observation focus your thinking about earlier parts of this psalm? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or a phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one thing you want to do because of the discussion today? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [ Isaiah 64:1-9 , 1 Corinthians 1:3-9 , Mark 13:24-37 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: O Shepherd of Israel, you bring forth guidance and protection from each of our struggles. We praise your name and give thanks for your provision and presence, even when the provision looks like the bread and drink of tears. We wait, and we hope, trusting that we will celebrate your presence and receive your gift of life. We trust that you will hear us when we call. Quicken our hearts and minds to hear your voice. Restore us, O God of hosts; let your face shine, that we may be saved. Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Come, You Blessed
body: Planning Worship Focus text : Matthew 25:31-46 Last week, we read the parable of the talents and wondered if perhaps Jesus was telling a story not about the kingdom of heaven, but about the kingdom of this world and its penchant for privileging wealth and productivity. This week, Jesus looks into the future, when the judgment of all nations will take place, and talks about…rewarding people for their good works. Really Jesus? You sure this is the direction you want to go? At least, that’s how some Christians have read this passage for centuries, including today. But that’s not the only interpretation of this teaching! In his Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament, John Wesley says of Matthew 25:35, “All these works of outward mercy suppose faith and love, and must needs be accompanied with works of spiritual mercy.” In other words, these works are not the admission price to God’s kingdom; they are the fruit of our salvation, the result of the work of God’s grace and love upon our hearts. This Sunday is also when we observe Reign of Christ Sunday, the end of the liturgical year, and the celebration of the kingdom Christ establishes that is simultaneously here and not yet. Next week, we begin Advent, a season of living into the “not yet,” the waiting for the fulfillment of God’s dream for all creation. So, I wonder if today is a moment to celebrate how God’s kingdom or kin-dom (a neologism emphasizing Christ’s reign as bringing us into family relationship with God, neighbor, and all creation) is already here among us. How do we experience the fruit of Christ’s reign right now? How are we experiencing the transforming power of God’s love among us? How do we look to Christ to guide us through the good and the bad of the whims, wiles, and woes of our earthly leaders? Perhaps we find the answers to these questions and more in Matthew 25. And perhaps we find more questions! This is a day that includes praise and celebration, yes, but also opportunities to wrestle with our calls to be disciples who feed the poor, tend the sick, and visit the prisoner in a world intent on pushing aside, hiding, and neglecting human suffering and the structures that cause it. So, sing the hymns in praise of God’s reign among us. Let your hearts soar with the choir as they sing “My Eternal King” (Marshall) or one of the many glorious arrangements of “Crown Him with Many Crowns.” And pray for wisdom and courage to recognize and follow the way of Christ when living as a disciple means living in conflict with the kingdom of this world. Name the griefs and challenges of living in a world where Christian nationalism falsely teaches people that particular political affiliations and God’s kingdom are the same thing. Encourage one another to persevere in following Christ when other leaders seek to lead us astray or pretend to represent Christ on earth. More than anything, embrace the complexity of this day, because, by grace, we have been blessed to choose to live under Christ’s reign, to wrestle with the difficult questions, and to persist in loving our neighbors as the fruit of our salvation in Christ.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Matthew 25:31-46 Are you as relieved to be here as I am? This is the parable by which many shape their understanding of discipleship. Some might argue that this teaching in Chapter 25 is the application of the Beatitudes in Chapter 5. It takes someone poor in spirit to serve the least of Christ’s brothers and sisters. It takes those who mourn the world's brokenness to want to serve those who are broken. It takes the meek to be willing to bend low enough to see those who are hurting. It takes … well, you can follow the pattern. It makes a compelling argument that Matthew and Jesus are bringing the story to its logical conclusion, or the most appropriate application. This passage seems to say what we know isn’t true: that we can earn our way into heaven by doing good works. But then, here is the king, Jesus in all his glory, with all his angels, telling us exactly that. Just do it. Just get out there and serve him by serving those who need—the least of these. And then, whether you realize it or not, you’ll be serving him. And you’ll get your reward. Of course, you sigh, we knew that. Jesus wants us to get out there and help people. OK, right, get to it. Another responsibility, another task, another chore to get done. Work it into our busy schedules to make Jesus happy. But saying it that way makes us realize we are still missing something. What is Jesus really asking for in this story? What are we supposed to understand? The goats missed it, but then you would expect them to; they’re goats, after all. But is it surprising that the sheep seem to have missed it too?  “When was it that we saw you hungry...?” Maybe their surprise is the point of the story. Jesus is saying that the goal is not to complete some task, like competing in a reality show, but to be the kind of person who loves as Christ loved, not because we’re supposed to, but just because we do. Christ wants us to give the gift of who we are, the loving, caring, giving person he has enabled us to become, or that we are becoming, since we are all in process. I suppose that is all anyone wants: the gift of ourselves—our better selves, our true selves, our Christ-like selves. This parable is not inconsistent with Jesus’ teaching all along. “What is the greatest commandment?” “Love God and love neighbor”  (Matthew 22:36-40). He couldn’t or wouldn’t separate love of God from love of neighbor. Our believing and our doing have to be two sides of the same coin. You can’t have one without the other. You can’t believe and have faith without acting on it. You can’t accept the saving power of Jesus Christ without being transformed into a servant of Christ. It is not just that good works are “nice”; they are essential. They are one and the same. Some scholars argue that “the nations” that are gathered before the throne in this parable include everyone but those who are already followers. This parable, they argue, is the answer to the ubiquitous question, “What about those who haven’t come to believe in Jesus but still live Christlike lives?” If they served people, they served Christ, whether they realized it or not. Christ was at work in them, whether they realized it or not. Because, as he told us, without him, we can do nothing. It seems more likely that with a beginning that states all the nations will be gathered, that we’re there too. Everyone is there. Judgment is not something we escape. But in this case, the judgment has already been made. “Come, you blessed” points to a prior relationship. A state of blessedness, we might say, already exists—maybe because of vows made and saviors claimed, or maybe because of behaviors that indicate the condition of the heart. Either way, the blessedness is claimed, pronounced, and, we might argue, experienced. What is this blessedness? How many times have you said or heard others say, “I got more out of that than I gave.” Often after a mission trip,  a shared activity of giving or caring or building or … whatever, there is a sense of something significant within the workers and the givers. That is the blessedness of which we speak. It is a sign of connection to God and to one another. It is what we were made for, this circle of caring, this sacrifice of loving beyond a commandment into a way of being. Come, you blessed and know what it is to love and to be loved. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Compassionate Shepherd, you have blessed us beyond measure and taught us to find your face in the hungry, the lonely, the stranger, and the forgotten. Receive these gifts and receive our lives, that we may become people whose generosity flows not from obligation but from love. Use our offerings to feed, welcome, comfort, and restore, so that others may glimpse your kingdom through our care. And when we serve our neighbors, awaken us to the holy mystery that we are serving you. Shape us into disciples whose greatest joy is to love as Christ first loved us. Amen. ( Matthew 25:31-46 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Gathering Time (5 minutes) . Divide participants into groups of two or three and ask,  “What are the things (actions, attitudes, behaviors, etc.) that you think God blesses? Why do you think that?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You likely won’t get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Prepare to read Matthew 25:31-46 by sharing the following: “This text is a parable that is the last of four that are considered ‘warning parables' (Matthew 24:45-51, Matthew 25:1-13, 14-30, and 31-46). Bring your questions and your curiosity as we approach this passage.” Read Matthew 25:31-46. Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: What are your first impressions of this parable? Feel free to share interpretations that may make you uncomfortable or that are confusing. What questions emerge  as you read this passage? This is a scene of the “final judgment” of Christ of the nations. [For a longer study, it may be helpful to read this section (starting in Matthew 24) with portions of Revelation (20:11-22:21).] Below are themes that are connected to the Final Judgment. Identify what this passage says about the following: All the nations gathered The Son of Man seated on the throne of his glory Separation Righteousness Eternity (damnation or life) There is repetition in this passage for the sake of comparison. The sheep (the “righteous,” those who fed the hungry, gave the thirsty something to drink, welcomed, clothed the naked, visited the sick and those in prison, etc.) and the goats (the “accursed,” those who did not do those things). How do you understand this comparison? What possible interpretations arise for you? John Wesley connected these actions as works of mercy, which was a “means of grace.” How do you think these actions are avenues for grace? The Preaching Notes for November 22 say: Some might argue that this teaching in Chapter 25 is the application of the Beatitudes in Chapter 5. It takes someone poor in spirit to serve the least of Christ’s brothers and sisters. It takes those who mourn the world's brokenness to want to serve those who are broken. It takes the meek to be willing to bend low enough to see those who are hurting. It takes … well, you can follow the pattern. It makes a compelling argument that Matthew and Jesus are bringing the story to its logical conclusion, or the most appropriate application. What do you think about the connection between the Beatitudes in Matthew 5 being exemplified by this parable about how the righteous and unrighteous are identified? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one action you might take because of our conversation/study today? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [ Ezekiel 34:11-16, 20-24 and Psalm 100 , Ezekiel 34:11-16, 20-24 and Psalm 95:1-7a , Ephesians 1:15-23 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Holy and Righteous King, as we ponder the judgment to which your Word speaks, we confess that there is much that we do not understand. Will you root us to your love and your righteousness, that we might demonstrate both to the world around us? And may we always see and serve “the least of these” as an expression of your love and generosity. We pray with gratitude and hope, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Come, You Blessed
body: Planning Worship Focus text : Matthew 25:31-46 Last week, we read the parable of the talents and wondered if perhaps Jesus was telling a story not about the kingdom of heaven, but about the kingdom of this world and its penchant for privileging wealth and productivity. This week, Jesus looks into the future, when the judgment of all nations will take place, and talks about…rewarding people for their good works. Really Jesus? You sure this is the direction you want to go? At least, that’s how some Christians have read this passage for centuries, including today. But that’s not the only interpretation of this teaching! In his Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament, John Wesley says of Matthew 25:35, “All these works of outward mercy suppose faith and love, and must needs be accompanied with works of spiritual mercy.” In other words, these works are not the admission price to God’s kingdom; they are the fruit of our salvation, the result of the work of God’s grace and love upon our hearts. This Sunday is also when we observe Reign of Christ Sunday, the end of the liturgical year, and the celebration of the kingdom Christ establishes that is simultaneously here and not yet. Next week, we begin Advent, a season of living into the “not yet,” the waiting for the fulfillment of God’s dream for all creation. So, I wonder if today is a moment to celebrate how God’s kingdom or kin-dom (a neologism emphasizing Christ’s reign as bringing us into family relationship with God, neighbor, and all creation) is already here among us. How do we experience the fruit of Christ’s reign right now? How are we experiencing the transforming power of God’s love among us? How do we look to Christ to guide us through the good and the bad of the whims, wiles, and woes of our earthly leaders? Perhaps we find the answers to these questions and more in Matthew 25. And perhaps we find more questions! This is a day that includes praise and celebration, yes, but also opportunities to wrestle with our calls to be disciples who feed the poor, tend the sick, and visit the prisoner in a world intent on pushing aside, hiding, and neglecting human suffering and the structures that cause it. So, sing the hymns in praise of God’s reign among us. Let your hearts soar with the choir as they sing “My Eternal King” (Marshall) or one of the many glorious arrangements of “Crown Him with Many Crowns.” And pray for wisdom and courage to recognize and follow the way of Christ when living as a disciple means living in conflict with the kingdom of this world. Name the griefs and challenges of living in a world where Christian nationalism falsely teaches people that particular political affiliations and God’s kingdom are the same thing. Encourage one another to persevere in following Christ when other leaders seek to lead us astray or pretend to represent Christ on earth. More than anything, embrace the complexity of this day, because, by grace, we have been blessed to choose to live under Christ’s reign, to wrestle with the difficult questions, and to persist in loving our neighbors as the fruit of our salvation in Christ.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Matthew 25:31-46 Are you as relieved to be here as I am? This is the parable by which many shape their understanding of discipleship. Some might argue that this teaching in Chapter 25 is the application of the Beatitudes in Chapter 5. It takes someone poor in spirit to serve the least of Christ’s brothers and sisters. It takes those who mourn the world's brokenness to want to serve those who are broken. It takes the meek to be willing to bend low enough to see those who are hurting. It takes … well, you can follow the pattern. It makes a compelling argument that Matthew and Jesus are bringing the story to its logical conclusion, or the most appropriate application. This passage seems to say what we know isn’t true: that we can earn our way into heaven by doing good works. But then, here is the king, Jesus in all his glory, with all his angels, telling us exactly that. Just do it. Just get out there and serve him by serving those who need—the least of these. And then, whether you realize it or not, you’ll be serving him. And you’ll get your reward. Of course, you sigh, we knew that. Jesus wants us to get out there and help people. OK, right, get to it. Another responsibility, another task, another chore to get done. Work it into our busy schedules to make Jesus happy. But saying it that way makes us realize we are still missing something. What is Jesus really asking for in this story? What are we supposed to understand? The goats missed it, but then you would expect them to; they’re goats, after all. But is it surprising that the sheep seem to have missed it too?  “When was it that we saw you hungry...?” Maybe their surprise is the point of the story. Jesus is saying that the goal is not to complete some task, like competing in a reality show, but to be the kind of person who loves as Christ loved, not because we’re supposed to, but just because we do. Christ wants us to give the gift of who we are, the loving, caring, giving person he has enabled us to become, or that we are becoming, since we are all in process. I suppose that is all anyone wants: the gift of ourselves—our better selves, our true selves, our Christ-like selves. This parable is not inconsistent with Jesus’ teaching all along. “What is the greatest commandment?” “Love God and love neighbor”  (Matthew 22:36-40). He couldn’t or wouldn’t separate love of God from love of neighbor. Our believing and our doing have to be two sides of the same coin. You can’t have one without the other. You can’t believe and have faith without acting on it. You can’t accept the saving power of Jesus Christ without being transformed into a servant of Christ. It is not just that good works are “nice”; they are essential. They are one and the same. Some scholars argue that “the nations” that are gathered before the throne in this parable include everyone but those who are already followers. This parable, they argue, is the answer to the ubiquitous question, “What about those who haven’t come to believe in Jesus but still live Christlike lives?” If they served people, they served Christ, whether they realized it or not. Christ was at work in them, whether they realized it or not. Because, as he told us, without him, we can do nothing. It seems more likely that with a beginning that states all the nations will be gathered, that we’re there too. Everyone is there. Judgment is not something we escape. But in this case, the judgment has already been made. “Come, you blessed” points to a prior relationship. A state of blessedness, we might say, already exists—maybe because of vows made and saviors claimed, or maybe because of behaviors that indicate the condition of the heart. Either way, the blessedness is claimed, pronounced, and, we might argue, experienced. What is this blessedness? How many times have you said or heard others say, “I got more out of that than I gave.” Often after a mission trip,  a shared activity of giving or caring or building or … whatever, there is a sense of something significant within the workers and the givers. That is the blessedness of which we speak. It is a sign of connection to God and to one another. It is what we were made for, this circle of caring, this sacrifice of loving beyond a commandment into a way of being. Come, you blessed and know what it is to love and to be loved. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Family of God, on this Reign of Christ Sunday, we celebrate and remember Christ, who reigns over all creation with love and grace, forming us as a family bound together by God. We come to worship Christ, who cares for the least of these and calls us to do the same. We gather to recount all the ways we encounter Christ in our midst—in our neighbor who checks in when we’re sick, in our unhoused friends who gather for a meal, in our friends who have been wounded in body and spirit. We come to worship Christ, who cares for the least of these and reminds us to do the same. We join our voices with Christians throughout the world and throughout time to give thanks and to seek guidance as we grow in love of God, neighbor, self, and creation. We come to worship Christ, who cares for the least of these and inspires us to do the same. Come, you blessed by God, with open hearts, open arms, and open doors to welcome and embrace all of our neighbors, because when we love our neighbors, we love Christ among us. We come to worship Christ, who cares for the least of these and empowers us to do the same. Thanks be to God! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, August 2026. Opening Prayer Sovereign God, the wind blows, the water flows, and the sun shines. All creation declares your majesty. In you, we move, live, and have our being. Be glorified in our worship. Be known by our testimony. We proclaim your goodness from the east and the west, from the north and the south. On countrysides and city blocks, you reign. In deep valleys and skyscrapers, we declare that your realm extends from everlasting to everlasting. We worship you, Holy One, in spirit and in truth. Amen. Written by Rev. Dr. Cheryl A. Lindsay and posted on the Worship Ways website of the United Church of Christ at https://www.ucc.org/worship-way/reign-of-christ-b-november-24/ . Prayer of Confession In the lives of neighbors who suffer brokenness and pain: We confess you are still speaking! In the struggle of the poor whose rights are not honored: We confess you are still speaking! In a world crying out for wisdom, love, and mercy: We confess you are still speaking! In a world calling for the blessing of truth: We confess you are still speaking!  Bless us to receive! Let us confess together: We confess that in our lives we often hide behind our work and play, schools and jobs, fun and fashion. We let ourselves get so busy that we forget the cause of the poor and the suffering. We confess we allow the powers of this world to seduce us into selfishness and silence our witness. Teach us to champion the cause of justice for all; strengthen us to love our neighbor and speak truth no matter the penalty.  Amen. Assurance of Pardon The Word of God assures us that we are able to love through the Spirit of Christ, whose grace forgives and empowers us to love our neighbors near and far, to speak up for those who are broken. Beloved, in the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Glory to God! Amen. Adapted from LT Leticia Rouser, chaplain in the United States Navy. Posted on the United Church of Christ’s Worship Ways website, http://www.ucc.org/worship/worship-ways/ . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2013/06/confession-you-are-still-speaking.html . Benediction May God bless you with open heart, open arms, and open doors to welcome the neighbor—known and unknown—with compassion and care, that in serving one another, we might build the kingdom of God among us here and now, one act of love at a time. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, August 2026.

title: Enter the Joy
body: Planning Worship Focus text : Matthew 25:14-30 Whom do you serve? Elsewhere in the book of Matthew, Jesus says, “No one can serve two masters…You cannot serve God and wealth” (Matthew 6:24). And then, we have this parable that portrays a master driven by wealth and productivity, a parable we often try to make fit the “kingdom of heaven,” because aren’t all of Jesus’ stories, especially in Matthew 25, about the kingdom of heaven? As Derek Weber proposes in the preaching notes , perhaps this is not a parable about the kingdom of heaven but the kingdom of this world, a story meant to tell us about the kingdom of heaven based on what it’s not. Now, I’ll stop there and let Derek get into the nitty-gritty of this interpretation of the parable of the talents. But this question, “Whom do you serve?” is a good question for us to ask as worship planners because, as we see in Matthew 25:23, whom we serve determines the joy we enter. As you prepare for worship this week, do you want to invite your people into the joy of the world or the joy of the kingdom of heaven, a joy dependent on wealth and productivity or on God’s love and grace? As you prepare the liturgy for this Sunday, take stock of the prayers, call to worship, and rituals you will engage in as a community. Do they portray God as a master with high expectations or a loving parent who nurtures and enables us to live as disciples of Jesus Christ through love and grace? Are there undercurrents in the ways your church talks about and prays to God that resonate with the old adage (not found in the Bible): "God helps those who help themselves"? This is a wonderful Sunday, not just to demonstrate a different understanding of God’s kingdom, but to explain it. So often, we either assume everyone knows why we do what we do in worship or we assume that explaining what we’re doing in worship will be boring or take the meaning out of it. Maybe this is a good Sunday to preface the prayers of the people with a note about how we pray to a loving God who listens to all of us, who works for the good of all of us, and who does not play favorites or prioritize those who “prove” their faithfulness to God. You may think your congregants know this, but knowing it in our heads and knowing it in our bones are two different things. Then, perhaps most importantly, find the joy--not the joy in material things or the joy that waits until we’re no longer stressed or anxious or fearful or tired, but the joy that meets us where we are and reminds us we are children of God, citizens of God’s kingdom. This is not joy we have to manufacture, but joy we create room for. Give people space to find some calm in worship. Acknowledge the difficult things we all carry right now. Tell stories of the good that is happening in your congregation, no matter how small it might seem. Show pictures of a senior-adult outing or of the children’s choir practicing. Invite everyone to have a two-minute dance party to shake it all out. Even simply turning to one another to say in worship, “I’m glad you’re here today,” may be one of the few positive interactions some of our congregants have all week. In a world that puts us in competition with one another and values us for our productivity, may church be a place where we enter into the joy of belonging to God and to one another for no other reason than that we are all children of God.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Matthew 25:14-30 “Is it possible that Matthew is out to subvert that model of judgment by exposing its ridiculous nature? Most of the evidence suggests otherwise, but this reader wants to know.”  So wrote Greg Carey, Professor of New Testament, Lancaster Theological Seminary, in 2014. https://www.workingpreacher.org/commentaries/revised-common-lectionary/ordinary-33/commentary-on-matthew-2514-30-5 . I suspect other readers want to know as well. This parable is troubling on many levels. Yet it can also be seen rather simply, and most commentators and preachers tend to lean toward the simple interpretation: that everyone must pull their own weight. Everyone must work and produce to be a part of the kingdom. That’s very Protestant when you think about it. Perhaps not earning one’s salvation— we can avoid works-righteousness theology—but as a result of salvation. We work because we have been saved, not in order to be saved. Perhaps more palatable is the use of the word talent to refer not to an outrageous sum of money, but to our inherent abilities or gifts, and to propagate the idea that talents are meant to be used for others, in service. This is Paul’s argument in I Corinthians 14, where he says, “Since you are eager for spiritual gifts, strive to excel in them for building up the church” (1 Cor. 14:12 NRSV). The purpose of the gift, or the ability or the talent, is to build up the whole church; it’s not simply for the benefit of the recipient of that gift. What is harder to comprehend is the harshness of the failure to produce that is presented in this text. Some argue that this is hyperbole and should not be taken so literally that those who are afraid or reluctant to use their talents will suffer eternal punishment. Others consider this to be the terrible consequence of not being a full participant in the life and work of a disciple. That brings us back to the works-righteousness question and implies that we can – or indeed must – work our way into the master's joy. The other side of the call to produce and the blessing of those who double their stake is a tendency toward prosperity-gospel thinking, that God wants us to be rich and to amass wealth for our own well-being. Verses such as For to all those who have, more will be given, and they will have an abundance; but from those who have nothing, even what they have will be taken away” (Matt. 25:29 NRSV) seem to argue for that interpretation. Maybe, we argue, if we think about talents, we observe that talented people seem to be talented in multiple ways. And those who don’t use their talents begin to lose them over time. What is the evidence that Dr. Carey points to when he says the evidence suggests that this is not a supreme reversal of a parable? Tradition? Certainly, he is right to argue that for centuries, this parable has been interpreted as similar to the others in this chapter, and indeed many others in the gospel. It has been presented as a straightforward representation of the kingdom. It is hard to venture out from that tradition. The parable itself reads like most of the others. There is a master, and there are servants or slaves in this case. There is uncertainty about the timing of the return, which is the main theme of this whole set of parables that began in the previous chapter. It is hard to argue against that traditional formation. Yet it doesn’t fit the image of Christ we have elsewhere in the gospels. If the master, the one who returns, is the Christ, then this one seems different from the one we have come to know. The third slave knows him as “a harsh man, reaping where you did not sow, and gathering where you did not scatter seed” (Matt. 25:24 NRSV). The master seemingly accepts this designation and then suggests that the slave should have broken the law to increase his wealth. Something seems off here. The story also begins differently. Instead of saying, as Jesus usually did, “The kingdom of heaven will be like this”, he says, “It is as if” (Matt. 25:14 NRSV). That begs the question, “What is it?” It is as if…? We supply the kingdom words, but they aren’t in the text as we have it. What if the “it” in this case isn’t the kingdom, but the way of this world? What if in chapter 25 of Matthew, we have a sandwich of sorts? We begin with the call to awareness, and we end with the call to serve the one of whom we are aware. But in the middle, we have a look out the window at the world around us. What do we value in our society these days? Who has power in our nation and world? What does it mean to be in the in crowd today? What happens to those who don’t fit the mold, who don’t measure up to the social standards? “Enter into the joy of your master” (25:21) begs the question, “Who is the master?” And what is that joy? If the master is the harsh taskmaster who drives us to produce, to increase, to make, to have more and more, and to take from those who have little, then the joy is an economy that favors the “haves” and punishes or dismisses the “have-nots.” But if the master is the one who says, “Come to me all you that are weary and carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest,” then that joy is something very different indeed. Maybe the hard thing we are called to do is to risk being cast out of the systems within which we live and stand against a cruel and oppressive economy that values profit over people. Maybe, like the third slave, we can protect what we’ve been given but not use it to oppress others. Maybe the joy of the master can be found in smaller, relational, and less expensive ways. Certainly, a message inviting us to use the gifts we have been given to help, heal, and create community is needed in our individualistic culture. But the joy we seek, the joy of our true master, is not found in what we produce, but in who we are in relationship with God and  neighbor. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Generous Christ, every good gift comes from your hand, and you entrust us with resources, abilities, and opportunities to serve your kingdom. Keep us from measuring our worth by what we produce or possess. Instead, teach us to invest our lives in love, mercy, and the building of community. Receive these offerings and use them to lift burdens, create hope, and strengthen your people. May we find joy not in accumulation, but in faithful relationship with you and our neighbors. May all that we offer today become a witness to your abundant grace. Amen. ( Matthew 25:14-30 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5 minutes). Divide participants into groups of two or three and ask, “What is one activity, community, or cause to which you happily donate time, talents, or treasure?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Prepare to read Matthew 25:14-30 by sharing the following: “This text is a parable that is the third of four that are considered 'warning parables' (Matthew 24:45-51, Matthew 25:1-13, 14-30, and 31-46). Bring your questions and your curiosity as we approach this passage.” Read Matthew 25:14-30. Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: What are your first impressions of this parable? Feel free to share interpretations that may make you uncomfortable or that confuse you. What questions emerge  as you read this passage? This parable includes themes of great wealth (a talent was equivalent to a lifetime of financial earning; it was a large amount of money), slaves/servants, and a harsh “master.” What do you think of the responses of the three slaves and their conversation with their master concerning how they negotiated the responsibility of such wealth? 5 talents 3 talents 1 talent Consider that this is a parable about talents (skills or abilities), as we use the word today. Does that change your interpretation of the parable? The Preaching Notes for November 15 say, “Enter into the joy of your master” (25:21) begs the question, “Who is the master?” And what is that joy? If the master is the harsh taskmaster who drives us to produce, to increase, to make, to have more and more, and to take from those who have little, then the joy is an economy that favors the “haves” and punishes or dismisses the “have-nots.” But if the master is the one who says, “Come to me all you that are weary and carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest,” then that joy is something very different indeed. Maybe the hard thing we are called to do is to risk being cast out of the systems within which we live and stand against a cruel and oppressive economy that values profit over people. Maybe, like the third slave, we can protect what we’ve been given but not use it to oppress others. Maybe the joy of the master can be found in smaller, relational, and less expensive ways. How does knowing the character/heart of the master determine the “joy of the master”? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a question, a word, or a phrase that stands out?  Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing : What is one action you might take because of our conversation/study today? Going Deeper on Your Own : This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the selected text [ Judges 4:1-7 and Psalm 123 , Zephaniah 1:7, 12-18 and Psalm 90:1-8, (9-11), 12 , 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11 ) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes) . Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes) . End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: God of all that is good, we confess that there are times when we do not trust the right one with our hearts, efforts, attention, or money. Forgive us, we pray, from burying our talents or wasting our time on that which does not bring honor to you. Free us for joyful obedience, that we might awaken to your purposes in our lives, bringing you glory and honor. In Christ’s name, whose return we await, we pray, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Keep Awake
body: Planning Worship Focus text : Matthew 25:1-13 Keep your lamps trimmed and burning, keep your lamps trimmed and burning, keep your lamps trimmed and burning, the day is drawing nigh. (African American Spiritual, public domain) Every time I read this Sunday’s gospel lesson, I feel this African American spiritual resonating in my bones. I’ve sung multiple arrangements over the years, but the simplest, most straightforward versions are the best. It’s just you, a chorus of other people, and this powerful marriage of tune and text sinking into the marrow, echoes of hope in the midst of profound and unjust suffering, a musical witness to the persistent belief that the good news of Jesus defies the power of the oppressor. I could wax poetic about this spiritual all day, but lest you think this is only for churches with large choirs, there is a singable, public domain version here that congregations of all sizes can sing. I’m not recommending that your congregation sing “Keep Your Lamps” this Sunday just because it directly references Jesus’ parable of the wise and foolish bridesmaids. Rather, this is an opportunity for the whole community to sing an interpretation of this text together. Through a simple, repetitive text paired with a minor tune full of pathos sung in community with others, “Keep Your Lamps” interprets Matthew 25:1-13 by drawing us toward one another, calling us to persevere in the midst of—not despite—the difficulties we face. Through this spiritual, the parable of the wise and foolish bridesmaids becomes not about judgment but about leaning in, supporting one another, and reminding one another that through Christ and in community together, we have hope. Throughout this series, we’re using the gospel texts in the lectionary to explore how Jesus describes the kingdom of heaven. It’s striking to me that Jesus doesn’t give us a list of action items complete with timelines, quotas, and scheduled progress reports. Imagine having a monthly check-in with Jesus: “The goal is world peace. We laid out a plan to make it happen, and you are, let’s see, two thousand years overdue on all tasks. Help me help you figure out the barriers here so we can make some progress.” But no, we don’t have a business plan or to-do lists. We have stories--stories that are culturally specific to Jesus’ day, yet all-too-human. We have parables that we, unfortunately, often read at a surface level when deeper meanings await us if we will stop and pay attention. So, this week, as you explore what it means to keep awake, consider the stories that shape your community. Where do some of those stories need a little extra light and attention? What are the stories we’ve forgotten or neglected? What are the stories that we need to replace about ourselves and our community so we can stay awake to what God is doing among us? Perhaps these aren’t questions we, as worship planners, must answer, but the questions we need to raise with our congregations in worship because the questions keep us awake and attentive to the work God lays before us to build the kingdom of heaven here and now.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Matthew 25:1-13 When did “woke” become such an offensive word in our polarized society? Perhaps the better question is, how? How did such an innocuous word become the ultimate put-down, the prime dismissal of whole groups of people and ways of thinking? Being awake, keeping awake, is a recurring theme for Jesus. This whole series of stories, of which there are four, we must note, begins with the call to keep awake. We have to grasp this invitation; we have to live into the possibility that being awake – being woke – is not only possible, but necessary for the follower of Christ. Before we unpack the text, we need to face realities. Preacher, you aren’t going to redeem the word “woke” in this sermon, even if you wanted to (and you may not). As “woke” has come to be defined in our political rhetoric – or misrepresented, if you will – it might not be worth the effort. Yet, using the title we gave this week’s theme might cause discomfort among some in your pews. It might cause echoes, unwanted echoes in the minds and hearts of the hearers. It might raise defenses. So, tread carefully. Four stories? Chapter 25 of Matthew’s Gospel only has three. True, but back up. This thread begins in chapter 24. It begins with a discourse on what really matters, occasioned by the disciples’ fascination with the Temple. The long discourse that follows has been presented as instructions for going to heaven or entering the kingdom of God. Indeed, there does seem to be an emphasis on eternity. Yet for Jesus, entry into eternity results from living with eternal, or kingdom, values today. In essence, this is about how to live today. The parables that follow the discourse are not simply about the next world, but about living in this one. That isn’t our text for this week, true. But it is the foundation of all of chapter 25 in Matthew. We skip over the first of the four parables: the wise and wicked slaves given charge over the master’s house. But all four parables are launched with the command to keep awake. At last, we get to this week's text! Our parable begins with “the kingdom of heaven will be like this.” This is one of those parables we would prefer to skip. It feels wrong to us. It seems to go against the faith we have learned from Jesus. Sharing seems fundamental to who we are called to be as followers of Christ, so saying there isn’t enough for you and for us seems selfish. So, how do we unpack this story in a helpful way? Preachers have wrestled with this passage for as long as we have attempted to preach it. Does it help to dive into the story's historical context and explain the wedding customs of the time? Maybe. It could allow the hearers to sit a little more comfortably with a complicated tale. It might, however, give people an out because their practice differs from ours, so we cannot relate. This is what “othering” means. It gives permission to set it aside as a quirky cultural event that we can’t duplicate. That isn’t the purpose of the sermon that delves into the history; we understand that. It is, on occasion, an unfortunate result. And this parable isn’t really about wedding behavior anyway. So, what is it about? Jesus tells us it is about being ready. When I was a kid, my mom would make sure I was ready for church. She would inspect the state of my clothes and the cleanliness of my hands and face, and then she would say, “Sit there and don’t do anything until it is time to go to church.” I was ready. And I had to be sure not to do anything to get myself unready, no risk taking, no adventures. Just sit there quietly, being ready. My mom knew me. But I don’t think she was giving me a parable about being ready. Jesus doesn’t say, "Sit still and don’t get messy.” He says to keep awake. “For you know neither the day nor the hour.” But what does that mean? Does our ignorance hinder our living? Does the lack of knowledge of the movement of the returning Messiah cripple our efforts, our ministry, our lives? Or does not knowing free us to live fully every day? Keeping awake is an invitation to engage in the joy of living. It is to embrace the presence of the kingdom. It is to recognize the kin-dom in the fellowship of the community around us. Keeping awake is an invitation to live the abundant life Jesus speaks of in John 10:10 (NRSV): "I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly." One curious observation is that both the wise and the foolish bridesmaids (or virgins – which might be another curious diversion. Is the reference about marital status or naivety?) behave in the exact same way—except for one difference, extra oil. So, what does the oil represent? That’s the question that captures everyone’s attention. Many have argued that the oil represents the good works that the one awaiting the Messiah's return performs in the meantime. That makes sense. That is why the wise ones are unwilling to share, because they can’t. But others point out that this hints at a works-righteousness theology that says that unless you do these things, you will be excluded from the wedding celebration. So what are we left with? It isn’t clear, to be honest. But what if the story is about presence? Waiting for a presence, to be sure, but also being present in the life of waiting. Keep awake, Jesus says, stay present. Pay attention to what is happening around you, in you, and to you. Listen to those who want to tell you their stories and hear the echoes of the story of the one who comes. Weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice: that’s the oil that brings light into a world too accustomed to darkness. “Keep awake” is a call to presence, to embodiment, to mindfulness. It’s not a selfish presence, however. It’s a presence awake to those around us. Bonhoeffer was speaking of this presence when he wrote, “We must be ready to allow ourselves to be interrupted by God. God will be constantly crossing our paths and canceling our plans by sending us people with claims and petitions” (Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Life Together: The Classic Exploration of Christian Community, cited in The Caring Congregation’s  Weekly Care Note email on April 28, 2026). We don’t know what day Christ will return. We don’t know what day we will catch a glimpse of him in the people and the needs around us. We don’t know that it just might be this day. So, keep awake. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Watchful God, you call us to keep awake—to live with open eyes and attentive hearts, ready to recognize Christ in the needs and joys that surround us each day. As we bring these gifts, keep the flame of compassion burning within us. Fill us with the oil of kindness, generosity, and holy attentiveness, that our lives may shine with your love in a world too often dimmed by fear and indifference. Use these offerings and our willing spirits to bring light, hope, and welcome to your children. Keep us awake to your presence and faithful in your service, through Christ our Lord. Amen. ( Matthew 25:1-13 )
