title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5 minutes). Divide participants into pairs or groups of three and have them answer, “Are you generally ready on time, or do you scramble to get out the door? What does ‘on time’ mean to you…early, at the agreed-upon time, or a few minutes late?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Matthew 25:1-13 aloud, inviting participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Ask group members the following questions: What are your first impressions of this parable? Feel free to share interpretations that may make you uncomfortable or that you find confusing. This is the second of four parables that are all considered “warning parables.” (Matthew 24:45-51 before this passage, and Matthew 25:14-30 and 31-46 after it. The two other parables in Matthew 25 will be introduced in the next two weeks.) In this one, part of the story is the affirmation of the bridesmaids who have extra oil to keep their lamps burning as they await the bridegroom. The listener to Jesus’ teaching is encouraged to “Keep awake” (NRSVUE)/”Keep watch” (NIV)/”Keep alert” (CEB)/”Stay alert” (The Message) “for you know neither the day nor the hour” (of Jesus’ return) (v. 23, NRSVUE). What are your thoughts or questions about Jesus’ return? Is there an emotion connected to that for you? The “present tense” nature of these words/phrases points to an active alertness or waiting that implies an ongoing state of alertness, not something that one did and now one is done. What do you think it means to “Keep watch/stay alert” for Jesus’ return in this season of life? What questions does this passage bring up for you? What could the following symbolize: The wise bridesmaids? The foolish bridesmaids? The oil? The bridegroom? The wedding? The door? The Preaching Notes for November 8 say: What if the story is about presence? Waiting for a presence, to be sure, but also being present in the life of waiting. “Keep awake,” Jesus says, “stay present.” Pay attention to what is happening around you, in you, and to you. Listen to those who want to tell you their stories and hear the echoes of the story of the one who comes. Weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice: that’s the oil that brings light into a world too accustomed to darkness. “Keep awake” is a call to presence, to embodiment, to mindfulness. It’s not a selfish presence, however. It’s a presence awake to those around us. What resonates with you about this idea? What challenges you? For personal reflection: how “awake” to the things of God do you feel in this season of your life? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or a phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one thing you want to do because of the discussion today? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [Joshua 24:1-3a, 14-25 and Psalm 78:1-7, Wisdom of Solomon 6:12-16 or Amos 5:18-24 and Wisdom of Solomon 6:17-20 or Psalm 70, 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Dear God, we confess that we may be asleep to your presence in some parts of our lives. Will you wake us up where we are asleep to your presence? And where we are awake, will you continue to stir us into active waiting on your return? Where we have questions, will you meet us, assuring us of your patient love, that we might be filled with your love and grow in patience. In Christ’s name, whose return we await, we pray, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Witnesses
body: Planning Worship Focus text: 1 Thessalonians 2:9-13 First, we are chosen, then we are tested. Now, we witness. Witness has a long history in the context of worship, but Paul isn’t really talking about speaking in worship when he writes to the Thessalonians. No, Paul is talking about a more holistic witness—the witness of our words and our life to the work of God among us. So, as you prepare for All Saints Day, consider the many different expressions that witness can take. What is the legacy of past saints that your church still witnesses in your midst? What does the witness of your church sound, smell, and taste like in your community? What stories shaped your witness in the past and today? What witness do you want to shape your future? Additionally, what does your congregation need to witness today? Where are people hurting and struggling in your community? Where are your neighbors struggling to survive, much less thrive? Where are the hidden places that your church needs to turn its attention to, the places where good news seems so far away? Paul’s witness to the Thessalonians allows us to exercise both parts of witness—noticing and proclaiming, paying attention and sharing the story. So, as you remember the saints today, let their witness guide your community to pay attention and pray for the people who need the gospel right now. Let your prayer of confession or intercession point your congregation to those places in your community and around the world where the vulnerable suffer and where injustice still reigns. And let the witnesses of the saints—the stories of the saints who have gone on and those present today—guide how the church responds to the needs in your community. Perhaps you invite a youth to tell a story about a grandparent, an aunt, an uncle, or another congregant who taught them something about God. Maybe have older adults and the children’s ministry work together to create a piece of art depicting how they notice God at work, and then include it on the altar. Or you might leaf through old bulletins and do a medley of hymns that have shaped the heart song and identity of your congregation. However, you choose to celebrate All Saints Day, in the midst of the grief and loss that this day brings, build in moments for gentle thanksgiving and joyful witness. This is a day of remembering that we are all part of the cloud of witnesses, bound together through Christ across all times and places because God’s word and grace are at work in us. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of the Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children initiative.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: 1 Thessalonians 2:9-13 Finally. All Saints Day falls on a Sunday this year. What an opportunity to truly celebrate this observance, one that Wesley considered his favorite. It is a celebration that lifts up the community of faith, that connects with history, that helps with the ongoing grief and the pride we have in those who have gone before. We honor those who sustained the church in powerful ways and who are now no longer visible in our midst. Yet their presence is felt in the rituals, traditions, and environment they helped shape. When we worship in the space they occupied, we bear witness to their ongoing influence on our lives and the identity of the church. We bear witness. That is a function of the church, of the community of faith: to bear witness. It is a part of our identity. So, it is both who we are and what we do. We are witnesses. As you know, there are two aspects of being a witness. First is the willingness to see. It is easy to avert our eyes and not see the world as it is, not see the suffering of our neighbors, not see the glory of God at work around us in surprising places and through surprising people. We are called to bear witness, to look into the eyes of the hurting, the marginalized, the broken and neglected. We are called to see those who are different from us and, therefore, require more work to truly see. We are not to assume we know but to see and investigate, to listen and learn, so that we can understand what we are seeing. We open our eyes to the world in all its glory and heartache. To follow Christ, to accept the gospel, is to live bearing witness to the world as it is and to hold on to the vision of the world as it could be—to see where the kingdom breaks through. Second, we bear witness by telling what we have seen. Today, perhaps, you’ll tell the stories of those who have gone before, bearing witness to their lives and their influence on the community of faith. At other times, you might tell your own story to bring hope to someone struggling with decisions. You are bearing witness to the work of the gospel by sharing your life with others. Paul asks the Thessalonians to remember the shared ministry they had while he was with them. He asks them to remember the intimacy, the familial relations, and caregiving. We can assume it was a happy memory for them and an inspiration for the work that is now theirs to do in their larger community. But then he makes an interesting shift in the final verse of our text for this week. We also constantly give thanks to God for this, that when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as a human word but as what it really is, God's word, which is also at work in you believers. (1 Thess. 2:13 NRSV) How often, preacher, are you aware of this two-tiered approach to proclamation and witness? Or perhaps more importantly, how often do members of your congregation understand that when they speak, when they give witness to what is happening in their lives, they too give voice to the word of God in the lives of their hearers as well? This might be a time for the community to wrestle with what this means. Most folks would not presume to speak for God when they speak, even words of faith. Most likely, many preachers would also step back from that understanding as well. “I’m just preaching” is not an uncommon attitude of preachers, whether articulated or not. Take another look at the verse, however. There are a couple of little words that we need to pay attention to. The first is “not.” Paul writes, “You accepted it not as a human word…” That’s a bold claim, to be sure. One wonders where he has evidence for this faith in the community at Thessalonica. Perhaps he is returning to the sentiments he expressed in the first part of the letter, where he tells the church that it is an example to churches everywhere. They must have, Paul reasons, understand God at work in the words to be motivated and empowered to live as disciples in their community and beyond so that the gospel can be seen in their lives. That’s how he is able to say that they heard God in those words and not Paul. Or maybe we should say, “not just Paul.” There is another important little word in this final verse of our text. That word is “also.” The Greek word is “ kai, ” which is usually translated as “and” when used as a conjunction. But here, the placement means that “also” is the best translation for the word. That’s a lot of attention to such an insignificant word. However, by using the word also, Paul shows that he understands that God works through our words, not in place of them or in spite of them. “God’s word is also at work in you,” he writes, “along with my instructions and example, along with the mentoring within the community and the experience that comes from walking in the faith.” God works alongside is an important understanding for all of us who would speak of faith. It doesn’t remove the responsibility we have for our words to be truthful and congruent with the gospel, but it adds a deeper dimension to our witness. This is what it means when we say God is using my witness or God is using me to proclaim grace or reconciliation. We don’t lose our agency in such an exchange. Our words and our witness still matter. But God speaks deeper in the exchange to bring a meeting of heart and mind and will and the possibility of transformation. Thus, we are chosen and tested and are witnesses in partnership with the whole church and the abiding presence of God, who confirms our words and receives our offering of praise and service. For that, we can always give thanks. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Call to Worship We are chosen children of God, bound together by the Holy Spirit. We belong to God, and through God, we belong to one another. As we gather to remember the saints who formed us in the faith, we give thanks for their living witnesses to God’s love, showing us that: We belong to God, and through God, we live as family in Christ, bound together by Love. We give thanks for the influence of the saints in our lives who demonstrated God’s love and saving grace, so that we could know in our bones that: We belong to God, and through God, we are saved to love one another. Come, let us worship God who blesses us with witnesses to divine love that we may be witnesses of Love with everyone we meet. We come to worship God who chooses us, empowers us, and inspires us to live as witnesses of Love in communion with the saints of every age. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Opening Prayer God, our Teacher, please instruct us in the ways of humility and love. Help us to live in community with one another rather than in competition with each other. Give us your heart for serving our neighbor. Assure us of your abiding presence and release us from the hierarchies of this world. May your kin-dom come with power and gentleness as we strive to live as embodied witnesses of the good news in Christ Jesus. Amen. Adapted from Cheryl A. Lindsay on the Worship Ways website of the United Church of Christ at https://www.ucc.org/worship-way/after-pentecost-23a-november-5/ . Prayer of Confession Beloved, we are God’s children now, but what we will be in the fullness of our time has not been revealed. What we do know is this: we will be like Jesus the Christ and saints of God. Let us consider how Jesus was revealed among us and pray to be more like the Christ in every way. Jesus embodied the unconditional love of God… We pray, may we be more like Jesus . Jesus fed those who were hungry… We pray, may we be more like Jesus . Jesus drew near to those living on the margins and excluded… We pray, may we be more like Jesus . Jesus brought healing and wholeness to those in need… We pray, may we be more like Jesus . Jesus hungered and thirsted for righteousness… We pray, may we be more like Jesus . Assurance of Pardon Beloved, through the love shown to us by Jesus, we can be sure that we are God’s children now. The Spirit of Christ is among us in this gathering, and the nature of Christ is revealed within us. We are becoming more and more like Christ each day, Living witness to the good news of God’s grace. Therefore, let us live joyfully as God’s people, saints and instruments of God’s way. Adapted from “All Saints Day (Year A),” posted on Seasons Online . . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/10/prayer-of-confession-1-john-3-1-3.html . Benediction May God bless you with reminders of the saints who have gone before, so that, inspired by their witness, you may live as witnesses to Love here and now. And may God surround you with the assurance that nothing—neither life, nor death, nor anything else in all creation—can separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Litany of Remembrance Living God, our Guide and Guardian, Who sits on the throne and delivers us into eternal life, we give you thanks for the saintswhose witness has shaped our lives who now rest in the shelter of your embrace. As we remember those saints Who have died and entered into glory during the last twelve months, we remember their witness to your love and grace with joy and gratitude. As each name is called, ring a bell and/or light a candle in honor of each person. Where possible, have family members or close friends of the person named come forward to light a candle or rise where they are sitting. We bless you for the life and love of these dear saints, and rejoice that they have entered into the fullness of life in your presence. We also remember those saints who We hold in our hearts who have not been With us for some time, yet whose life and witness Continue to form and shape us as your disciples. We honor them now by lifting their names aloud or in our hearts. Allow space for people to speak names aloud from where they are seated. On this All Saints Sunday, we remember that we too are living saints, members of the family of God with all the saints of the past, the present, and the future. And so, we proclaim: We are God's children, witnesses of God’s word that is at work in us and in the saints who have gone before. Today and every day, may we put on Christ and live as saints who tend the poor, comfort the mourners, learn from the meek, affirm those who seek righteousness, offer mercy alongside the merciful, and work for peace with the peacemakers until Christ comes in final victory and we feast as the family of God at Christ’s heavenly banquet. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Eternal God, we give you thanks for the saints who have gone before us—those whose lives bore witness to your grace and whose faith still shapes the church we share today. As we remember them with gratitude, we offer these gifts as signs that their witness continues through us. Open our eyes to see your work in the world. Use our voices to give witness to what we have seen of your love and mercy. Use these offerings to strengthen your church, that our lives may also become a testimony to your living Word at work among us. Through Christ, our Lord. Amen. ( 1 Thessalonians 2:9–13 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson is meant to help students begin to understand the importance of telling their stories.  Even as youth, they have an important role in sharing their story about how God has been present in their lives. This is not an easy thing to do, even for adults, so this lesson should be the first of many you use to help students start telling their stories. Times are based on a fifty-minute lesson period but may be adjusted. NEEDED RESOURCES: Butcher paper or posterboards Markers/other writing utensils Icebreaker - Say What? (10 min.) In this activity, you will ask students to share what they think the following phrases/sayings mean. Encourage all students to share. Adult volunteers can share if students are hesitant, but allow students to lead, with adults asking questions or reframing ideas for clarity1: Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to repeat it. The past actually happened, but history is only what someone wrote down. History is a myth that people agree to believe. We are not makers of history. We are made by history. Where I’m from, we believe in all sorts of things that aren’t true…we call it history. Is one a crusader or a ruthless invader? It’s all about which label is able to persist. Read Scripture (5 min.) Our scripture reading today comes from Philippians. Paul, the author, wrote it while in prison, awaiting trial. He wrote the entire book to the church in Philippi, a young church facing societal opposition. In this section of scripture, he gives a history lesson before moving on to the mission of the church. He shares his story, something we all should learn to do more easily. Have someone read Philippians 3:4b-14 (CEB). Discussion (15 min.) Paul begins this section of scripture by giving the readers a history lesson of all he’s been through and accomplished as a follower of Jesus. Paul went from persecuting the church (as Saul) to becoming the author of many letters to new and emerging churches, instructing them on how to follow Jesus and organize the church. How do you feel as you learn about Paul’s zeal (and conversion) for Jesus, knowing he was once an enemy of the church? Have you ever known someone whose very strong opinions were changed or reversed because of a specific experience? Paul says he is a Hebrew born of Hebrews. Why do you think Paul includes that specific line for his audience?2 Paul uses his story as an invitation to others to walk with Christ. How might hearing a story like Paul’s help others to walk with Christ? Paul speaks of pressing on to the prize - the prize of righteousness. What does righteousness mean to you? Have you ever experienced “righteousness”?3 Read Ephesians 5:1-2 (CEB). What practices help you press on toward righteousness in Christ and imitate God like “dearly loved children”?4 Activity and Discussion: Map out My Story (20 min.) Give each student a large piece of butcher paper or posterboard. Have them draw a timeline of their life from birth until the present day. Then have them brainstorm different occasions where they experienced God’s presence in their lives. This encourages them to start thinking about where they have seen God. If you have room in your youth space, hang these up after the lesson. Encourage the students to add “God sightings” throughout the year. Have students share their timelines/stories with the group. Close in the manner that is typical for you. Consider taking joys/concerns from the students, then asking for a volunteer to close in prayer.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). Say the following: “Think about the people in your life who have shaped you spiritually. Who has been an example in the faith for you? In pairs or groups of three, talk about that person, taking a few moments to give honor and gratitude to them today.” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You likely won’t get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read 1 Thessalonians 2:9-13 . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: This passage is a part of Paul’s letter to the church of the Thessalonians. He references the past hard work so that “we might not burden any of you while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God” (2:9). What do you think he might be referencing? What questions does this bring up for you, either about the context in which Paul is writing, or about hospitality and financial support as a part of the church today? Verse 2:10 says: “You are witnesses, and God also, how pure, upright, and blameless our conduct was toward you believers.” How do you understand being a witness in this context? Why is being a witness important? What bearing does the character of the witness have on what they’re bearing witness to? The Preaching Notes for November 1 say: “We bear witness. That is a function of the church, of the community of faith: to bear witness. It is a part of our identity. So, it is both who we are and what we do. We are witnesses. As you know, there are two aspects of being a witness. First is the willingness to see. It is easy to avert our eyes and not see the world as it is, not see the suffering of our neighbors, not see the glory of God at work around us in surprising places and through surprising people...Second, we bear witness by telling what we have seen…you might tell your own story to bring hope to someone struggling with decisions. You are bearing witness to the work of the gospel by sharing your life with others.” Is one aspect of “bearing witness” easier for you than the other? Which one? If so, why do you think that is? How do you understand bearing witness to the gospel in your own life? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: How can you share your gratitude for the person who has been a witness in your faith? Find one way to honor them/their memory. Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [ Joshua 3:7-17 ; Psalm 107:1-7, 33-37 ; Micah 3:5-12 ; Psalm 43 ; Matthew 23:1-12 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Gracious heavenly father, you are a wonderful parent to us, pure, upright, and blameless. May we receive the gift of your generous love that sometimes shows up as people in our lives. We thank you for the witness of those who have pointed to your love and pray that we might be those people for others as well. Give us grace to live a life worthy of you, who called us to be your people in the world around us. We pray this in the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Tested
body: Planning Worship Focus text: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-8 Worship planners, let me say upfront, moving from “chosen” to “tested” is hard. People who have been harmed by the church hear “God tests our hearts…” and are likely plotting their escape. People who have been in the church a long time may hear the same words and assume they know what they mean, when in fact, we could all use a refresher on what Paul is and is not doing in this passage (see Preaching Notes). So, as worship planners, how do we keep everyone engaged? How do we provide the safe space and the brave space to explore what Paul is talking about in today’s passage? First, we create a safe space by reminding ourselves of the truth of who God is and who God calls and empowers us to be. We recall how God chooses us in the call to worship. We sing of God’s never-failing, always-active love. We pray for one another and our world in the context of God’s faithfulness to listen to our pain and to act for the flourishing of all creation. We prepare the congregation for the possibility that the scripture may hit a few buttons, but we’re going to wrestle with it, not just accept easy, surface-level readings. Then we create a brave space by encouraging vulnerability with boundaries , critical thinking, and mindfulness. This is a place where the preacher and, possibly, the worship leader/liturgist will do much of the heavy lifting. We have to admit the harmful ways passages of scripture have been used, endeavor to ask hard questions of God and the Bible, and expect that we are all doing our best and none of us has the full picture. That’s why we need one another! But we do all of this with boundaries in place. We don’t expect others to agree with us, but we do expect others to address our disagreements with charity and respect. We may leave the worship space with more questions than answers. This is not an invitation to blame those who lead worship, but an opportunity to listen for what God might be saying to us. Brave spaces welcome critical thinking—unpacking the text, being curious and open to new ways to read the same words, and examining multiple viewpoints. To do all of this, we have to be mindful. So, perhaps you begin and end proclamation with a time of silent meditation or a guided practice for paying attention to our bodies, our breathing, and the space we inhabit together. It is difficult to be brave when we’re distracted and disconnected from ourselves and from one another. If you are in a season of stewardship, I encourage you to avoid the idea that God is somehow testing our giving. This can lead to a transactional understanding of faith that leans dangerously close to prosperity gospel teachings. Rather, give thanks that God who chooses us also empowers, encourages, and supports us in the growth of our faith, because that’s what the testing is really about. God isn’t grading us. God invites us, by grace, to join in the process of being molded and formed to be more like Christ, so that we may be a community of thanksgiving and generosity modeled after our generous Creator. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of the Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children initiative.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-8 We are chosen: that’s where we start in this exploration of I Thessalonians. But now we take another step and discover that we are also tested , a tricky word, to say the least. What comes to mind when you hear that we as Christians are tested? Or our faith is tested? Or that God tests us? Consider what you think, and then consider what many in your congregation might think. How does that sound? How is God portrayed in those understandings? How does God come across to those who think about being tested? Arbitrary? Capricious? Maybe even cruel? We need to reflect on what Paul means by “God tests our hearts” (I Thess. 2:4 NRSV). One thing that is clear from the whole text assigned this week is that he includes himself in that testing. This text is primarily about Paul as an example of what it means to live the life of faith. We can be upset about that and see Paul as a braggart, or self-centered, or whatever terms have been used to describe him by people throughout history. But in the end, what do we have to give witness to our faith other than the text of our own lives? That is what communicates; that is what is persuasive and potentially transformative. Our own stories, our own efforts to live out the demands and the grace of the gospel are the means by which every Christian is called to bear witness to the world. Paul is a part of the tradition. He doesn’t raise himself above either the Thessalonians or above us thousands of years later. Instead, he joins us in the struggle. He, too, is tested. “God tests our hearts.” (Emphasis mine!) Paul stands in solidarity with any Christian who faces hard times. That’s his consistent theme: “I have suffered for this faith.” In that context, then, and in that solidarity, he lays out a pattern for gospel sharing or witness giving. Gospel sharing is not about flattery, says Paul, nor about greed – about feathering one’s own nest. It is not about gaining notoriety or receiving awards. It is about the gospel itself, or rather, it is about the God behind the gospel, within the gospel. It is about the one who embodied the gospel, Jesus of Nazareth, the Christ of God. It is only by setting ourselves aside that we can approach sharing this gospel as Paul describes. Paul may have been responding to accusations that he was in it for himself or for the notoriety that comes from gathering folks together and leading them. There is a suspicion that everyone is notoriously self-centered and that personal enrichment – in many forms – is the primary motivator of our actions. Certainly, the well-publicized cases of religious leaders and their lavish lifestyles don’t help with this perception, this suspicion. Paul’s response to these accusations is interesting. It begins with denial, as we have seen— I did not come for myself or to please people. I came to give glory to God. That’s where he starts. But from there, he adds a deeper dimension. I could have come in, says Paul, and flashed my credentials. I could have put pressure on you to follow, to obey, because I am an apostle. That’s an interesting flex. What kind of pressure would that have put on a new bunch of believers? Regardless, he declares that isn’t what he did. Instead, he says, But we were gentle among you, like a nurse tenderly caring for her own children. (1 Thess. 2:7 NRSV) There is some debate in biblical scholarship circles about the word that the NRSV translates as “gentle.” There are authoritative manuscripts of the letter that render the word as “infants.” Many scholars lean toward this word in the context of the letter. (See Prof. David Carr’s argument in Working Preacher, https://www.workingpreacher.org/commentaries/revised-common-lectionary/ordinary-30/commentary-on-1-thessalonians-21-8-6 .) By switching the infant for gentle in verse 7, we have a sense of mutuality in the relationship between Paul and the church. We came to you as infants, needing care. We put ourselves in your hands, perhaps. Or we relied on you, even as you relied on us. Do you hear the implication in this switch? Keeping the word gentle can get you there, but it is more likely to be interpreted as holding back, as still holding all the power but choosing not to use it. Coming as infants and as a nurse implies a sharing of power or agency. This is emphasized in the following verse where Paul says that their intent, or their process, was to share the gospel, and also to share themselves. In other words, he argues that the gospel is not something that is separate from the life of the disciple. It is not a thing out there but is woven into the life of the person following Christ. That brings us back to the idea of testing mentioned at the beginning of the text. Testing in this sense is not an arbitrary or extraneous challenge or burden laid upon those who decide to be believers. Rather, it is living out of one’s faith day by day. Our faith is tested because we use it. The testing is in acting as people of faith. It is not a hoop to jump through or even a job evaluation exercise. Our faith is tested whenever we step out in faith, whenever we stand up against injustice, whenever we act out of love for God or neighbor, whenever we swim against the cultural current and put ourselves at risk. We are chosen because we responded to the call of the gospel, and we are tested because we live our faith. Surrounding all of this is a profound gratitude to the God who called us and walks with us, and to the community with whom we are woven into relationships of love, respect, and service. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship We are chosen children of God, bound together by the Holy Spirit. We belong to God, and through God, we belong to one another. When we feel tested by hard decisions, calls to advocate against injustice, competing narratives, and worrying misinformation, we remember: We belong to God, and through God, we belong to one another. When we struggle with damaged trust and the need to repair our relationships with God and one another, when we are called to go against the social current to build communities of mercy and justice, we remember: We belong to God, and through God, we belong to one another. Come, let us worship God whose grace surrounds us when we feel tested and tried, empowering us to remain faithful disciples of Jesus Christ when we face chaos, division, injustice, and hardship. We come to worship God who chooses us, empowers us, and inspires us to live as the Body of Christ in a broken and hurting world. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Opening Prayer Happy are we, O God, when our hearts are full, our ways are yours, our spirits enlivened by your call. Happy are we, O God, when our lives are guided by delight. We gather here today for just that, holy God. We gather to draw on all you would give us to be more fully yours.  In Jesus’ name. Amen . Written by Rev. Kaji S. Douša and posted on the Worship Ways website of the United Church of Christ at https://www.ucc.org/worship-way/pentecost_21_october_25/ . Prayer of Confession Almighty God, you love us, but we have not loved you; you call, but we have not listened. We walk away from neighbors in need, wrapped up in our own concerns. We have gone along with evil, with pride, quarreling, and divisiveness. Holy God, help us to face up to ourselves, so that, as you move toward us in mercy, we may repent, turn to you, and receive mercy; through Jesus Christ our Lord.  Amen. Words of Assurance Receive this good news: God, who tests our hearts, gives us abundant grace to turn from sin and back to God again and again and again. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Glory to God! Amen. Adapted from a prayer of confession posted on the PCUSA website, http://www.pcusa.org/ . Re-posted on the re: Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2014/09/prayer-of-confession-as-you-have-loved.html . Benediction May God bless you with the courage and the wisdom to respond to division, confusion, injustice, and hardship as imitators of Christ and agents of divine love as we work for the well-being and flourishing of all God’s creation today and every day. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Loving God, you call us not only to believe the gospel, but to live it. You test our hearts not with trials meant to break us, but through the daily invitation to serve, to love, and to share our lives with one another. Receive these gifts as signs of our gratitude and our willingness to embody the good news of Christ. Use what we offer to nurture communities of compassion, where faith is lived gently, courageously, and with humility. May our witness—like Paul’s—be rooted not in pride or gain, but in love that gives itself freely for others. Amen. ( 1 Thessalonians 2:1–8 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson explores what it means for faith to be “tested” not through impossible spiritual challenges, but through everyday acts of love, courage, and integrity. The icebreaker uses a collaborative communication challenge that helps students experience trust, misunderstanding, and teamwork in a playful way. After reading 1 Thessalonians, students discuss how Paul describes leadership rooted in gentleness, mutuality, and shared life rather than status or power. In the activity, students work together to create a human-scale “web” of connection and responsibility, discovering that faith is lived and strengthened through relationships, vulnerability, and daily action. Times are based on a 50-minute lesson period, but can be adjusted. Icebreaker:  “Silent Line-Up” (10 min) Challenge students to line themselves up in a specific order without speaking. Start simple: Birthday month and day Height Number of siblings Then add one funny or unexpected round: How awake they currently feel How much they like pineapple on pizza How likely they are to survive a zombie apocalypse Students can gesture, mime, and move around, but they cannot talk. Keep the pace quick and playful. The goal is awkward teamwork and laughter, not perfection. Bible Reading (5 min) 1 Thessalonians 2:1–8 Discussion Questions (10 min) According to Paul, what motivations should not drive leadership or sharing faith? How does Paul describe the way he treated the Thessalonian community? What differences have you noticed in your own life between people who have led based on power and people who have led based on gentleness or mutual care? What do you think Paul is meaning when he encourages sharing “ourselves” along with the gospel? What are some cultural values or ideas right now about strength, influence, or success that are different from what this passage shows? How might living out faith day by day feel like a kind of testing? Active Learning Activity:  “The Web We Carry” (20 min) Have students stand in a circle. Give one student a ball of yarn. The first student shares one short answer to this prompt: “Name one way people help carry each other through hard times.” After answering, they hold onto one part of the yarn and toss the ball across the circle to someone else, who answers and repeats the process. Continue until a web forms across the circle and every student is holding some of the yarn. Once the web is complete, ask students to gently pull on the yarn. Invite them to notice how movement in one part affects everyone else. Then add a challenge: Ask one student to let go completely. Ask another to pull too hard. Ask two people to carefully support tension together. Pause after each change and notice what happens to the web. Take a moment to name that faith is not something people carry alone. Communities hold, support, stretch, and affect one another constantly, which is why leadership and discipleship require care, honesty, and mutual responsibility. Reflection Questions: What did you notice about how the web changed when one person changed their role? How does this activity connect to Paul’s emphasis on shared life and mutual care? What does this reveal about the way communities influence and support one another? Prayer (5 min) Close with prayer or your group’s weekly blessing. Supplies: Ball of yarn or string large enough for the group Open space for students to stand in a circle

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “Are you a person who likes tests or dreads them? Why?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read 1 Thessalonians 2:1-8 . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. After reading it, ask the following questions: Paul is addressing a community of believers with whom he has a relationship. What evidence of that relationship do you see in this passage? What questions do you have about this relationship? Chapter 1 emphasizes that the people are “chosen” by God (1:4), visible by the “message of the gospel [that] came to you not in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction.” Chapter 2 builds on this foundation but notes that “just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the message of the gospel (chosen), even so we speak, not to please mortals, but to please God who tests our hearts” (2:4). What do you think about God “testing our hearts”? Does this have a positive, neutral, or negative association for you? What would help you decide which it is? Have you ever felt that God was testing you? What was that experience like? What did you learn about God through that experience? About yourself? The image of the relationship between Paul (and Silvanus and Timothy, who are the “we” to whom Paul is referring in this passage—see 1:1) and the people in the church of the Thessalonians is a tender image, a nurse caring for her own children (v. 7). What foundation does this create when there is this kind of trusted relationship? The Preaching Notes for October 25 say, “Testing…[by God] is not an arbitrary or extraneous challenge or burden laid upon those who decide to be believers. Rather, it is living out of one’s faith day by day. Our faith is tested because we use it. The testing is in acting as people of faith. It is not a hoop to jump through or even a job evaluation exercise. Our faith is tested whenever we step out in faith, whenever we stand up against injustice, whenever we act out of love for God or neighbor, whenever we swim against the cultural current and put ourselves at risk.” How does this passage resonate or conflict with your understanding of testing by God? How does it expand upon what you thought about testing by God? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or a phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one action you might take because of our conversation/study today? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the selected text [ Deuteronomy 34:1-12 ; Psalm 90:1-6, 13-17 ; Leviticus 19:1-2, 15-18 ; Psalm 1 ; Matthew 22:34-46 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: God of all goodness, we give you thanks for entrusting us with your gospel and giving us the witness of your faithful followers across time. May we be people who are tested—and approved—by you as disciples who are full of your love for one another and for the world. Give us awareness of your invitations to be tangible expressions of your love in the world around us. In the name of Jesus, we pray, Amen. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. title: Chosen
body: Planning Worship Focus text: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10 During a time of year when many churches are focused on giving, we turn for the next three weeks toward thanks giving. Too early? Are you wondering if this series is better suited for November instead of October? Maybe so. But the lectionary invites us to start our thanksgiving early. Before the turkey and pumpkin pie and even before the trick-or-treaters come to our doors, we have the opening salutation of Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians: “We always give thanks to God for all of you and mention you in our prayers, constantly…” (verse 2). You know that warm feeling you have inside when a friend of a friend meets you, and says, “I have heard so many good things about you!”? I have to imagine that’s how the Thessalonians felt when they received this letter. Before Paul begins discussing their chosen-ness, he claims them. He remembers them with thanksgiving. He prays for them and feels connected to them despite their being apart. I wonder, what relationships in your congregation feel like this? What neighborhood partnerships produce this feeling of gratitude? What connections are you giving thanks for right here and now? How can you express this thanksgiving in worship? To emphasize the theme of thanksgiving, consider whether you want to use a hymn of thanksgiving or gratitude as a thread woven throughout the three weeks of this series. Some traditional options include “Now Thank We All Our God” ( United Methodist Hymnal 102), “Come, Ye Thankful People, Come” ( United Methodist Hymnal 694), and “For the Beauty of the Earth ( United Methodist Hymnal 92). These well-known hymns offer opportunities to hear the familiar in new ways—whether by changing the tune or using a verse as a prayer response—while also leaning into a heart song in your community. You might also consider a newer song that is less familiar to your congregation, such as “Praise God for This Holy Ground” ( Worship & Song 3009) or “All My Days” ( Worship & Song 3011). Vary how you use the hymn from week to week, and by the end of three weeks, it may become a new favorite! If you do happen to be in a season focused on stewardship, remember: thanksgiving and generosity go hand in hand. In one of his final articles as Director of Stewardship and Generosity, Rev. Ken Sloane notes the power of saying thank you . Thanksgiving and joy are at the root of true generosity. We don’t tell people to be thankful as a transaction to receive their gifts. We start with thankfulness, because we have all been richly blessed by our Creator and our community, a community that chooses to follow God because we have been chosen and sustained by God. In times when stewardship campaigns can feel like an exercise in noticing all that we do not have, let thanksgiving turn you and your congregation toward the abundance of what God has already provided and trust that God will guide, provide, and equip you to live, work, and rest as the body of Christ planted just where you are for a time such as this. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of the Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children initiative.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10 What does it mean to be chosen? Paul calls the Christians in Thessalonica “beloved by God” and says that God has chosen them. It must have made them feel good. We know what it is to be chosen (or maybe we know the pain of not being chosen). We know about exclusion and inclusion. We understand what it means to be part of something bigger than ourselves, or we long to. That’s what Paul is talking about: that participation. He claims to know that the Thessalonians are chosen because the Word came to them. That’s an interesting claim. He knows their chosenness, their inclusion, because the word, the word he brought, came to them, and they received it. So, is listening to the word being chosen? Or is it that only those who are chosen can hear it —or hear into it? Is it only the chosen who can hear something bigger, something deeper? That is how your chosenness is identified, says Paul. Actually, he says something more. It wasn’t just hearing the word; it was receiving the power. Ah, there we have it. The special ones are the ones chosen, the ones we read about in our history, the ones we’re not a hundred percent sure we believe. But wouldn’t it be great? Those miracles, those unexplained actions that a special few can do, or pretend to do, or convince people that they can do. That is what this is about, isn’t it? Wonder workers, celebrities, heroes, and heroines of the faith: those are the chosen. Admit it: that has long been a suspicion we’ve had. We’ve felt that it wasn’t about us, the ordinary ones, but about the special ones. And good for them. Really. We need heroes and heroines. We need models to look up to, to emulate, or to imitate. Paul throws that in: “And you became imitators of me” (I Thess. 1:6 NRSV). You, not you individually, but you all, all y’all. You became a community that lived faith, that grew in faith, that sought ways to act out faith. You—all y’all—did that. That’s how he knows you were chosen, because you are living it, because others are encouraged by you, by the example you are setting, and by the hope you are living. Chosenness is about ripples. Like any gift of the Spirit, it isn’t given primarily for you, for the one receiving it. You are chosen to be an influence, to be an example. Many wonder what it means to be a disciple of Jesus Christ in today's crazy world. They figure it out by looking to you, to your community, to the witness that you give in word and deed, in mission and in service. You can ask how the surrounding countries learned about the faithfulness, the chosenness of the disciples in Thessalonica. We don’t know. Paul says he didn’t need to talk about it. Maybe he meant he didn’t need to keep talking about it. Maybe he told, but then the word spread. We don’t know. And in the end, it doesn’t really matter. The message here is that you are an example, the light on the hill that Jesus talked about. That’s you. That’s all y’all. Parents learn early on that they are being watched by the little ones they are raising, even when they aren’t “on” or intentionally parenting. They are being watched. There are folks in your town who wonder what it means to follow Christ. They wonder what it means to belong to a church. Sure, they could go to church themselves to find out, but they don’t need to. They just see you. Are you an example of the joys of discipleship? Are you one who loves God and neighbor with equal passion and commitment? What do your neighbors see when they look at you? At your church? Do they wonder if they might be welcomed if they wander in one day? Or is your church like a social club that they don’t have the credentials to join? Paul says you are chosen because you responded. Being chosen is not an award or a medal that you can wear with pride. It is a call to follow Christ, to put on the yoke, to live outwardly and openly in a way that increasingly stands out in the culture around us these days. That call begins with gratitude. Paul addresses his hearers by saying he always gives thanks to God for them. For us. For those who have been chosen, for those who have responded. We join him in this thankfulness and give thanks for the call on our lives and for the disciples who stand with us for support and encouragement. We give thanks for the opportunity for the ripples to go out from the little things we do to lift up those around us. We give thanks for the gift of life itself and the blessing of living in a world of wonders. We have been chosen for all of this and more. Thanks be to God. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship We are chosen children of God, bound together by the Holy Spirit. We belong to God, and through God, we belong to one another. The Spirit empowers us to live as imitators of Christ in love of God, neighbor, self, and all creation. We belong to God, and through God, we learn to love one another. The Spirit inspires us to receive God’s Word with joy in a world that rejects the good news. We belong to God, and through God, we live in joy with one another. Come, let us worship in the assurance of God’s love that chooses us, empowers us, and inspires us to live as the family of Christ. We come to worship God in the assurance that we belong to God, and through God, we belong to one another. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Opening Prayer Loving, living God, be among us now. Show us your ways. Guide our steps. Live in us, that we may be people of steadfast hope and powerful giving. Help us hear your words, challenging us to give you all the things that are yours. Help us remember that all we are and all we have are gifts from you, gifts to be shared in service and love. Holy One among us, help us be a holy people who receive your word with joy and live your message with love. Amen. Written by Mary Scifres on the Ministry Matters website, http://www.ministrymatters.com/all/blog/entry/1779/worship-elements-october-16-2011 . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/10/call-to-worship-prayer-proper-24a.html . Prayer of Confession God of Grace, we know that you have chosen us, but we often forget that you have also chosen others. You call us to be imitators of Christ, yet many times we are imitators of the world. You challenge us to turn from our idols, but we are tempted to turn back to them again and again. Rescue us, Lord, from ourselves. Show us your way. Guide our every action, that we may live as you call us to live. Prayers of silent confession Words of Assurance Beloved children of God, receive this good news: God loves us, chooses us, Forgives us, and renews us to live in love and service of God and neighbor. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Glory to God! Amen. Adapted from Amy Loving, The Worship Closet.  Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/10/confession-1-thessalonians-1-1-10.html . Benediction May God bless you with the assurance that you are chosen children of God, empowered and equipped by the Spirit to live as the Family of God in a world in desperate need of the good news. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Gracious God, you choose ordinary people and weave them into a community that shines with your love. We thank you for the gift of belonging—for the call to live our faith in ways that ripple outward into the lives of others. Receive these gifts as signs of our gratitude and our willingness to be witnesses to your grace. Use what we offer to encourage the weary, welcome the searching, and strengthen your church as a living example of hope. May our shared life together always point to Christ, whose love calls and sends us. Amen. ( 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10)

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson explores what it means to be “chosen” not as superiority or exclusion, but as a call to live in ways that create hope and encouragement for others. The icebreaker uses a collaborative puzzle challenge that helps students notice one another’s instincts and strengths while working together under pressure. After reading 1 Thessalonians, students discuss how faith spreads through example, community, and everyday actions rather than celebrity or status. In the activity, students create a ripple installation that visually traces how small acts of encouragement and faithfulness can influence people far beyond what we immediately see, discovering that discipleship is communal, visible, and contagious. Times are based on a 50-minute lesson period , but can be adjusted. Icebreaker:  “Puzzle Relay Mix-Up” (10 min) Before students arrive, prepare several simple puzzles or image cutouts and secretly mix the pieces between groups. Divide students into small teams and give each team a pile of puzzle pieces. Explain that the first group to finish their puzzle wins. Students will quickly realize they are missing pieces and have extras that belong to other groups. The only way to complete the puzzle is to communicate, trade, and help one another. Do not explain this ahead of time. Let them discover it naturally. Once all groups finish, briefly celebrate the chaos and teamwork before moving on. Bible Reading (5 min) Read : 1 Thessalonians 1:1–10 Discussion Questions (10 min) What words or phrases from this passage stood out to you most? According to Paul, how did the Thessalonians respond to the message they received? What does Paul seem to mean when he says they became an “example” to others? How is being “chosen” described differently here than how people sometimes think about it? What do you think is the reason that people learn more from watching others than from being told what to do? How can churches or faith communities accidentally make people feel excluded instead of welcomed? What kind of example do you think makes faith feel believable or attractive to others? If your group wanted to create positive ripples in your school or community this week, what might you actually do? Active Learning Activity:  “Ripple Wall” (20 min) Tape a large sheet of paper to a wall or spread it across a table. In the center, write the phrase, “Small things change people.” Give each student several strips or circles of colored paper and markers. Ask students to think of small actions, habits, encouragements, or examples that have positively affected them. These should be ordinary things, not huge dramatic moments. Examples: Someone noticed I was having a bad day A coach kept encouraging me Someone invited me to sit with them A teacher believed in me A friend checked in on me Students write one example per paper piece. Then invite them to tape their pieces outward from the center phrase like expanding ripples in water. As the wall grows, students will visually see how small acts spread outward into wider influence. When finished, step back together and look at the full installation. Name that Paul describes discipleship like ripples: ordinary people living faithfully in ways that quietly spread hope and encouragement. Reflection Questions (for the Activity) What kinds of small actions showed up most often in the ripples? What surprised you about how influence spreads? How does this activity connect to Paul’s idea of being an example to others? Prayer (5 min) Close with prayer or your group’s weekly blessing. Supplies: Simple puzzles or printed images cut into puzzle pieces Large sheet of paper or butcher paper Colored paper strips or circles Markers Tape

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “Who has been an example of a Christian for you? What do you see in their faith or action that compels you?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in the time you have together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10 aloud, inviting participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Ask group members the following questions: What positive affirmation does Paul, the author of this letter (or “epistle”), give the church of the Thessalonians based on this passage? Verse 4 refers to the people as “chosen.” Consider what it means in scripture when someone is “chosen.” When have you been “chosen” for something? What about not being chosen? How does being chosen—or being excluded—shape one’s identity? What do you think Paul means by the gospel not just being “word,” but also in “power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction”? How do you understand the gospel having power and conviction? Paul references them becoming imitators and being “an example to all the believers.” How does the idea of imitating Paul/Christian leaders sit with you? How does the idea of being an example to all believers sit with you? Which do you struggle with more? Why might that be? The Preaching Notes for October 18 say: “There are folks in your town who wonder what it means to follow Christ. They wonder what it means to belong to a church. Sure, they could go to church themselves to find out, but they don’t need to. They just see you. Are you an example of the joys of discipleship? Are you one who loves God and neighbor with equal passion and commitment? What do your neighbors see when they look at you? At your church? Do they wonder if they might be welcomed if they wander in one day? Or is your church like a social club that they don’t have the credentials to join?” What resonates with you about these questions? What challenges you? Read back through the scripture passage. Is there a word or a phrase that stands out? Write it down for consideration in the week ahead. Just One Thing: What is one thing you want to do because of the discussion today? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice [ Exodus 33:12-23, Psalm 99 , Isaiah 45:1-7 , Psalm 96:1-9, (10-13) , Matthew 22:15-22 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Loving God, the power of your resurrection raised Jesus from the dead, and it raises us, too. We can sometimes feel less than “qualified” to be an example for others. But you choose us anyway, before we do anything to be worthy of being chosen. May we be encouraged by the witness of the church of the Thessalonians, who served you, the Loving and True God. And may we also be found faithful. In Christ’s name, we pray, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Rejoice in the Lord!
body: Planning Worship Focus text: Philippians 4:1-9 I don’t know about you, but oftentimes, joy feels like a luxury. An add-on. An I’ll-get-to-that-if-I-ever-have-free-time kind of thing. So, when Paul says, “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice,” I’m tempted to respond, “Got that covered on Sundays, but there’s too much going on in this world to spend time on joy or rejoicing the other six days of the week.” But then, I come across an article or a podcast ( like this one with Brené Brown and Karen Walrond ) that stops me in my tracks and calls me out on just how wrong I am. What Paul, Brené, and Karen all know that I all too quickly forget is that joy isn’t a luxury or a distraction. Joy is vital . We can’t do this thing called life without it. And more importantly, we don’t have to manufacture it. Joy is a gift, an act of grace in our lives that points us back to God and flows out of us to others. Joy gives us sustenance to maintain life, hope, resilience, and perseverance, even in the most impossible circumstances. Joy isn’t an escape. True joy accompanies us in and through the realness of our lives. So, even as you focus on rejoicing today, don’t forget the prayer of confession or the prayers of the people. Speak the truth about how we fall short. Name the places of hurt and suffering in your community. We can rejoice in God because in all of our faults and our pain, we are not alone. God is with us. So, bring out the noisemakers; pull out all the stops on the organ; lift up your voices. Find extra moments of celebration and praise throughout the service. Let the joy come in response to God’s never-ending, always-loving presence among us, in response to God’s acts of pardon, nurture, and provision. Whatever you do, don’t just talk about joy. Practice full, embodied joy together! As we end this series, consider using the following breath prayer to draw attention to God’s acts and our joyful response: (Breathe in) I rejoice in God, (breathe out) because God’s love will never let me go. Encourage congregants to use this prayer in the week ahead and beyond to focus attention on God’s love at work among us and the joy that sustains us as we press on together. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.

title: Preaching Notes
body:
Preaching Notes Focus Text: Philippians 4:1-9 “Always” is a hard word. In many ways, it’s an inhuman word. Always . Who says that? How do we guarantee “always” in a temporary kind of world? Who knows what might be next? I heard about a wedding couple who wanted to change the vows from “until death do us part” to “as long as love shall last.” Now, it is possible that they meant always , that they were confident in that love. It was an Irving Berlin kind of love. (Yes, I AM old.) “I’ll be loving you Always / with a love that’s true Always / when the things you’ve planned / need a helping hand / I will understand Always.” 

(Writer: Irving Berlin. Copyright: Lyrics © Kanjian Music, BMG Rights Management, Universal Music Publishing Group, O/B/O DistroKid, Capitol CMG Publishing, Songtrust Ave.) Maybe that is what the couple meant when they wanted to change the vows to “as long as love will last.” Maybe they were proclaiming an Irving Berlin kind of love. Always. Too old for you? How about a Jon Bon Jovi love? “And I will love you, baby - Always / And I'll be there forever and a day - Always / I'll be there till the stars don't shine / Till the heavens burst and / The words don't rhyme / And I know when I die, you'll be on my mind / And I'll love you - Always.” Writer: Jon Bon Jovi. Copyright: Lyrics © Universal Music Publishing Group, Kobalt Music Publishing Ltd., Spirit Music Group Okay, Bon Jovi isn’t necessarily current either. But, Berlin or Bon Jovi, always is still a big word, a romantic word, not a very practical word. Always —not a very doable word. Always —for now, that fits, that works. For a while, we can handle that. But who has the capacity to say “always”? Not me. And I suspect, not you. Am I right? “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, Rejoice (Philippians 4:4 NRSV). Dang it, Paul. Why’d you throw that word in there? That unreachable, impossible word? That “always” word. Take that word out, and this is a nice little passage about being happy, finding your joy, walking on the sunny side of life. “It’s got a nice beat, and you can dance to it.” A spoonful of sugar, all that sort of stuff. But no, you weren’t happy with that. You wanted something more, something deeper. You wanted something (dare I say it?) eternal. Cover one eye and read this without that scary word. Just for a moment. “Rejoice in the Lord.” Well, of course! Who would say no to that? “Again, I say rejoice.” Sure, keep reminding me; I need the boost. I also need to be reminded of the source of this joy: “Rejoice in the Lord.” Certainly, I can do that. I have done that. I remember a time when there was joy in the Lord, in worship, in fellowship. Sure, it happens. Been there, done that. And then, Paul says, let it spill out. That joy in the Lord is not just for you, not just so that you get a boost, a lift, a skip in your step. Let it come out. “Let your gentleness be known to everyone.” Gentleness? Hmm. I’m not sure that’s the best word, actually. It’s a good word, but not the best. It doesn’t quite convey what Paul is getting at here. “Patience,” some say, “forbearance,” if anyone uses that word anymore; “magnanimity,” if you want a real tongue twister. Peterson’s The Message says, “Make it as clear as you can to all you meet that you’re on their side, working with them and not against them.” [2] I like that. An earlier paraphrase said, “Let all the world know that you’ll meet them half-way.” It’s about hospitality, welcome, inclusion; it’s about the fact that we aren’t the judge; we don’t point fingers; we don’t accuse; we dropped our stones long ago, even since Jesus told us that only the sinless can throw them. We aren’t looking to pick fights, to call names. What we have to share is joy—joy in the Lord. “Let your gentleness be known to everyone.” Everyone? Paul almost slipped in an “always” there, didn’t he? Everyone. Hmmm. Don’t worry about anything. Yeah, ok, thanks, Paul. But no thanks. I mean, how in the world are we going to do that? It’s one thing to know we aren’t supposed to worry, but how do we stop? And then, because we can’t stop, we end up worrying about worrying. I guess that’s why there is a comma there and not a period. “Do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.” “Don’t worry,” says Paul, but get on your knees. Don’t worry, but pour it out. Don’t worry, but beg and plead and pound on the doorways of heaven with both fists, even as you know—not hope, not assume, but know—that you are heard and that answers are already all around you when you open your eyes again and put one foot in front of the other. Don’t worry because you don’t have time to worry, you are so busy bending God’s divine ear. Don’t worry because your life is now a prayer, and the answers are coming fast and furious and surprising. Don’t worry, because from somewhere comes this sense that maybe, just maybe, you are not alone in the universe—this sense that maybe you do have a place, a home, an identity, an existence right here and right now that is meaningful, useful, transformed, and transforming. From somewhere, who knows where, God, it must be, comes a peace that even on your best days you can’t define or even describe. It just is, passing all understanding, or your understanding anyway. Where does it come from? Choose joy. Rejoice in the Lord. Always . We’ve come back to that. It is still there. We can squint it away only so long. We can ignore it only for a time. Rejoice in the Lord, always. Maybe we could negotiate with Paul. Rejoice in the Lord, when it is convenient. Rejoice in the Lord, when we’ve got the time, when we’re in the mood, when the world hasn’t taken yet another sideswipe at my confidence. Rejoice in the Lord when I’ve run out of excuses not to. Rejoice in the Lord ... Always. Always? How do we do that? Focus on the next one? No, focus more deeply on this one. “Finally, brothers and sisters, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is pleasing, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.” Think on, dwell on, meditate on, take your cue from, be obsessed with these things. Look at the list: True, honorable, just, pure, pleasing, commendable, excellent, praiseworthy . What is that? Who is that? Implied in the directive is the confidence that there is enough of this out there to fill us up, and not only fill us up but give us joy—real joy, in the Lord joy. Always joy. Paul says, "Go find Christ in the world." Go find the one you love, the one who loves you, focus on that, and you will know joy. The fruit of the Spirit is love that then brings us into joy, the joy of the Lord, always. Always. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh.
