title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Beloved, God’s never-ending love spills out all around us, drawing us together in beloved community with God, neighbor, and all creation. Rejoice in the Lord always, and again we say, rejoice! God’s always-present grace surrounds us, enlivening us to love ourselves and our neighbors just as Christ loves us. Rejoice in the Lord always, and again we say, rejoice! God’s persistent peace sweeps through us, guarding our hearts and empowering us to live as agents of God’s mercy and justice wherever we go. Rejoice in the Lord always, and again we say, rejoice! May our rejoicing overflow into our families, neighborhoods, and the whole earth that through our living, working, resting, and playing, God may be glorified. Rejoice in the Lord always, and again we say, rejoice! Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Prayer of Intercession God, we come into Your presence with praise and thanksgiving for Your faithful love. Your love never fails—not even when we turn away from You: when we ignore Your invitation, or desert You for gods of our own making. Even then, You do not abandon us, but reach out—again and again— inviting us back into relationship once more. As You welcome us, so You welcome our prayers. We bring them to You with confidence, knowing that You will hear and answer. We pray for the world You created and the people who share it with us: - for countries caught up in war or violent conflict, - for those whose homes and lives are threatened by natural disaster; For these and all the other areas in our worldwhere there is need and despair, Lord, hear our prayer. We pray for our country and for its people: - for our government leaders, federal and local, - for our judicial system, police forces, and military, - for our cities, towns, and rural communities, - for employers and employees, for young and old, For all who are part of this great country, Lord, hear our prayer. We pray for our local community—the people of this city/town, - for those who are unemployed, - for those in prison - for those who are hungry, - for those who are alone and afraid, For all our neighbors, both known and unknown to us, Lord, hear our prayer. We pray for this congregation—our siblings in Christ, - for those who are ill or whose loved ones are ill, - for those who are anxious about the future, - for those struggling with their faith, - for those who minister among us, For all Your people in this place, Lord, hear our prayer. Pour out Your Spirit on us! Fix our hearts and minds on what is true and honourable and right. Give us the joy and peace that comes from knowing and doing Your will. Keep us faithful to the call we have received in Christ Jesus, our Lord, extending Your loving invitation to the world around us. In Jesus’ name. Amen . Adapted from Christine Longhurst, posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/09/prayers-of-people-october-9-2011.html . Prayer of Confession God pours blessings upon us, even as we choose to go our own way. God is present and seeks to bring healing and wholeness to all. Therefore, I invite you to confess all that would separate you from God or one another. Let us pray. When we have fashioned idols of our own desire or worshiped the temples of our own tradition, Lord, have mercy. Time for personal reflection and confession. When we have denied your invitation to the banquet of love and justice, or failed to extend the invitation to others, Christ, have mercy. Time for personal reflection and confession. When we have adorned ourselves with worry rather than joy or failed to be gentle, knowing you are near, Lord, have mercy. Time for personal reflection and confession. Assurance of Pardon Praise be to God, our sins are forgiven. God’s steadfast love endures forever. Praise God! From Standing in the Gap , written by Rev. Dr. Bob Gross, OCC, pastor at Lake Avenue United Church of Christ, Elyria, OH, and posted on the United Church of Christ website. Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/09/confession-of-sin-proper-23a.html . Benediction Beloved, as you go from this place, may the peace of God that surpasses all understanding surround you, centering your minds on whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, pleasing, commendable, excellent, and worthy of praise and empowering you to press on toward the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026.

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson includes a random act of kindness for the ending activity and can be continued to a subsequent lesson if needed.  It covers the fruits of the Spirit and explains how we can rejoice in the Lord always.  Times are based on a fifty-minute lesson period but may be adjusted. NEEDED RESOURCES: Small rocks to be painted (big enough to write words on but not too big and heavy/bulky Paint, paint brushes, permanent markers or paint markers for writing words, and drop cloths if needed to protect surfaces. Icebreaker - Fruit of the Spirit? (10 min.) In this activity, students will be asked to vote if a certain virtue is a fruit of the Spirit listed in Galatians 5:22-23. Below is the list of virtues that are fruits of the Spirit and those that are not. Feel free to mix them up. You may want to let students vote by a show of hands or by walking/running to a designated corner of the room if they need to burn off some energy! After each virtue that is not on the list of fruits of the Spirit, have a quick discussion about why it’s not a fruit of the Spirit. 1 1.    Love (yes) 2.    Quietness (no) 3.    Joy (yes) 4.    Rigid Doctrinal purity (no) 5.    Peace (yes) 6.    Patience (yes) 7.    Hiding your emotions (no) 8.    Kindness (yes) 9.    Goodness (yes) 10.    Fear (no) 11.    Faithfulness (yes) 12.    Gentleness (yes) 13.    Passivity (no) 14.    Self-Control (yes) Read Scripture (5 min.) Our scripture reading today comes from Philippians. Paul, the author, wrote it while in prison, awaiting trial. He wrote the entire book to the church in Philippi, a young church facing societal opposition. Have someone read Philippians 4:1-9 CEB. Discussion (15 min.) Paul says to rejoice in the Lord always.  Can you think of songs or movies that use the word “always”? (“I Will Always Love You” and “Always Something There to Remind Me” might be examples.) “Always” is a strong word, much like “forever.” Do you find it challenging to commit to doing anything ALWAYS? Why or why not? Is there anything you ALWAYS do, no matter what? (Breathing might be a funny answer…but it is true. Perhaps the things that we ALWAYS do for God should be as natural as taking a breath.) Does rejoicing in the Lord always mean we have to be happy all the time? Why or why not? How are “rejoicing” and “being happy” different? 2 Paul also encourages us to let our joy spill out: “Let your gentleness show in your treatment of all people.” Have you ever been in a place where joy or positive energy seemed to be contagious? How can we let our gentleness and our joy show to all people? Read Galatians 5:22-23 (CEB) . Which fruit of the Spirit do you find most challenging to notice in yourself? To notice in others? Which ones do you find the most natural to live out? How does living into the fruits of the Spirit help you “rejoice in the Lord always”? Activity and Discussion: Don’t Throw These Stones (20 min.) Have students paint rocks.  After the rocks have dried, instruct the students to write down words of affirmation they heard during the lesson. Some examples include “rejoice,” “joy,” “always,” and any of the fruits of the Spirit. After the students have finished their work on the rocks (possibly the next time your group meets), have them take the rocks and either give them directly to community members or leave them for community members to find. This can be a random act of kindness for your group. (Remind your group not to throw the rocks. We don’t cast [the first] stones around here.) Close in the manner that is typical for you. Consider taking joys/concerns from the students, then asking for a volunteer to close in prayer.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Steadfast Joy, when “always” feels larger than our capacity, you remain near. In gratitude, we bring these gifts, signs of love learned from you. Quiet our anxious hearts and turn our attention toward what is true, honorable, and worthy of praise. Shape us into a people whose generosity is gentleness made visible, whose offerings declare we are on the side of our neighbors. Receive what we place in your hands and let it become courage, welcome, and hope. Guard us with your peace as we press on in Christ. Amen. ( Philippians 4:1-9 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer the question, “What is the most peaceful place you have ever been to?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Philippians 4:1-9 aloud. Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Encourage participants to highlight or write down the word or phrase which stands out to them. Pay attention to themes of peace, praise, and prayer. Share these with the group. In Philippians 4:2, Paul names two women, Euodia and Syntyche. It is implied there is a disagreement between them and Paul encourages unity. How do you resolve disagreements in your church community? What would it look like to resolve conflicts with gentleness and the mind of Christ? Paul encourages the church to not be anxious about anything but instead turn to prayer. (Philippians 4:6) How do you use prayer when you feel worried or fearful? Do you feel as though you can bring every concern or worry to God in prayer? In the midst of conflict and worry, how do you still rejoice and give thanks to God? Reread Philippians 4:8. Paul says to praise the things which are true, honorable, just, pure, pleasing, and commendable. Create a list of things which are true, honorable, just, pure, pleasing, and commendable. How can you praise and rejoice in these items this week? Taking Action This week, focus on peace, prayer, and praise. Peace Spend time centering yourself to be at peace. If there are conflicts or disagreements in your life, work to resolve them. Remember to work for unity and be gentle with others. Prayer When you feel as though you are worried or unsure about the world, pray to God. Remember nothing is too great for God. Praise Be sure to give thanks to God each and every day. Create a gratitude list of the items you are grateful for. Turn on your favorite worship songs and remember to give thanks to God. Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests. After each prayer respond: Hear our Prayer. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer. Peaceful God, we praise you! We rejoice knowing you are present with each of us in the ups and downs of life. You are with us in our disagreements and worries. You are there in our celebrations and elation. You encourage us to press on and continue to be of the same mind of Christ. May we continue to focus on what is true, honorable, just, pure, pleasing, and commendable knowing your peace will surrounds us. We praise you and together we pray. Amen. Rev. Maddi Baugous is an ordained elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference where she serves as University Minister at Nebraska Wesleyan University in Lincoln, Nebraska. Maddi is passionate about encouraging young adults in their faith through justice and education.

title: The Heavenly Call
body: Planning Worship Focus text: Philippians 3:4b-14 “What’s Paul’s problem with bodies?” I asked myself this (paraphrased) question often as a teenager, especially since Paul’s letters were a popular source for Sunday school and youth group Bible studies. It also didn’t help that I heard preachers and teachers over the years warn about the temptations and dangers of the flesh, using their own riffs on Paul to encourage young people to flee the ways of the flesh and choose the way of Christ. So, it’s no wonder that I started to read Philippians 3 as promoting a kind of escapist faith instead of an embodied one. You may have congregants in your pews who feel the same. The thirty-year-old who was taught not to trust his instincts when something doesn’t feel right. The eighty-year-old who learned not to be honest with the community about her pain because her body doesn’t matter as much as her faith. The eight-year-old born with cerebral palsy who uses a wheelchair and is told it’s all ok because in heaven, he’ll be whole and able to walk again. They’ve all received the message: our heavenly call, our journey of faith in Christ, is an escape from the body. Thank Jesus, then, that’s not what Paul is writing. For Paul, faith is a deeply embodied journey that calls us into the present, embodied reality of loving and living with God, self, neighbor, and all creation. We press on together here and now by the grace through which Christ saves us, the grace that gives us confidence and perseverance to continue. That’s the other thing Paul tells us—we’re not there yet! That is why we need one another. So, this week, consider using the following breath prayer in worship and throughout the week: (Breathe in) Help me press on, (breathe out) because I belong to Christ. May this prayer be a reminder that we are not alone—we belong to God, and through God, we belong to one another. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: Philippians 3:4b-14 In October 2008, United Methodist representatives from across Indiana gathered to vote on whether the two conferences would remain separate or merge into a single new conference. This is a common occurrence throughout our denomination, and there are many reasons it has happened and will continue to happen. Some of the reasons are self-preservation and institutional survival. Some of the reasons are about shared vision and mission. “The face of unity,” some posited; “an attempt to circle the wagons,” others declared. All the above, it could be argued, and more. I bring up this historic moment not to pass judgment on the act itself, but to consider a minor detail of the moment. The joint conference gathering that October was held at the State Fairgrounds in Indianapolis, in the Toyota Pavilion. Now, you may not know what the Toyota Pavilion is at the Indiana Fairgrounds. It is the sheep barn. Someone told me it is the only public building in Indiana dedicated entirely to sheep. And there we met to form a new conference. It was there we met to press on toward the goal of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus, the Great Shepherd of the sheep. That’ll preach, as they say. But what does it have to do with this text from the letter to the Philippians? Paul gives a history lesson, then sets that history aside in favor of the mission of the church. Okay, granted it reads like a humble brag. Paul, who was big on humility in his writing, manages to sneak in some considerable self-referential information that sounds like one-upmanship. The familiar “I’m better than you, so you should listen to me.” More than that, he actually says, "Do what I do." “Join in imitating me,” he says a couple of verses past the reading for this week. This sort of thing has turned people off of Paul for a long time. And it is hard not to see their point. But look a little deeper. After his catalogue of suffering and attributes (which are, surprisingly, in the same list), he says it doesn’t really matter. Moreover, he says he considers all that stuff garbage. The Greek word is skubala , translated as rubbish , garbage , or dung . It’s a strong word, offensive in some circles. That’s how he feels about his own resume—at least compared to knowing Jesus, compared to the call to share the gospel, to widen the circle, to embrace the hope and encourage others to embrace with him. What Paul knows is that when it comes to all of that, to … well, let’s just say it … evangelism. Another strong word, offensive in some circles. But when it comes to evangelism, all we have is our stories. All we have is the witness of our lives. Paul isn’t ashamed to use what he has to tell of the relationship he has with the Risen Christ. He is ready to lay his life down as a witness to the power of the redeeming spirit of Jesus—not to use it as a way to increase his own glory, climb some social ladder, or enrich himself. He chooses to let his story be an invitation for another to hear, embrace, move closer, and know the one who gives Paul his strength and purpose. The best thing about Paul’s story, he would no doubt point out, is not his history, but his future; not who he has been, but who he is becoming. The invitation is to come along for the journey of discipleship. The invitation is not “look at me,” but “walk with me as we look to Christ.” “We’re pressing on,” Paul argues. But pressing on toward what? What does Paul call us to do or be? Pressing on toward the goal of the heavenly prize means what, exactly? Well, we think it is obvious, isn’t it? It’s about getting to heaven, about lounging on a cloud with halo and harp, about basking in the presence of the Lamb on the throne, or however we might envision that realm. Indeed, Paul talks about leaving to be with Jesus in other passages. That escape into a place where kingdom rules apply sounds enticing in today's world. Yet it seems unlikely that Paul is arguing here for an escapist mentality. Rather, for Paul, the prize is righteousness , and righteousness is not a strict adherence to rules and laws, but an embodiment of God’s mercy and justice. Embodiment is an important concept. It is how we live. It is the actions we take, the positions we hold, and the values we embrace. We are, in other words, called to become like Christ. When Paul rails against “flesh,” he doesn’t mean bodies. What we do with our bodies matters a lot to him. And we can express our faith through our bodies, our words, and our inner being. “Flesh” represents anything that gets in the way of embodying faith in a Christlike way. Flesh is self-centered as opposed to other-centered. Flesh prioritizes empire – status quo – nation over the kingdom of God. When we press on, we press on through many avenues. We press on through spiritual disciplines. We press on through acts of mercy. We press on through justice work and world-transforming efforts that bring wholeness to all people. We press on to build community, not just to take care of ourselves. Through his story, Paul issues an invitation to partner with the Spirit in working toward the vision that Jesus the Christ gave to us. That heavenly prize is—as we regularly pray —the kingdom come on earth as it is in heaven. Press on. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship We live in a world that entices us with influence, power, and accolades. We choose to press on toward the prize of the heavenly call. Sometimes we find ourselves wishing for heaven without working to bring heaven to earth. We choose to press on toward the prize of the heavenly call to live righteously here and now. Other times, we find ourselves exhausted by working for the gospel, wondering if anything we do is making a difference. We remind one another to press on toward the prize of the heavenly call, leaning on Christ as the source of our perseverance and hope. Beloved, God calls us not to escape this world but to build the kingdom of God in this place and in this time. We choose to press on toward the prize of the heavenly call to embody God’s mercy and justice as we build God’s kingdom on earth as it is in heaven. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Prayer of Intercession Holy God, bless our lives, sanctify us, and in your way, grant us our hearts’ desire. Anoint us with your grace, that what we desire is also what you desire. Help us to understand that our hearts’ true desire is the love of you. May the love of Christ urge us on; may we walk by faith. Thank you, God, for all our blessings. Holy God, bless those who govern – Bless the leaders of nations, countries, towns, and cities. And those who lead in all manner – social, political, and religious – Bless us all. Fill the hearts of all with your wisdom. Guide us in the way of justice and integrity for all. Guide us to walk by faith. Holy God, tend to those who suffer in mind, body, and spirit. Tend to the tired, the dying, the poor and the hungry. Help us to follow the love of Christ, a love which urges us on. Help us to seek and serve Christ in others, bringing forth a new creation. Holy God, we ask all this in the name of Christ, our redeemer. Holy God, we ask all this by the Holy Spirit who activates your love in us. Holy God, we ask all this that your love may be like seed scattered— manifesting in small and unexpected ways—the greatness of You. May your love take root in our lives, that we may walk by faith. Amen. Written by Rev. Terri C. Pilarski, on the Words Matter.Episcopal site, http://expansivelanguage.blogspot.ca/. Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/search?q=Terri+C.+Pilarski. Prayer of Confession Loving God, present and near. You are beyond our words and our understanding. Help us to remember that You are at once infinite, boundless, timeless, and eternal, but, at the same time, intimately entwined with our lives. You are with us no matter where we find ourselves. When we have forgotten You, Lord, have mercy. When we have failed to speak words of love, Lord, have mercy. When we have neglected the need of another, Lord, have mercy. Loving God, present and near, help us to recognise Your presence and nearness with us as we worship together. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen. Written by Thomas Sutcliffe and posted on the Church of Scotland’s Weekly Worship website. http://www.churchofscotland.org.uk/worship/weekly_worship/ . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/10/prayers-of-approach-and-confession.html Benediction Disciples of Christ, may God bless you with perseverance, that together we may persist in following the way of Christ toward the heavenly call by embodying God’s mercy and justice here now. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026.

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson is meant to help students begin to understand the importance of telling their stories.  Even as youth, they have an important role in sharing their story about how God has been present in their lives. This is not an easy thing to do, even for adults, so this lesson should be the first of many you use to help students start telling their stories. Times are based on a fifty-minute lesson period but may be adjusted. NEEDED RESOURCES: Butcher paper or posterboards Markers/other writing utensils Icebreaker - Say What? (10 min.) In this activity, you will ask students to share what they think the following phrases/sayings mean. Encourage all students to share. Adult volunteers can share if students are hesitant, but allow students to lead, with adults asking questions or reframing ideas for clarity 7 : Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to repeat it. The past actually happened, but history is only what someone wrote down. History is a myth that people agree to believe. We are not makers of history. We are made by history. Where I’m from, we believe in all sorts of things that aren’t true…we call it history. Is one a crusader or a ruthless invader? It’s all about which label is able to persist. Read Scripture (5 min.) Our scripture reading today comes from Philippians. Paul, the author, wrote it while in prison, awaiting trial. He wrote the entire book to the church in Philippi, a young church facing societal opposition. In this section of scripture, he gives a history lesson before moving on to the mission of the church. He shares his story, something we all should learn to do more easily. Have someone read Philippians 3:4b-14 (CEB) . Discussion (15 min.) Paul begins this section of scripture by giving the readers a history lesson of all he’s been through and accomplished as a follower of Jesus. Paul went from persecuting the church (as Saul) to becoming the author of many letters to new and emerging churches, instructing them on how to follow Jesus and organize the church. How do you feel as you learn about Paul’s zeal (and conversion) for Jesus, knowing he was once an enemy of the church? Have you ever known someone whose very strong opinions were changed or reversed because of a specific experience? Paul says he is a Hebrew born of Hebrews. Why do you think Paul includes that specific line for his audience?8 Paul uses his story as an invitation to others to walk with Christ. How might hearing a story like Paul’s help others to walk with Christ? Paul speaks of pressing on to the prize - the prize of righteousness. What does righteousness mean to you? Have you ever experienced “righteousness”? 9 Read Ephesians 5:1-2 (CEB) . What practices help you press on toward righteousness in Christ and imitate God like “dearly loved children”?10 Activity and Discussion: Map out My Story (20 min.) Give each student a large piece of butcher paper or posterboard. Have them draw a timeline of their life from birth until the present day. Then have them brainstorm different occasions where they experienced God’s presence in their lives. This encourages them to start thinking about where they have seen God. If you have room in your youth space, hang these up after the lesson. Encourage the students to add “God sightings” throughout the year. Have students share their timelines/stories with the group. Close in the manner that is typical for you. Consider taking joys/concerns from the students, then asking for a volunteer to close in prayer.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Faithful Shepherd, you call us beyond our resumes and our trophies, beyond what we have been toward who we are becoming in Christ. As we lay these gifts before you, free us from clinging to what we think gives us worth. Turn our eyes toward the future you are unfolding. Let our giving press us deeper into mercy, widen the circle of belonging, and shape us into people who embody your justice and grace. Keep us moving; keep us growing; keep us following. We press on toward your kingdom, trusting you to lead. Amen. ( Philippians 3:4b-14 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer the question, “If you could only describe yourself in three words, what words would you use?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Philippians 3:4b-14 aloud. Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Encourage participants to highlight or write down the word or phrase which stands out to them. Share these with the group. In Philippians 3:5-6, Paul is sharing his religious background. He is naming the privileges he had in the Jewish society, being a religious leader. What privileges or advantages do you have in our society? (Think about your race, religious background, socio-economic status.) Paul later refers to all his previous achievements and accomplishments as “rubbish”, because he has experienced new life in Christ. (Philippians 3:8) What are some of the achievements or accomplishments you could discard or let go of? Paul no longer needs the law or a list of requirements to receive God’s love. (Philippians 3: 9) Have you ever felt like you had a check list of items to complete to earn God’s love? How did this hinder your relationship with Christ? In Philippians 3:10, Paul writes “I want to know Christ.” The Greek word is ginōskō which is not just about intellectual knowing but also experience. What does it mean to know Christ? How have you experienced the power of the resurrection in your own life? How do you “press on toward the goal?” (Philippians 3:14) What does this look like in your faith journey? Taking Action This week, allow yourself to let go of your achievements and accomplishments. Make a check list of all the things you feel you “must do” to receive the grace of God. Maybe you list out attending worship or leading a Bible study. Even list out the privileges or achievements you hold to be most important. Then cross out every single one of them. Check them off. Instead, write over them or on a new sheet of paper, “I know Jesus Christ.” Write it as many times as you need to remember Jesus’ love for you. Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests. After each prayer respond: Hear our Prayer. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer. God of new life, you do not need our earthly accomplishments. You do not desire us to complete a check list for us to receive your love. May we lay down our privileges to trust you your faithfulness and compassion. Help us to experience the power of Jesus Christ so that all may know the hope of resurrection. Together we pray. Amen. Rev. Maddi Baugous is an ordained elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference where she serves as University Minister at Nebraska Wesleyan University in Lincoln, Nebraska. Maddi is passionate about encouraging young adults in their faith through justice and education.

title: In Full Accord
body: Planning Worship Focus text: Philippians 2:1-13 How do we press on together? What does it take to live well as a community? In Philippians 2, Paul lays it out clearly: “Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus.” Easy to say, but difficult to understand, much less do. Even for Paul. I often wonder if that’s why he chooses a song to explain what he means—because a theological treatise is not nearly as effective as a song at describing what it means to have the same mind as Christ. And not just any song—a hymn, a song sung in community with others. How do we live like Christ? We live in humility and grace together. In full accord. So, as you plan worship this week, find hymns that reference Philippians 2:1-13, so that your congregation can join their minds and their singing with Christians across the generations. Some hymns that more fully quote the passage include “At the Name of Jesus” ( United Methodist Hymnal 168) or “All Praise to Thee, for Thou, O King Divine” ( United Methodist Hymnal 166). Philippians 2 was also a favorite passage of John and Charles Wesley, and it is referenced in hymns such as “And Can It Be” ( United Methodist Hymnal 363) and “Jesus! the Name High over All” ( United Methodist Hymnal 193). Consider, too, how you can model the call for all to live in humility and grace together through worship. For centuries, Philippians 2 was used to keep some people humble at the expense of making others powerful. So, when we pray, sing, and preach about living according to Christ’s example, we must recognize and confess how humility without grace has been used as a spiritual weapon against the vulnerable, and repent that we may receive grace to live in Christ’s humility, marked by just and merciful love. Whether you choose to explain the history of this passage in the sermon or incorporate a prayer of confession, consider using the following breath prayer to either prepare for or respond to the sermon: (Breathe in) Unite us through grace, (breathe out) to love like Jesus. Encourage your congregants to continue praying this prayer throughout the week, paying attention to how our shared journey in grace leads us back to one another to praise, exalt, and set our minds on Christ in full accord. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: Philippians 2:1-13 Paul seems very concerned about thinking—maybe because he is in prison and doesn’t have much else to do but think. In the first few verses of this passage, he tells us that we should think alike and think as Christ does. Right? Well, sort of. “Being of the same mind” doesn’t stifle creativity or even differences of opinion. He is not trying to remove all the differences in the body of Christ. Those differences make us the rich tapestry we are. Finding new perspectives, new ways of looking at the same things, is part of the excitement of living in community. So, what does he mean by “having the same mind”? How can a diverse collection of humanity—like the church—ever hope to achieve unanimity of thought? We are too different, have too many varied experiences and backgrounds, and too many diverse abilities to hope to think alike on any issue of substance. Don’t you think? Paul has a solution. Wake up in the morning with your mind stayed on Christ. Do you know that spiritual? The first line goes “Woke up this mornin’ with my mind...” ( The Faith We Sing , 2082). Stop there for a moment. Woke up with my mind? Well, good for you! We were wondering. The song doesn’t say much about yesterday, or tomorrow, for that matter. You wonder, “It’s a good thing, don’t you think, to wake up with your mind?” (Especially considering the alternative.) However, this isn’t a hymn about mental health. It is an invitation to think as Christ does. The song, while it pauses at the end of the first line, goes on to make a very profound statement: “Woke up this mornin with my mind ... and it was stayed on Jesus.” Some versions simply say, “with my mind stayin’ on Jesus. “ It’s an early morning act of faith. It is claiming Christ first thing. It is claiming that living the day that lies ahead in the way we say we want to live is possible only by focusing on the mind of Christ. That is exactly what Paul says in our text from Philippians this week. He wants us to think as Christ does. The thought process he is particularly interested in is humility: “set yourself aside.” Set aside your need to be right. Set aside your need to have it your way. Set aside ... Wouldn’t it be wonderful if those who claimed to be followers of Christ—in business, in politics, in the church—would set their minds on Christ and embrace humility, self-sacrifice, and a desire for unity and hope? Some do, I know. But most don’t, or most of us don’t all the time. That’s why we need daily reminders. “Woke up THIS morning...” The “same mind” doesn’t mean the same thoughts, but the same goals. It means that love always trumps prejudice. It means that sacrifice always wins over selfishness. It means giving always triumphs over hoarding. It means ... well, you get the idea. How we go about becoming more like Christ, having that mind of Christ, may be different, as each of us is different. But we all seek the same Christ, the same kingdom, the same hope. This is what being in full accord means. It means thinking, acting, and being as much like Christ as we can day by day. It means choosing again and again to have a mind “stayed” on Jesus. That is what causes Paul to break into song in the last verses of the passage. He hopes that one day we won’t have to wonder what Jesus would do, because we would all be doing it, not because we were forced or coerced, but because it was what we all wanted to do. It was the natural response to any situation— the loving response, the caring and giving response, the Christlike response. “Woke up this morning with my mind stayed on Jesus.” At least, that’s my hope. How about you? Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship The apostle Paul calls us to “let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus.” What is the mind of Jesus? The mind of Jesus is to love God, neighbor, self, and all creation. Paul reminds us that “it is God who is at work in you.” How is God at work in us? God enables us through grace to love God, neighbor, self, and all creation. Paul exhorts us to “work on your own salvation with fear and trembling.” How do we work on our own salvation? We cooperate with grace to love God, neighbor, self, and all creation. Beloved, we gather to worship God who, through Jesus, shows us how to love and enables us to love as Christ loves us. We gather to learn how to live in full accord through our love of God, neighbor, self, and all creation. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Opening Prayer Most wonderful God, the beauty we see in Jesus is your beauty veiled in human flesh, the love we witness from Bethlehem to Golgotha is your love contracted to a span. If Christ’s life is so holy as to fill us with wonder, how much more would your unveiled beauty leave us overwhelmed and trembling? You are more than the eye could bear, more than the mind can ever fathom. Yet you have so carefully made us that although we cannot fathom you, we can yet love you. Gratefully, we bring our little lives to you, asking that our worship may arise from love and be shaped by love, and be directed towards that larger loving which is our soul’s desire. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen! Written by Bruce Prewer, posted on Bruce Prewer’s Homepage. Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/09/opening-prayer-philippians-2-6-11.html. Prayer of Confession Within the strength of community, in the power of silence, we come before God with the truth of our lives, trusting in the mercy and love of our Creator. Let us offer our confession before God and each other. Holy God, we know that in so many ways We have run from you, We have ignored your call, We have closed our eyes to your presence, We have disbelieved your mercy, We have disregarded your words, We have belittled ourselves, We have forsaken others. So we ask, once again, for your forgiveness. We ask you to stay with us as we turn away from what is wrong and hurtful to what is bright and life-giving. And hear now our silent prayers. Receive the good news: God’s love abounds for us, Forgiving us and restoring us to Community with God and one another. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Glory to God! Amen. Written by Beth Merrill Neel on her blog, “Hold Fast to What Is Good.”  Used with permission. Posted at https://holdfasttowhatisgood.com/liturgy/prayer-of-confession/ . Benediction Beloved, remember: God is at work in you, enabling you to will and to work for God’s pleasure. May God bless you with a spirit of joyful cooperation and Christian love as together we work with God and neighbor for the flourishing of all God’s creation. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026.

body: Music Notes The “same mind” doesn’t mean the same thoughts, but the same goals. It means that love always trumps prejudice. It means that sacrifice always wins over selfishness. It means giving always triumphs over hoarding. How we go about becoming more like Christ, having that mind of Christ, may be different, as each of us is different. But we all seek the same Christ, the same kingdom, the same hope. This is what being “in full accord” means. title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This is an opinion-heavy lesson.  Encourage students to think outside the box and be creative, particularly during the activity and discussion portion of the lesson. They do not have to be songwriters or poets to come up with some great ideas! Times are based on a fifty-minute lesson period but may be adjusted. NEEDED RESOURCES: YouTube lyric video for Woke Up This Morning TV or screens to view the video (with sound) Printed lyric sheet of the song for reference (see within lesson) Paper and writing utensils for students to write their song/poem Icebreaker: Good Morning! (10 min.) Play the lyric video for the spiritual "Woke Up This Morning" on YouTube or read the lyrics to your group if you can’t play it. Once the video is done, ask the students to share their typical morning routine. Do they wake up and listen to any music? Do they wake up cranky or happy? Are they slow or quick to wake up? What is typically the first thing on their mind in the morning? Read Scripture (5 min.) Our scripture reading today comes from Philippians. Paul, the author, wrote it while he was in prison, awaiting trial. He wrote the entire book to the church in Philippi, a young church facing societal opposition. Have someone read Philippians 2:1-13 (CEB). Discussion (15 min.) Paul is still in prison when he writes this letter. Because of his situation, he has PLENTY of time to think. When was the last time you took some time to think - only to think - about what it means to follow Christ? What sort of things did you think about? If you’ve never thought about it, take a few minutes to think about it now.  What does it look like to follow Christ? How might you find time and space between Sundays for time like this? In the scripture, Paul says we are to have the same mind. How can that be in a world full of diverse individuals? 3 Read Hebrews 12:2 . Are there activities that benefit when we focus our vision, or concentrate, on one specific area or action? What activities, and how does focusing help? If we think about a life of discipleship as filled with activities and action, how can we fix our eyes on Jesus? 4 Why do you think the author of Hebrews calls Jesus the pioneer and perfecter of our faith? 5 You saw a video at the beginning of the lesson that starts with the lyric: “Don’t you know that I woke up this morning with my mind stayed on Jesus?” Have you ever had a day when you woke up excited about something, and you kept thinking about it all day? Are you willing to share what that was? How might your morning or day change if you woke up with your mind on Jesus? What easy and short activities could you add to your morning routine to stay focused on Jesus?6 Activity and Discussion: Rewriting Lyrics (20 min.) Take some time to think again about what it means to follow Christ.  Then try rewriting the song's lyrics to fit YOUR life.  You could write the lyrics as a poem.  Be creative. What does staying your mind on Jesus look like for you? Close in the manner that is typical for you. Consider taking joys/concerns from the students, then asking for a volunteer to close in prayer. title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Humble Savior, you meet us at the start of every day and invite us to take on the mind of Christ. As we bring these gifts, set aside in us the need to win, to hoard, to be first. Shape us instead for love, for shared work, for joy in serving side by side. Use what we offer to build a community where sacrifice is natural, mercy is instinctive, and hope rises in every heart. Keep forming us, not by force but by grace, until our living begins to look like Jesus. We place our offerings—and ourselves—in your hands. Amen. ( Philippians 2:1-13)

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer the question, “Who is the humblest person in your life? What qualities do they embody?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Philippians 2:1-13 aloud. Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Encourage participants to highlight or write down the word or phrase which stands out to them. Pay close attention to what Paul writes about “the mind of Christ” and “humility”. Share these with the group. Paul shares we should do things with humility and “do nothing from selfish ambition or empty conceit”. (Philippians 2:3) What do you think he means by this? What are some of examples of selfish ambition and empty conceit, which prevent us from showing humility? In Philippians 2:5, Paul “Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus”. What does it mean to have the mind of Jesus? Does this mean we all must think the same? The Greek word for mind is phroneo. It is not just about thinking but also one’s attitude and behavior. Reflect on the life of Jesus. How did Jesus live his life? What behaviors or actions did he take in his lifetime? Are there specific stories which come to mind to show Jesus’ humility? Paul concludes by encouraging the church to “work on your own salvation.” (Philippians 2:12) What does it mean for you work on your salvation? How can you best emulate the life of Jesus? Taking Action This week, focus on humility. Instead of turning towards selfishness, put others’ needs before your own. You could be intentional about letting people go ahead of you at the grocery store or donate food to those in need. You might take time to listen to someone who needs to be heard or advocate for a cause. Ensure you are lifting up the needs of others. Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests. After each prayer respond: Hear our Prayer. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer. Modest God, you entered the world as a humble servant, Jesus Christ. You put the needs of others first. You feed the hungry, healed the sick, and ultimately took on the cross for each of us. May we press on, living as you lived. Help us put aside our own egos and desires, to instead show humility to all. Guide us on the path of salvation. Together we pray. Amen. Rev. Maddi Baugous is an ordained elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference where she serves as University Minister at Nebraska Wesleyan University in Lincoln, Nebraska. Maddi is passionate about encouraging young adults in their faith through justice and education.

title: Striving Side by Side
body: Planning Worship Focus text: Philippians 1:21-30 Are you feeling life pressing in all around you? The global events, the local concerns, the too-full schedules, the sudden surprises? Are you staring at your calendar, social media feed, or news app, wondering how we’ll all get through this? I recently saw a reel from a therapist who was talking about how common it is for eldest daughters who are now in adulthood to daydream about having a minor medical emergency so they can get some rest. Maybe it’s because I’m an eldest daughter, or maybe it’s the world we’re in right now, but I found myself resonating just a little too much with what that therapist was saying. Whether we’re in the pulpit or the pew, a lot of us are wishing for a way out of the stress and worry that inundate our lives. Thankfully, we’re not alone. Though they weren’t facing stressors like 24-hour news alerts, the uncertainties of AI, and a constantly fluctuating economy, Paul and the Philippians were not strangers to stress, worry, and the struggle to live faithfully amid it all . So, consider this an invitation over the next four weeks to stop, take a breath, and mine Paul’s wisdom for pressing on toward Christ as we move through the struggle together. As you begin this series, think about the heart songs in your congregation. What hymns or choruses might you weave into worship over the next four weeks? Maybe you sing a traditional hymn like “How Firm a Foundation” ( United Methodist Hymnal 529) in a new way by singing one verse a week in preparation for prayer or singing the hymn in a variety of styles throughout the series. Maybe one week, the congregation meditates on the words while a pianist plays an arrangement of the tune, and another, you sing the hymn congregationally but in a new way—a folk style or with a small instrumental ensemble. This might also be an opportunity to introduce a new hymn into your congregation’s musical and spiritual vocabulary, such as “ We Labor Unto Glory” by Porter’s Gates or “We Will Follow”/“Somlandela” ( Worship & Song 3160). One of the key points to remember throughout this series is that we are not called to wear ourselves out. Pressing on is not about throwing ourselves against brick walls with no regard for our own well-being. Rather, pressing on is about persevering faithfully in love for God, self, neighbor, and creation. So, throughout this series, we encourage you to incorporate a breath prayer—a simple, meditative prayer practice—into worship and/or as an offering for the week ahead that reflects on Paul’s words to the Philippians and the theme of pressing on. For this first week, consider using this breath prayer: (Breathe in) We are God’s people; (breathe out) together, we press on. May it be so. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences, as well as the New Day Amani/Upendo house churches in Dallas. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, Lisa earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text: Philippians 1:21-30 Does the fact that Paul writes this letter from prison add an important dimension to the words we will reflect upon in this series? Next week, when he asks us to have the same mind as Christ, does that feel different knowing he is incarcerated by the empire? In week three, when he tells us his story of suffering and of privilege, does it land differently because he speaks from a position of being bound? And in the final week, when he tells us to rejoice—and not just rejoice but rejoice always—do the echoes of that proclamation through the bars of his cell ring more profoundly? He begins this epistle by reminding the believers in Philippi that he is praying for them—from prison. He prays for them, and by extension, for us. In our text for this week, he wrestles with life and death. That’s understandable, perhaps, except his isn’t the usual prison despair, but an inner debate about the purpose of faith and life. It’s stunning, and it’s especially stunning when we realize that his decision to stay is so that he can be in service to others. It is not his own good that drives him, but that of the flock that follows him, including this group from Philippi. He writes from prison that he is motivated to live and work for the cause of Christ because of them. And let’s not assume that he was contemplating ending his life in prison, but that he was considering surrendering his ministry and waiting for the sentence to be pronounced against him, which it ultimately was. No one would have faulted him for sitting back and worrying about his fate. No one would have blamed him for being concerned about the state of his soul in these perhaps final moments of freedom and life itself. Instead, he sets himself aside to continue encouraging the church and building up the body. So how shall we respond to this act of self-sacrifice? Paul asks the Philippians to “live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ” (Phil 1:27 NRSVUE [1] ) “Live your life,” he says. Live it well, as Christ would have you live. But there are signs that this was more than simply being good boys and girls. First, there is the call to unity. A life worthy of the gospel is a life lived in community, in shared mission and ministry. Striving side by side is not a byproduct of the gospel; it is in the very design. This unity, this shared striving, is where the strength comes from—the strength to stand against those who would oppose the mission. Enemies : a complicated word. Some of us don’t think we have enemies. Others see their mission is to conquer enemies, destroy enemies, vanquish enemies. But Paul doesn’t give permission to do that here. Instead, he suggests that faith and unity are protection against enemies. “To not be intimidated by those who oppose” is the way we read it here. It’s about perseverance and commitment to the cause of Christ, regardless of the obstacles. It’s a reminder that the best way to do this is together. Striving side by side while we stand together is what Paul looks for. “Striving while we live our lives in a manner worthy of the gospel” sounds like just getting on with it, or, as a famous shoe manufacturer says, “Just do it!” It’s that, but more. The word here is “ polituesthe ”- “live your life.” Look again, it is the word we get politics from. Some translate the word as “conduct yourselves as a citizen” in a manner worthy of the gospel. But we’re not supposed to get political, we’re told. The worlds are separate, we hear. Just deal with faith stuff, spirit stuff, and not political stuff. Paul’s argument is that there is no separation. How you conduct yourself as a citizen is a faith issue. If the spiritual dimension of your life never leaks into the political dimension, what good is it? If your faith in Jesus has no impact on the priorities by which you live, the values you hold, the causes you support, then is it really transforming? Is it really sanctifying if it never changes how you live? This is not a call to be partisan, to promote a party or a candidate, but a call to let your faith and the community within which you live and work and grow together guide you in living life in human society. We are called, invited, and encouraged to strive side by side for the kingdom of God as envisioned by the one we follow. We let the gospel be the measure by which our lives are shaped. And we press on. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship In times of busyness and stress when we feel surrounded by challenges on all sides… We gather to learn to strive side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel. In times of joy and rest when we feel the goodness of God’s provision and abundance deep in our bones… We gather to learn to strive side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel. In times of conflict and distress when we feel just how hard it is to live in unity together… We gather to learn to strive side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel. Disciples of Christ, come, let us worship God who empowers us to press on… As we learn to strive side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026. Opening Prayer Mighty God, we enter your presence with thanksgiving and hope. You have formed us as your people. You join us on the journey of life through valleys, upon mountains, and on the plains. We set our attention and seek your wisdom, encouragement, and grace. Reveal your will and display your glory among your people as we worship your holy name. Amen. Written by Rev. Dr. Cheryl Lindsay and posted on the Worship Ways website of the United Church of Christ at https://www.ucc.org/worship-way/after-pentecost-17a-september-24/. Prayer of Confession We continue to believe that we must earn our way into God's heart. But God's grace is given to each of us, for all of us, freely, unconditionally, always. Let us open our lives to this mercy as we pray, saying, It seems we cannot decide, Cloud of Glory. We say we will live to serve others, but end up meeting only our needs. We claim to live in a way that honors Christ, but we do not take him to work, school, home. We believe that the gospel can transform lives, (at least, for those who need it - not us). Forgive us, Presence of Peace. Instead of grumblers, may we be ambassadors of grace. Instead of continual complaining, may we carry compassion to the hurting. Instead of whiners, may we be workers with Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, to reach out and bring the kingdom of God to everyone we meet. Silence is kept Assurance of Pardon This is the good news: there is no ranking in God's kingdom. God graces everyone with the same gifts: mercy, restoration, new life. God has kept the covenant. We have been forgiven, we have been made new people. Thanks be to God. Amen. Written by Thom Shuman, from Lectionary Liturgies . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/09/prayer-of-confession-september-18-2011.html . Benediction As you go from this place, may God bless you with wisdom, courage, and perseverance to live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ as you work, rest, play, and strive side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, July 2026.

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher To save time, you can precut the prison cell doors instead of having the students do it. Ideally, students can cut out the bars and contemplate the lesson at the same time. Times are based on a fifty-minute lesson period but may be adjusted as needed. NEEDED RESOURCES: Construction paper Scissors Writing utensilsAn example prison cell door would help visual learners see what they are supposed to create. Icebreaker: Best Gift Ever? (10 min.) Students will take turns sharing the best gift they’ve ever received. Ask them to talk about the occasion and the gift itself, but not why it was special. As they answer, sort students into small groups (4-5 students per group ideally) based on the gift (either type of gift or occasion). Once the youth have been sorted into groups, have them share their names, then have them share with their small groups why the gift was so special to them. Adult volunteers should participate as well. Read Scripture (5 min.) Our scripture reading today comes from Philippians. Paul, the author, wrote it while he was in prison, awaiting trial. He wrote the entire book to the church in Philippi, a young church facing societal opposition. Ask someone to read Philippians 1:21-30 (CEB). Discussion (15 min.) Paul keeps on writing, even while in prison, for the good of the church that is full of new believers to benefit those young Christians. That is his gift to them. We talked about the best gift you’ve ever gotten, but what’s the best gift you’ve ever given someone else? Paul says in verse 29 that it is a privilege (a gift) to not only believe in Christ but to suffer for Christ’s sake. What does that mean to you?1 Paul calls for unity in the body of Christ. What does it mean for a group of believers to have unity? Does it mean they agree on everything all the time? Why or why not? Read Romans 5:3-4 . In this scripture, also written by Paul, he says that we should be happy when we have problems (endure suffering).  What was his reasoning? Paul likely wrote this book of Romans before he wrote the book of Philippians.2  Do you think he would have written something different after being imprisoned for so long? Activity and Discussion (20 min.): A prison of your own making. Have the students create a paper prison cell door from construction paper by cutting strips out of a piece of construction paper, leaving the paper intact at the top and bottom (see sample below). Then have them write on each of the “bars” how they think being imprisoned would affect them. In the space at the top and the bottom, have them write “gifts” they could work on while imprisoned that would help their group reach others for Christ. After they finish, have them share what they created with the group.  Adult volunteers should also participate. Close in the manner that is typical for you. Consider taking joys/concerns from the students, then asking for a volunteer to close in prayer. Sample "Prison Cell Door"

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Steadfast God, for us to live is Christ. In every season, you hold us, and in every struggle, you knit us together as one body. Receive these gifts as signs that we choose to stand firm, striving side by side, living as citizens of your kin-dom. Use what we offer to encourage the weary, strengthen your church, and bear witness that love is stronger than fear. Shape our common life to be worthy of the gospel, until our unity itself proclaims your grace. Amen. ( Philippians 1:21-30 )

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer the question, “When you need encouragement, who do you turn to? Why?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Philippians 1:21-30 aloud. Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Encourage participants to highlight or write down the word or phrase which stands out to them. Share these with the group. In Philippians 1:21, Paul states, “For to me, living is Christ, and dying is gain.” What do you think Paul means by this? Paul is writing this letter to the church of Philippi while he is in prison. He is facing uncertainty about what his future might look like. Living in prison is not enjoyable, and he finds it challenging. What does Paul discover is his reason to continue living? Following Jesus is not always easy. In our own faith journeys, we can be discouraged or uncertain. Think of a time in your faith where you were discouraged. What brought you joy to press on? What do you think it means to “live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ?” (Philippians 1:27) The Greek for “live your life” can also be translated as “live as citizens” indicating when we live for Christ our faith is public and should be seen by others. In what ways do you want to make your faith a public act? (ex: evangelism, advocacy, volunteering) Taking Action: This week, be intentional about living your life in a manner of Christ. Write down three ways you can show your faith to others. Then throughout the week check them off whenever you do it. For example, your list might include- volunteer at my local food bank, call and pray with my friend, write a thank you letter to your biggest encourager. Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests. After each prayer respond: Hear our Prayer. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer. Generous God, at times we face challenges in our faith and in our world. We want to journey faithfully, yet we struggle with doubt and discouragement. When we face these troubles, help us to live fully as true citizens of Christ: showing compassion to our neighbors and encouraging our friends. May we experience the joy of Christ to press on every day. Together we pray. Amen. Rev. Maddi Baugous is an ordained elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference where she serves as University Minister at Nebraska Wesleyan University in Lincoln, Nebraska. Maddi is passionate about encouraging young adults in their faith through justice and education.

title: Grace
body: Worship Planning Notes Focus text: Exodus 14:19-31 , Matthew 18:21-35 Have you ever had one of those moments where your perspective on life shifted? A moment you can mark as the time everything changed? I’ve had a couple, but the earliest was the summer I was twelve and went to church camp for the first time. I grew up in a United Methodist congregation, and, to use the verbiage of that time, accepted Jesus Christ as my savior when I was seven. But for a couple of years before that summer, I had gone through moments of doubting if I was truly saved. I know; it’s a lot for a kid to navigate, but it happened, and I was often quite scared I hadn’t done something right. So, there I am at camp, praying for help as I had for so long, and suddenly, I knew. Like a flood, assurance washed over me. John Wesley’s whole “heart strangely warmed thing”? I believe it because I experienced it. To this day, that experience is a grounding point for my faith journey. With that experience of assurance came an overwhelming sense of the vastness and abundance of God’s grace for me, yes, but also for everyone. When we talk about leadership and grace, it’s easy to confuse our terms. In the context of Exodus and Matthew, leading with grace is not about keeping one’s composure or aligning with societal expectations. It’s also not about being permissive and submissive to others for the sake of avoiding conflict. Rather, leading with grace is about living as a conduit of the grace that flows abundantly for us and therefore through us to our neighbors. We are cleansed, inspired, redeemed, and formed by grace that we may be God’s agents of grace. Grace holds boundaries while extending forgiveness when boundaries are crossed. Grace tells the truth without shaming others. Grace recognizes that we all have gifts and strengths that benefit the community and finds ways for us to work collectively rather than in competition. All of this and more is made possible by grace and, by extension, forgiveness. If last week was about navigating conflict, this week is about reconciliation. Without grace, reconciliation is impossible. Through grace, Jesus tells us we keep the door open to reconciliation always. Over and over. We don’t write people off as irredeemable. We don’t throw people out because they keep making the same mistakes. We expect people to grow, but we don’t give up on them when they don’t grow as fast as or in the ways we expect. As we conclude this series, consider how the previous weeks might build into this final week. Are there examples of leadership from week one that you might bring back for this final week? Is there a hymn you already sang that bears repeating? Perhaps you want to explore a ritual of reconciliation that holds space for people to extend forgiveness to themselves and to take even small steps toward forgiving others who have hurt them. Sometimes all we need is space to lament what hurts and confess where we’ve messed up to discern the next right step to take. Throughout your planning, find ways to acknowledge communal sin and communal pain. It is quite easy to take these passages and focus on individual responses. And there’s certainly room and reason to do so. But consider, too, how your congregation as a community may need tending and space to lament, confess, and forgive as an exercise in gracious leadership now and in the future.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus text: Exodus 14:19-31 , Matthew 18:21-35 I’m sure you’ll join me in leaning into the Gospel text this time. It feels like a contrast, like opposites from the Exodus Sea of Reeds experience and the conversation on forgiveness between Peter and Jesus. One seems to advocate a final-solution approach to dealing with oppressors, and the other rests on mercy—not because it is easy, comfortable, or even preferred, but because it is more like Christ. You can imagine Peter’s exasperation growing throughout this encounter. He comes to Jesus to show that he’s been paying attention. He wants another gold star like the one he got a few chapters ago. If anything, he might even have expected Jesus to tell him to slow down because he had gone a bit too far with this forgiveness thing. Standard rabbinic teaching was that one ought to forgive four times to follow the law of mercy. Four times is pretty lenient, most would think. So, Peter, after hearing Jesus talk about reconciliation and bringing the whole church into the conversation to bring people back into right relationship, swaggers up and says, “I got it now. We should forgive one another seven times.” Waiting for Jesus to say, " Whoa, slow down there, Sparky. Four is enough.” But Jesus doesn’t say that. He doesn’t put the brakes on. Instead, he steps on the gas. Seven? Hardly. How about seventy-seven times? Or seventy times seven, depending on how you read the math here. And Jesus would be the first to say that it isn’t a math problem anyway. All those sevens aren’t about keeping score or tallying up forgiveness, but a way of saying, “Quit counting, just forgive.” That should be our default mode. That should be our lead. We start with forgiveness; we lead with grace. Not very practical, though. Right? A clergy member recounted a conversation with a parishioner after preaching on the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew. The preacher was approached by an angry listener who demanded to know where he got this “woke nonsense.” His calm reply was “from Jesus,” expecting an immediate apology and acceptance. But instead, the parishioner responded with “Well, that just doesn’t work anymore!” “Blessed are the peacemakers” just doesn’t work anymore. “Blessed are the meek” doesn’t work anymore. Forgiving seventy-seven times doesn’t work anymore. Is that our proclamation? Is that the gospel we will stand for? It doesn’t work anymore? Jesus illustrates his point with a story that verges into the absurd. “There is this slave,” says Jesus, “who owed his master ten thousand talents.” Wait, what? Ten thousand talents. He owed ten thousand talents. A slave, a servant, a laborer owed ten thousand talents. There is some debate about the value of a talent. Some scholars place it at around twenty years’ worth of a day laborer’s salary, give or take; twenty years, one talent. So, okay; do the math. This slave owed two hundred thousand years of salary to his master: 200,000 years. This is a nation’s gross domestic product- level money we are talking about. How in the world did a slave run up such a debt? But the real corker in this story is the debtor's comment: “Have patience with me, and I will pay you everything.” How might that happen? That is asking for a whole lot of patience on the part of the debt holder—200,000 years’ worth of patience. That is a lot. And then, instead of patience, the master has pity. This word is also translated as compassion, a word often used about Jesus. He had compassion. His heart went out. He had, in other words, empathy. He felt the other’s pain. The master in the story knew there was no way his servant could repay such a debt. And rather than holding him accountable for such an outrageous, unimaginable debt, the master simply forgives him. He wipes it away, as if it had never happened, never been accrued – however that might have occurred. But then, the plot thickens. This man, who was forgiven such an outlandish debt, grabs a fellow worker who owed him a hundred denarii. Now, a hundred denarii is not an insubstantial sum. If a denarius is one day’s wage, then this was one hundred days of hard labor. That’s significant,  until you laid it alongside ten thousand talents. Then it is microscopic, insignificant, nothing in comparison. The servant had been forgiven a debt that would bankrupt nations, so you would think that he would be generous to the person who owed him such a sum. After all, in financial terms, he is now up ten thousand talents. Of course, he should forgive the smaller debt. But he didn’t. He prosecutes this person to the fullest extent of the law. Here's the thing about this story,  and remember, it is a story: Jesus is making a point, not reporting the news. But the man who prosecuted the debtor was within the law. It was his right to do what he did. Some might argue that he should have done exactly what he did. After all, how can folks learn that borrowing has consequences? To forgive a debt is to unfairly benefit an individual and ultimately destroy the economic system of the people. Is this parable a commentary on capitalism? No, not really. But it does speak against the idea that commerce comes before humanity, or that systems matter more than people. We are hearing that forgiveness doesn’t work anymore. Jesus has a different set of priorities. But how does the story end? What is the moral that Jesus leaves his hearers with? It is hard not to hear those final verses as a threat. When you read verses 34 and 35, you hear the Sea of Reeds crashing down over the Egyptian army. This is the God who destroys, who punishes. Those who seek divine judgment can find it and wield it like a sword against enemies and oppressors. But look again. This judgment is not about breaking the law. It is about not showing mercy. It is about learning how to forgive. Those who say forgiveness doesn’t work anymore need to look at this story again. There are rabbinical stories that accompany the Exodus passage and cast a different light on the event. Supposedly, while the Hebrew refugees were celebrating their freedom on the far side of the Sea of Reeds, or Red Sea as some translate, God was weeping at the death of the Egyptians. “Are they not my children too?” the grieving God declares. Jesus came to be the face of God. If the gospel no longer works in our world, then what needs to change is the world. What needs to change is the way we live in community, the values we place on systems over people, the “thoughts and prayers” approach to poverty and circumstance. To lead like Christ is to lead with grace. It is to walk alongside those who are oppressed by debt and by generational poverty, to find solidarity with those who have been marginalized because of race or country of origin, to build community based on shared respect and empowerment. Jesus’ parable declares that we don’t live in a zero-sum game where some have to lose for others to win. Rather, we live in a world of abundance, but with a messed-up delivery system that favors a few over the many. We are called, invited, and encouraged to lead with grace and partner with the Spirit as we build toward the kingdom, the kin-dom, the homespace that Jesus proclaimed.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Followers of Christ, we live in a world where we hurt one another, where sin divides us one from another and makes us enemies instead of neighbors. Yet we are a people of grace, called by Christ to forgive and repair the rifts between us. The divisions in our world seem like too much to overcome, and we wonder if this forgiveness thing really works anymore. Maybe it worked for Jesus, but not for us. Yet we are a people of grace, called by Christ to forgive and repair the rifts between us. We find ourselves tempted by easy answers and quick solutions, reticent to do the slow and difficult work of reconciliation. Yet we are a people of grace, called by Christ to forgive and repair the rifts between us. In this place, may we encounter Christ who meets us in the places where we want to give up, where we despair that life-giving change is even possible, with abundant grace to sustain us on the journey. God, form us today as people of grace, called by Christ to forgive and repair the rifts between us. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026. Opening Prayer Liberating God, we worship you. We praise you for delivering your people of old from enslavement in Egypt by opening up a new and unexpected future before them. They experienced your grace and mercy in awesome and life-sustaining ways, which must have been like an impossible dream coming true. Through these acts, you showed your compassion for the weak and powerless of this world. We praise and adore you for opening up a new future for us when your love and compassion, your mercy and grace became enfleshed in Jesus Christ. He delivered us from the bondage of evil and sin through his death on the cross. The impossible once more became reality when love defeated evil once and for all. We pray that this time of worship will be a true offering of our wonder and praise that you should care for us so deeply and so faithfully. This we pray in Jesus’ name.  Amen. Written by Moira Laidlaw on Liturgies Online . Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/09/opening-prayer-exodus-14-19-31.html . Prayer of Confession O God, we seek your mercy… yet we ourselves look for payback when we are wronged. We think it “only fair” and “what is right” when we retaliate and use harsh words and withdraw from relationship. The forgiveness you offer on our account is larger than we can comprehend; still, we withhold forgiveness and carry the grudge over petty items. We are eager to do your judging. And the worst: we conspire our inner thoughts to secure your forgiveness while avoiding honest repentance. Forgive us, Lord, for the sins we know in our hearts. Save us, Lord, from the sins we hide. Silent prayer of confession God’s gift of forgiveness makes us able, with the power of Holy Spirit, to choose to forgive, renew, and live again in right relationship with each other and with our God. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Glory to God! Amen. Adapted from Bill Wessner and posted on Confession RCL blog . Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/09/confession-matthew-18-21-35.html . Benediction Followers of Christ, go now in the blessing and assurance that you are a forgiven people empowered by grace to forgive and heal the divisions that keep us from truly loving God, self, neighbor, and all creation with the fullness of our beings. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026.
