title: Children's Message
body: Children's Message INTRODUCTION Does the summer seem too long? Are the dog days barking at you and your congregation? Maybe it is time for a praise break! The songbook of the people of God can be a refresher, an encourager, or even a challenge that our faith needs from time to time. We invite you to take this short three-week pause from the busyness of a summer of activities to remind yourselves that the God we worship and the Christ we follow are with us every step of the way. And the only appropriate response to encountering the divine among us is to sing, to shout, to declare our praise. Enjoy a Praise Break! The bell teaches children that praise is how our bodies respond when we notice God’s love—quietly, joyfully, and together. The bell teaches children that praise is how our bodies respond when we notice God’s love—quietly, joyfully, and together. Scripture: Psalm 105:1-6, 16-22, 45b Psalm 105:1-6, New International Reader's Version 105 Give praise to the Lord and announce who he is. Tell the nations what he has done. 2 Sing to him, sing praise to him. Tell about all the wonderful things he has done. 3 Praise him, because his name is holy. Let the hearts of those who trust in the Lord be glad. 4 Seek the Lord and the strength he gives. Always seek him. 5 Remember the wonderful things he has done. Remember his miracles and how he judged our enemies. 6 Remember what he has done, you children of his servant Abraham. Remember it, you people of Jacob, God's chosen ones. Psalm 105:16-22, New International Reader's Version 16 He made the people in the land go hungry. He destroyed all their food supplies. 17 He sent a man ahead of them into Egypt. That man was Joseph. He had been sold as a slave. 18 The Egyptians put his feet in chains. They put an iron collar around his neck. 19 He was in prison until what he said would happen came true. The word of the Lord proved that he was right. 20 The king of Egypt sent for Joseph and let him out of prison. The ruler of many nations set him free. 21 He put Joseph in charge of his palace. He made him ruler over everything he owned. 22 Joseph was in charge of teaching the princes. He taught the elders how to think and live wisely. Psalm 105:45, New International Reader's Version 45 He did it so they might obey his rules and follow his laws. Praise the Lord. New International Reader's Version (NIRV) Copyright © 1995, 1996, 1998, 2014 by Biblica, Inc.® . Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. Object: A bell Message: Friends, do you remember this bell from last week? What did it help us do? ( Allow children to answer: listen, notice, be quiet .) Today, the bell has another job. The psalm we heard today says, "Give praise to the Lord. Tell about the wonderful things God has done. Sing to God!" That means praise is not quietly hiding praise; it's praise we share. Let's think together for a moment. What is something good that happened this week? It doesn't have to be big. It could be something small, like a hug, a favorite snack, a funny moment, or a sunny day. ( Invite several responses .) Every time we name something good, we're going to ring the bell. ( Ring once after each response .) Listen carefully. That sound doesn't disappear right away, does it? It rings… and then it fades… but it comes back again. That's what God's goodness is like. God's goodness doesn't just show up once and leave. It keeps coming back, again and again and again. The psalm we heard today tells the story of people who had a really hard time. Some were hungry. Some were far from home. Some were stuck in places they didn't want to be. Those people might have wondered, "Did God forget us?" But God didn't! God helped them step by step. God stayed with them. And later, when the people told those stories again, they didn't whisper them. They sang them. They shared them. They praised God together. Let's try that now. When I ring the bell, you can say, "Thank you, God!" Or you can say, "Praise the Lord!" ( Practice once . Ring the bell and invite responses multiple times .) Listen to all those voices. Do you hear how different they sound? Some are loud. Some are quiet. Some are excited. That's what praise sounds like. Many voices. Many stories. One God, who keeps showing up with goodness. Prayer: God, thank you for the good things you do. Help us remember and praise you together. Amen. Praise Break: Between-the-Sundays Family Practices Threaded Object: A bell (or any gentle sound: phone chime, spoon on mug, wind chime) Families: If you don't have a bell, any soft sound will work. The point is noticing, remembering, and praising together. Week 2 – Sing Praises Theme: Remembering and Telling God's Goodness Conversation Starters What was one good thing that happened today? Share with other family members. Who helped you this week? What is something you're thankful for right now? Activity: "Bell of Thanks" During dinner or bedtime: Place the bell in the center of the table or room. Take turns naming something you are thankful for. After each person shares, everyone says together: "Thank you, God," and someone rings the bell. Optional extension: Let children draw a picture of one thing they thanked God for and place it near the bell. Simple Prayer God, thank you for the good things you give us. Help us remember and share them with joy. Amen.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, "If you were to identify songs to put on a 'Playlist/Soundtrack/Album' for your life, what one or two songs would you include? Why?" Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Psalm 105:1-6, 16-22, 45b . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. Though this selection skips part of the story that leads to the final verse of praise, how could you explain the connection between the first part (vv. 1-6) and the second part (vv. 16-22)? The story being summarized in verses 16-22 is from Genesis 37-41 and focuses on how God uses Joseph to rescue the Israelites. Whether the story is familiar to you or not, where do you see opportunities to praise God? What questions do you have about this part of the story? Read Genesis 37:1-4, 12-28 . This is the beginning of Joseph's story. While it's a difficult story of injustice, where do you see God's grace or mercy? Based on this part of the story, for what could we praise God? Part of the power of Joseph's story that is highlighted in Psalm 105 is that the faithful actions of one man (Joseph) would have ripple effects much broader than his circumstances. How have you witnessed a positive impact for many from a faithful act of one? The Preaching Note for August 9 says, "God's instruments are at hand. That is what we celebrate or at least acknowledge. The underlying message is that we may be those instruments. We may be the undercover agents for the kingdom of God at work in the world around us. We may be the seed planted, the yeast embedded, the salt applied to give flavor or provide traction in a slippery time. We may be Joseph appointed to lead God's people through a famine of the lack of righteousness." How do you feel about the notion that you may have a "seed planted," "yeast embedded," or "salt applied" to "provide traction in a slippery time"? Just One Thing: Commit to taking five minutes this week (set a timer!) to look back at your life to find one thing that has had a positive "ripple effect" because of faithfulness (yours or someone else's). Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the selected text [ 1 Kings 19:9-18 , Psalm 85:8-13 , Romans 10:5-15 , Matthew 14:22-33 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord's Prayer: God of faithfulness, we praise your name and give you thanks for release from mistreatment. God, would you help us recognize the places where your grace is at work, where your people are faithful amid suffering, where your presence is felt even in the darkest of times? May we be people who say yes to righteousness and serve as your hands and feet to accomplish your purpose of restoration. And when we don't see it, may we praise you until we have eyes to see your victory. In Christ's name, we pray, amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford, Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Behold the Face
body: Worship Planning Notes Focus text: Psalm 17:1-7, 15 Praise Jesus! It’s a phrase I utter regularly. Sometimes it comes on the tail of a sigh, as relief floods through my body when potentially bad news turns out better than expected. Sometimes it bursts forth in excitement when I finally find a parking spot that’s not a half mile away from the entrance to the mall. And sometimes it fills my heart without ever leaving my lips, as I take in the majesty of snow-capped mountains. The praise we give to God in the large and small moments of our lives matters. Praise is a fruit of our growth in love for God and neighbor, an expression of our recognition of and cooperation with God’s grace at work all around us. But how do we praise? Over the next three weeks, we turn to the psalmist to help us start answering that question. As you plan for this series, consider how you might incorporate the themes of each week into the acts of worship. This first week focuses on awareness. How might you practice awareness of God’s presence and work during gathered worship? The psalmist focuses on embodiment. How might you cultivate embodied awareness of God’s presence and work? You might try a grounding exercise together, like the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique, where you focus on five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. If your congregation tends to have a lot of wiggles, you might try something more active by inviting everyone to test out how different parts of the body can give praise. How do hands give praise? How do lips give praise? How do feet give praise? How do ears give praise? How do knees give praise? Anything that helps the group embody their response to God! And then , reflect in worship (and in planning) on how these embodied responses help us cultivate awareness of God. If you do a grounding practice, follow up with a time to meditate and reflect on how awareness of God among us changes after we ground ourselves in our bodies. Or, if you do something more active, invite your congregation to use those same body parts to notice and tell the truth about God’s work all around you. What truths do hands tell about God? What truths do our lips tell about God? How do feet demonstrate God at work? Whether you have your congregation actively respond to these questions or you enter into a time of prayer and reflection around these questions, this is an opportunity to connect action with contemplation, to learn to be aware of God’s presence and give God praise, not just in our minds but with our full, embodied selves.
liturgical: Tenth Sunday after Pentecost, Year A

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus text: Psalm 17:1-7, 15 What does it mean to behold the face of God? Isn’t there a verse that says something about seeing the face of God and not living through the encounter? (Exodus 33:20, if you’re wondering.) So, is seeing the face of God a terrifying experience or a source of comfort and strength? And of course, the answer to this conundrum would have to be “yes.” Maybe we should set aside the what and why questions for a moment and focus on the how. Psalm 17 is full of advice on seeking the face of God. In this “Praise Break,” we hope to help followers embrace the need for praise at regular times in their lives, beyond the weekly gathering for worship. We are called to pay attention to opportunities to praise throughout our day. We cultivate an awareness of God's presence that then bursts forth in spontaneous praise—sometimes loud; more often, quiet. But how? How do we cultivate this awareness? How do we make room for praise in our daily lives? The expected answer is that we must become more spiritual. Tune out the world and focus on the unseen. Look beyond the horizon—geographical, occupational, and relational horizons— and seek the face of God beyond. That is not the advice Psalm 17 gives, however. Look again at how physical the psalm is. Count the body parts; for example, ear and lips, eyes and heart, mouth and feet. It is an anatomical inventory of praise. The psalmist grounds us in the physical, even in the call for the face of God to appear—or perhaps as the means by which the face of God will appear. Maybe it is through our faces, as part of our faces, that the face of God is seen. But the psalm is not a static inventory of body parts. No, these lips speak; these feet walk; this heart passes the test of faithfulness in action. There is a kinetic quality to this act of praise. There is movement, action, effort in the search for the face of God. There is a time when stillness is necessary. “Be still, and know that I am God,” another psalm tells us (Psalm 46:10 NRSV). But that is not the only way to encounter the face of God. As a pastor, I was asked how someone might find the will of God for their lives. “I’ve prayed,” they told me, “But I’m not getting a clear answer. How do I know what God wants me to do?” My advice was to keep moving. God seems to work best with moving targets. Keep moving. Pick a direction, and if it isn’t working, then make a change. Like a river that sometimes has to meander until it finds its true path, course corrections can come if we keep moving forward. “Give ear to my prayer” means keep praying. “Let your eyes see the right” means that you keep looking, listening, and discerning. “My steps have held fast to your paths” (verse 5) means that you were walking as best you could, walking by the light you could see. And in this light, “Wondrously show your steadfast love, O Savior of those who seek refuge from their adversaries at your right hand” (17:70. Here is a key piece to seeing the face of God and finding the strength to praise at all times. We can’t wait; we don’t wait until all is well before we seek God’s face. We don’t wait until all the pieces are in place or the coast is clear and the living is easy. No, we go; we seek; we praise when we feel threatened and when we feel secure. We praise when we feel satisfied and when we are unsettled. That’s the beauty of praise; it comes from many sources within us. It carries many moods. Read through the psalms and find an emotion not contained there. It is difficult. Yet they are all invitations to praise. But then how, in our multidimensional, multifaceted, multi-emotional praise, do we encounter the face of God? What does the psalmist offer to us as a way of experiencing that presence? Verse 15 is key: As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake I shall be satisfied, beholding your likeness. (Psalm 17:15 NRSV) I shall behold your face in righteousness. Or we might say, “I shall behold your face as I honor my relationships.” Righteousness is a relational concept. It is being faithful to our relationships, with God first of all, but also with one another, with those around us. We see God as we honor and keep those relationships. Jesus told us that when we serve others, we serve him; when we see others— particularly the ones our society doesn’t see— we see him. I shall behold your face in righteousness. But wait, there’s more! “When I awake, I shall be satisfied, beholding your likeness.” So … a dream? Is that what it means to encounter God? Do we dream our face-to-face moments? And that’s enough, apparently, when I awake, I shall be satisfied. Good enough, we think. The dream was enough. But is that what is being offered? “I shall be satisfied beholding your likeness.” Connect those last two phases of the verse, not the first two. When I awake, then I shall be satisfied beholding your likeness. Where? Everywhere? In the mirror as I get ready for the day. In the faces, the needs, and the energy of our loved ones, as together we launch out into the world. In our coworkers with whom we wrestle, in the neighbors we encounter, in the needy who ask for recognition, in the adversaries who seem to want to oppress us. In short, everywhere. Disciples seek the face of God and find that face in the work to which we are called and in the worship by which we are strengthened. Beholding the face of God is more about taking a faith stance toward the community around us than about developing an individualized devotional practice. When we expect to see God in the world around us, then we will be blessed to see that divine presence in surprising places. And in moments worthy of a praise break.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship As we gather and as we disperse, as we rise and as we sleep, as we eat and play and work, We offer God praise. As we wash our car, scrub the dishes, rinse the grime of the day from our hands, We offer God praise. As we feel the tips of the grass on our feet, the wind against our face, the sun on our backs, We offer God praise. Come, let us worship God who creates, redeems, and sustains us to live out our praise in all we do! We come as people formed by grace to offer God praise with our whole selves now and in all the ordinary moments of our lives! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026. Opening Prayer Awesome and majestic God, your creative power, your glory and holiness were experienced by your people of old as clouds and fire guiding them to freedom. They believed that no one could see your face and live. How blessed, therefore, are we, for you have revealed your face to us in Jesus— the human face of your love. You also equip us for our journey through life and beyond, by breathing new and everlasting life into our very beings, through the gift of the Holy Spirit. These people of old believed that it was your presence with them which made them a chosen and special people. We praise and adore you, O God, for making our lives so special, by choosing to share your life with us in and through Jesus. May this time of worship and the service of our lives reveal our thanksgiving and our wonder that you should so care for us. This we pray in Jesus’ name. Amen. Written by Moira Laidlaw and posted on her Liturgies Online website. Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/10/call-to-worship-prayer-october-16.html . Prayer of Confession O God, listen to our prayer of confession, for we would speak honestly before You. We confess that we haven’t always done what is right; that some of our attitudes and actions have hurt others and ourselves, and have grieved You. Forgive us. In Your mercy, look deeply into our hearts. Examine our thoughts and our actions. Test our motivations. Bring to light all the things in our lives that dishonor You. We want to follow You with integrity, to obey the commandments You have given us, and to walk in ways that bring honor to Your name. Words of Assurance Siblings in Christ, our God never fails to hear us when we call. Trust in God’s forgiveness and unfailing love, and be at peace, for God rescues all who take refuge in God. Amen. Adapted from “Confession & Assurance: Psalm 17” on the re:Worship blog, https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/07/confession-assurance-psalm-17.html . Benediction Beloved, may God bless you with the discernment to stop and notice God at work all around you, the inspiration to offer up praise in the middle of the busyness of life, and the peace that comes from beholding the face of God and knowing deep in your bones that we are not alone—God is with us. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, May 2026.

title: Offertory Prayers
body: Offertory Prayer Attentive God, you see us as we are and meet us in the movement of our days. As we bring these gifts, shape our lives to reflect your righteousness—faithful in love, honest in action, steady in compassion. Open our eyes to behold your face in the neighbors we serve and the work we share. Let our giving become praise in motion, a testimony that we seek your presence not only in stillness, but in faithful steps forward. Receive these offerings as signs of our trust and our desire to live in right relationship with you and with one another, until we are satisfied in the likeness of your grace. Amen. ( Psalm 17:1-7, 15 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson invites students to explore what it means to seek and behold the face of God, not by escaping the world but by paying attention as they move through it. The icebreaker uses a playful ball game to help students learn one another’s names and something about their daily lives. After reading Psalm 17, students discuss how praise is physical, relational, and active, showing up through our bodies, relationships, and choices. In the activity, students work together to build a shared structure that represents how we notice and respond to God’s presence in everyday life, discovering that praise often emerges while we are already in motion. NEEDED RESOURCES: One soft ball Building materials such as wooden blocks, LEGO bricks, plastic cups, cardboard pieces, or similar items Open floor or table space for building Icebreaker: Name Toss Connect (10 min.) Have students stand in a circle. Hold a soft ball. The first player starts by saying their name and one simple, everyday fact about themselves, then gently tosses the ball to someone across the circle. That person repeats what the player before them said, then tosses the ball to someone new who hasn’t received it yet. Depending on the size of your group, you can keep going after everyone has received the ball. If you want to make it more challenging, have the statements be cumulative: each person repeats all the statements that came before, and the last person throws the ball to the first person, who then says everything that has been said before them. Scripture (5 min.) Read Psalm 17:1–7, 15 . Discussion (15 min.) What parts of the body does the psalm mention, and what are they doing? What are the ways this psalm describes seeking God as something active rather than passive? What is one reason you think the psalm connects praise with movement, speaking, and walking? Have you ever been in a place where praise or prayer also included movement? When and where? What did that feel like? How does the idea of “beholding God’s face” shift when it is connected to relationships? Where do you notice moments of praise or awareness showing up in ordinary life? Do you think people tend to pray more when they are having a great time or a terrible time in life? Why might praying and praise be important to remember? How does this psalm challenge the idea that we praise only when everything is going well? What role do other people play in helping us notice God’s presence? Activity and Discussion: Build the Path (20 min.) Divide students into small groups. Give each group a set of building materials and a flat surface on the floor or a table. Explain the task: each group will build a “path” or structure that represents how people seek and notice God’s presence while living everyday life. The structure should have movement built into it, such as steps, turns, connections, or bridges. After a few minutes of building, pause and give a second instruction: each group must add at least one new element that represents relationships, such as connection points, shared supports, or places where paths meet. When the students have finished, invite the groups to explain their structure briefly. Encourage them to name where movement, attention, and relationships show up in what they built. Emphasize that praise is not just stillness or sound, but a way of moving through the world with awareness of God’s presence. Reflection Questions (for the activity) What did you notice about how your group decided what to build together? Where did movement or connection become important in your structure? How does this activity change how you think about praise in everyday life? Close in a manner that is consistent with your group’s practice.

title: Children's Message
body: Children's Message INTRODUCTION Does the summer seem too long? Are the dog days barking at you and your congregation? Maybe it is time for a praise break! The songbook of the people of God can be a refresher, an encourager, or even a challenge that our faith needs from time to time. We invite you to take this short three-week pause from the busyness of a summer of activities to remind yourselves that the God we worship and the Christ we follow are with us every step of the way. And the only appropriate response to encountering the divine among us is to sing, to shout, to declare our praise. Enjoy a Praise Break! The bell teaches children that praise is how our bodies respond when we notice God’s love—quietly, joyfully, and together. The bell teaches children that praise is how our bodies respond when we notice God’s love—quietly, joyfully, and together. Scripture: Psalm 17:1-7, 15, New International Reader's Version A prayer of David. 17 Lord, hear me, because I ask for what is right. Listen to my cry for help. Hear my prayer. It doesn't come from lips that tell lies. 2 When you hand down your sentence, may it be in my favor. May your eyes see what is right. 3 Look deep down into my heart. Study me carefully at night and test me. You won't find anything wrong. I have planned nothing evil. My mouth has not said sinful things. 4 Though evil people tried to pay me to do wrong, I have not done what they wanted. Instead I have done what you commanded. 5 My steps have stayed on your paths. My feet have not slipped. 6 My God, I call out to you because you will answer me. Listen to me. Hear my prayer. 7 Show me the wonders of your great love. By using your great power, you save those who go to you for safety from their enemies. Psalm 17:15, New International Reader's Version 15 You will show that I am right; I will enjoy your blessing. When I wake up, I will be satisfied because I will see you. New International Reader's Version (NIRV) Copyright © 1995, 1996, 1998, 2014 by Biblica, Inc.® . Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. Object: A bell Message: Good morning, friends. I'm really glad to see you today. Before we begin, I want to show you something. ( Hold up the bell but keep it still .) Do you recognize what this is? ( Allow children to affirm .) This is a bell. It doesn't look very big, does it? But even something small can help us notice important things. Have you ever been so busy playing, running, or talking that you didn't hear someone calling your name right away? ( Allow children to respond .) That happens to all of us. The palm we heard today was written by David. David was talking to God, and he said, "God, listen to me. God, look at me. God, when I wake up, I want to see you." That tells us something important: David believed God was close enough to hear and see him. Let's see how the bell works. When I ring it, I want you to listen carefully, not just with your ears, but with your whole body. ( Ring the bell once and wait .) Did you notice how the sound didn't stop right away? The sound just slowly faded. Even when no one touched the bell anymore, the sound was still there. That's a little like God's presence. Even when we stop talking… even when we stop moving… even when we are very quiet… God is still with us. David trusted that God was watching over him, not looking for mistakes or waiting for him to mess up, looking at a checklist, but watching over him because God cared. David believed God looked at him with love. Sometimes we think being "seen" means someone is checking to see if we did something wrong. But David tells us something different. God watches us because God loves us. Let's think about that together. If God were looking at you right now, not to catch your mistakes, not to correct you, but just to watch you with love…what do you think would make God smile? ( Invite responses: "When I help my sister." "When I try again." "When I sing." "When I tell the truth." ) Yes. God smiles at those things. God smiles when you try. God smiles when you are kind. God smiles when you keep going, even when something is hard. ( Quietly ring the bell once .) This bell doesn't mean, "Uh-oh, stop." It means, "God is close." The sound reminds us to pause and remember: God is not far away. God is not waiting to be disappointed. God is near, and God delights in you. Prayer: God, thank you for being close to us. Help us notice you with us today and every day. Amen. Praise Break: Between-the-Sundays Family Practices Threaded Object: A bell (or any gentle sound: phone chime, spoon on mug, wind chime) Families: If you don't have a bell, any soft sound will work. The point is noticing, remembering, and praising together. Week 1 – Behold the Face Theme: Noticing God's Nearness Conversation Starters What is something you noticed today that you usually hurry past? When do you feel calmest or safest? What do you think God notices about you? Activity: "Notice and Ring" Choose one moment each day, before school, at bedtime, or during a meal to: Ring the bell once to get everyone's attention. Sit or stand quietly for a few seconds. Invite each person to name one thing they noticed that day (a sound, a feeling, a kind act, something beautiful). Ring the bell once after each sharing. This practice helps children connect noticing with God's presence, without needing to explain it fully. Simple Prayer: God, thank you for being close to us. Help us notice you with us every day. Amen.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, "What kinds of conversations do you like to have 'face-to-face'? Why is that?" Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Psalm 17:1-7, 15 aloud. Invite participants to listen for ways the psalmist pays attention to God. Encourage group members to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. This passage shares a "bodily" way of conversation between the psalmist and God. Identify the various "physical" interactions described in this passage. What do you think is at the heart of what the psalmist is saying in these verses? Share with participants the context of Genesis 32:22-31 . Jacob deceived both his twin brother, Esau, and his father, Issac, to receive the birthright blessing that conventionally should have gone to Esau (Genesis 25-27). This passage depicts Jacob's interaction with a mysterious "man" as he prepares to meet Esau for the first time after the stolen blessing. Read Genesis 32:22-31 aloud. Encourage group members to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. What does this encounter tell you about Jacob? In this story, Jacob is given a new name, "Israel," which means "The one who strives with God" or "God strives." Jacob names the place, "Peniel," meaning, "The face of God." While we don't expect to encounter God physically in this way, how does this encounter give insight into God's presence? Read Psalm 17:15 again. What do you think it means to "behold" God's face "in righteousness"? The following includes some ways people might describe experiencing God's presence. Identify which of these resonate with you: An inner "knowing." Thoughts that align with scripture or things you know about God. Joy/peace/confidence around something that has been troubling you. Experiencing nature. Clarity in your spirit. Connection with another person, place, or encounter in a way that defies explanation. Reconciliation with God/forgiveness for sins. Unexplainable love. Something else? What questions do you have about God's presence? How do you experience God's presence in your life most often? The Preaching Notes for August 2 say: "Here is a key piece to seeing the face of God and finding the strength to praise at all times. We can't wait; we don't wait until all is well before we seek God's face. We don't wait until all the pieces are in place, or the coast is clear, and the living is easy. No, we go; we seek; we praise when we feel threatened and when we feel secure. We praise when we feel satisfied and when we are unsettled. That's the beauty of praise. It comes from many sources within us. It carries many moods. Read through the psalms and find an emotion not contained there. It is difficult. Yet they are all invitations to praise." How often do you feel the impulse to praise God? Just One Thing : What is one thing for which you can praise God? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice (Isaiah 55:1-5, Psalm 145:8-9, 14-21, Romans 9:1-5, Matthew 14:13-21) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord's Prayer: O God, we call upon you and trust that you hear our prayers. Will you make us aware of your presence this week? Even now, will you give us insight into what it means to walk in your ways and encounter you? We want to be people of praise who give thanks to you and honor your name in every circumstance. Thank you for your willingness to meet us face-to-face. May we do the same. In the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford, Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: More Than Conquerors
body: Worship Planning Notes
liturgical: Ninth Sunday after Pentecost, Year A

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Romans 8:26-39 “What then are we to say about these things?” (Romans 8:31 NRSV) . That is a question preachers should be asking as we approach this text. There is a lot to say, and Paul has said plenty. Some we might wrestle with from our theological perspective. What do we say about verses 29 and 30? How do we understand predestination in the Wesleyan tradition? How might we proclaim the good news of verse 28 without dismissing real suffering in our world today? Of course, we have responses and ways of understanding these words, but we might also figure out how we can leave space for the Spirit to intercede with sighs too deep for words. Where can we give hearers breathing space to listen for those sighs? To be affirmed by that presence? Out of all the themes that can emerge from these layered verses and deep theological wrestling, two rise to the top in the current climate in which we live. The first is toward the end, where Paul declares us “more than conquerors.” The second theme is a bit more subtle, but it permeates the whole passage with repeated emphasis and is the nature of community. What are we claiming, and what is Paul claiming, when he declares that as Christians, we are more than conquerors? In the ongoing struggle with Christian nationalism pulling all the oxygen out of the room, with the warrior ethos echoing through the halls of political power, it is incumbent upon the church to watch its language—not to dismiss the concept, but to explore a little deeper and move beyond a militaristic understanding of conquering. Some commentators argue that Paul is here attempting to contradict, or at least challenge, the Stoic view that we “conquer” suffering by enduring it without complaint or response. His position is that we are more than this kind of conqueror, more than one who endures; rather, we are redeemed in our suffering. And we are conquerors not because of what we have done, but because of what Christ has done in us. To claim that we are more than conquerors does not feed into the rhetoric of nationalism; in fact, it does the opposite. Paul claims that the victory is not ours but a gift from our savior.  This is not about power, in other words, but about suffering that can bring us closer to God and to one another. This leads to another dimension that needs amplification in our current culture. From the first verse of this text, Paul suggests that all of this is a corporate experience. “Likewise,” he writes, “the Spirit helps us in our weakness” (Romans 8:26a). Do you hear that? Us, we, the saints, those who … Paul’s argument from the start is that we must understand the nature of community to participate fully in this grace. To hear the sighs from the Spirit, to see the good being worked even in desperate circumstances, to be more than conquerors, we have to have a grasp of corporality. Discipleship has never been an individualistic exercise. This is not to say that the individual isn’t important. Individual choices and decisions need to be made. There is such a thing as a personal relationship with Jesus that can shape an individual follower's life and discipleship. But we have focused on the individual’s walk with Christ to the exclusion of participation in the community of faith. We have neglected to emphasize that the call to faith is a call to relationship with God and with the body of Christ. Declaring this, we are not talking about a benefit of faith or an extra. No, we are saying something about the essence of discipleship. Faith, at its core, is a corporate experience. It is not that we benefit from being a part of a community; we require it. Pastors are often fielding the question, “Do I need to be a part of the church to be a follower of Jesus?” Being familiar with the history of the desert fathers and mothers, we might perhaps answer, “No, not necessary, but very important.” Even those so-called hermits engaged with pilgrims and disciples who came and learned from them. So, perhaps the answer, and the one it appears that Paul advocates, is that “Yes, to be a Christian, you need a community around you.” You need a sense of belonging, a way to live out your discipleship day by day. You (you plural) need a God to worship and a neighbor to show kindness to. And you need the support of a caring community that will lift you up when you begin to flag. That’s what it means to declare that we are more than conquerors. Not that we are the strongest, the most warrior-like, but that we are the most supported, the most connected, the most loved, even in our suffering, even in our weakness.  Together, we are part of something so much bigger than ourselves. Therefore, we are more than conquerors. Thanks be to God. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Beloved, this is the core of our faith: nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Thanks be to God! God’s never-ending love surrounds us and calls us, assuring us that through God’s love, all things will work together for God’s good purposes. Thanks be to God! God’s never-breaking love empowers us in the face of temptation, distress, division, and scarcity to hold onto our faith and work together for the flourishing of all God’s good creation. Thanks be to God! Come, let us worship God who is Love, trusting that through joy and sorrow, happiness and despair, contentment and pain, Love will carry us through. Thanks be to God who forms, connects, and guides us through Love. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, February 2026. Opening Prayer God, Your extravagant love has called us together. Long before we even knew You, You already knew us, and had chosen us to be part of Your own family— sisters and brothers with our Lord Jesus Christ Himself. What amazing love You have shown toward us! And so we come before You with praise and thanksgiving, offering You the worship of our hearts and lives, and opening ourselves to the prompting and leading of Your Holy Spirit. Receive our worship—our praise and prayers and offerings— through the intercession of Your Son, Jesus Christ, our Saviour and Lord. May the time we spend here in Your presence bring honour and glory to Your Name. Amen. Posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/07/opening-prayer-romans-826-34.html . Prayer of Confession Creator of all things, who rejoiced in your creation at the beginning of the world; forgive us our sins of greed, selfishness, and carelessness by which we daily damage the beauty to which we have become insensitive. By war and violence, we destroy families and their means of livelihood. We cut down great forests that are the homes of people, animals, and birds. We ill-treat our farm animals in the race to outstrip our rivals in food production, yet still leave millions of people starving. We pollute our air and water with the excess of our greed, without thought for the disposal of what we waste. For all this, we ask not only forgiveness, but also the power to turn away from our headlong course of destruction, and instead to share in your constant work of creation in preparation for the time when our kingdom comes to earth as it is in heaven. This we ask through Jesus Christ, our Savior, who became part of your creation and gave his life for the whole world. Silent prayer Receive this good news: There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, for the power of the life-giving Spirit has freed us from the power of sin that leads to death. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven! In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven! Glory to God! Amen. Adapted from Helen Lamb (Ireland) found in Prayers Encircling the World: An International Anthology (Louisville: Westminster John Knox Press, 1998), 148. Benediction Go now in the blessing and assurance that nothing can separate us from the love of God. May this good news inspire us all to take up the hard work of building community and acting for the flourishing of all our neighbors, because we do not act on our own—we act on the power of God’s never-ending love. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, February 2026.

title: Music Notes
body: Music Notes What does it mean to declare that we are more than conquerors? Not that we are the strongest, the most warrior-like, but that we are the most supported, the most connected, the most loved, even in our suffering, even in our weakness. Together, we are part of something so much bigger than ourselves. Therefore, we are more than conquerors. Thanks be to God. title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Steadfast God, you search our hearts and know our needs even when we struggle to find the words. In your mercy, you strengthen us in our weakness and bind us together in love that cannot be broken. As we bring these gifts today, may they bear witness to your enduring promise: that nothing—not hardship, nor fear, nor even death itself—can separate us from your love in Christ Jesus. Bless these offerings, that they may bring hope to the weary, peace to the troubled, and joy to the hearts of your people. Through Christ, our Redeemer and Companion, we pray. Amen. ( Romans 8:26-39 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson invites students to explore Paul’s claim that we are “more than conquerors,” not through power or winning, but through shared love, support, and community. The icebreaker helps students learn more about one another in a playful, low-pressure way that builds connection. After reading Romans 8:26–39, students discuss how the Spirit shows up in weakness, how suffering is held in community, and why faith is never meant to be lived alone. In the arts-and-crafts activity, students create a shared visual representation of support and connection, discovering that being “more than conquerors” means being deeply held together rather than standing strong on our own. Needed Resources: Blank paper or cardstock cut into equal squares (one per student) Markers, crayons, or colored pencils Tape Pens or pencils for the icebreaker Blank paper with 3×3 grids (one per student) Icebreaker: Common Ground Bingo (10 Min.) Give each student a blank 3×3 grid on a sheet of paper and a pen (or have them draw a Tic-Tac-Toe board on a blank sheet of paper). Ask them to fill each square with something that might be true of people in the room. Keep the activity light and non-personal. Examples to suggest (they choose their own): Has a pet Likes spicy food Has moved houses Loves music Hates mornings Enjoys being outside Plays a sport or game Likes art or creating things Once the grids are filled, students move around the room asking yes-or-no questions to find someone who matches a square and write that person’s name in the box. The goal is not speed or winning but conversation. Stop after a few minutes and ask what surprised them about what they learned. Scripture (5 Min.) Read Romans 8:26–39 . Discussion (15 Min.) What does Paul say the Spirit does when people feel weak or unsure? Have you experienced this or believe it to be true? What do you think Paul means by “more than conquerors”? How does Paul’s idea of conquering seem different from how the world usually talks about winning or strength? What do you notice about how often Paul uses words like “we,” “us,” and “together” in this passage? Is that important? Why do you think Paul ties faith so closely to community instead of individual strength? How does being part of a community change how people experience and get through hard things? What parts of this passage feel comforting, and what parts feel challenging? If being “more than conquerors” is about connection and love, what might that look like in your school or youth group? Activity and Discussion: Quilt of Endurance (20 Min.) Give each student a square of paper or cardstock and access to markers, crayons, or colored pencils. Explain that they are each creating one “panel” of a shared quilt. On their square, invite students to respond creatively to this prompt (words, symbols, colors, or images all count): “What helps people endure, heal, or keep going together?” Encourage them to think about support, love, presence, prayer, listening, laughter, rest, or hope rather than individual strength or toughness. After several minutes, gather all the squares and get the students to tape them together on a wall or table to form a large, shared collage or quilt. Take a moment to step back and look at it together. Talk about the fact that no single square tells the whole story, but together they show what it means to be “more than conquerors” through connection and shared care. Reflection Questions What did you notice when you saw everyone’s squares together? How did the meaning change when individual pieces became part of a whole? How does this help you understand Paul’s emphasis on community and shared strength? Close in a manner that is consistent with your group’s practice.

title: Children’s Message
body: Children's Message Introduction The eighth chapter of the letter to the Romans is one of the most loved chapters in the Bible. As the crux of this important epistle, this chapter provides insight into some of the core elements of our faith. How does the law function in our faith? What does it mean to set our mind on the Spirit? What is our relationship with all creation? How are we bound together with other disciples in suffering and joy? St. Paul sets out to answer these and many other questions as he weaves a poetic vision of what it means to be a follower of Jesus and a part of the body of Christ. We invite you and your congregation to explore “Core Faith” this summer. Scripture Romans 8:26-39, New International Reader's Version 26 In the same way, the Holy Spirit helps us when we are weak. We don’t know what we should pray for. But the Spirit himself prays for us. He prays through groans too deep for words. 27 God, who looks into our hearts, knows the mind of the Spirit. And the Spirit prays for God’s people just as God wants him to pray. 28 We know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him. He appointed them to be saved in keeping with his purpose. 29 God planned that those he had chosen would become like his Son. In that way, Christ will be the first and most honored among many brothers and sisters. 30 And those God has planned for, he has also appointed to be saved. Those he has appointed, he has made right with himself. To those he has made right with himself, he has given his glory. We Are More Than Winners 31 What should we say then? Since God is on our side, who can be against us? 32 God did not spare his own Son. He gave him up for us all. Then won’t he also freely give us everything else? 33 Who can bring any charge against God’s chosen ones? God makes us right with himself. 34 Then who can sentence us to death? No one. Christ Jesus is at the right hand of God and is also praying for us. He died. More than that, he was raised to life. 35 Who can separate us from Christ’s love? Can trouble or hard times or harm or hunger? Can nakedness or danger or war? 36 It is written, “Because of you, we face death all day long. We are considered as sheep to be killed.” (Psalm 44:22) 37 No! In all these things we are more than winners! We owe it all to Christ, who has loved us. 38 I am absolutely sure that not even death or life can separate us from God’s love. Not even angels or demons, the present or the future, or any powers can separate us. 39 Not even the highest places or the lowest, or anything else in all creation can separate us. Nothing at all can ever separate us from God’s love. That’s because of what Christ Jesus our Lord has done. New International Reader's Version (NIRV) Copyright © 1995, 1996, 1998, 2014 by Biblica, Inc.®. Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. Objects Four linked hearts. Message Good morning, friends. Come a little closer so you can see. Look at our hearts. (Point to the chain.) We started with one heart, God’s love for each of us. Then we added more, God’s Spirit, waiting and growing, love for the whole world. Today our hearts are complete. (Add the final heart to the chain.) One heart became many. Just like God’s love. In today’s Bible passage, Paul tells us the biggest, strongest truth of all. Are you ready? (Build anticipation.) Are you ready? Nothing! Nothing at all! Nothing at all can separate us from God’s love. Let’s see if that’s really true. Everyone hug yourself as tight as you can. (Count to three together.) Now open your arms wide, like you’re ready for the biggest hug ever. God’s love is not tight. God’s love is open. Let’s test some things. When I name something, you help me decide. Is it stronger than God’s love? Ready? Not sadness. Is sadness stronger than God’s love? (Invite children to shake their heads “no.”) Not fear. Is fear stronger than God’s love? (Stomp once together.) Not mistakes. Are mistakes stronger than God’s love? (Wiggle fingers like “uh-oh,” then smile.) Not being left out. Is the feeling of being left out stronger than God’s love? (Arms crossed, then opened again.) Not even hard days. Are hard days stronger than God’s love? (Take a deep breath together.) None of these are stronger than God’s love. Now, everyone gently hold the heart chain. (Invite a few children to help or have all reach toward it.) Feel how the hearts stay connected. We are held by God’s love. Not alone. Not apart. Together. Let’s say it loud enough for the whole world to hear. Say it with me: “Nothing can separate us from God’s love!” (Say it again—this time louder.) “Nothing can separate us from God’s love!” Paul says we are more than conquerors. That means God’s love wins. Every time. Nothing can separate us from God’s love. I wonder who needs to hear this good news today. Can you think of someone who needs to hear this good news? (Allow children to pause to reflect.) I wonder how we can share God’s love this week. Let’s create four ways (to represent the four hearts) that we can share God’s love this week. I’ll count. (While counting, touch each heart from the chain. Allow children to provide ways that they can share God’s love.) Wow! Those are all great ways to share the love of God with someone. Consistent Closing Ritual (Each Week) Now let’s end the way we always do. Put your hands on your heart. (Pause.) Now reach out and link hands with someone nearby, or imagine our hearts all connected together. Leader: God’s love holds me. Children: God’s love holds us. Prayer (Hands on hearts, slow breathing) God of love, thank you for holding us always. Help us share your love with the world. Amen. Between the Sundays A Family Faith Practice for the “Core Faith” Series Each week includes: A short scripture idea. Conversation starters. A hands-on or movement-based activity. A simple prayer. The consistent ritual used in worship. Week 4 – More Than Conquerors Scripture Focus: Romans 8:26–39 Theme: Nothing can separate us from God’s love. Talk Together What are some things that feel scary or hard? Talk about a time you felt scared or had difficulty this week. What helped you feel safe again? Who might need to hear that God loves them no matter what? Share a story of how you shared God’s love this week. Try This Together Love Test Hug yourself tightly. Open your arms wide. Say together: “Nothing can separate us from God’s love.” Complete your heart chain and display it together. Wonder Together I wonder who needs to hear this good news. Have each family member provide a name of someone who needs to hear this good news. I wonder how we can share God’s love this week. As a family, come up with four ideas of how to share the love of God this week. Prayer God of love, thank you for holding us always. Help us share your love with the world. Amen. Family Ritual Hands on hearts; then hands linked together. Leader: God’s love holds me. All: God’s love holds us.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “Think of a time when you felt weak—physically, mentally, or emotionally. What did you do in response to that experience of weakness?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You likely won’t get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Romans 8:26-30 . This may be a familiar section of the larger text for today. What do you notice about what the text says about the Spirit in the first few verses? What words or ideas from this passage bring comfort or consolation to you? What words or ideas from this passage are challenging for you? Read Romans 8:31-34 . In this section of the passage, Paul is making an “argument” that despite the difficulties of a person’s life, God is still “for us.” (v. 31). The evidence he cites is that he gave up his son, Jesus, “who died, or rather, who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (v. 34). This concept is at the heart of the Christian faith. How do you grapple with these ideas? How does knowing that Jesus suffered, died, and was raised impact you? Have you thought about Jesus interceding for us? How does that affect you? Read Romans 8:35-39 . In this passage, Paul lists several things that have power or are destructive. Why do you think God’s love is more powerful than any of these things? The Preaching Note for July 26 says, “[In reference to being ‘more than conquerors’] Some commentators argue that Paul is here attempting to contradict, or at least challenge, the Stoic view that we ‘conquer’ suffering by enduring it without complaint or response. [Paul’s] position is that we are more than this kind of conqueror, more than one who endures; rather, we are redeemed in our suffering. And we are conquerors not because of what we have done, but because of what Christ has done in us… Paul claims that the victory is not ours but a gift from our savior. This is not about power, in other words, but about suffering that can bring us closer to God and to one another.” (emphasis mine) Have you ever thought about how suffering can bring us closer to God and to one another? How do you understand that we are “more than conquerors”? Just One Thing: This passage concludes with the reminder that nothing (absolutely nothing ) can separate us from God’s love. What is one way that you can remind yourself of this awareness this week? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the selected text ([ Genesis 29:15-28 Psalm 105:1-11, 45b Romans 8:26-39 Matthew 13:31-33, 44-52 ]) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Loving God, we confess that it is hard to wrap our minds around how much you truly love us. And yet, your word tells us of that love, and with help from your Holy Spirit, we claim that love. In our weakness, may we look to you, and in our wavering, may we have the grace to believe your promises. In the name of the Father who created all things, and the Son who was raised as our Savior, and the Holy Spirit who sustains us, we pray, Amen. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Romans 8:12-25 It is difficult to know where to start with this text. There is so much packed into these verses that one could preach a season’s worth of sermons from the ideas and images found here. Almost any verse could become the center of the sermon or the focus of worship this week. How do we choose? Then there is what seems at first to be a significant conflict in this long text. We begin with a call to live not by flesh but by spirit. Then, midway through, we have a lyrical passage about our relationship with creation itself. Can you get more fleshly than worrying about the environment? And is that what we are asked to consider here? Years ago, my wife came to one of my Bible studies because the members had heard me talk about all the things we do or don’t do to be “green,” to be ecological. So, she came and made a presentation on the choices we make daily, the homework we should do on companies and their impact on the environment, and which companies we should support and which ones we should avoid. There were weights and counterweights, balances and trade-offs, choices around every turn. Finally, after some time, members of the class said, “This is hard!  Maybe too hard.” Why should we bother worrying about our impact on the environment, reducing our carbon footprint, and “reduce, reuse, recycle”? Surely, my little bit isn’t going to make much of a difference. And are things really that bad? Aren’t we being alarmist? Aren’t there conflicting views of the human impact on climate and the planet as a whole? Can’t we wait and see? Go about our business and trust that it will all come out okay? And if not, if worst comes to worst, aren’t we as Christians not really all that worried about this world anyway? It’s just temporary; we’re just passing through. Right? It’ll all get swept away, and the new heaven will be established, better than this one by far. Right? Who better to look beyond this world to the next one than Paul? Who better to get our priorities straight, our vision properly focused, our eyes on the prize? We’re straining forward, he tells us, for the finish line, the goal that lies ahead. Surely, he won’t be concerned about this world, since his whole focus is on the next one. Right? For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the children of God; for the creation was subjected to futility, not of its own will but by the will of the one who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and will obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Romans 8:19-21 NRSV Well, now that’s a bit of a surprise. “The whole creation,” he writes. Groaning in labor pains, hurting because of what it wants to birth, what it wants to bring forth. Of course, we say, he’s talking spiritually, he’s speaking metaphorically, about spiritual matters, not physical ones. Or is he? It seems like Paul is hinting that our salvation is tied up with the bondage and decay of all creation. The fate of the world, the fate of the plane, is woven into our fate, into our future, and our hope. Not only that, but all that God has made relies on us. Not just us, but our better selves, our true selves, our lives as the sons and daughters of God. That is a roundabout way of saying that we treat our world as though it were part of God and part of us. It is not God; that’s an important distinction. We don’t worship the creation. We aren’t tree worshipers and mountain disciples; we’re not grass gurus (any kind of grass, for that matter!) or flora and fauna followers. No, we are followers of Jesus the Christ, worshipers of the Creator of all we see and all we are. Creation is not God. Yet, we get a glimpse of the Creator when we comprehend the creation. We know the artist when we examine and protect the work of art. We commune with the author when we spend time in the writing. When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you have established; what are human beings that you are mindful of them, mortals that you care for them? Yet you have made them a little lower than God, and crowned them with glory and honor. You have given them dominion over the works of your hands… Psalm 8:3-6a NRSV To approach God, we need a better sense of ourselves. We need a proper perspective on who we are. One of the places to grasp that perspective is in the contemplation of nature. You can’t stand on the rim of the Grand Canyon and not be humbled by the grandeur and beauty of the place, overwhelmed by the forces of time and nature that carved this natural wonder. You can’t walk the beach of any ocean and watch the pounding of the surf and the power of the currents and not feel small and helpless despite our ability to fashion machinery and dwellings we think can withstand this power, until the storm surge comes and our efforts are swept away in a few tumultuous seconds. You can’t contemplate the vastness of the universe and feel more significant than a speck of dust. Yet, the psalmist tells us, God loves us, cares for us, blesses us, honors us,  and gives us dominion. Now there’s a word that needs another look: dominion. It’s a word that has gotten us into trouble, I believe, because we look at one side only—the power side, the authority side. “You have made them” – people, that is, you and me – “a little lower than God.” “You have crowned them with glory and honor.” Woo hoo! I don’t know the Hebrew for woo hoo, frankly. And even if I did, I wouldn’t find it in this psalm. It’s not there. This isn’t about power. This isn’t about dominating, about using, exploiting, abusing, and casting aside. No, it is about caring, as God cares for creation. It is being mindful of the planet where we live. It is caring for creatures and habitats as God cares for us. Don’t think creation deserves that care? Do we? The psalm begins and ends with a doublet about God. Our translation reads, “O Lord, our Sovereign.” Older translations read, “O Lord, our Lord.” It is a reminder that all our “dominion” is the power to care as God cares, to be mindful—to be woke!—as God is mindful of all of creation, including us. Yeah, it’s hard. It takes effort and energy. It takes planning and going out of our way to be mindful and caring. But it’s worth it, because it’s our home, and it is the world that is dying to be born again, groaning to be fulfilled as God intended—groaning in hope. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Today, we gather to join our voices with winds and seas, sunshine and rain, mountains and grassy plains to worship God, our Creator. We gather as children of God, stewards of God’s creation. We gather to join our hearts with creatures who creep and crawl, slither and squirm, swim and soar, to worship God, our Creator. We gather as children of God, stewards of God’s creation. We gather as witnesses of the harm that has been done to God’s creation, to the groanings of the earth and all the earth’s inhabitants who long for peace and flourishing. We gather as children of God, stewards of God’s creation. Come, let us worship God who strengthens and equips us, guiding us to live out our faith as good stewards of God’s good creation. Come, let us worship God who inspires and empowers us to be stewards of hope and redemption in a wounded and hurting world! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026. Opening Prayer God of grace and love, We rely on Your love extended to us in all ways and at all times, extravagantly and with generosity. We live day by day knowing that Your care and concern is poured out for us in Your provision for our needs and beyond our imagining. You entrust us with the gift of the good news of the Gospel and invite us to be partners in the sharing of the message of grace. Day by day, we realise the many gifts lavished upon us. We come to You to acknowledge and praise You for all Your goodness to us. Amen. Written by Rev. Nigel Robb and posted at https://pilgrimwr.unitingchurch.org.au/?p=7107 . Prayer of Confession Holy God, we confess that we do not always love our neighbor. We confess that we have despised others, even to the point of hatred. We confess that we have been hurt by others. We confess that forgiveness and reconciliation at times are just impossible for us. We know that nothing is impossible in You. We come to You, seeking healing and wholeness for us. Help us, whenever possible, to live in peace with others, to seek reconciliation and healing and forgiveness. For Your Son came and lived among us, was betrayed and denied, abused and put to death. He rose again and came with the message of peace to those who had denied him and abandoned him. May we walk in his ways. Amen. Blessing/Assurance of Pardon For nothing is impossible with God. There is no place you can go, no end of the earth you can run, where God cannot find you. There is nothing on earth or beyond death that can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. In the name of Jesus Christ, you are forgiven. Amen. Written by Rev. Mindi and posted on Rev-o-lution , http://rev-o-lution.org/ . Reposted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/02/prayer-of-confession-loving-others.html . Benediction Beloved, the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the children of God. May the Spirit bless us and empower us to reveal ourselves as the children of God as we work for the flourishing of all creation. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Compassionate Creator, you formed us from the dust of the earth and breathed into us life and purpose. In these gifts we return, we offer more than resources; we offer our hope. Let these gifts, given in trust, be signs of our partnership in the renewal of all creation. Awaken in us a holy longing, as deep as the groaning of the earth itself, for justice, healing, and new life. May our giving participate in your redemption, until the world rejoices in freedom and glory as your children. We offer this with joy, in the name of Christ our Redeemer. Amen. ( Romans 8:12-25 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson invites students to explore Paul’s surprising claim that our faith, our lives, and the fate of creation are deeply connected. The icebreaker uses a playful guessing game to help students learn more about one another and notice how differently people experience the same world. After reading Romans 8:12–25, students discuss how creation’s groaning and hope are woven together and what responsibility looks like without blame or fear. In the activity, students move through the room in response to real-life scenarios, discovering that discipleship means living in the tension between groaning and hope, while choosing care, trust, and shared responsibility. Needed Resources: Index cards (one per student) Pens or pencils An open space large enough for students to move comfortably Icebreaker: Who’s This About? (10 Min.) Before the lesson, give each student an index card and a pen. Ask them to answer one fun, low-stakes prompt on the card without putting their name on it. Choose one prompt, such as: One thing that helps me feel calm A place I feel small in a good way Something in nature I really like One thing that annoys me about the world A small thing that gives me hope Collect all the cards, shuffle them, and read them aloud one at a time. After each card is read, the group guesses who they think wrote it. The students may reveal themselves or stay anonymous if they prefer. Keep the activity moving, light, and curious. The goal is connection, not accuracy. Scripture (5 Min.) Read Romans 8:12–25 . Discussion (15 Min.) In this passage, what does Paul say is happening with creation? In your own words, what do you think Paul means by “groaning” and “hope”? Where do you notice “groaning” in the world around you in ways you can see or feel? What is one small way you have seen people bring “hope” into something that feels broken or stuck? Why do you think Paul ties the future of creation to the “revealing of the children of God”? What might he be getting at? Are we participants in that future? When people talk about caring for the environment, what helps it feel like a shared responsibility rather than a matter of blame or guilt? What do you think faithful hope looks like when you cannot fix everything or see results right away? If your group wanted to live this passage for one week, what is one concrete practice you would try together? Activity and Discussion: Groaning and Hope Walk (20 Min.) Clear a large open space in the room. Designate one end of the room as “Groaning” and the opposite end as “Hope.” Explain that there are no right or wrong answers; this is about noticing where things feel true right now. Read each statement aloud. After each one, invite students to move and stand somewhere along the spectrum between groaning and hope. Example statements: Seeing environmental damage in a place you care about Hearing about people working together to protect land or communities Feeling like your individual actions do not really matter Learning about ways communities are responding to climate challenges Thinking about the future of the planet After each movement, invite a few students to share why they chose their spot. Close in a manner that is consistent with your group’s practice.
