title: Children’s Message
body: Children's Message Introduction The eighth chapter of the letter to the Romans is one of the most loved chapters in the Bible. As the crux of this important epistle, this chapter provides insight into some of the core elements of our faith. How does the law function in our faith? What does it mean to set our mind on the Spirit? What is our relationship with all creation? How are we bound together with other disciples in suffering and joy? St. Paul sets out to answer these and many other questions as he weaves a poetic vision of what it means to be a follower of Jesus and a part of the body of Christ. We invite you and your congregation to explore “Core Faith” this summer. Scripture Romans 8:12-25, New International Reader's Version 12 Brothers and sisters, we have a duty. Our duty is not to live under the power of sin. 13 If you live under the power of sin, you will die. But by the Spirit’s power you can put to death the sins you commit. Then you will live. 14 Those who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God. 15 The Spirit you received doesn’t make you slaves. Otherwise you would live in fear again. Instead, the Holy Spirit you received made you God’s adopted child. By the Spirit’s power we call God Abba. Abba means Father. 16 The Spirit himself joins with our spirits. Together they tell us that we are God’s children. 17 As his children, we will receive all that he has for us. We will share what Christ receives. But we must share in his sufferings if we want to share in his glory. Suffering Now and Glory in the Future 18 What we are suffering now is nothing compared with our future glory. 19 Everything God created looks forward to the future. That will be the time when his children appear in their full and final glory. 20 The created world was held back from fulfilling its purpose. But this was not the result of its own choice. It was planned that way by the one who held it back. God planned 21 to set the created world free. He didn’t want it to rot away. Instead, God wanted it to have the same freedom and glory that his children have. 22 We know that all that God created has been groaning. It is in pain as if it were giving birth to a child. The created world continues to groan even now. 23 And that’s not all. We have the Holy Spirit as the promise of future blessing. But we also groan inside ourselves. We do this as we look forward to the time when God adopts us as full members of his family. Then he will give us everything he has for us. He will raise our bodies and give glory to them. 24 That’s the hope we had when we were saved. But hope that can be seen is no hope at all. Who hopes for what they already have? 25 We hope for what we don’t have yet. So we are patient as we wait for it. New International Reader's Version (NIRV) Copyright © 1995, 1996, 1998, 2014 by Biblica, Inc.®. Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. Objects Three linked hearts. Message Good morning, friends. I have a question for you. Have you ever had to wait for something really special? (Pause. Invite a few short responses: “My birthday.” “Christmas.” “A visit.”) Waiting can be exciting…and waiting can be very hard. Let’s see your waiting face. (Encourage exaggerated faces. Smile.) Now show me your waiting body. Everyone freeze like a statue. (Freeze with them.) Let’s wait together. (Silently, count to five. Let the quiet stretch just a bit.) Whew! That felt long, didn’t it? (Allow children to respond.) Paul tells us something surprising in today’s Bible passage. He says that God’s whole world is waiting. (Repeat.) God’s whole world is waiting. Not just people, but trees. Not just people, but animals. Not just people, but the Earth. Waiting for healing. Waiting for joy. Waiting for peace. That’s a lot of waiting. (Bring out the third heart.) Remember our hearts? We started with one, God’s love for us. Then added a second, God’s Spirit helping our minds and hearts. Today, we add one more, making three hearts linked together. (Link the third heart.) While we wait, God is still working. Let’s try something. Wiggle your fingers low to the ground, like tiny seeds in the soil. (Allow children to wiggle.) Nothing looks like it’s happening yet. Now wiggle them just a little higher. Waiting can feel slow. It can feel quiet. It can feel like nothing is happening. But watch: Slowly stretch your arms up high, like a plant reaching for the sun. Stand tall. Even when we can’t see it, God’s love is growing. Now, let’s touch each heart together. (Touch first heart.) God’s love is with you when you wait. (Touch second heart.) God’s love is with us when we wait together. (Touch third heart.) God’s love is with the whole world while it waits. Take a slow breath in…and out. Waiting doesn’t mean God is gone. I wonder how God’s love grows while we wait. Waiting means God is still at work. I wonder what you are waiting for right now. God is working, even while we wait. Shared Closing (Weekly Ritual) Now we’ll end the same way we always do. Put one hand on your heart. (Wait.) Now reach out and link hands with someone nearby, or imagine all our hearts are all connected. Leader: God’s love holds me. Children: God’s love holds us. Prayer (Hands on heart, slow breathing) Patient God, waiting is hard. Help us trust that you are always working. Amen. Between the Sundays A Family Faith Practice for the “Core Faith” Series Each week includes: A short scripture idea. Conversation starters. A hands-on or movement-based activity. A simple prayer. The consistent ritual used in worship. Week 3 – Wait with Eager Longing Scripture Focus: Romans 8:12–25 Theme: God is working even while we wait. Talk Together What is something you are waiting for right now? How does waiting feel in your body? Have you ever seen something grow slowly? Try This Together Freeze and Grow Game Freeze like a statue. Count silently to five. Slowly stretch upward like a growing plant. Say together, “God’s love is growing.” Add a third heart to your chain. Wonder Together I wonder what God is growing that we cannot see yet. I wonder how hope feels while we wait. Talk about a time this week when you needed to wait. Prayer Patient God, waiting is hard. Help us trust that you are always working. Amen. Family Ritual Hands on hearts, then hands linked together. Leader: God’s love holds me. All: God’s love holds us.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer these questions: “Who in your life demonstrates patience? What does that patience look like?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You likely won’t get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Romans 8:12-25 . In verses 12-17, Paul writes about those who are “children of God.” Make a list of what you see noted in these scriptures related to this idea. [Answers could include: those led by the Spirit are children of God (v. 14); spirit of adoption does not fall back into fear (v. 15); the Spirit bears witness with an individual’s spirit affirming that the person is a child of God (v. 16); being a child of God means that a person is a joint heir with Jesus (v. 17); suffering with Jesus also implies sharing in his glory (v. 17).] How do you understand the concept of being a child of God and a joint heir with Jesus? What is one aspect of this that you readily accept? Is there any part of it that is more challenging? Read again Romans 8:19-23. What does this text say about creation? [Answers could include: it waits with eager longing for the revealing of the children of God. (v. 19); it was subjected to futility (v. 20); creation is in bondage to decay (21); creation has been groaning in “labor pains” (22)] In which of the following ways do you view creation? Something to enjoy (and what do you mean by enjoy ?) Something to steward Something to restore Something else? The Preaching Notes for July 19 say: “To approach God, we need a better sense of ourselves. We need a proper perspective on who we are. One of the places to grasp that perspective is in the contemplation of nature. You can’t stand on the rim of the Grand Canyon and not be humbled by the grandeur and beauty of the place, overwhelmed by the forces of time and nature that carved this natural wonder.” How does spending time in nature provide a perspective of who God is, especially in relationship to who we are? Psalm 139 points to an intimacy with which God knows us. Read Psalm 139:1-12, 23-24 aloud and invite group members to allow a verse to become a prayer for the week. Read again Romans 9:24-25. What is the relationship between hope and patience? How could you connect this idea to creation? Just One Thing: What one thing could you do this week to embrace patience in an aspect of your life?~~ ~~ Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice ( Genesis 28:10-19a , Psalm 139:1-12, 23-24 , Romans 8:12-25 , Matthew 13:24-30, 36-43 ) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Oh God, you have searched us and know us. You adopted us as your children. There is nowhere we can go away from your Spirit or flee from your presence. Forgive us for preferring our way over yours. Would you grow the spiritual fruit of patience in our lives, so that we might be people of hope, awaiting your full restoration? Thank you for your grace that sustains us as we wait. In the name of Christ, our Savior, we pray, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Romans 8:1-11 Woke up this mornin' with my mind, stayed on Jesus. Woke up this mornin' with my mind, stayed on Jesus. Woke up this mornin' with my mind, stayed on Jesus. Hallelu, hallelu, hallelujah. “Woke Up This Mornin’”, African American Traditional, Public Domain A traditional approach to the letter to the Romans is to declare that it is Paul’s most coherent systematic theology. It is presented as his introduction to the Christians in Rome, a theological resume, if you will. Even if that is true, it is not merely an academic exercise for Paul. Instead, as with all his writing and preaching, it is an invitation into the new life in Christ. Paul carries his faith, his invitational faith, on his sleeve and shows it, offers it, gives it away every chance he gets. We could argue that he didn’t set out to build a church, an institution, but to make disciples of Jesus Christ. And not only does he issue an invitation, but he also describes a process. In other words, he doesn’t just give us the “what”; he gives us the “how.” “Set your mind,” says Paul. That is a part of the process. But what is all this “flesh and spirit” stuff? We need to wrestle with this to understand how we become disciples of Jesus Christ. There are many of these polarities in the Bible, and Paul is particularly fond of using them. But we need to hear them for what they are, not make surface assumptions about the intent. In our text for this week, we have the duality of flesh versus spirit. It seems straightforward enough, particularly when Paul identifies flesh with the adjective “sinful.” So, we know the attitude we need to take toward each of these polarities. But what is he pointing toward here? Flesh seems like corporality, like bodies, like the tangible life we live every day. Some hear this text saying that our whole lives, caring for our bodies, living the human pleasures that are given to us, are somehow bad, evil, or sinful. That anything bodily is a distraction from the pure life of the spirit. To hold such a position would be a denial of Incarnation. The fact that God chose to be born in the flesh of a human baby and live the human life with all its needs and gifts is an antidote to the idea that bodies are inherently sinful. Further, to use this polarity as an excuse not to care for an individual’s or a community’s physical well-being would be counter to the declaration from Jesus himself that to care—to physically care—for the “least of these” is to care for him. So, what is the polarity that Paul is drawing attention to in this text? It is hard to simplify this rich theological proposition with a single statement, but Paul himself uses the phrase “set your mind” as the key to understanding. What does it mean to set our minds? Is he talking about a fixation? Is he saying that over-observing any one thing is the problem? Well, kind of, but not really. It isn’t about a fixation; it is more like a filter or a lens through which we approach the world. The question Paul asks is, “Are you the center of your world, or is God in Christ?” This isn’t a call to neglect oneself, however. But it is a call to have a proper perspective on life, to set one’s mind according to the Spirit, to seek God’s will in all things, to see what would benefit the community and world, not just oneself. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. That is Paul’s argument, the proposition. But it isn’t a club to which we gain membership. Instead, it is a way of living, a way of being in the world. There is no condemnation for those who seek Christ’s will in all things. There is no condemnation for those who seek the healing, the caring, the uniting that Christ sought. There is no condemnation for those who take up the towel and basin to care for neighbors. There is no condemnation for those … well, you get the idea. This is where life is, says Paul, setting your mind on Christ. “I woke up this morning with my mind stayed on Jesus,” says the spiritual. “No condemnation with my mind stayed on Jesus,” says another verse. “Can’t hate your neighbor with your mind stayed on Jesus,” in another.  “Devil can’t catch you in your mind stayed on Jesus.” Paul says to set the mind of the flesh (on the self as the center of all your thinking) is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace (Romans 8:6 NRSV). You are not “in the flesh.” Maybe Paul gives us more credit than we deserve here. At my best, I’ll agree. At other times, well, the flesh is awfully seductive, drawing me away from the better angels of my mind. Maybe what he means is that we have the means to not be in the flesh, to not be self-centered, but to be other-centered, to be Christ-centered. We have the knowledge and the opportunity. We have the gospel, he would argue. We have the Spirit; let it take over. Set your mind to the guidance of the Spirit. I woke up this morning with my mind. That in itself is a needed thing these days: to have a mind; even better, to use it. Or as Paul would have it, to offer it, to be transformed by the renewing of the mind, to let the Spirit dwell in your mind. Or simply, wake up this morning with your mind stayed on Jesus. That’s a start. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship We gather today in the midst of busy lives and hectic schedules that mirror the chaotic pace of the world around us. We come to set our minds on the guidance of the Spirit. We gather as people inundated with constant information, fast-moving news cycles, and ever-present alerts vying for our attention. We come to set our minds on the guidance of the Spirit. We gather as people seeking to anchor ourselves in the faith as the world around us is blown to and fro by waves of fear, scarcity, and reactivity. We come to set our minds on the guidance of the Spirit. Beloved, come. Come to find rest, grounding, and guidance in the Spirit who dwells in you. We come to set our minds on the Spirit who guides us and draws us together toward life, peace, and flourishing. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026. Opening Prayer Loving God, you created life in us and all around us. Open us to receive your gifts of your world and your word that we may be not just hearers of the word, but doers also. Amen. Written by Rev. Ruth Garwood and posted on the Worship Ways website at https://www.ucc.org/worship-way/pentecost_6_july_12/ . Prayer of Confession O God who loves us, hear our prayer. So often we come to you at a loss – at a loss for the right words, the right deeds, the right feelings. We know all is not right, but we cannot say with certainty what is wrong. There are deep divisions between us and others. There are too many who live in poverty and fear. There are too many horrific stories, and not enough hopeful ones. So we pray to you, our Creator and Redeemer, to make things right, and to make us right with you and each other. Turn us around from that which destroys toward that which heals and brings joy. And hear us again, as we offer you our confession in silence. Silent confession Assurance of Forgiveness Friends, let us proclaim the Good News: In Jesus Christ, we are forgiven! Let us go out into the world as people made new by God. Amen. Written by Beth Merrill Neel on her blog, “Hold Fast to What Is Good.” Used with permission. https://holdfasttowhatisgood.com/liturgy/prayer-of-confession/ Benediction May the Spirit who dwells in you bless you with open minds to receive God’s wisdom, open hearts to follow God’s guidance, and open doors that we may together build God’s kingdom of life and peace on earth as it is in heaven. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Living God, you meet us this day with grace that frees and a Spirit that gives life. You tell us there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, and we cling to that good news with grateful hearts. As we bring these gifts, we set our minds on you—not on fear or self-interest, but on the life and peace you promise. Shape us by your Spirit to live generously, to seek the good of our neighbors, and to share in your work of healing and reconciliation. Receive these offerings as signs of our attention being fixed on Christ and our lives opened to your renewing power. We give thanks; we give ourselves, and we trust your Spirit to lead us into abundant life. Amen. ( Romans 8:1-11 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Note to the Teacher This lesson invites students to explore Paul’s idea of “setting your mind” as a way of seeing the world rather than a rule about bodies or behavior. The icebreaker uses a fast, playful guessing game with everyday objects to get students talking about assumptions and perspective. After reading Romans 8:1–11, students discuss how Paul contrasts self-centered and Spirit-centered ways of living. In the activity, students use physical filters to experience how the same world can look different through different lenses, discovering that life and peace grow when our minds are oriented toward Christ rather than ourselves. Needed Resources: Small everyday objects for the icebreaker (spoon, key, coin, rubber band, etc.) Table or open surface for sorting objects Transparent colored plastic, cellophane, or page protectors (one per group) Icebreaker: What’s the Rule? (10 Min.) Before the lesson, gather a small set of simple objects and place them on a table or in the center of the room. Examples of objects: A spoon A key A rubber band A coin A sticky note Tell students you are secretly sorting the objects according to a rule in your head. Pick up one object at a time and place it into either Group A or Group B (two visible piles). Students must talk to one another and guess which rule you are using. After a few guesses, reveal the rule. Keep it surprising or arbitrary, such as: Objects you would keep versus objects you would throw away Objects that make noise versus objects that don’t Objects that feel “useful” versus objects that are “easy to forget” Then briefly note that we often assume the world works according to certain rules, but sometimes the real question is which lens or mindset we’re using. Scripture (5 Min.) Read Romans 8:1–11 . Discussion (15 Min.) What words or phrases from this passage stood out to you? How does Paul describe the difference between “flesh” and “Spirit”? What do you think Paul means by “set your mind”? What misunderstandings might people have about this passage? How does this text push back against the idea that bodies or physical life are bad? What does Paul say is the result of setting the mind on the Spirit? Where do you notice different “lenses” shaping how people see situations today? How does this passage connect mindset with care for others? What feels challenging about shifting the perspective away from yourself as the center? What might it look like to set your mind toward life and peace in everyday life? Activity and Discussion: Changing the Lens (20 Min.) Divide students into small groups. Give each group a transparent “filter,” such as colored plastic, cellophane, or a tinted page protector. Invite groups to look around the room through the filter and name what changes and what stays the same. Then read a series of everyday situations aloud. After each one, groups briefly discuss how the situation might look when viewed through a self-centered lens or a Spirit-centered lens. Invite a few groups to share after each prompt. Example situations: A disagreement with a friend Choosing how to spend free time Noticing someone being left out Feeling stressed or overwhelmed Responding to criticism Emphasize that the world does not change; the lens does. Paul invites us to live in the world with renewed minds. Reflection Questions (for the activity) What changed when you looked at the same space through a different filter? Which situation felt most affected by perspective and why? How does this help you understand Paul’s idea of setting your mind ? Close in a manner that is consistent with your group’s practice.

title: Children’s Message
body: Children's Message Introduction The eighth chapter of the letter to the Romans is one of the most loved chapters in the Bible. As the crux of this important epistle, this chapter provides insight into some of the core elements of our faith. How does the law function in our faith? What does it mean to set our mind on the Spirit? What is our relationship with all creation? How are we bound together with other disciples in suffering and joy? St. Paul sets out to answer these and many other questions as he weaves a poetic vision of what it means to be a follower of Jesus and a part of the body of Christ. We invite you and your congregation to explore “Core Faith” this summer. Scripture Romans 8:1-11, New International Reader's Version The Holy Spirit Gives Life 8 Those who belong to Christ Jesus are no longer under God’s judgment. 2 Because of what Christ Jesus has done, you are free. You are now controlled by the law of the Holy Spirit who gives you life. The law of the Spirit frees you from the law of sin that brings death. 3 The written law was made weak by the power of sin. But God did what the written law could not do. He made his Son to be like those who live under the power of sin. God sent him to be an offering for sin. Jesus suffered God’s judgment against our sin. 4 Jesus does for us everything the holy law requires. The power of sin should no longer control the way we live. The Holy Spirit should control the way we live. 5 So don’t live under the control of sin. If you do, you will think about what sin wants. Live under the control of the Holy Spirit. If you do, you will think about what the Spirit wants. 6 The thoughts of a person ruled by sin bring death. But the mind ruled by the Spirit brings life and peace. 7 The mind ruled by the power of sin is at war with God. It does not obey God’s law. It can’t. 8 Those who are under the power of sin can’t please God. 9 But you are not ruled by the power of sin. Instead, the Holy Spirit rules over you. This is true if the Spirit of God lives in you. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Christ. 10 If Christ lives in you, you will live. Though your body will die because of sin, the Spirit gives you life. The Spirit does this because you have been made right with God. 11 The Spirit of the God who raised Jesus from the dead is living in you. So the God who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your bodies. He will do this because of his Spirit who lives in you. New International Reader's Version (NIRV) Copyright © 1995, 1996, 1998, 2014 by Biblica, Inc.®. Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. Objects One soft or paper heart from last week and a second heart to attach to the first to begin creating a chain of hearts. Message Good morning, friends. Do you remember this heart from last week? (Hold up one heart. Pause.) What did it help us remember? (Allow responses: “God loves us.” “God forgives us.”) Yes. God loves us no matter what. Today, I brought something new. (Hold up the second heart but don’t link it yet.) Before we talk about it, let’s wake up our bodies again, because our bodies help us learn. Everyone, sit down. Now stand back up. Now, stand tall like a tree. Stretch your arms up high. Can you feel your feet on the ground? Press them down just a little. Let’s breathe together. Slow breath in…and out. One more time. In…and out. Paul from the Bible tells us something important today. He says God gives us the Spirit to help us think about loving things. Our minds think. Our hearts feel. And God helps both. Let’s try something: Turn your whole body this way. (Pause.) Now turn your body the other way. That was easy. But sometimes choosing which way to go isn’t easy. Sometimes, we choose kindness. Sometimes, we choose to yell. Sometimes, we want to do the right thing…and sometimes, we don’t. Does that ever happen to you? (Pause for nods or quiet “yes.”) That’s why God doesn’t leave us by ourselves. (Link the two hearts together.) When God’s Spirit is with us, our hearts connect. We are not alone when we make choices. God’s Spirit helps our minds think loving thoughts and our hearts choose loving actions. Let’s feel that. Put one hand on your head. Put one hand on your heart. Your mind. Your heart. God cares about both. Now we’re going to practice together. When I say “Spirit,” breathe in. When I say “love,” breathe out. Ready? Spirit… (Let children breathe in.) Love… (Breathe out.) Spirit… Love… One more time. Spirit… Love… Does your body feel calmer? God’s Spirit helps us slow down, pay attention, and choose love. I wonder how God helps you when you feel angry. (Allow children to answer.) God’s Spirit helps us choose love. I wonder what loving choice you might make this week. (Allow children to respond.) Shared Closing (Repeat Weekly Ritual) Now, just like last week, we’ll end together. Put one hand on your heart. (Wait.) Now reach out and link your hands with someone near you; imagine your hearts are linked together. Leader: God’s love holds me. Children: God’s love holds us. Prayer (Hands on heart, slow breathing) God, thank you for your Spirit. Help our minds and hearts follow your love. Amen. Between the Sundays A Family Faith Practice for the “Core Faith” Series Each week includes: A short scripture idea. Conversation starters. A hands-on or movement-based activity. A simple prayer. The consistent ritual used in worship. Week 2 – Set the Mind Scripture Focus: Romans 8:1–11 Theme: God’s Spirit helps us choose love. Talk Together What helps you calm down when you feel upset? How does your body feel when you make a kind choice? Who helps you choose loving actions? Try This Together Spirit and Love Breathing Sit or stand tall. When someone says “Spirit,” breathe in slowly. When someone says “love,” breathe out slowly. Repeat three times. Optional: Add a second heart next to last week’s heart. Wonder Together I wonder how God helps us when we feel angry. I wonder what loving choice we can make this week. I wonder what loving choice you offered this week. Share with other family members. Prayer God, thank you for your Spirit. Help our minds and hearts choose love. Amen. Family Ritual Hands on hearts; then hands linked together: Leader: God’s love holds me. All: God’s love holds us.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “What are two or three thoughts you consider throughout the day?” (For example, does your mind drift to your “to-do” list? To people in your life? A mantra or breath prayer? A worry or anxiety? How your body feels? Your responsibilities? The latest news story?) Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Romans 8:1-11 . Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. This text contains complex ideas and invites slowing down and looking at the words. Ask the group what they notice from the text about the following: The law Sin The Spirit Life Peace Verse 5 talks about the following: “Living according to the flesh.” Look ahead to verses 6-9 to answer, “What do you think that means?” “Living according to the Spirit.” Look ahead to verses 6-9 to answer, “What do you think that means?” This passage centers on the idea of “setting one’s mind.” What does it mean to set your mind on the flesh or on the Spirit, as mentioned in verse 5? How have you experienced “setting your mind” on the Spirit? Would you talk about that with members of your group? Verse 11 says, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies also through his Spirit that dwells in you” (NRSVUE). How do you understand this idea? What could it mean for day-to-day life? The Preaching Note for July 12 says, “So, what is the polarity that Paul is drawing attention to in this text? It is hard to simplify this rich theological proposition with a single statement, but Paul himself uses the phrase “set your mind” as the key to understanding…It isn’t about a fixation; it is more like a filter or a lens through which we approach the world. The question Paul asks is, “Are you the center of your world, or is God in Christ?”…[It] is a call to have a proper perspective on life, to set one’s mind according to the Spirit, to seek God’s will in all things, to see what would benefit the community and world, not just oneself. Just One Thing : Where can you write out the words of Romans 8:11 so that you can read it daily in the week ahead? Going Deeper on Your Own : This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the selected text [ Genesis 25:19-34 , Psalm 119:105-112 , Romans 8:1-11 , Matthew 13:1-9, 18-23 ] out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Spirit of God, you raised Jesus from the dead, and you want to dwell in us! Forgive us when we set our minds on the things of the flesh. Help us to choose life and to set our minds on the things of the Spirit. And as we grow in the life of the Spirit, I pray that our thoughts, actions, and very being would point others to you. Set our minds on you in all that we do today. In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Romans 7:15-25a 250 years: those of us who live in the US are still reeling from the celebration of 250 years as a nation. Was it a celebration of all the history and ideals the nation was founded upon? Or was it a sober reflection upon all that has been lost in recent years and the ways this nation has failed to live up to those ideals? Maybe both? Is such a thing possible? Can we celebrate, give thanks, and be proud even while we are concerned about where we are going these days? Can we enjoy ourselves even when we have serious reservations? Surely, such a thing is possible. We can sing in prison like Paul and Barnabas. We can be grateful even when we are afraid. We do it all the time in our personal lives as well as in our national and communal existence. We can be on the road to perfection and constantly at war with ourselves.  Same old, same old. Wait, what was that? Something about war? Not a word you expect to see on such a list, in such a moment. Wars start when we are down, or angry, attacked, hurting, or... right? Well, right, they do. The struggle arises at our low points, no question. But in our text for this week, it seems that our problem is more than just “having a bad day.” Paul sees it as something more fundamental than that;  more ubiquitous than that; much more... human than that. Good old Paul. You can always count on him to spoil a perfect celebration. Paul seems to be having a bad day to end all bad days. Or maybe even a bad life. “Wretched man that I am!” He seems to shout to the heavens. “Nothing good dwells within me.” Yeah, I’ve been there. I’ve had those moments when it seemed like all my choices were bad ones, when all my mistakes were big ones, when all my thoughts were broken ones. Yeah, I’ve been there with ya, Paul. So, buck up. Hang in there, and it will get better. You just gotta hold on until the storm passes. “No,” he replies, “You aren’t listening.” This isn’t a momentary weakness in your impenetrable armored will. This isn’t a “didn’t get enough sleep last night, my biorhythms are out of whack, or “the moon isn’t in the right phase for me right now” kind of thing. This is you. This is the real you. This is the consequence of living in the world as it is now, rather than as it was originally designed. This is the result of sin running loose in the world. This is the universal human condition; it’s not just you, not just an individual. It is corporate; it is national; it is worldwide; it is empire. Yeah, you say, I get that. I do bad stuff from time to time. I mess up, my bad. I make a goof, a boo- boo, an “open mouth, insert foot moment” in the conversation. I know that I’ll do better; I really will. I can hoist myself up by my bootstraps and try a little harder. Thanks for the reminder there, Paul. Whew, close call there. Thanks for the boost; thanks for the lift. Just thanks. “No,” says Paul. “You still aren’t listening. I’m not talking about an exercise program. This isn’t about trying harder, digging deeper, climbing higher in your attempt to do good things, to embrace the good, to be good. This is about admitting that there is nothing good in you.” Whoa there, Paul. There might have been a time when that sort of approach would have worked. When you wanted to scare folks into the faith, when you wanted to shame them into responding to the altar call on your sawdust revival trail. But we’ve gotten a bit more sophisticated these days. We need goal-setting and strategic plans. We need behavior modification and checks and balances. We need self-esteem raising and awareness training. We need the rules explained and defined, the boundaries clearly marked, and the punishment delineated. We need self-help books: five days to be a better you, six minutes to tighter abs, seven ways to total transformation. “What you need,” says Paul, “What you’ve always needed and will always need is a savior.” Who will rescue me from this body of death? “We need rescuing,” he says. We can’t save ourselves. And while we know that intellectually, it is hard for us to claim this truth. It is hard for us to live into it every day. Okay, we might accept the need one time for a rescue or a hand up. But then we tend to live the rest of our lives with an “I got this Jesus, thanks anyway” attitude. We live in a world that tells us we can be anything we want to be, which is both true and false at the same time. It is true that opportunities abound for many of us—maybe not all of us—that is the tragic inequality of the world in which we live. Even so, even without that imbalance, the war within us means we cannot consistently choose the good. We cannot will the right, live in the light. Sin, Paul says, is not an act or even a pattern of behaviors that we choose or to which we succumb. It is, instead, a power and a presence that dwells within us. As long as it is there, our efforts might be successful for a time, but they cannot last, will not last. One commentator likens Paul’s view of sin to the disease called shingles, a viral infection that continues to live in our bodies and —every now and then— breaks out in the rash that causes so much pain. Even when the rash goes away, the virus remains. Even when we don’t engage in sinful acts, Paul says, sin still dwells within us. And the war goes on. No one is strong enough to win that battle on their own. They may hold out for a while; we may hold out for a while. We may want the good and not want the evil, but, says Paul, but ... Perhaps the illness or the battle metaphors don’t work for you. Both are problematic for many. Maybe we could claim another image from this text. At the center of his struggle, Paul claims that, deep down, he delights in the law of God. He is able, even in his weakened or wavering self, to see the goodness of following God. But he doesn’t have the will to embrace it fully. He doesn’t have the courage to claim this way of living, way of being. It is beyond him, he writes. “Who will rescue me?” That’s the key to the passage. That question is a cry of faith. It follows the cry of despair, “wretched man that I am.” Wretched woman. Wretched creature. In a world without hope, that is the final cry. But praise be to God, there is another cry to follow. “Who will rescue me from this body of death?” The Lord of life, that’s who. The promise here is that this disease, this lack of will that dwells within us, can be replaced by the Christ who dwells within. We can be transformed from the inside out. It is sometimes instantaneous, but more often it is a lifetime of inviting the indwelling Christ to come and take up residence within us. I guess that means there is a struggle either way. Either we struggle against the sin that threatens our existence in the world, that makes us ill-equipped to live in community, to maintain relationships, to be content within our own hearts, and we live that constant battle, knowing we will ultimately lose. Or we struggle against our own will that doesn’t want to be given over to a loving God who can remake us into what we really want to become. That struggle was described by the late songwriter Rich Mullins in the song “ Hold Me Jesus ”: Surrender don't come natural to me / I'd rather fight You for something / I don't really want / Than to take what You give that I need / And I've beat my head against so many walls / Now I'm falling down, I'm falling on my knees. Written by Richard Mullins, Lyrics © Capitol CMG Publishing When we finally fall to our knees, when we finally surrender, when we embrace a delight in obedience to the law, then we find a new strength; we find a new support network; we find a new possibility. We find the sun still shining even though the clouds have rolled in. We find hope instead of despair. We find joy instead of shame. We find goodness within and all around us. Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship We gather to worship God with our full, imperfect selves. We come to delight in the law of God, who is Love. We gather as people who don’t always know what to do in the face of difficult and complex circumstances. We come to delight in the law of God, who is Love. We gather as people who desire to follow God with our actions but struggle to connect what we want to do with what we actually do. We come to delight in the law of God, who is Love. Whether you come to worship today wondering if there is anything good left in the world or rejoicing in the small moments of goodness that remind you grace is still at work among us, you are welcome here. We come to delight in the law of God, whose grace shows us how to live, work, play, and rest as a community of faith woven together by Love. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026. Opening Prayer God of heaven and earth, we gather in Your presence with thanksgiving and praise for the way in which You have revealed Yourself to us. Through Jesus Christ, your Son, we have come to know and love You; we have witnessed Your love and mercy in action; we have caught a glimpse of Your heart, and we have received the call to follow. Continue to reveal Yourself to us as we worship. May Your Holy Spirit open our minds and hearts to Your presence here, and to the word that You have for us this morning. We long to meet You here, and to know You better. In the name of Jesus Christ, Your Son and our Savior. Amen. Adapted from “Opening Prayer: Proper 9A” posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/06/opening-prayer-proper-9a.html . Prayer of Confession Lord, we come before you this day confessing that we don’t understand our own actions. The very things we want to do, we don’t do. Too often, we find ourselves doing the very things we hate. We need you this day, Lord. The harmful behaviors we tried to put down, we keep picking back up, and our soul is hurting. The chance we had to fix that broken relationship came, But anger and rage rose up again, Inflicting harm and abuse upon the very people we said we loved. We need you this day, Lord. The opportunities we have been praying for came, But fear, lack of confidence, and low self-esteem drove them away. Lord, the good we want to do, we don’t do; and the evil we hate doing, we just keep doing. Lord, what messed-up souls we are. We need you now, Lord, this day. Rescue us from works that lead to death; save us from self-destructive behaviors. We submit our lives into your hands right now. (Silence) Thank you, God, for your Son Jesus, who will make it all right. Thank you for your Son Jesus. He will heal our sin-sick souls. Thank you, God, for Jesus Christ, our Lord. When we find it difficult to do the right thing, we will place our trust in you. We are convinced that we can do all things through Christ who gives us strength. Glory to God! Amen. Adapted from Joseph W. Daniels, Jr. in The African Worship Book, Year A (Nashville: Discipleship Resources, 2006), 147, 155. Benediction May Christ who dwells in you continue to do good work in you, blessing you with grace and perseverance to continue on in the journey of faith as you grow into the image of Christ more and more every day. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026.

title: Music Notes
body: Music Notes The eighth chapter of the letter to the Romans is one of the most loved chapters in the Bible. As the crux of this important epistle, this chapter provides insight into some of the core elements of our faith. How does the law function in our faith? What does it mean to set our mind on the Spirit? What is our relationship with all creation? How are we bound together with other disciples in suffering and joy? St. Paul sets out to answer these and many other questions as he weaves a poetic vision of what it means to be a follower of Jesus and a part of the body of Christ. We invite you and your congregation to explore “Core Faith” this summer. title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Gracious Redeemer, you know us completely—our good intentions, our wavering will, our stumbling steps. Like Paul, we confess the war within us: we long to do what is right, yet too often fall short. Still, you meet us not with condemnation, but with mercy and grace. So, we bring these offerings, not to earn your favor, but to respond in gratitude for a Savior who rescues us from sin’s grip. Use these gifts, and use us, to offer hope where there is despair, light where there is shadow, and love where there is brokenness. We give because you gave first—and because your Spirit empowers us to live not by our strength, but by your grace. In Christ’s name, we pray, Amen. ( Romans 7:15-25a )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons This lesson invites students to explore the human experience of wanting to do what is right while feeling stuck or conflicted. The icebreaker uses a playful, hands-on game to get students talking and laughing about mixed signals and crossed intentions. After reading Paul’s honest words about inner struggles, students discuss how faith is not about trying harder or being perfect, but about naming what is real and asking for help. The movement-based activity helps students physically experience internal conflict and surrender, discovering that delighting in God’s way does not erase struggle but opens us to transformation that happens with grace, not willpower. Needed Resources: Two small cards or slips of paper per student (labeled YES and NO) Tape to mark a center line on the floor An open space that is large enough for students to move comfortably Icebreaker: Mixed Signals (10 Min.) Give each student two small cards or pieces of paper, one labeled YES and one labeled NO. Have students stand in an open space. Explain that you will read a series of light, everyday statements. After each one, students must quickly raise either YES or NO cards, but they may change their answer once after seeing what others chose. Keep it fast and playful. Example statements: I like surprises. I enjoy being the center of attention. I hate being told what to do. I like rules when they help people. I say I’m fine even when I’m not. After several rounds, briefly note how easy it is to feel pulled in two directions at once. Scripture (5 Min.) Read Romans 7:15–25a . Discussion (15 Min.) What phrases or emotions from this passage stood out to you? In this text, how does Paul describe what it feels like to be human? What seems confusing or frustrating about Paul’s experience? How is this passage different from messages that say, “Just try harder”? Why do you think Paul names this struggle out loud instead of hiding it? What does Paul seem to believe is the real problem, not just bad choices? Where do you see similar inner conflict in everyday life? How does naming our struggles change the way we think about faith? What does the question “Who will rescue me?” suggest about trust and dependence? Have you ever heard the phrase, “Be a participant in your own rescue”? Do you think that is good advice? What might it mean to delight in God’s way even when following it feels hard? Activity and Discussion: Tug of Will (20 Min.) Clear a large open space. Place a line of tape on the floor to mark the center. Explain that one side of the room represents, “I can handle this on my own,” and the other side represents, “I need help beyond myself.” Students will move back and forth silently in response to prompts. Read each prompt slowly. After each one, invite students to stand where they feel pulled , not where they think they should stand. Example prompts: Trying to change a habit you keep falling back into. Wanting to do the right thing but feeling exhausted. Knowing what is good but not feeling able to choose it. Asking for help when you would rather stay in control. Trusting grace instead of effort. After several prompts, invite students to notice how often they moved and how it felt to stand in different places. Emphasize that Paul is not condemning this movement or struggle. He names it honestly and points toward grace that meets us there. Reflection Questions (for the activity) What did you notice about how often you shifted positions? Which side felt harder to stand on and why? How does this activity help you understand Paul’s struggle in a new way? Close in a manner that is consistent with your group’s practice.

title: Children’s Message
body: Children's Message Introduction The eighth chapter of the letter to the Romans is one of the most loved chapters in the Bible. As the crux of this important epistle, this chapter provides insight into some of the core elements of our faith. How does the law function in our faith? What does it mean to set our mind on the Spirit? What is our relationship with all creation? How are we bound together with other disciples in suffering and joy? St. Paul sets out to answer these and many other questions as he weaves a poetic vision of what it means to be a follower of Jesus and a part of the body of Christ. We invite you and your congregation to explore “Core Faith” this summer. Scripture: Romans 7:15-25, New International Reader's Version 15 I don’t understand what I do. I don’t do what I want to do. Instead, I do what I hate to do. 16 I do what I don’t want to do. So I agree that the law is good. 17 As it is, I am no longer the one who does these things. It is sin living in me that does them. 18 I know there is nothing good in my desires controlled by sin. I want to do what is good, but I can’t. 19 I don’t do the good things I want to do. I keep on doing the evil things I don’t want to do. 20 I do what I don’t want to do. But I am not really the one who is doing it. It is sin living in me that does it. 21 Here is the law I find working in me. When I want to do good, evil is right there with me. 22 Deep inside me I find joy in God’s law. 23 But I see another law working in me. It fights against the law of my mind. It makes me a prisoner of the law of sin. That law controls me. 24 What a terrible failure I am! Who will save me from this sin that brings death to my body? 25 I give thanks to God who saves me. He saves me through Jesus Christ our Lord. So in my mind I am a slave to God’s law. But sin controls my desires. So I am a slave to the law of sin. New International Reader's Version (NIRV) Copyright © 1995, 1996, 1998, 2014 by Biblica, Inc.®. Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. Object One soft or paper heart. Message Good morning, friends. I’m really glad you’re here today. I have a question to ask you, “Have you ever noticed that something in your body keeps working even when you forget about it?” (Pause. Let children respond: “Your heart!” “Your brain!”) Yes! Your heart. Let’s check. Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel your heart? Is it fast or slow today? (Tap gently together.) Your heart keeps beating while you sleep… while you play… even when you’re not thinking about it at all. That’s a little bit like God’s love. God’s love doesn’t stop just because we forget about it. Now let’s wake up our bodies. Stand up with me. Let’s see how good we are at listening. Touch your toes. (Wait and laugh together.) Now jump one time. Freeze! Wow! You did that so well. That was easy, wasn’t it? But I wonder…is it always that easy to do the right thing? Let’s try something different. When I say something kind, show me a thumbs up. When I say something unkind, cross your arms. Ready? Sharing toys Pushing in line Helping a friend who fell down. Yelling when you’re really, really mad. You’re really good at knowing what’s kind and what’s not. But here’s something important. Sometimes we know the kind thing, but we still do the other thing. Has that ever happened to you? (Pause for nods, quiet “yes,” or shared smiles.) It happens to grown-ups, too. A man in the Bible named Paul once said, “I want to do good… but sometimes I don’t.” (Show the heart.) When Paul said that, God didn’t stop loving him. This heart reminds us of that. Let’s try something with our hands. Squeeze them into tight fists. Really tight. (Wait.) Now open them wide. That’s what God’s love is like. It’s not tight. Not angry. Not gone. It’s always open, always here. (Place the heart somewhere the children can still see it.) God loves us, even when we make mistakes. When we make mistakes, we need someone to forgive us. I wonder how it feels when someone forgives you. (Allow children to answer.) I wonder how it feels knowing that God forgives. (Allow children to answer.) When God forgives, God also helps our hearts get another chance. I wonder how God helps our hearts try again tomorrow. Each week, we will end our time together this way. Put your hand on your heart. I will say, “God’s love holds me.” Place a hand on your heart, then link your other hand with the person next to you. Leader: God’s love holds me. Children: God’s love holds us. Prayer (Hands on hearts, breathing slowly together.) God, thank you for loving us when we do the right thing and when we don’t. Help our hearts learn, and help us try again. Amen. Between the Sundays A Family Faith Practice for the “Core Faith” Series Each week includes: A short scripture idea. Conversation starters. A hands-on or movement-based activity. A simple prayer. The consistent ritual used in worship. Week 1 – Delight in the Law Scripture Focus: Romans 7:15–25a Theme: God loves us even when we mess up. Talk Together Talk about a time you tried to do the right thing, but it was hard. What helps you feel better when you make a mistake? How do you know someone still loves you after a hard moment? Try This Together Open Hands Practice All squeeze their hands into tight fists. Ask, “How does that feel?” Slowly open your hands wide. Say together, “God’s love is open to us.” Optional: Draw or cut out a paper heart and place it somewhere visible this week. Wonder Together I wonder how it feels to be forgiven. I wonder how God helps us try again. Prayer God, thank you for loving us when we do the right thing and when we don’t. Help our hearts grow. Amen. Family Ritual One hand on the heart; the other linked to the next person. Leader: God’s love holds me. All: God’s love holds us.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer the question, “Did you make any New Year’s resolutions? Why or why not? Do you remember what your resolution was this year? Are you keeping it?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). You may not get through all the questions in your time together. Consider inviting group members to work through any remaining questions on their own throughout the week. Read Romans 7:15-25a aloud. Invite participants to have the scripture in front of them, either in a Bible, on a phone app, or printed on paper. This text contains many repeated ideas. It invites slowing down and looking at the words. Ask the group what they notice from the text about the following: What Paul says about what he does The law Sin and evil Good Can you think of a time when this phrase would have described you? “I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” If that no longer describes you, why do you think that is? In Romans 7:22, Paul writes, “For I delight in the law of God in my inmost self.” What do you think Paul means? The following verse (v. 23) points to the tension of sin at work “in my members” and “with the law of my mind.” What do you think Paul means? The Preaching Notes for July 5 say: “’Who will rescue me?’ That’s the key to the passage. That question is a cry of faith. It follows the cry of despair, ‘wretched man that I am.’ Wretched woman. Wretched creature. In a world without hope, that is the final cry. But praise be to God, there is another cry to follow. ‘Who will rescue me from this body of death?’ The Lord of life, that’s who.” How does the possibility of rescue give you permission to vulnerably confess your need of it? The idea of being rescued is complicated. Which of these statements resonates the most with you? I’ve got things under control in my life, and I do not need to be rescued. I’m too [busy/distracted/___________] to know whether I need to be rescued. I’m fully aware of many ways that I need to be rescued, but I struggle to relinquish control. I can surrender to the Rescuer in some things, but struggle in others. When I need to be rescued, my first possibility of it comes from surrendering to the Rescuer. Just One Thing: This week, share with someone in your life a time when you needed rescue; then commit to pray for each other for “the Lord of life” to provide rescue. Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text of your choice ( Genesis 24:34-38, 42-49, 58-67 , Psalm 45:10-17 , Romans 7:15-25a , Matthew 11:16-19, 25-30 ) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: O Lord of Life, you see all the times that we desire to follow you, but we desire more to do what we really want to do. Forgive us and help us know that your rescue in our lives is good. You are our Savior. Help us to delight in your law and see what is truly good about your way. Thanks be to God who delivers us through Jesus Christ, our Lord. Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Focus Text : Genesis 22:1-14 Many years ago, I was a young pastor on the staff of a large church. I remember a debate I had with another member of that staff about this text. It was while I served the church that the adoption of our son came through, and we were living in the glow and haze of being new parents. Suddenly, this story of the near–sacrifice of Isaac hit a little differently. I shared some of those feelings in a staff meeting, and my colleague said he believed Abraham knew the sacrifice of Isaac would not happen. That is the only way, he said, that this story made sense to him. I didn’t quite know how to process that idea, to be honest. It changed everything, it seemed to me. It would be like the Docetic heresy that claimed Jesus didn’t really suffer on the cross, that he only appeared to do so. It was a “seeming.” Abraham seemed to be offering up his only son, the son he loved, because he knew it wasn’t real. I understand that, to make sense of a text like this — far from our cultural experience — we have to find ways of interpreting it that give us some peace. My colleague had opted for the interpretation that it was only an act. Abraham was acting out something here, perhaps allowing God to end child sacrifice, perhaps modeling total obedience. Knowing seems important to the text, however you choose to interpret it. “What did Abraham know?” is an important question. But we could also ask, “What did God know?” I know that sounds ridiculous, since we hold to the omniscience of God, that God knows everything. But Genesis 22 seems to argue differently. As the voice of God stops Abraham from using the knife on his son, the text gives God’s words as “now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me” (Gen 22:12 NRSV). “Now I know” — as in he didn’t before? As in, this was a test, and God was being tested as well as Abraham? Abraham’s track record hasn’t been great, frankly. Yes, when God called ten chapters ago, Abraham didn’t waver; he just went. Dragging along extended family and as much wealth as he could gather, he  went. At the beginning of this chapter, Abraham doesn’t argue, doesn’t waver; he just goes. But in the middle, things are a little messy. There is the Hagar incident. There is the passing off of Sarai as a sister rather than a wife, and we can’t help but wonder who he was trying to protect. So, yeah, maybe he did need to pass a test to be the launch of a new plan of redemption for all of creation. But this seems … harsh. Even Jewish interpreters approach this harshness with some distance. While in Christian scriptures, this text is titled “the sacrifice of Isaac,” the rabbis have consistently named it “the binding (“the akedah”) of Isaac.” They are more accurate, we could argue, because while Isaac was indeed bound, he wasn’t sacrificed. There was that last-minute reprieve, a pardon from the governor before the switch was thrown. There is some debate as to whether child sacrifice was actually practiced in the surrounding nations and cultic groups. But it certainly seems possible. Maybe the intention was to establish that child sacrifice was not an accepted practice among the people of God. But then why not make a decree about it? Why this charade of a ritual killing? It’s true that we haven’t gotten to the law-writing stage of development for this nation-to-be. But this seems a good place to start. If we could set aside questions of blame, as in whose fault is it that we are even here, and recognize that horrifying things happen on an all too regular basis, then maybe the message is that God is with us and that solutions, even for impossible situations, can often be found if we take a moment to breathe and to look. The message we cling to is that God will provide. We cannot always know how and with what, but we can trust that, through means that may seem miraculous or simply the people of God being who they are called and gifted to be, God will provide. I have consistently declared that it is not the preacher’s job to explain God or to excuse or defend God. Our honest confession is that we don’t know what all this means or how we are to live with this text. So, what do we do then? While most of the time it seems best to take texts from the Hebrew scriptures on their own, perhaps this one needs a Christian lens through which we can look for meaning and even hope. Isaac carries the wood for the sacrifice on his own back. When he asks his father where the lamb is,  Abraham’s cryptic response is, “God will provide the lamb.” The pathos of this verse is heavy with the realization that Isaac was indeed provided through miraculous means. But for us Christians, the sentence echoes through the centuries to another mountain, not Moriah but Golgotha, where the son carried the wood for his sacrifice and then became the lamb that was slaughtered. We cannot read this text and not see that terrible grace, that horrifying beauty, opening a door to salvation for all. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber , Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Focus Text : Genesis 22:1-14 Call to Worship When our way seems unclear, and we are surrounded by loud and conflicting voices… God will provide. When we, like Abraham, are trying to be faithful and seem to have no good choices available to us… God will provide. When we, like Isaac, are led by those we trust into unjust and harmful situations… God will provide. Family in Christ, we gather today to worship God, who meets us in places of fear, confusion, and despair. We gather to worship God, who provides a way toward abundant life when no way can be found. Thanks be to God! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026. Opening Prayer Lord, the hearts of all turn to You in hope; and You give them what they need. You open Your hand and satisfy the hunger and thirst of every living thing. We, too, turn to You again, longing to be filled— to eat of the Bread of Life, to drink from Your life-giving streams, to taste Your goodness and live. May the time we spend together in Your presence nourish our hearts and minds; may it strengthen our relationship with You, and renew our commitment to live in this world as Your faithful disciples. For You alone are God, the Source and Sustainer of life. In Jesus’ name, Amen. Written by Christine Longhurst at the re:Worship blog, https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2011/07/opening-prayer-feed-us-lord.html . Prayer of Confession Comforter, draw near, for You have waited and watched, as we have stumbled through the tasks of life. Our ears have not been open to the sound of Your gentleness, and so with frustration and anger, we have turned on those we love and cherish and brought hurt and division to life. Our eyes have not noticed the beauty of our surroundings, and in resentment of being restrained from living, we have played our part in the changing pattern of creation, forgetting to steward all You have made. In prayer, we remember You invite us to choose between the path of darkness and the path of light, and laying our sorrow and failure on the ground, we long for Your forgiveness to call us towards life with You. We wait to be reshaped by the fire of Your Holy Spirit, as new vigour spurs us to walk with You. Silence God’s gift of eternal life has been given in Jesus Christ, who offers us forgiveness from our sins and welcomes us to the way of holiness. Amen. Written by Rev MaryAnn Rennie, Church of Scotland . Reposted on the Pilgrim WR Uniting Church website at https://pilgrimwr.unitingchurch.org.au/?p=7103 . Benediction May God go with you, blessing you with divine provision, making paths where there were none before, and leading you into flourishing in the most impossible of places. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, January 2026.

title: Music Notes
body: Music Notes Focus Text : Genesis 21:8-21 Isaac carries the wood for the sacrifice on his own back. When he asks his father where the lamb is, Abraham’s cryptic response is, “God will provide the lamb.” The pathos of this verse is heavy with the realization that Isaac was indeed provided through miraculous means. But for us Christians, the sentence echoes through the centuries to another mountain, not Moriah but Golgotha, where the son carried the wood for his sacrifice and then became the lamb that was slaughtered. We cannot read this text and not see that terrible grace, that horrifying beauty, opening a door to salvation for all. title: Offertory Prayer
body: Offertory Prayer Faithful Provider, we bring our gifts with trembling hands and trusting hearts. Like Abraham on the mountain, we don’t always understand the path ahead, but we believe in your promise: that you will provide. We offer these gifts, not as bargains or sacrifices to earn your love, but as signs of our trust in you. Use them, we pray, to bless others—to meet needs, to heal hurts, to build hope. And as you provide for the world through us, keep us faithful to your calling, even when the way is unclear. May our giving be our “Here I am,” ready and willing to serve. In Christ’s name, Amen. ( Genesis 22:1-14 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Focus text : Genesis 22:1-14, CEB NEEDED RESOURCES: Blindfolds (scarves, bandanas, or fabric strips work fine) Items to create obstacle course (chairs, cones, tape, or whatever is available Open space safe enough to navigate blindfolded Note to the Teacher This may be the most challenging text in the series. God asks Abraham to sacrifice Isaac, his son, his promise, his future. Abraham doesn't argue. He goes. This is a deeply difficult story, and we don't need to explain it away or defend God here. Instead, we listen for what the text is trying to teach us: that God provides. In Hebrew practice, sacrifice was a way people made offerings to God and showed their commitment. Abraham's willingness to offer everything shows the depth of his trust and his covenant relationship with God. The core message isn't that God will hurt you to test you. It's that God provides. Even in impossible situations, even when we can't see the way forward, God provides. The icebreaker explores how people respond when they're stuck. The discussion works through how hard this story is without rushing to easy answers. The activity puts youth in a position of having to trust without knowing the outcome, then reflecting on what that teaches us about faith. 1. Icebreaker: What Would You Do? (10 min.) Present this scenario: You're stuck. You don't know what to do next. Maybe it's a problem with a friend, a decision you have to make, something that scares you, or something that just feels impossible. When you're in that kind of situation, what's your gut reaction? Do you ask for help? Do you freeze? Do you try to figure it out on your own? Do you panic? Do you wait and see what happens? Go around the circle quickly. The youth can give one word, a phrase, or a sentence about their instinct. No judgment, no fixing, just noticing what people naturally do. After everyone shares, you might ask: “Did you notice any patterns? Are there times you do one thing and at other times you do another? What changes?” 2. Scripture (5 min.) Read Genesis 22:1-14 (CEB), Binding of Isaac. Our scripture today might just be the most difficult in this set of lessons. God asks Abraham to offer his son, Isaac, as a sacrifice. Abraham goes, trusting that somehow God will provide. 3. Discussion (15 min.) Start with some of these questions to get the conversation going: This is a really difficult story. What's your first reaction to it? Have you heard this story before? What are you bringing in terms of knowledge or opinions to this text before we start talking about it? Abraham doesn't argue or refuse when God asks him to do this. What does that tell us about him or about his relationship with God? What do you think Isaac was feeling at different points in the story? When do you think Isaac realized he was going to be the sacrifice and not a ram? What do you think Sarah thought or felt when Isaac and Abraham left? Do you think Abraham told Sarah what God had asked him to sacrifice? In the culture at the time, when Abraham built that altar and made an offering, he was showing his trust and commitment to God. His willingness to offer even what was most precious showed the depth of his covenant relationship with God. Abraham was willing to give up everything. What's something you hold onto tightly? What would it take to let go of it? If you want to explore further, consider: The passage says, "God will provide the lamb for the offering." Abraham says this to his son…do you think Abraham was speaking figuratively (meaning that Isaac is the lamb that God provided, and Isaac just doesn’t realize it yet) OR literally, meaning that even in the midst of the hike up to the altar, Abraham believes God will provide a sacrifice besides Isaac? What does it mean to trust something you can't see or guarantee? Is faith the same as certainty? At the end, God provides a ram instead of Isaac. What does that change about the story for you? What does "God will provide" mean in this moment? Have you ever been in a situation where you had to trust that things would work out, but you couldn't see how? What was that like? What does "God will provide" mean to you? Does it mean God will fix everything? Or something else? How does this story help you understand what provision means? Have you heard that phrase used in helpful ways? In harmful ways? Explain. 4. Activity and Discussion: The Unknown Path (20 min. ) Set up a simple obstacle course or path in your meeting space, using chairs, cones, tape lines, or whatever you have. Keep it simple and safe - nothing too high or dangerous. Before you start, ask for three or four volunteers. Explain that each volunteer will walk the path blindfolded while the rest of the group gives them step-by-step directions. The group can tell the volunteer the NEXT step ("Step left," "Duck under," "Step over," "Keep going straight"), not multiple steps ahead. Each walker has one person designated as a safety spotter who walks beside them to make sure they don't hurt themselves. After each person goes through, they take off the blindfold and rejoin the group. After all volunteers have gone, bring everyone together and ask: “What was it like being blindfolded and having to trust the group's directions?” “Did it feel easier or harder when you couldn't see what was coming?” “Abraham doesn't know where he's going or how things will work out, but he trusts God. How is that like what you just experienced?” “What's the difference between blind trust and trust based on knowing someone cares about you and won't let you get hurt?” Close out your time however you usually do. Invite youth to share joys and concerns, then ask for a volunteer to close in prayer. 50 minutes total
