title: Children's Message
body: Children's Message Introduction: The story of Abraham and Sarah is complex, full of twists and turns, great faith, and crippling fear. Through it all, it is a story about a family that struggles and learns to love in ways that could be an invitation to the whole world. It is a story about the people of God who want to follow, even when their wisdom falls short. It is a story about blessing, about receiving a blessing, and then being a blessing. We begin this season after Pentecost by thinking about the church and about these examples of faith as we consider forming a family and preparing a people. This children’s message series offers a summer theme, a great fit for this season after Pentecost. These messages provide a fresh, distinct summer theme that feels light and joyful, while still honoring the Abraham stories. “God’s Big Summer Adventure” Big Idea theme throughout this series: God invites us into God’s family, goes with us wherever we go, listens when we are scared, and takes care of us, just as a loving guide would do on a summer adventure. “God goes with us on every adventure.” Genesis 12:1–9, New International Reader's Version God Chooses Abram 12 The Lord had said to Abram, “Go from your country, your people and your father’s family. Go to the land I will show you. 2 “I will make you into a great nation. And I will bless you. I will make your name great. You will be a blessing to others. 3 I will bless those who bless you. I will put a curse on anyone who puts a curse on you. All nations on earth will be blessed because of you.” 4 So Abram went, just as the Lord had told him. Lot went with him. Abram was 75 years old when he left Harran. 5 He took his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot. They took all the people and possessions they had acquired in Harran. They started out for the land of Canaan. And they arrived there. 6 Abram traveled through the land. He went as far as the large tree of Moreh at Shechem. At that time the Canaanites were living in the land. 7 The Lord appeared to Abram at Shechem. He said, “I will give this land to your family who comes after you.” So Abram built an altar there to honor the Lord, who had appeared to him. 8 From there, Abram went on toward the hills east of Bethel. He set up his tent there. Bethel was to the west, and Ai was to the east. Abram built an altar there and called on the name of the Lord. 9 Then Abram left and continued south toward the Negev Desert. New International Reader's Version (NIRV) Copyright © 1995, 1996, 1998, 2014 by Biblica, Inc.® . Used by permission. All rights reserved worldwide. Object: Beach sun hat. Message: ( Hold the sun hat in your hands, but don’t put it on yet. ) Good morning, friends! Have you ever gone somewhere new in the summer, maybe on a trip to the beach, to a park, or to a friend’s house? ( Pause for a few responses. Repeat one or two answers aloud. ) Going somewhere new can be really exciting, but it can also make you feel a little bit nervous , right? When you go somewhere new, what do you need to take with you? Shoes? A grown-up? A favorite toy or stuffed animal? ( Pause and nod as children answer. ) On a bright summer day, when the sun is shining, what might you need? ( Allow children to respond. ) That’s right, you will need a hat to protect you from the hot sun! ( Lift the sun hat so everyone can see. ) This hat is going to help us remember something important today. Today’s story is about a man named Abraham . One day, God said to Abraham, “Go to a place I will show you.” Now, listen carefully, God didn’t give Abraham a map. God didn’t give Abraham directions like, “Turn left here” or “Turn right there.” God didn’t tell Abraham how long the trip would be. God simply said, “Go… and I will be with you.” That might feel a little scary, right? To go somewhere new without knowing exactly where you’re going? ( Put your hand on your heart. ) Let’s all put a hand on our hearts for a moment. Can you feel your heart beating? Sometimes when we feel unsure or nervous, our hearts beat a little faster. Abraham probably felt that way, too. But God didn’t just say, “Go.” God also made Abraham a promise. God said, “I will bless you… and you will be a blessing.” That means God was going to give Abraham love, help, and care, and Abraham was going to share that love with others. Can you show me with your hands what it looks like to share? ( Have children pretend to give something away. ) Yes! Abraham wasn’t going on this big adventure just for himself. He was going to help, care for, and show God’s love to others. ( Slowly and intentionally, put the sun hat on your head. ) This hat reminds us of something very important: When God sends us out, to the beach, to the playground, to the pool, to a friend’s house, to church, God goes with us. Let’s say that together nice and loud: “God goes with us!” ( Say it again while gently marching in place. ) One more time, but this time whisper it: “God goes with us.” This summer, wherever we go, God is with us. God helps us be kind , ( Show kindness with a gentle wave. ) God helps us be brave , ( Stand up tall. ) And God helps us be loving , ( Give yourself a hug. ) Because we are part of God’s big family . ( Smile and gently tip the hat. ) Prayer: Loving God, Thank you for loving us. Thank you for going with us wherever we go. Help us trust you when we feel unsure. Help us share your love with others. And help us remember that we are part of your big family. Amen. Between the Sundays Family Guide Series: “God’s Big Summer Adventure” Theme Object: Sun Hat Week 1 – To Be a Blessing Core Truth: God goes with us. Conversation Starters Can you think of a time when you went somewhere new? How did you feel about going there? Excited? Nervous? Brave? How do you think God was with you on that adventure? Family Activities Sun Hat Adventure Walk: Take a walk outside, wearing a hat or cap. Talk about ways God is with you wherever you go. Point out signs of God’s care (flowers, trees, birds, sunshine). Kindness Map: Draw a map of places you go during the week. Write or draw one way you can share God’s love or be a blessing at each place. Storytime Extension: Read a story of someone showing kindness. Discuss how God helps us bless others.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer the question, “What do you think God’s voice sounds like?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). Read Genesis 12:1-9 . Other scriptures for this week include Psalm 33:1-12 , Romans 4:13-25 , and Matthew 9:9-13, 18-26 . Put together a profile of Abram and Sarai based on Genesis 12:1-9. What is the “demographic” information about each of them? (Name, age, where they live, where they go.) Read the “Call” part of this text again, Genesis 12:1-3. What are the promises God gives to Abram? For the leader: 1) I will make you into a great nation; 2) I will bless you; 3) I will make your name great (and you will be a blessing); 4) I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; 5) All peoples on earth will be blessed through you. Use your imagination: what are some possible reactions Abram and Sarai could have had to this “invitation” from God? What questions emerge for you about the blessings that God promises Abram and Sarai? The Preaching Note for June 7 says, “Notice that [Abram] didn’t get complete information about what he would be doing or where he would be going. It would be revealed as he went. ‘Leave the familiar, God said, and go to a place that I will show you—not a place I am showing you, not a place known to you, an unknown place.’ That is like life, don’t you think?” Have you ever been asked by God (or someone else—a parent, a spouse, a work or school opportunity) to go to an unknown place—literally or figuratively? What emotions, thoughts, or bodily experiences emerge during a season of uncertainty? This story connects three things: God’s call, new experiences, and blessings. Explore how these come together by considering these questions: How do you understand God’s call? Do you think everyone can hear God’s call? How do new experiences create space for God’s presence to be noticed? What do new experiences produce in you? In this story, God says they are blessed and will be a blessing to all nations. How do you understand being blessed and blessing others? Just One Thing: What could you do in the week ahead to explore what it means to be blessed to be a blessing to others? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the other lectionary texts using the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture (Psalm 119:18). Read the text (Psalm 33:1-12, Romans 4:13-25, or Matthew 9:9-13, 18-26) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with this prayer or the Lord’s Prayer: Open our ears that we may hear your voice, O God. Open our eyes that we may see your invitations to your Spirit. Open our hearts that we may receive your blessings and keep them open so that we may freely share them with others. Would you fill us with faith to follow you into unknown places and give us the sensitivity to your Spirit to know we’re not going it alone? In Christ’s name, we pray, Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in conference leadership for over a decade. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary and a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: Spirit in Partnership

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Color : White Focus Texts : Genesis 1:1-2:4a , Matthew 28:16-20 How do we tell the story of the Trinity? Some might be bold enough to point out that Trinity as a description or understanding of God does not appear as such anywhere in the Bible. It’s true. No prophet said, “Let me tell you about God as Trinity.” Neither Paul nor any other Epistle writer ever said, “The best way to understand God is by naming the Godhead as Trinity.” It just isn’t there. So, maybe a thing like Trinity Sunday is a theological non-starter, if not a waste of everyone’s time. Except what is in there is a richness about the experience of God that we often neglect when we begin to talk about who God is for us. The biblical witness is that God is so multidimensional, so nuanced, so accessible and yet inaccessible at the same time, that words often fail to describe this reality we claim by faith. So, Trinity is an approximation of how we understand and approach our God. At its simplest level, we take the words of Jesus in Matthew 28 as a guide to this understanding. “Baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (verse 19b). This is our entry into Trinity. We can argue whether Jesus actually said this or whether these words were put in his mouth by those who wanted to establish a theological doctrine or tradition. There may be some editorial work going on here, to be sure. But the words remain. The invitation or the commandment remains. And the implication seems clear. We are meant to understand how God works in partnership. Go back to the beginning. Take some time, preacher, to read the poem that begins our Bible. Read it in preparation, surely, but read it in worship. It preaches better than many of our sermons anyway. Give it space to be heard. Hear the unfolding of all that is. Hear the blessing that is imparted upon creation. Hear the divine presence throughout. Hear the “we,” the “us,” in the very act of creation. Let it seep into our beings, since we, too, are a part of this creation. This is our beginning; this is our origin—not as science, not as a historical reflection of the beginnings of the universe, but as a theological tone poem that speaks to the glory of who we are and who we might be as a part of the wonderous whole. It is a gift, this poetry, a prayer and a blessing, a reminder of our interdependence on all creation, and a belonging to a Creator who loves us and breathes life into us each and every day. The NRSV and CEB translations of “wind” in verse two are correct, but unfortunate. We know that the Hebrew word here (ruach) can be translated as wind, as breath, and as Spirit. We know that. However, on Trinity Sunday, we need to hear Spirit. We need to hear that partnership, that blessing, but also the effort involved in creation. The word translated as “swept across” in the NRSV is translated as hovering or as moving elsewhere. The Hebrew carries the sense of movement, but also of trembling and of exertion. Something is stirring, or the Spirit is stirring something. There is effort here, exertion. God, through the Spirit, is bringing something to life, and that is never an easy or effortless process. Ask any mother. The partnership of Creator and Spirit is clear. Is there a true separation in these “persons”? Is there a difference between you and your breath? Well, yes. And no. There is oneness and duality at the same time. There is effort expended and direction given. And all that is flows from that partnership. But wait, we think, duality is not trinity. Where is the third actor in this drama? John gives us the answer to that quandary in the prologue to his gospel. “In the beginning was the word” (John 1:1 NRSV). There is God creating; there is Spirit causing a trembling; and there is a word spoken: Let there be. And there is. God is the author, the vision-caster. Spirit is the environment prepared and preparing for something to be. The Word is the conduit for creation to happen. And creation happens. Again and again, it happens. And it still happens. God, Spirit, Word are still at work in the world. The incarnated Word invites us to be partners in that creation. “Go into all the world,” we are told. Go into creation and create. Go and envision; go and incarnate the kingdom, which is a kin-dom of relationship, hospitality, and transformation. Go and grow disciples. Grow seems better than make. Make can lead to colonial thinking. Grow is a dynamic relationship over time. Go and grow disciples. Invite them in through the water of new creation in the name of the Trinity. And then teach them, you’re not done at baptism. You’ve only begun. Teach them everything I have taught you. Teach them how to live in community. Teach them how to cross the boundaries we have created that keep people apart. Teach them how to care for bodies as well as souls. Teach them how to heal from their brokenness and find their identity in community and in him. Teach them how to follow, how to pick themselves up when they fall, or to be picked up by a caring community. Teach them how to practice faith, see Spirit, acknowledge the Creator, and live in the Son. Teach them everything. Because you are partnering with God in creation itself. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship On this Trinity Sunday, we come to praise the Triune God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit! We praise God who creates, redeems, and sustains all creation! We come to wade into the depths of the divine mystery of God, the One-in-Three and Three-in-One. We seek an ever-deepening faith in God who creates, redeems, and sustains all creation! We come to witness the interconnectedness of the Triune God, to marvel at the divine dance of partnership and cooperation. We receive the invitation to join the divine dance of God who creates, redeems, and sustains all creation! Come, let us worship the Triune God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit! Come, let us worship the Triune God who creates, redeems, and sustains all creation! Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, December 2025. Opening Prayer Out of our ordinary, everyday lives, you have gathered us here, Holy God, to this time of worship, to this time of praise. We join with angels and archangels and all the company of the saints to bless you, to listen for your Word, to immerse ourselves in your grace, in your love. Open our hearts And our minds to your presence with us. Take the chaos of the world that has found its way into our hearts — speak your Word and give order and form and new creation. Take the failures and defeats, the guilt and the shame that bind our spirits — speak your Word and set us free. Take our longings for your goodness to shape our lives, this community, the hurting world — speak your Word and infuse us with your courage and your hope and your love. Then, awaken us to your Holy Spirit who is making all things new, even us. We ask in Jesus’ name, who sends us out to speak love and mercy and grace to those who are waiting, longing, hoping, for a sign that they are not alone, that you are a God of love, that you are a Saviour who knows their name, that the Holy Spirit is leading them home. Amen. Adapted from Christine Jerrett, https://christinejerrett.wordpress.com/ . Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2019/06/prayer-matthew-28-16-20.html . Prayer of Confession As heirs of God, let us come to lay before God our sin and wrongdoings and lack of faith. Let us come with hearts that seek newness. Holy One, we acknowledge that too often we try to live not acknowledging the mystery of your Being. Even though you have shown us your truth, we allow ourselves to rest in our own uncertainties. We find ourselves unable or unwilling to embrace the love through which you sent Christ to live among us. We take for granted the grandeur of you as Creator, Redeemer, and ever-present Sustainer. We do not live out the beloved community you desire for all. Forgive us, we pray, and help us give testimony to your love. Assurance of Pardon We trust in these promises: that the Triune God, in each of its persons, promises us newness of life, a gift of new birth. The Divine Trinity invites us to testify to its Being as the foundation for reconciliation of all of God’s people and for Creation. In these truths, we trust and give thanks. Thanks Be to God! Written by Rev. Dr. Bertrice Wood, posted on the Worship Ways website at https://www.ucc.org/worship-way/trinity-sunday-may-30/ . Benediction Go now in the blessing of the Triune God who draws you into the divine dance, inviting you to partner in God’s life-giving work to bring flourishing and abundant life to all creation! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, December 2025.

title: Offertory Prayers
body: Offertory Prayer Creating God, from the beginning, you formed light out of darkness, breath from dust, and life from love. In Christ, you walked among us, and through your Spirit, you empower us still. Today, we offer our gifts—signs of our desire to partner with you in your ongoing work of creation, healing, and discipleship. Use these offerings to build communities of compassion, to welcome the stranger, and to teach your ways of justice and joy. May our giving reflect the wonder of your Triune love and our willingness to go and grow disciples in your name. Amen. ( Genesis 1:1-2:4a , Matthew 28:16-20 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Genesis 1:1-2, 4a, Matthew 28:16-20 (CEB) Supplies Needed: Blocks or other building materials Paper Drawing materials Art supplies (markers, pens, crayons, etc.) Note to the Facilitator Trinity Sunday can be challenging for some students (and facilitators!). It can be challenging to understand that God exists as one, but also as three. This is a mystery, and it is okay for students—especially the more concrete thinkers—to feel frustrated that they cannot fully describe this beautiful mystery. This lesson encourages students to think deeply and imagine, not necessarily arrive at a correct answer. Encourage students and assure them that many of the adults in their lives struggle with this idea! Our goal together is not a perfect definition, but thoughtful exploration and faithful curiosity. Icebreaker: Our Origin Story (10 min.) Many good characters become great characters when they have an origin story. The Wicked Witch of the West ( The Wizard of Oz ) becomes a fully developed character as Elphaba ( Wicked ). Darth Vader from the original Star Wars trilogy (episodes 4, 5, 6) grows from a child, Anakin Skywalker, in episodes 1, 2, and 3. Nearly every superhero (or villain, for that matter) becomes more interesting when writers tell the story of how they came to be the way they are. Invite students to come up with a list of any other origin stories (for characters or franchises!) they can think of. Suggest to students that, as individuals, we each have our own origin story. (And yes, God has indeed been with us since the beginning.) Some of the stories are dramatic, like the ones in the movies. Some have calm, simple origin stories. And many of our origin stories overlap. Those common origins, therefore, can provide us, as a group, a collective origin story…how our group came to be, and why. Encourage the students to work together for five minutes to write a communal origin story. Make sure that each part of the story works for the entire class. If there is an outlier, ask students to rewrite the story to include the whole group. These can be playful stories set in a fantasy world or stories with a movie-like plot. One group might say the head of the [your church name] branch of the FBI has assembled a group of new recruits to investigate the meaning of the Bible. Here is how our team of recruits came to be here… Pose the questions, “What about our church? Do you know how our local church came to be? Where do we find our origin story? Who would be considered the hero (or heroes) in our church life?” Scripture (10 min.) Read Genesis 1:1-2 , 4a out loud. Remember, the origin story isn’t the whole story. Read the communal origin story the group wrote. What if this were the only part of our story that anyone knew!? We are so much more and do so much more than that! Invite students to view the Bible as one ongoing story. That story starts with the three verses we just read. Remember how we learned in elementary school, the plot line in a story? “In the beginning” sets the stage for every character and community that follows, including the lives we lead today! (Be prepared here to give a basic description of plot lines in case anyone has forgotten this lesson!) One surprising thing we all share is how God is already present at the beginning; the plot lines and origin stories in scripture rise and fall, peak and (sometimes) find resolution. One of the peaks of the Bible is the Great Commission that Jesus gives in Matthew. Read Matthew 28:16-20 . Explain to the students that you would like to look at this passage as the peak (or climax of action) in a plotline. Jesus asks us all to do our best each day to keep stepping forward in this ongoing resolution to “go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Because of this peak, we are part of the continuing story of God and people’s relationship with God. How do we do this? To lead others to this Holy Mystery of the Trinity, first we must consider it ourselves! Discussion (10 min.) Explain to students that this piece of our faith, the Trinity, the “Father, the Son, and Holy Spirit,” is a concept a lot of people have a hard time putting into words or even understanding. But today, we are going to dive into it together! Introduce students to commonly used examples and descriptions of the Trinity. Use as many or as few of these as you think appropriate for your context. H 2 O — The chemical compound of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom can exist in three separate forms— water, ice, and steam—and remain the same chemical compound. Although they share the same chemical compound, these are three distinctly separate “modes” of the compound, and we experience them differently. The sun, light, and heat. The sun is a star that can be perceived as visible light and the warmth it produces. We know we only have one sun, but sometimes we see it in our sky; sometimes we see the light it provides, and sometimes we feel its warmth. These different ways we experience the sun are unique and distinct; they all come from being our sun. They all can exist together, even if we experience only one aspect. A shamrock with its three leaves connected to one stem demonstrates three distinct parts forming one whole. This shows that there are three different parts of God, although they all come from one central source of being. Which of the symbols helps you understand God most easily? Which do you like the best? Which do you like the least? Where do any of these symbols fall short? If you took any of the metaphors too literally, what misunderstanding might it create about God, Jesus, or the Holy Spirit? Is there an analogy you have heard that wasn’t included here? Are you willing to share? Picture It (20 mins) Give students paper and drawing materials. Invite them —individually or with partners— to create a symbol for the Trinity. They may use their imagination or use any of the analogies previously discussed. If they are not comfortable drawing, encourage them to write down what they have in mind in as much detail as possible! Give students ten to fifteen minutes to create their symbols. They may need some help thinking deeply. Regular interaction and encouragement to explain further or “say more” may help push them to think deeply and articulate their thoughts. After the allotted time, invite students to share if they wish. Closing. Invite three students to collectively close the class in prayer, with one praying to God the Father, one to God the Son, and one to the Holy Spirit. Collectively close with an “Amen!” Total time: 50 minutes

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Trinity Sunday - May 31, 2026 – Spirit in Partnership Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, obviously, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “When did you first learn about the Trinity? What do you remember about God being Three-in-One?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). Read Genesis 1:1-2:4a and Matthew 28:16-20 . Genesis 1 provides a poetic description of creation. Where do you see elements of partnership in this story of creation? Where do you see partnership in Matthew 28:16-20? What does partnership look like at the end of Jesus’ earthly life? Matthew 28:16-20 includes the instruction to baptize disciples in “the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” This phrase is known as the “Trinitarian Formula.” How does thinking of God as Trinity affect your understanding of: Creation (Genesis 1:1-2:4a; it may be helpful to also read John 1:1); Baptism (Matthew 28:16-20; it may be helpful to also read about Jesus’ baptism in Matthew 3:13-17). The preaching note for May 31 says, “Go and grow disciples. Invite them in through the water of new creation in the name of the Trinity. And then teach them that they are not done at baptism. They have only begun. Teach them everything I have taught you.” How do you feel about the idea that baptism is the starting place to grow as a disciple? What does growing as a disciple mean to you at this point in your life? The concept of Three-in-One and One-in-Three is challenging: three persons, one God; one nature, three distinctions. How do you understand that unifying nature? What character, personality, or attribute of God is visible in all three persons of the Trinity? Just One Thing: What can you do this week to grow as a disciple, knowing that the Holy Spirit is with you? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text (Genesis 1:1-2:4a or Matthew 28:16-20) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Triune God, we pause in awareness that there is much about your nature as Three-in-One that feels complicated, confusing, or mysterious. But even in the mystery, we can see unity of purpose that is rooted in Love and invites us into partnership. Open our hearts and minds and equip our hands as we become co-creators with you and grow as your disciples. We pray this in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the UMC, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction

title: Preaching Notes
body: Preaching Notes Day of Pentecost - May 24, 2026 – Spirit Unbounded Color : Red Focus Texts : Numbers 11:24-30 , Acts 2:1-21 Would that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would put his spirit on them! (Numbers 11:29 NRSV) Would that we were! Would that we had a statement to make, a stand to take. Would that we advocate for justice, represent the marginalized, and welcome the stranger. “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets!” says Moses with some exasperation, perhaps. Why is God so stingy with the Spirit? Moses had to share what was within him. Does God have a limited supply? That seems to be part of Joshua’s fear. “Stop them” is his response to the word that there might be some unauthorized prophesying, that something leaked out that needed to be nipped in the bud before it flowered into something that was against them or that diminished them. Worse yet, something that steals some of the authority of Moses. Joshua is “team Moses” all the way and doesn’t want to see anyone stepping into the place and stealing that primacy. Moses has different ideas about leadership, which, for Moses, are different ideas about the Spirit. Moses is happy to share. He is happy to offer what is within him to the seventy elders so that they, too, can prophesy to the people. But what does that mean, exactly? What is being shared, and what are they prophesying about? Has Moses just created a team of fortune tellers predicting the future? No, this Spirit that now is shared is what a leader needs to lead God’s people. It is the ability to tell the truth and have empathy to care for the people one is leading. That seems a stretch, I know, but that is what appears to be at the heart of this event. Let us tell the truth about what God is doing in our midst and the truth about what we are doing (or not doing) in response. And let us do it because we care about the people we lead. We care about their well-being; we care about their survival. We care about their relationships within the community of pilgrims. We care about their thriving as whole people, and we care about their walk with God every single day of their lives. This is leading with the Spirit, not with human power and authority. Those authoritarians are right to be afraid of or concerned about empathy. It is a dangerous effect. But they are wrong to claim it makes you soft. Empathy makes you strong because it is so difficult. Even Moses wanted to get out from under it more than once. He argued with God on the mountain, saying your people are a pain in my existential ground of being! Your people! But in the end, he protected his people; he led his people; he cared about his people because that is what good leaders, Spirit-filled leaders, do. Moses was not diminished by sharing the Spirit that was within him with the seventy elders. He lost none of the empathetic leadership and authority that he had. He could still tell the truth. He could still lead toward a vision given to him by God. He was not diminished by sharing this Spirit any more than love is diminished by giving it away. The more we love, the more capacity we have to love. The more we care for the people around us, the more we are able to tell them the truth about the world, about themselves and their behaviors, about the consequences and the benefits to come. We tell the truth to the people we care about. Leaders who wield power through lies, threats, and othering are not leading with the Spirit given to them by God. Moses’s complaint was that there weren’t more out there leading with this Spirit. “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets” – prophets who tell the truth, prophets who care for the people, prophets who claim the vision that comes from God of a new way of living in this world and the next. “Would that all the Lord’s people …” And God heard that prayer, and we have Pentecost. Peter stands in for Moses on this incredible day and announces that Moses’s prayer has been answered. This Spirit, once sparsely shared, is now poured out on all flesh, as the Prophet Joel predicted. All flesh. Sons and daughters shall prophesy (Acts 2:17 NRSV). Did you hear that? In the church that has struggled with women in leadership, the Pentecostal message is that the Spirit has been poured out on all flesh, sons and daughters. Daughters and sons. Young shall see visions, and old shall dream dreams (Acts 2:17 NRSV). Did you hear that? For the church that has struggled with youth in leadership or with ignoring the wisdom of the elders, the Pentecostal message is that age is no barrier to the ability to prophesy, to tell the truth with empathy to God’s people. “Even upon my slaves, both men and women, in those days I shall pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy” (Acts 2:18 NRSV). Did you hear that? In the church that has struggled with marginalized and economically disadvantaged people and their role in the church and society, the Pentecostal message is that even the poor, even those bound by economic and racial systems of oppression, have a truth to tell and a story to be heard. Pentecost is the fulfillment of the heartfelt hope of Moses wandering through the wilderness with people who were only barely on board with the vision. What seemed like lack of access to the Spirit would be one day unbound by that limitation and poured out on all flesh. “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets.” We can wonder whether the Spirit was really that limited in Moses’s day. But we can’t really know. All we can be sure of if it was limited is that it no longer is. The Spirit is unbound, if it ever was. Or maybe we have been unbound so we can now receive that Spirit and learn to tell the truth with empathy in a world desperately in need of both. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Liturgical Resources Call to Worship Beloved, the Spirit of Truth gathers us here to receive and discern God’s good news working among us. Come, Holy Spirit, come! The Spirit of Love draws us together to receive and restore life-giving relationships with God and one another. Come, Holy Spirit, come! The Spirit of Freedom knits us together to receive and renew the bonds of empathy, justice, and peace that bind us together in the work for liberation and wholeness. Come, Holy Spirit, come! Beloved, the Holy Spirit is here, moving and working among us. Will you come and receive all the Spirit has to give? We come to receive the Spirit’s abundant and gracious gifts that we may be a people who live out God’s truth, love, and freedom in our neighborhood, community, and throughout all creation. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, December 2025. Opening Prayer Send forth your Spirit, O God, and renew the face of the earth. Dwell among us, even though your presence will startle and unsettle us. Grant us your peace, we pray, as justice and love pour down upon the yearning earth. Amen. Written by Mary Sue Gast in Touch Holiness: Resources for Worship, Updated, ed. Ruth C. Duck and Maren C. Tirabassi (Cleveland: The Pilgrim Press, 2012), 105. For use in worship services, include the following permissions statement: Reprinted by permission of the publisher from Touch Holiness , ed. Ruth C. Duck and Maren C. Tirabassi. Copyright © 1990 by The Pilgrim Press. Prayer of Confession The act of confessing our sin is not simply a recitation of our faults and wrongs, but also an opportunity to receive God’s mercy and share in that abundant grace. Confident of God’s love for us, let us offer our prayers, first in silence. Silent prayer Holy God, we ask for your help, your power, your Spirit, so that we can amend our lives and grow more each day into the image of Christ. We confess that we fear what is different. We confess that it’s easier to lock the doors of our community than to receive those who don’t look like we look, love like we love, or vote the way we vote. We confess that we have not lived out your call to share in abundant life and unconditional love. We believe that you have the power to turn us around to a more inclusive way of living, so we ask you to do that. We ask you to give us the courage to change. We ask that you give us the energy, intelligence, imagination, and love to be your people in all we say and do. Amen. Written by Beth Merrill Neel on her blog, “Hold Fast to What Is Good.” Used with permission. https://holdfasttowhatisgood.com/liturgy/prayer-of-confession/ . Benediction Family of God, go now in the blessing of the Spirit who inspires you to seek God’s truth, empowers you to share God’s love with empathy and compassion, and emboldens you to live in the freedom of the Spirit who binds us to God and one another that we may be truly free. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, December 2025.

title: Music Notes
body: Music Notes Pentecost and Trinity Sunday are not about a God far off and incomprehensible, but about a God poured out on God’s people. Embrace these days with passion and purpose, and with a promise to be partnered with a God poured out. Abbreviations UMH=United Methodist Hymnal TFWS=The Faith We Sing Numbers 11:24-30 , Acts 2:1-21 Pentecost is the fulfillment of the heartfelt hope of Moses wandering through the wilderness with people who were only barely on board with the vision. What seemed like a lack of access to the Spirit would be one day unbound by that limitation and poured out on all flesh. God the Spirit, Guide and Guardian        UMH 648 As a Fire Is Meant for Burning                  TFWS 2237 God of Grace and God of Glory                  UMH 577 In the Midst of New Dimensions              TFWS 2238 Spirit of Faith, Come Down                         UMH 332

title: Offertory Prayers
body: Offertory Prayer Empowering God, you are the one who pours out your Spirit on sons and daughters, on young and old, on leaders and servants alike. You have not withheld your gifts, but have shared them freely:  truth, empathy, vision, and power. As your Spirit-filled people, we now offer our gifts—not out of fear or obligation, but in response to your boundless generosity. Use these offerings to fuel the prophetic witness of your church, to bless those still yearning for hope, and to build a community where all are seen, heard, and loved. May our giving, like your Spirit, be poured out without limit. Amen. ( Numbers 11:24-30 )

title: Youth Lessons
body: Youth Lessons Numbers 11:24-30,  Acts 2:1-21 (CEB) Focus Verse: Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? If only all the Lord’s people were prophets with the Lord placing his spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29 CEB) Supplies: Paper Pens or pencils Note to the Facilitator This lesson moves from the physical description of what happened at Pentecost to a consideration of Pentecost moments in our lives today. It asks students to consider what it would be like for God to speak through each of us. We learn that Moses wanted this for the Hebrew people, and we reflect on this desire being fulfilled at Pentecost and look for it to continue today! The goal is for students to place themselves in this moment and consider ways the Holy Spirit may speak through them here and now. Icebreaker: The Common Thread (10 min.) Break into groups of three and give students forty-five seconds to find one weird, unexpected thing that everyone in the group has in common. Have each group, in rapid-fire fashion, share the common thread they found. Immediately, switch groups to new groups of three and repeat the process. This round, they need to find DIFFERENT threads that haven’t yet been discovered. Continue for three or four rounds, as time allows. Read Scripture (5 min.) Recall with the students that we learned about Moses leading the Hebrew people out of Egypt. They were on this wilderness journey for so long—forty years! Sometimes, this journey seemed like an epic group project. The Hebrew people were accustomed to having a single prophet who served as the link between the people and their God. If you have ever been the “leader” in a group project, you can probably relate to Moses a little earlier in the chapter, when he became overwhelmed and didn’t think he could do it all. Relatable, right? Invite students to open their Bibles to Numbers, chapter 11, and look at what happens when two other leaders rise up as prophets, which helped Moses, but definitely made some of the Hebrew people a little nervous. Invite a student to read Numbers 11:24-30. Discussion (10 min.) When have you felt you were carrying the workload for a whole group? How would it feel to have two other leaders be there suddenly and willing to take some of the lead? How do you think Moses felt about that? (Not only did these two men, Eldad and Medad, take some of the load off Moses, but the other people recognized that they could follow other leaders. They didn’t need to rely solely on Moses.) Share a time when you saw someone make people uncomfortable by stepping into a leadership position. Explain what happened. What do you think the people in this passage felt when they realized there could be multiple leaders within one community? Where in your life do you see people “gatekeeping” as leaders or wanting to look to a particular leader only? What might it mean for YOU to be someone through whom God speaks? If the Holy Spirit showed up at your school tomorrow, what do you think it would look like? Activity: Pentecost Remix (30 min.) Explain to students that the Holy Spirit did show up in the New Testament at an awesome celebration that was taking place! Read the story of Pentecost in Acts 2:1-21. Point out that we often don’t understand those around us. Invite students to think about speaking with people from different generations. When we use slang, or the person we are talking to uses slang, it can be hard to understand what the other person is saying! What are some phrases or sayings from other generations that the youngest generations in the room wouldn’t understand? Discuss that sometimes when we read the words in the Bible, it can feel a little like this, too, like it’s another language. In Numbers, Moses wishes that others could be prophets. What if WE can be those prophets for people around us? Let’s try it. Invite students to break into groups of up to four people and give each group paper and pens or pencils. Invite the groups to rewrite the Acts passage in a modern setting (maybe in a school hallway or in an online gaming chat—somewhere they are comfortable and could see this type of experience happen). After fifteen minutes, invite the groups to share their remix with the larger group. Closing: In Numbers 11:29, Moses says, “If only all the Lord’s people were prophets with the Lord placing his spirit on them.” What if Moses were here right now? What if he were saying, “I wish that all God’s people…” How do you think he would finish that sentence today? Invite students to share how they think Moses would finish the sentence. Close the session in prayer. Total time: 50 minutes

title: Children's Message
body: Children's Message Object: Stickers or small trinkets Stuffed animal Sermon: Good morning! Our Scripture today is about sharing so I brought something to share with all of you. Pass out stickers or small trinkets. Oh no! We seem to have a problem. There’s enough for all of you but not enough for everybody else. I don’t have enough for the adults to have some too. Bummer. It’s a real problem when you run out and don’t have enough for everyone right? Has that ever happened to you? Allow time for kids to answer. I have an idea. I brought this stuffed animal today and it’s so soft and cuddly, I just love to give it hugs. Hug stuffed animal. Would you like to hug it too? Pass around for kids to hug. You know what’s so cool? Everyone got to hug my special stuffed animal but we didn’t run out of hugs, right? If I passed it around again, we would still have more hugs to share. We could even pass it around to the adults and there would still be more than enough hugs. The amount of hugs is limitless, it’s infinite! In the Scripture today, Peter says that God’s Spirit is poured out on all people. The boys and the girls, the young and the old, the rich and the poor. Everyone gets to share in the Spirit. The Holy Spirit isn’t like the stickers. It can’t run out after just a few people. The Holy Spirit is like the hugs: limitless, infinite. It gets poured onto us but it will never run out. And that’s a good thing! See, when we have the Spirit of God, we can lead with truth, with empathy, and with love. We get to share with the world and we don’t have to be afraid that the more we share, the less we have. God’s Spirit will never run out. Prayer: Dear God, we praise you for the Spirit that guides us each day. Show us how to share in the Spirit with a heart of abundance, unbound by our own limits, so that we can live in your infinite love. Amen. Between the Sundays Ideas: Family Activities and Conversation Starters Look up videos of small little streams, rushing rivers, and flowing waterfalls. Which do you think is most like the pouring out of God’s Spirit? When do you feel like the slow flowing stream? What about the rushing river? Dress up in red to celebrate Pentecost. What does the color red remind you of? What other colors might represent God? Why? Read Acts 2:1-21 or look up the Pentecost story in a children’s Bible. What do you think tongues of fire would look like on someone’s head? If you could start speaking another language, what would you want it to be? Written by Sammy Waters. Sammy has served in family ministry in the North Georgia and Horizon Texas Conferences over the past 6 years. After receiving her Master of Divinity from Candler School of Theology, she moved to Texas where she has enjoyed working with children, youth, and families to design new ways to engage in worship, learn the stories of God, and create space for wonder.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship – Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, obviously, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or groups of three, have participants answer, “What do people look like when God has poured out the Holy Spirit on them?” Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). Read Numbers 11:24-30 ; Acts 2:1-21 . What do you notice about what each of the following people said about the activity of the Spirit in these stories: Joshua (Numbers 11:28), Moses (Numbers 11:29), the “devout Jews” (Acts 2:5), and Peter (Acts 2:14-21)? How do you see a “pouring out” in these encounters? The Preaching Note for May 24 says , “ Moses was not diminished by sharing the Spirit that was within him with the seventy elders…The more we care for the people around us, the more we are able to tell them the truth about the world, about themselves and their behaviors, about the consequences and the benefits to come. We tell the truth to the people we care about.” How do you understand the connections among these three things: (1) the Spirit’s presence, (2) telling the truth, and (3) caring for others? Moses complained that there weren’t more people leading as “prophets.” What questions does this bring up for you? Even though Joshua seems to place boundaries on the work of the Spirit and is concerned by the two men, Eldad and Medad, who prophesied in the camp, Moses welcomes the gift of prophesy—speaking in the power of the Spirit—that is continuing in their community. How do you understand a prophetic gift in today’s context? May 24, “Aldersgate Day,” recalls and celebrates John Wesley encountering the Holy Spirit in what he described as his heart being “strangely warmed.” When have you experienced the pouring out of the Holy Spirit or a “heart-warming” encounter? Just One Thing: What could you do in the week ahead to explore what it means to be unbounded by the Holy Spirit? Going Deeper on Your Own: This week, consider studying one of the lectionary texts in the following pattern: Prayerfully ask God to open your eyes to the scripture. (Psalm 119:18) Read the text (Numbers 11:24-30 or Acts 2:1-21) out loud. What do you notice about the text? What questions arise? What do you think God might be saying to you in this text? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Spirit of the Living God, we sometimes place boundaries on how we understand or experience you. On this day of celebrating the gift of Pentecost, may we be open to how you want to pour out your Spirit on our lives. Give us ears to hear your voice and the conviction to be truth-tellers. Transform us with your love to all around us. Amen. Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Rev. Dr. Ashlee Alley Crawford , Director of Adult Discipleship, an elder in the Great Plains Annual Conference of the UMC, served in campus ministry for twelve years and in leadership with the Great Plains Conference for over a decade. She has a passion for connecting people with resources and encouraging them to nurture their faith and walk in step with Jesus Christ through the power of the Holy Spirit. She has a D.Min. in spiritual direction from Asbury Theological Seminary. Ashlee also has a Certificate in Discipleship Coaching through Discipleship Ministries.

title: So That They May Be One
body: If you have decided not to observe Ascension of the Lord Sunday for the final Sunday in Eastertide this year, you are in the right place! In nearly every music ministry I have worked or participated in, this Sunday tended to feel overshadowed by Pentecost. The choir had recovered from Easter Sunday and would focus on an extra special anthem for Pentecost. I would prepare an extra special organ voluntary and/or coordinate with other musicians for hymns and special music…for Pentecost. The altar guild would start gathering materials to mark the shift…to Pentecost. With our limited time and resources, we would focus much more on the celebration of Pentecost than on the completion of Eastertide, almost to the point that it felt like Pentecost was the end of Eastertide. But it’s not. Today marks the end of Eastertide, the culmination of the season in which we celebrate Christ’s resurrection and reflect on what it means to live as Easter people. So, as you reflect on Jesus’ farewell prayer in John 17, consider how it paints a picture of who we are to be as followers of Jesus as the body of Christ in the world. How do Jesus’ words speak to you and your congregation right here and right now? What would it look like for your church to take these words to heart? Perhaps you could give everyone (not just the kids) paper and crayons before the service and ask them to draw what they think “so they may be one” looks like for your church. Or perhaps you invite an active lay member to discuss with the pastor during part of the sermon what it means for Jesus to be glorified in us, as those who have received and known the truth about who Jesus is. You might even consider having a “theology moment” to dive into a bit of Trinitarian theology and the impact our understanding of the Trinity has on our understanding of how we live and act as the church, based on John 17:11. This is such a rich passage, and while we can easily get lost in parsing it out, find ways to make the passage real to your congregants. Jesus was not giving a seminary lecture. He was praying for us. So, how do we, members of the body of Christ of all times and places, live as answers to Jesus’ prayer? Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.

title: Preaching Notes
body: There are so many threads in this tapestry that the picture might be a bit obscured. To spend the time picking them all apart is beyond the realm of these notes. We could extend the verses a little bit and talk about that sanctify request. He says don’t take them out of the world but protect them. Help them; help us live in the world as though we belong to him. Jesus calls on the Spirit of protection so that we could be made fit for God’s purposes. Jesus hands us over to God and asks God to let us live and work in this world, but as signs of God’s presence, pointing beyond the world in which we work. We could talk about what this protection means and what it doesn’t mean. Or we could talk about unity, one of my favorite themes. That’s what I’m supposed to talk about. It fits the title, “so that they may be one.” Jesus prays that we (that’s you and I and everyone else) would be one as “we are one.” We are to be as close as Jesus and God. We are called to function as parts of the Trinity, aspects of the same thing, different, but one in essence and in hope. That is what community really means. It doesn’t mean individuality is lost; differences make the whole what it is. But it does mean that we acknowledge our need for the other and acknowledge that we are somehow incomplete without the other. How can we fight amongst ourselves? How can we hate and cast stones at one another when we are part of the same whole? We are hating and casting stones at ourselves. The church is many things, but in this prayer, it is clear that the church is called to be one. Or we could talk about that “in the world” and “out of the world” language in the prayer. Yes, on one level, it is Jesus’ farewell address. He is on his way out of the world. But then we also believe that Jesus is in the world, still today. Just as we live in this world, but we don’t belong to the world. Our eyes are on eternity; our true home is in the kingdom, which might have embassies here in this world, which might break through, which might peek around the edges, but it isn’t here. At least not yet. Or we could talk about the hundreds of other things that I haven’t figured out yet. Maybe you saw something or wonder something or figured something out from this prayer that you didn’t know before or that confirmed something inside of you. Or maybe we could simply talk about what it is like to know that Jesus is praying for us, what a blessing that is, even when we don’t always know what is in that prayer, even when we don’t know how to respond to that prayer, or what we should be looking for. Just knowing about the prayer means something. In a week, it will be May 24, known as Aldersgate Day, the day we remember John Wesley and his heart strangely warmed experience, as he finally understood that Jesus’ love and salvation was a gift for him too. But instead of all that, the words that jumped out at me were those in verse ten: “All mine are yours and yours are mind and I have been glorified in them.” I know that really says more about who Jesus is than it does about us. But it also speaks deeply of relationships and f community. Peterson translates the last part of the verse like this: “my life is on display in them” (John 17:10 The Message [1] ) .How we live and love in this world is the presentation of Christ to those who don’t know him yet. How we share and give does not just reflect on us, but on Jesus. How we treat one another, honor one another, and celebrate one another and the commitments we have made is part of our faith. Christ is glorified by the way we live in community. Unity matters, in other words. It is part of our witness, part of our telling the story that matters. Disunity is a denial of the very content we claim to want to present. To belong to him, to belong to the story that matters, is to be in partnership with the whole church. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Call to Worship Easter people, Christ has completed the work of salvation, reconciling us to God so that we may know eternal life. Through Christ, we are made one with God. In life, death, and Resurrection, Christ guides us into eternal life with God here and now. Through Christ, we are made one in God. Through prayer and teaching, healing and serving, Christ draws us together as the people of God, diverse members of the one body. Through Christ, we are made one with God and one another. So, come, let us worship God who saves us into eternal life with God and one another! Thanks be to God! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, October 2025. Prayer for Unity God of all creation, who called every being into life, who is mindful of humankind in all its diversity, who embodies us with dignity, granting different gifts and talents to shape life in this world, we ask for your Spirit to unite us where we face lack of understanding and disunity in our churches, in our communities, in our countries. And in silence, we lay before you the burdens of our hearts. (Silence) We ask for your Spirit to unite us in the face of the conflicts, hatred, and violation of life experienced in so many regions of the earth and, in silence, we bring to you the pain of the victims. (Silence) We ask for your Spirit to unite us wherever fear prevents us from caring for our neighbour, from meeting people of different ethnicities, cultures, and faith communities with respect, and, in silence, we bring to you the brokenness of human relationships. (Silence) God of all creation, in Christ we are reconciled, and so we ask for your uniting Spirit to help us to overcome all our divisions that we may live in peace. Posted on the Monthly Prayers page of the Christian Aid website, http://www.christianaid.org.uk/http://www.christianaid.org.uk/. Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/09/prayer-for-unity-amidst-diversity.htmlhttps://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/09/prayer-for-unity-amidst-diversity.html. Prayer of Confession God, we believe you have called us to unity, but often we have isolated ourselves from others. God, forgive us for the times we have turned our backs on those who are different. God, we believe you have called us to live together as one body. God, forgive us for the times we have created division within your worldwide church. God, we believe you ask us to look, listen, and learn from others. God, forgive us for the times we have ridiculed and attacked those with different viewpoints. God, we believe you ask us to accept and seek to understand all who are called by your name. Forgive us for the times we have offended you by failing to love others as we do ourselves. God, we believe you call us to be one, even as you are one. Forgive us for the disunity we have harbored and make us one. (Pause to offer up prayers for unity within the church.) God and Creator of all humankind, your son Jesus Christ prayed that your church might be one, even as you our God are one. May you renew our minds and rekindle your love in our hearts, so that by the power of the Spirit, we might find the Oneness that you intend for us. God, may we recognize in your Oneness our need for unity. God, may we recognize in your Three-ness, our need for community. God, may we recognize in your creativity, our need for diversity. God, may we recognize in your Self, our need to love each other. Amen. Adapted from the Lenten series Journey into Wholeness written by Christine Sine. Published in 2009 by Mustard Seed Associates. The entire series is available on the Godspace website, http://godspace.wordpress.com . Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/01/prayer-called-to-be-one.htmlhttps://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/01/prayer-called-to-be-one.html . Benediction Beloved, go now in the blessing of the Triune God to live as diverse members of the one body of Christ, choosing unity over division, cooperation over conformity, and collaboration over exclusion as we work together for the flourishing of all creation. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, October 2025.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Unifying God of Grace, you have entrusted us with the joy of community and the calling of witness. As Jesus prayed that we might be one, we bring these gifts as a sign of our shared commitment to your mission in the world. Let our giving reflect our love, our unity declare your glory, and our generosity embody Christ’s presence among us. Use these offerings to strengthen the church, to bless our neighbors, and to glorify your name. In Christ, we belong to you. In Christ, you are glorified in us. Amen. (John 17:1-11)

title: Youth Lessons
body: Supplies: A whiteboard or individual paper and markers Note to the Teacher In John 17, Jesus prays for his followers just before his arrest. He centered his prayer on unity because he knew that the disciples would soon face fear and confusion. This lesson uses games and creative collaboration to help students practice finding unity and connections with those around them. Icebreaker: Common Thread Sprint (10 min.) When I announce, “They may be one!” get into a group of three or four people. You have ten seconds to find a “common thread” that ties your group together. Share your common thread with the group. When you hear “They may be one!” again, you need to find a new group. Again, you will have ten seconds to find a “common thread” that ties this group together. However, this one has a catch: your common thread must be a new thread that no one in your group has already used. Read scripture (5 min.) Supplies: Bible or printed handouts of John 17:1-11. Today, we are reading from the words that Jesus spoke to his disciples right before his arrest. When we know we have to leave a place, many of us will offer a goodbye or some lasting words of wisdom. In this passage, Jesus, instead, prays for his friends. He prays that the disciples “may be one,” knowing that in a short time, they would likely all feel alone. Jesus knows that being together and finding strength in their community would be important for them. As we read these words, remember that Jesus also prays for our unity. Read John 17:1-11 . Discussion (10 min.) What stood out to you in Jesus’ prayer? What’s the difference between being “one” and being identical? What divisions do you see in your daily life? Who seems to make or enforce those divisions? How did they come to be? What does it mean to be “in the world but not of it” for students? What habits create or destroy unity? Activity: One Team (30 min.) Supplies: A whiteboard or individual paper and markers Today, we will start our activity with a familiar game, but with a twist! Many of us have played “Two Truths and a Lie.” Today, we will play “Two Truths and a Thread.” Hopefully, you remember some of our ideas from the “Common Thread Sprint” we played earlier! When it is your turn, tell us two interesting facts about yourself and something you have in common with another person in this room. In our group today, we found many common threads that help us connect with one another. We are all unique, but we are all made in the image of God! That is such a cool thing: to all be uniquely ourselves while still being similar to one another. Now that we have found many things in common, let’s imagine we are a team: a sports team or any team you would like! First, let’s come up with a team name and mascot. If you have a whiteboard available, invite students to write or draw their ideas on the board. If students prefer, they can individually draw their ideas on paper and share them. As a group, select your team’s name and motto. What if this team had a jersey? What would be printed on each jersey to remind you throughout the week of this amazing team? Spend time as a group identifying what unites your group and what people should know about it. Create a short jersey motto as a group. If you have time, create a cheer for the team! Closing To close this session, stand in a circle and hold hands. If it is more comfortable, everyone can place their left hand on the right shoulder of the person next to them. After pointing out that this group is a unified body, go around the circle and ask each youth to offer a one-word prayer. After each word, the leader will start by squeezing the hand or shoulder of the person next to them. As you feel the squeeze, squeeze the hand or shoulder of the person next to you. After each word, we can feel the pulse go around the group, uniting us in prayer.

title: Children's Message
body: Sermon Good morning! I’m so glad to see you because I was thinking about all of us this week and I wonder if we have more similarities than differences. Let’s test it out. I’ll list some things about myself and you raise your hand for each one that is the same for you, okay? I like pepperoni pizza. My favorite book is The Very Busy Spider. My family has a black car. I like cats more than dogs. I love coming to church! Substitute these for facts about yourself and give a moment after each one for hands to raise. So cool! Did that seem like a lot or a little that were the same? Now this time I need you to tell me something about yourself and we’ll have the whole church raise their hand if they share that trait too. Ready church? Let the kids tell you facts about themselves as the congregation raises hands on ones that they share. If kids are too shy to share, substitute with a few more facts about yourself. Wow! That was a lot more hands raised than the first time! We all share a lot in common but I noticed something, there were some things that were special to just some of us. Like our favorite book or how many pets we have. Do you think the differences between us are important, or just the similarities? Give time for the kids to think and answer. In our Scripture today, Jesus is praying to God the Father and he asks that we (all of us) should be one, just like Jesus and the Father are one. Now that’s kind of tricky, because are Jesus and God the Father exactly the same? We’ll avoid deep theological answers today, but the short answer is no, not exactly. So what does that mean for us? Maybe it means that it’s not just the similarities between us that are important, but the differences too. We can be different and yet still be united. Like how in your family you might all like different foods but still you all sit down together to share a meal. When we bring all of our special and individual selves together, we can be one. And that is good news! It means that who we are is important to God and important to the church. When we bring our whole selves to this community, we are doing exactly what Jesus wanted, we are being one. Prayer God, thank you for all the special and unique people here today. Show us how our similarities and differences make Your church stronger. Teach us to be one together, one in You. Amen. Between the Sundays Family Activities and Conversation Starters Make a Venn diagram of similarities and differences in your family members. Which of the shared traits or preferences can we lean into this week? Which of the unique traits or preferences makes you feel most special Hold hands and try all walking in opposite directions. What happened when we all went different ways? How could we help each other get where we want to go?

title: Small Groups
body: Fellowship — Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, obviously, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes) Our church and nation seem to be rife with conflict, controversy, distrust, and disunity, yet God calls us to “be one.” What would this unity look like to you? What would have to change? Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes) Read John 17:1-11. This passage logically continues through verse 19, so consider including it in your discussion. The text is not neatly divided among these themes, but for this session, consider these sections: verses 1-5 discuss the glorification of the Son, who did the work of the Father; verses 6-10 discuss the preparation of the disciples; and verses 11-18 discuss that Jesus is leaving the world, and thus giving it over to the ministry of the disciples. Form three smaller groups, if you can, and assign one of these sections to each small group to read and examine. When they have had time to consider their text, bring the group together to compare notes. If you can, print out these questions for each group before the session. If you have fewer participants, feel free to remain as one group and explore all the questions together rather than dividing into three smaller groups. For Group 1: Verses 1-5 What does it mean that God has “glorified the Son” and the Son glorifies the Father? God has given Jesus authority “over all people.” In what ways do you see this authority exhibited (if at all)? If God has given this authority, is it possible for someone to choose not to be under that authority? If so, what does that authority mean, and what does it encompass? Eternal life is defined or described as “know(ing) you, the only true God and Jesus Christ whom (he) sent.” Does this conform to your understanding of eternal life? What sort of “knowing” could confer eternal life? For Group 2: Verses 6-10 These verses speak about the complete union God desires for all people: everyone belongs to God; God entrusted them to Jesus; Jesus taught and molded them and gave them back over to God and God’s purposes. Do you see yourself that way? Do you feel that sort of kinship with Christ and with others who claim the name of Christ? If not, what interferes with that sense of unity? Jesus taught the disciples God’s word, which they received and believed. What, for you, is the most important word from God? How have you received and believed it? How do you share the word? Jesus spoke first about glorifying God and being glorified by God. Now he says he has been glorified in the disciples. What does that mean? How does that happen? In what way could Jesus be glorified in you as a disciple? For Group 3: Verses 11-19 In this section, Jesus speaks about the world; he is leaving it, and the disciples are remaining. The state of the world is such that Jesus had to protect the disciples from it. What does this mean now? In what ways is the world a threat to faith in general or to disciples in particular? (Note: Being criticized or disagreed with is not the same thing as being persecuted.) Jesus spoke about being hated and suggested that genuine ministry begets this hatred. Why would love, generosity, forgiveness, and compassion beget hatred? Do you see this in our current social or political climate? In what ways? How should genuine ministry address this? When Jesus comes to the Father, he says the disciples may have “my joy made complete in themselves.” What is this joy? Do you feel a complete joy in your faith? Does joy characterize your personal discipleship? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: God of the world, we give you thanks that Jesus, the Christ, has saved us and that the Spirit has molded us to be your disciples in the world. We are often overwhelmed by the needs of the world and our own unworthy efforts, yet we yearn for peace with justice. Empower us for the task of discipleship and make us bold in the face of the world’s sin. Help us to employ our gifts and stand resolute in faith. We ask this in Jesus’ holy name. Amen Subscribe to receive the Discipleship Email Newsletters at https://www.umcdiscipleship.org/subscribe . Diana Hynson is a retired elder, living in Lebanon, PA. She has served in local churches, as an editor at The United Methodist Publishing House, and as Director of Learning and Teaching Ministries at Discipleship Ministries. She teaches Sunday school to a lively group of older adults who still enjoy learning.

title: Living the Sequel
body: Every year, the lectionary provides a choice for the last Sunday in Eastertide: either observe the Ascension of the Lord or the Seventh Sunday of Easter. This choice comes from the fact that historically, the Feast of the Ascension of the Lord has been observed on the fortieth day after Easter in both Eastern and Western Christianity. If you’re doing the math and realizing that means Ascension is always on a Thursday, you are correct! For liturgical traditions that observe feast days throughout the week (i.e., not solely on Sunday), Ascension is always observed on a Thursday, and the Seventh Sunday of Eastertide is observed on the following Sunday. However, for many Protestant traditions that do not observe weekday feasts (outside of Holy Week), we are left to decide whether to observe the Ascension of the Lord on the final Sunday of Eastertide or skip it altogether. This year, the Worship Team at Discipleship Ministries is offering resources for both options! If your congregation rarely, if ever, observes Ascension, consider making a change this year. The Ascension of the Lord has been a feast day in Christian communities for centuries. In general, the feast is meant to celebrate the completion of Christ’s work of salvation and Christ’s entry into heaven with our human nature glorified. What we would like to add to this understanding of Ascension is the sense of blessing or benediction (discussed further in the preaching notes). Jesus does not leave us without blessing, without promise, without equipping us for what is to come. I can think of no better way, then, to observe Ascension of the Lord than to approach the whole of worship as an act of blessing—blessing God and blessing our neighbors. Yes, I said, “Bless God.” We often think of blessing as something God graciously gives us. In the case of Luke 24:44-53, Jesus blesses the disciples, and their response is to bless God in return. So, as you prepare to observe the Ascension of the Lord, be intentional about noting who receives and gives blessings throughout the service. As you gather, name the good and gracious gifts God bestows that draw us together for worship and call the congregation to reciprocate by blessing God with praise. As you pray, declare the blessing of God’s relationship with creation that grounds our trust that God receives our prayers. Pray for discernment and guidance to be conduits of this blessing with and for our neighbors. As you go forth, call upon God to bless the gathered body and call on the gathered body to continually bless God—to praise and tell the truth about God’s good news—in all of their thoughts, words, and actions in the week to come. Let this be a worship service that, from beginning to end, embodies the blessing that Jesus demonstrates as he ascends into heaven, making the story real and present to us as present-day disciples of the Risen One. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.
