title: Preaching Notes
body: Some years ago, I was part of a small group that decided to study a wonderful book by Barbara Brown Taylor, titled An Altar in the World . It was a book about paying attention to the world around us, about recognizing that God was present in the most unlikely situations, in small things and big ones too. Taylor took a spiritual disciplines approach, and each chapter was titled “The Practice of ...” and included such items “Waking up to God,” “Wearing Skin,” “Saying No,” “Feeling Pain,” and many more. Things that most of us don’t consider spiritual practices suddenly were doorways into the experience of the presence of God. We finished the book with the last chapter, “The Practice of Pronouncing Blessings.” It was a great way to end the study and the book, with a benediction. I was surprised during that church’s Followership Retreat (that’s what we called it, instead of a Leadership Retreat) when someone said they liked the benedictions. There was a feeling of being gathered up and sent off, made complete by the word that provided an amen to the hymn that is worship week by week. A blessing, on the one hand, is a casual comment recognizing the presence of another. Sneeze in public, and a total stranger will bless you. Spending time around Southerners blessing someone is a way of empathizing, even when the person being blessed isn’t present. Tell of a difficult time in someone’s life, and you will get a heartfelt, “Bless their heart” when you are in the South. Blessings are prayers of support as well. Even “goodbye” is shorthand for “God be with you.” We invoke that presence when we wish one another well, when we part from those we know and love. And when that parting is going to be for a long time, the words almost choke in our throats, not because we are reluctant to confer the blessing, but because we know that our words are inadequate to convey such power and presence and hope. And for a moment, we wish we had a better way of blessing those we love. One wonders about the tone in Jesus’ voice as he conveyed yet another blessing on those he called and now will leave behind. It is Ascension Sunday this week, when Jesus said his goodbyes and was taken up to his place alongside the Father in heaven. We’re reading Luke’s version—or his first version, because he retells the story in part two, the Acts of the Apostles. But this is the ending of the Gospel bearing Luke’s name. “While he was blessing them.” It sounds like something he was used to doing, a habit, a way of being. There are some people who are like that. When you are with them, you feel like you are being blessed. Even if there are no formal words to that effect, no pronouncement or prayer, just being with them feels like God is smiling on you. Maybe that is what was remembered here. They were talking together about a lot of things. Jesus wanted them to finally understand. They spent most of his earthly ministry with their mouths hanging open and scratching their heads. The most common response to most of Jesus’ teaching, even from those closest to him, had to have been “Huh?” But the waiting had to be over. So, he taught them —about himself. He told them plainly. He looked back at everything that was written about him, and he pointed it out with painstaking detail. Luke says, “He opened their minds.” For some of them, it took a crowbar or the mental equivalent. Maybe it was mystical powers, maybe it was divine patience, maybe it was drawing pictures, or maybe it was the ability to move them beyond themselves long enough to see something significant in front of them. It is curious that Luke messes up the Greek in this passage. We cleaned it up for him in translation, but what he wrote was that Jesus opened their mind, not their minds. I know, the grammar instructor would have pointed out the need for the plural word there, to match the plural object - they, their needs minds , so we supplied it. But what if it wasn’t an accident? What if he meant it? What if part of what Jesus showed them was that they needed one another to figure this stuff out? He was telling them that on their own, they would be hopelessly inadequate for the task of understanding, but that together - one heart and one mind - they just might make it. Maybe a part of what he opened in them was the recognition of how much they needed one another. Then he gave them a task: to be witnesses to the world, proclaimers of repentance - getting people back on track—and forgiveness of sins - doing it without judgment or division, but with love and compassion. And then because that would be beyond the capabilities of all of them - and all of us - he promised them help. In fact, he gave them a task and then told them to wait until they received the help they needed to do that task, until they were clothed with power. That means that this power would not come from within; it wasn’t something they could generate for themselves. It had to be given; it had an outside origin. It was like a blessing. While he was blessing them, he withdrew and was carried up. It was as if the task of blessing was incomplete, at least for now. There was more to come, more that they needed, a further blessing. I mentioned that my small group finished the study, but I should have pointed out that they finished it without me. I missed the final session because I was with my brother and sister while we cared for our mom and dad. It had been a difficult time with far too many unanswered questions. Mom had a particularly bad day and told my sister that she wasn’t sure how much longer she could do this. “This” was rehab from a broken hip and the struggles with her mind about who she is and who she was, and all the worries about what might be next. Early Alzheimer’s was beginning to take its toll. After many tears and few words, my sister and my mom sat in the darkening room and held hands, while my dad expressed his grief by going for a walk. Alerted by my sister, I arrived a little later and came and sat with Mom, while she and Dad went out for some air. By the time I got there, the tears were gone and, instead, there was peace. She smiled as she took my hand and said, “I love you” about a hundred times in the hour or so we sat together, interspersed with “I am so proud of you.” I told her that it was her love that made me who I am, and that I couldn’t be prouder to have her as my mother. And then, out of nowhere it seemed, she said, “I’ll always be there. Right behind you.” It sounded like goodbye —a least to us, and it broke our hearts. But maybe we were wrong. Maybe it was a blessing, not an ending, not a parting, but something new. Physically, she is improving and could be with us a lot longer. Who knows? Something was changing, slipping away into something new, and we didn’t quite know how to handle it. She didn’t, and we didn’t. But as I held her hand in that room that seemed to close in on us, she began to glow. It was as if her love for me became visible for a moment. And I pray that mine for her was just as evident. It was a benediction, a good word in the silence of that moment, and in that love, we were both clothed with power. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Call to Worship Easter people, in this season of Eastertide, we remember the blessings God gives us—the blessings of Resurrection, salvation, and new life in Christ. We come to praise God for the blessings of Easter! We recall the blessings of creation—of clean air and water, of food and shelter, of beauty and awe. We come to praise God for the blessings of creation! We share in the blessings of community—of family and friends, of church and home, of help that is given and received. We come to praise God for the blessings of community! Easter people, we gather today to remember Christ’s Ascension, when Jesus was taken up into heaven while blessing his disciples, marking not the end but the next chapter of God’s salvific work among us. We come to bless God with our praise as God continues to bless us with all that we need to live as God’s Resurrection people. Thanks be to God! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, October 2025. Pastoral Prayer Today, Jesus, we are faced with a wonderful truth to proclaim, but also an awesome and uncomfortable responsibility. We praise you and celebrate you as Ascended Lord; we recognise that you have authority over all things, but we live in a world where greed and power and violence seem to be in control. And so, as you call us, we pray: Come as Lord, Jesus, and set the world to rights. We praise you and celebrate you as the Way, Truth, and Life; we recognise that in you our life is made whole and full; but we live in a world where death, brokenness, and need appear to be everywhere. And so, as you call us, we pray: Come as Lord, Jesus, and set the world to rights. We praise you and celebrate you as God among us; we receive your invitation to live God’s dream; but we live in a world where dreams and hearts are broken daily, and hope seems all but lost. And so, as you call us, we pray: Come as Lord, Jesus, and set the world to rights. And we pray as you taught us: Our Father… Written by John van de Laar and posted on his http://sacredise.com/Sacredise website. Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2012/04/prayers-of-people-ascension.htmlhttps://re-worship.blogspot.com/2012/04/prayers-of-people-ascension.html. Prayer of Confession While we claim to celebrate the ascension of our Lord, the way we live proclaims our lack of faith in his power to deal with the world. Let us confess the incongruity between our faith and practice. Let us pray: We come, O Lord, on this day of glory to confess our lack of trust. While we sing of your lordship over all creation, we have too often acted as though you are powerless in the face of today's events. Help us to live with confidence in your presence today and in hope for life with you forever. Amen. title: Youth Lessons
body: Supplies: Wallet-size cards: “I am a witness when I ____.” Pens or Pencils Note to the Teacher In the United States, we have seen standalone movies grow into sequels, then into franchises, and eventually into entire universes. (Pick an example that makes sense for your context: Star Wars, Marvel, Wizarding Worlds, Percy Jackson, and more.) Interconnected characters and stories, released at different times in young people's lives, can shape how they understand them. Likewise, today’s session looks at Jesus after the crucifixion. The disciples did not expect to see him again. They reconnected with their rabbi even though the disciples went in different directions immediately following the crucifixion. Icebreaker (10 min.): Today’s icebreaker is “You: The Sequel.” Imagine your life as a movie, but not just any movie, a sequel, a real blockbuster. The box office has never seen such an amazing film! Come up with your sequel! First, what is the title?  It can be anything you want! You might choose something like “The Chaos Continues” or a very hopeful drama called “A New Chapter.” Be creative! After you come up with your title, tell us the movie's genre. Is it a comedy? Sci-Fi? A drama? After giving students time to think, ask them to share their sequels. Read scripture (5 min.) As the disciples walked, Jesus walked with them, but none of them knew it was Jesus. When they realized Jesus was with them, they were afraid he was a ghost! Once they realized he wasn’t a ghost, they did the best thing you can do when you see an old friend: they fed him. Today’s scripture concerns what Jesus told the disciples after they recognized who he was. This scripture leads to the Ascension, when Jesus returned to heaven. Read Luke 24:44-53 . Discussion (10 min.) What’s the best (or funniest) “goodbye” you’ve heard? It may be in real life or the media. Think of famous goodbyes from literature, television, radio, or movies. How about the worst goodbye? What kinds of things make a goodbye easy or difficult? If you were present at the Ascension, would it feel more like a commissioning or abandonment? What do you think would make you feel that way? Where do you see the church living like a sequel right now? What parts of Jesus’ story are easiest to carry forward? What parts are the hardest? What kind of sequel do you want your faith to have? Activity (30 min.) Supplies: Paper Pens or pencils Today, we are going to imagine what it would have been like to hear Jesus explain the Ascension to the disciples. What would it have been like to hear his words and see Jesus ascend? How do you think you would react if you were there? How would you feel? Would you be scared, surprised, excited, or angry? What would you say to the people around you? Talk as a group about what that experience might have looked like. As a group, you will write a one-page script about what you imagine happened right after this passage. Take into consideration what everyone there was thinking, feeling, and saying. Your script should include one character for each person in your group. If there is time, we will take turns performing the short scenes for the group. Closing Commission Cards: Make wallet-size cards that say, “I am a witness when I ____.” Add one concrete action. Closing Prayer May we all live the sequel with courage and carry the story of Jesus into the world. Amen.

title: Children's Message
body: Sermon Good morning! I love your [insert special trait about one of your kids here] . Whoops, do you know what I just did? I gave you a compliment! Do you know what a compliment is? Take a couple answers. Yes! A compliment is something nice we say to people. How do you feel when someone gives you a compliment? Take a few answers. Compliments can make us feel warm inside, they might even make us feel a little embarrassed. They show that someone sees and cares about us. The opposite is true of mean comments. Even if the person didn’t intend to be mean, it can still make us feel sad and hurt, right? Our words are so powerful. They have the ability to make someone feel good or bad, we can use words to tell people where to go or what to do, words can create a story or paint a picture. Words can even be a gift. Do you know what a blessing is? A blessing is something we say to one another to give them the gift of words. It shows that we care about someone else and want good things for them. Share about a blessing your church does. This could be the benediction at the end of worship, a blessing you give graduates each year, a blessing you say each week after the children’s sermon, or another common instance of blessing that the kids will recognize. Right before Jesus left his disciples, he gave them a gift - he gave them a blessing. He promised them that when they go out, telling the whole world about Jesus’ forgiveness and love, that they would be clothed with power. This promise and the ones we say here in church, are a present we can give one another. They give us comfort and peace when life gets hard. This is the gift of a blessing. Prayer God, thank you for the blessings you give us each day. Help us to give others the gift of blessings this week. Amen. Between the Sundays Family Activities and Conversation Starters Work together as a family to write a short blessing you can share. What could we say that is a gift to someone? Will these words encourage, comfort, or empower? Make a list of people you can bless with your family blessing. Why are these people important to you? How do you think they’ll feel when we/you bless them? Find an easy time in your daily routine to bless your children with the family blessing. It could be as they jump out of the car for school, at the breakfast/dinner table, or as part of a bedtime ritual. Does this feel different than praying with or for your children? Consider what God’s daily blessing for you might be. Written by Sammy Waters. Sammy has served in family ministry in the North Georgia and Horizon Texas Conferences over the past 6 years. After receiving her Master of Divinity from Candler School of Theology, she moved to Texas where she has enjoyed working with children, youth, and families to design new ways to engage in worship, learn the stories of God, and create space for wonder.

body: Blessing God of Presence, even as Christ ascended, you did not leave us alone. While he was blessing them, you were preparing us to carry the story forward, to be your witnesses, to live in hope and power. title: The Story Abides
body: What is our story? I think it’s a good question to ask from time to time. We tell ourselves all kinds of stories about our lives, our church, our workplaces, our community. Stories help us make sense of our experiences, even when some of them may not be the most helpful and/or leave out details. That’s the way our brains work. We are limited in what each of us alone can remember and interpret about our experiences. So, in the church—and significantly, in worship—we have to pay attention to our individual stories and how we bring those stories together to tell our shared story of life in the body of Christ. In this week’s reading from John 14, Jesus reminds us that the Spirit abides in us. To give it a bit of a literary/library spin, the Spirit is our archivist. The Spirit lives in us, guides us, and gathers us together, preserving us as the living story of the body of Christ. So, how do we tell that story in worship? In one sense, every time we gather for worship, we tell our story. Every time we read scripture or sing the songs of the faith, we tell our story. But what is the story of your community? Of your local church? Of your experience as the church in your particular context? As you plan worship, draw on the heart songs of your congregation. Sing the words and the tunes that have accompanied your people through the ups and downs of the last several years or even decades. Lean into the music that tells your story. Find people who can witness to your church’s story right now. Include a time for testimony or ministry moments where one or two members share how they’ve experienced Resurrection life within your congregation. Show pictures from the last year in the life of the church. Pray for the present needs and concerns as your church seeks to share love and make disciples in your particular corner of the world. As you reflect on the past and the present, pray and bless one another to continue the story into the future. Remember: the Spirit abides in us, weaving a living, breathing narrative of God’s love that unfolds in and through each of us as we live together in the body of Christ. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.

title: Preaching Notes
body: The Farewell Discourse is an amazing document. We have taken these words as instructional, and indeed they are. Like a professor attempting to prepare students for the upcoming final exam, Jesus wants to make sure his followers have everything they need for what comes next. And we are grateful for that. We have lived through these words for the centuries that have followed. We have learned about how to be the church, how to be disciples, how to see all the people and invite them into a deeper relationship with the Christ we have come to know. There is so much to learn from these powerful words. Perhaps the mirror to Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount, the Farewell Discourse in John’s Gospel gives us a picture of the church at its best. It is a vision to live into—a practice that is simple on the surface but takes a lifetime to perfect. Let me not diminish that informational or instructional function of these verses. But there is also something more intimate going on here. There is a binding, a gathering up that happens as Jesus shares his heart and his future with those who have been following him. He is offering a legacy, a continuation in and through those disciples. He is putting all his theological eggs in their basket. All of his missional hopes now reside in these somewhat inept followers. And he wants to make sure how okay he is with that. Not just okay. This is the plan. This is the next step on the world-changing effort, this kin-dom-building transformation. And here’s the difficult part: he will be with them. It’s difficult to comprehend, that is. Yeah, it’s the next chapter when he talks about abiding, but he plants the seed here. “On that day you will know that I am in my father and you in me and I in you” (John 14:20 NRSV. “That day”? That day where they see him, but the world does not. That day where they understand life a little bit better. That day. On that day, they will know that the story abides, because it abides in them. They are the story. They live the story. They are the witnesses that this was more than just a dream. They are proof that hope is possible; that there is something beyond our vision. The story abides in them. That’s the gift that he offers them in this instructional, intimate moment—a promise of presence, his presence, the story’s presence, the Spirit’s presence. Ah, the Spirit. That is how we hold on to something beyond our grasp. That is how we make sense of the story, the experience, the relationship with this one we call Lord. The Spirit gives us utterance, we say. But how does this work? How does this Spirit abide and become the means by which we become the story, the gospel on the hoof, as it were? There is a lot that we don’t know about the Spirit, no question about that. The Spirit blows where it will and all of that. But if we listen carefully to what Jesus tells us here, there is a lot we do know or can believe in, anyway. We need to extend the reading a few verses, though. You are hereby given permission to extend the lectionary gospel reading for this week. Take thou authority! First of all, we can know or believe that access to or awareness of the Spirit is a function of faith. It involves a relationship with Jesus Christ. “The world,” John quotes, “cannot receive” the Spirit. The world doesn’t know the Spirit, not because they aren’t worthy, but simply because they don’t have this relationship of love that opens the door to the experience of the Spirit. Oh, it is possible to have an experience of God without a relationship with Jesus the Christ. But to know and be known by the Spirit takes something deeper, an act of will, an offering of self to the Lordship of Christ. “I will not leave you orphaned” says Jesus. I will not leave you Fatherless, out of touch with the Father. There is a connection, a link to the Father that once came from the person of Jesus and now comes through the Spirit. The function of the Spirit, according to Jesus in verse 26, is to teach and to remind. This Advocate (which is the Greek word “ paraklete ” and is sometimes translated Helper, or Comforter, or Counselor) is the abiding presence that connects to our sense of who we are. We are reminded of what we already know. We are reminded of the teachings that we learned as children but may have forgotten or chose to set aside for a time. It is the Spirit that comes and whispers in our ears to remind us that we are better than we sometimes behave. It is the Spirit that comes to remind us even in the darkest of nights that we are not alone. It is the Spirit that reminds us that we are loved - especially in those moments when we feel most unlovable. It is not just what we already know that is recalled by the prompting of the Spirit. We are pushed further; we are asked to climb higher. The Spirit also teaches, calling us to new levels of understanding and experience. The Spirit works with our spirits to claim deeper truths and new applications. We are stretched beyond our childhood faith as we grow and learn and live into the realm of the Spirit. We have much to learn under the tutelage of the Spirit, and much of it is learned by doing. When we tell the story, even the part of the story that abides in us, that intersects with our lives, then we learn more about what it means to be alive, to abide in him and know he abides in us. We grow into the story we tell. And in us and in the community of which we are a part, the story abides. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Call to Worship Easter people, no matter the bends and curves in our path, Jesus does not leave us alone on this journey of faith. God gives us the Spirit, our Advocate and Helper. The Spirit lives in and among us, pointing us all toward the way, the truth, and the life of Jesus. God gives us the Spirit, our Guide and Guardian. The Spirit draws us into God’s story, showing us how to cooperate in writing God’s dream into reality. God gives us the Spirit, our Dream-Giver and Story-Keeper. Easter people, God’s story abides in you, calling you to live as co-creators of love and abundant life. We come to worship God and listen for the Spirit who inspires, guides, and helps us join in God’s story, until God’s kingdom comes on earth as it is in heaven. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, October 2025. Prayer for the Day God of all time and space, you initiated the relationship of love and generosity with creation at a time before and beyond all knowing. Through the Word and the Spirit, you continue in eternal love for all beings. Fill us with a deep and abiding awareness of your presence, your call, and your grace in our lives and in our world. Shape us into the people you have made us to be – poured out in creative mercy for the sake of Jesus Christ in all creation. Amen. Written by Lutheran Julia and posted on RevGalBlogPals. Re-posted on the re:Worship website at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/05/prayer-eternal-love.htmlhttps://re-worship.blogspot.com/2017/05/prayer-eternal-love.html . Prayer of Confession Eternal God, Creator of all that is, In you, we live and move and have our being. You have placed us on earth and sustained our being through the produce of the land and the cleanness of the air we breathe. You have made us for each other, to tend and care for the weak and ensure a just sharing of the earth’s resources. But we are part of a proud and hard-hearted people who hoard what the earth provides and seem loathe to share the fruits of our labours, who live for today with little thought for tomorrow, who are afraid to let pain and suffering affect us. Incarnate God, you know us in our inner being. In your grace, you offer us forgiveness even before we have the chance to articulate our sorrow. You embrace us in all our sinfulness And, in doing so, give us the chance to start again to learn from the example you have given us in Jesus, who chose the way of the Cross that all might know the depth of your love for all you have made. Spirit of God, open our hearts and minds that we may grasp your forgiveness, and forgiven, seek to forgive others and to live a life of reconciling love modelled on the example of Jesus Christ, in whose name we make this prayer. Amen. Written by the Very Rev. Dr. Sheilagh Kesting on the Church of Scotland’s Starters for Sunday, http://www.churchofscotland.org.uk/http://www.churchofscotland.org.uk/. Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2016/02/prayer-of-confession-reconciliation.htmlhttps://re-worship.blogspot.com/2016/02/prayer-of-confession-reconciliation.html. Benediction Go now to love and serve God in the blessing of the Spirit who journeys with you as we live the unfolding story of God’s dream for creation here and now. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, October 2025.

body: Abiding Spirit of Love, you have not left us orphaned. Even in our uncertainty, you draw near, whispering truth, stirring memory, teaching us to live as those who know we are loved. title: Youth Lessons
body: Supplies: Sticky notes Markers, pens, or pencils Small stickers (any shape- stars, circles, etc.) Note to the Teacher This week, we are talking about how the story of Jesus abides with us. Teens may not be familiar with the word abide. To abide is to keep showing up, to stay connected and close, to stay rooted. In this lesson, we talk about how God shows up for us and to us, where we see God, the Holy Spirit, and Jesus in our lives. The words “God,” “Holy Spirit,” and “Jesus” are used interchangeably in this lesson to demonstrate the different ways we see God in our lives. Icebreaker (15 min.) Supplies: None (but students may request items such as paper for their lesson) Everyone is an expert in something! You may be an expert at curling your hair or doing yo-yo tricks. You might be an expert toast toaster. You may be an expert in silence or in folding a paper football. You have sixty seconds to teach me something, anything. If we don’t have the supplies you need (for example, if you want to teach how to ride a unicycle), you will have to simply describe what you would use if you had it! Read Scripture (5 min.) Supplies: Bibles or handouts with John 14:15-21. This is a continuation of what Jesus told his disciples at the Last Supper. In the midst of explaining that he would soon be going somewhere that they could not, Jesus said that the Holy Spirit would always be with the disciples. Read John 14:15-21 . Discussion (10 min.) What words in this scripture passage describe the Holy Spirit? How have you heard someone else describe the Holy Spirit? Even though Jesus says that the world “doesn’t see” the Spirit, how might you see the Spirit in the world today? What’s the difference between memorizing a story and living it? Where do you see the story of Jesus alive today? How do you compare, experience, or understand God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit? (If your pastor or another church leader is interested in joining this time and discussing the Trinity, it is an opportune moment!) Activity: Sightings Gallery (25 min.) Supplies: Sticky notes Markers, pens, or pencils Small stickers (any shape—stars, circles, etc.) We talk a lot about God being with us. Sometimes that is hard to understand. Today, we are thinking about where we see God, the Holy Spirit, and Jesus in our lives. Sometimes, these are personal sightings when we see Jesus in the people around us or in our experience of peace and hope. Sometimes, we see God at school, in our family, or in our community. Sometimes we see God when we read scripture and find comfort or meaning. In today’s “Sightings Gallery,” we will think about where we see the Spirit in many forms and many places. Take four to six sticky notes and write on each one a different place you have seen God. You can be as specific or as general as you are comfortable. Once you have written your sightings, place your sticky note on the wall. After you post your sightings on the wall, quietly take a walk through our “Sightings Gallery,” carrying your small stickers. You have three small stickers to place on sticky notes that resonate with you—whether you agree, disagree, or just like it! Break into small groups to discuss any sightings with a lot of stickers. Why do you think these sightings resonated with so many people? What does this tell us about where we should pay attention and look for the Spirit this week? As a group, finish this sentence together: “God, help us notice you when…” We will share these with the larger group. For today’s closing, we will stand in a circle so that we can see one another. Think of one word you want to carry with you throughout this week to help you remember that God is there. God abides with us. We are rooted in God’s story. We will go around the circle and share our word. It’s okay if your word is the same as someone else’s. You do not have to share if you are not comfortable. Simply say “pass” if you do not want to speak. Blessing: Invite the students to join you in a simple breath prayer as you dismiss them. Practice this together three times before the group parts ways. Inhale : “You are with me.” Exhale : “Help me notice.”

title: Children's Messages
body: Children's Message Scripture: John 14:15-21 Good morning! I’m so happy to see you today because this week I learned something interesting and really want to share it with you. Share something you learned, no matter how small. Ex: learned about a new bug in your garden, what the moon is made of, or how fast tuna fish can swim (up to 43 miles per hour!). Did anyone else learn something new this week? At school, at home, or out in the world? Take a few answers. Wow! You all sure learned a lot. There are lots of different ways to learn. We could sit at our desks and listen to a teacher. Or we could investigate with microscopes. We could read a book or look at pictures. We could even sing to learn - that’s what we do each week when we sing in church! What songs do you love to sing when you come to church? Give time for the kids to think and answer. Each time we sing a song in church, we learn a little more about God and grow a little closer to one another. God’s love is for each of us (point at kids individually) and for all of us (spread arms wide to encompass everyone) . Do you ever get a warm, fuzzy feeling when everyone is singing, and the whole space is filled with music? The Gospel of John tells us that the Holy Spirit abides in us; that means that God is in you and me, teaching us about love and pulling us towards one another to share that love. We are all gathered together, even when we can’t see each other, by the Spirit that lives in us and teaches us to love. Make the shape of a heart with your hands. Let’s share the love of God this week! Prayer: God, we thank you for the Holy Spirit that pulls us together and teaches us to love. Help us to share your love with one another this week. Amen. Between the Sundays Ideas: Family Activities and Conversation Starters Add family members’ favorite songs to your car ride or walking playlist. What makes those songs special to you? What do you think about when you sing these songs? Spend 5-10 minutes learning something new together by checking out a library book, running a simple experiment, or looking closely at something unexpected. How did you feel learning something new together? I wonder who else might be interested in this new thing we learned? Try holding hands while you pray this week. Do you feel more connected this way or when you pray alone? Brainstorm other ways you could connect during prayer time. Written by Sammy Waters. Sammy has served in family ministry in the North Georgia and Horizon Texas Conferences over the past 6 years. After receiving her Master of Divinity from Candler School of Theology, she moved to Texas where she has enjoyed working with children, youth, and families to design new ways to engage in worship, learn the stories of God, and create space for wonder.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship — Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, obviously, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes) Father and Son seem easy to describe and discuss, but the Spirit may be more elusive. In pairs or small groups, talk about what you believe about the Holy Spirit. How is the Spirit identified? What is the role or function of the Holy Spirit? Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes) Read John 14:15-21 . Share this background of United Methodist theology: We receive God’s grace in (at least) three distinct ways. First is God’s prevenient grace, going before us to prepare our hearts and minds for belief and relationship. Second is God’s justifying grace, which leads to our acceptance of and commitment to our call to faith and discipleship. Third is God’s sanctifying grace, which nurtures our spirits and deepens our love of God and our surrender to God’s will. Optional : Have a copy of The United Methodist Hymnal available. Take a look at the “Affirmations of Faith” (880, 883, 884, 885) that describe the Holy Spirit. List those attributes as support for the other teaching activities. The Preaching Notes (5/10/2026) suggest three insights to the Holy Spirit. The first is that the Spirit brings us to awareness of God and God’s activity in our lives and the world (prevenient grace). Think about your earliest experiences of church, God, and faith. In what ways were you prepared to believe in God? For a relationship with God and with others in the faith? Who was your mentor or teacher? Who modeled the faith for you? The second insight is that the Holy Spirit reminds us (justifying grace). At some point, we must take responsibility for our own beliefs and growth. What was the turning point for you? When did you realize that you were forging your own beliefs and relationship with God apart from your childhood (or other) lessons? When we face novel, disturbing, painful, or challenging circumstances, it is easy to simply react, but the Spirit’s role is to remind us of all that Jesus taught us. When has this reminding function helped you? What changed? The third insight is that the Holy Spirit teaches u s, lifting us to new, deeper levels of understanding (sanctifying grace). Simply growing older does not guarantee maturity in life or in faith. Still, the Spirit is present to teach us to dig deeper, think more critically, pray more diligently, and practice the spiritual disciplines more faithfully. How do you put yourself in the hands of the Spirit for this sort of growth? What spiritual disciplines do you practice? What new discipline might stretch you beyond your comfort zone? How would you learn? Who might help you try? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Most Holy God, who comes to us as Creator, Savior, and Spirit, we thank you for your abiding presence in our lives. Open our hearts and minds more fully to your reminders and teachings. Help us to grow more deeply in our surrender to your will. We ask this in Jesus’ name and for his sake. Amen.

title: You Know the Way
body: If you’ve been planning worship using the Revised Common Lectionary for a while, you’ve probably noticed that the first few Sundays after Easter usually focus on post-Resurrection appearances. However, as we enter the later weeks of Eastertide, our Gospel readings revisit Jesus' pre-Resurrection teachings, which elaborate on his salvific work. That is why our reading this week features Thomas again (or, rather, for the first time) questioning Jesus’ words. I sometimes imagine Thomas as a six-year-old, sitting in front of his teacher who says, “And you know the way to the place where I am going,” and immediately shooting his hand in the air while interjecting, “Nuh-uh! I don’t know! How can we know the way?” It might be tempting to good-naturedly roll our eyes at Thomas’s outburst, but in this story and in John 20, Thomas serves as a stand-in for us. Thomas asks the questions (or, later, expresses the doubts) that we hold in our hearts, speaking what we might not be ready to utter. Thankfully, Jesus gives Thomas (and us) an answer: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Follow Jesus, and we’ll know the way to the place where Jesus is going. Great. Now, how do we do that? I think it is interesting that Jesus doesn’t just answer that he is the way—he adds truth and life. It is as if to say, “I am the way, and to follow the way, you have to both believe the truth of who I am and live the way I show you to live.” Charles Wesley picked up on this interplay of belief and ethics when he wrote in a hymn for children, “Unite the pair so long disjoined,/Knowledge and vital piety.” (Follow the link to find the hymn set to the tune ST. CATHERINE. It would make an excellent opening hymn!) So, consider how you will unite belief with holy living in worship. If you regularly recite the Apostles’ Creed or another statement of faith, take a moment before speaking it together or after, perhaps even in the sermon, to highlight how the beliefs we proclaim in the creed guide the way we live. As you pray for the community, draw connections between our trust in God’s faithfulness and our call to love and serve our neighbors, to live the answers to the prayers we pray because of God’s steadfast love. Also, create space for the community to raise their questions, to embody Thomas in response to the scripture reading. What is the way? How do I know the truth? What does life in God look like? This might involve offering a litany of questions woven with a prayer response, or having a time of silent prayer for congregants to offer up their questions and listen for God’s voice, or inviting people to speak their questions out loud during the sermon. As we discussed a few weeks ago, Thomas is not wrong for asking questions. We learn to follow the Way when we bring our questions into the open, trust God to hold them, and seek after the truth and life God gives together. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.

title: Preaching Notes
body: I love exploring new cities. Although Minneapolis isn't a new city for me (I have been there for the Festival of Homiletics many times, and I recommend this event highly, https://festivalofhomiletics.com/why-foh/), I love walking for miles through the "skyway system," building to building without ever going outside and at least two stories up. The views are interesting, and I got lost only once. But not for long. Minneapolis has impressive art and architecture, and a fascinating cultural mix in this former Norwegian Lutheran bastion. Minneapolis has sports enthusiasm that rivals any city. Plus, I have spent hours sitting in churches in the center of Minneapolis and could give a review on the comfort levels of the pew padding. While wandering around looking for the next church I was to attend, I ran across a street sign that made me stop in my tracks. That, of course meant that people behind me had to adjust their pace as well. What was the surprising sign, the one that led to the title of this piece? There on a post alongside the downtown street was a sign that read, "Bus Doesn't Stop Here." Think about that for a moment. All over the place are signs saying, “Bus Stop.” That makes some sense, doesn't it? That's what we expect. Isn't it? But then there it was, in black and white, posted on a pole beside a busy road in the center of Minneapolis: “Bus Doesn't Stop Here.” I tried to imagine what the need was for such a sign. Was there a regular occurrence of people standing at that spot waiting in vain for a bus that wasn't going to come? Was there a time when the bus did stop there and now they were letting us all know that it wasn't stopping there anymore? Or was it just an arbitrary action by a bored bureaucrat who wanted to make a statement? Someone's idea of a joke, perhaps. Trying to bring a smile to the busy downtowners who were hurrying to jobs and errands and back again. Or maybe they were deadly serious. Maybe this was only the first of the signs to come. Anywhere there was a bus-sized space on the road, they were going to put up a sign—just in case there was some doubt. They were trying to draw the lines clearly: This is a bus stopping place. This is not a bus stopping place. They wanted certainty and clarity on where the lines were drawn. My mind began to reel at the sheer number of signs that would be necessary for such an endeavor. To mark every place where the bus didn't stop seemed a monumental task. It would keep the sign makers in business for years, if not forever. It seemed an exercise in futility. Why not concentrate on telling us where the bus did stop and not worry about where it didn't. Then it occurred to me that this is some people's view of the church. We need to put up signs so that people know where we won't go, what we won't do, or what we won't allow. For many people, often people on the outside, our faith is a "no" faith. We want to make very clear what the boundaries are and what is outside the lines. So, we put up the "bus doesn't stop here" signs to make sure everyone is clear on what we consider wrong, or bad, or evil. Now, you might argue that if we aren't clear about what is wrong, or bad, or evil, then pretty soon people will begin to assume that nothing is. And then we'll be the church of anything goes, which is pretty much what the culture has become. So, no wonder we are becoming irrelevant. It might explain why some of the more conservative churches seem to be growing, because people want to be clear where the boundaries are. If we are too vague on that, then no one wants to bother. So, draw those lines; put up the signs; make sure people know where the bus doesn't stop. That's what people want. Or is it? Do people really want to know what is bad, what is evil, where the bus won't stop? Or do they want to know where it does stop? Maybe what draws people to those churches is not negativity, but certainty. And since the only certainty in town is negative, they'll go with that. But what if we offered an alternative? What if we were certain too? But certain of where the bus stopped, not where it doesn’t. Or better yet, what if we were certain about where it was going? Not just in an otherworldly way, but in a “this is what life is about” way. What if instead of telling folks what is wrong with their lives, we spend our time talking about what a good life consists of? That's what I think Jesus came to do. That's what I hear in our passage for this week. Most of the time, we think the passage is about heaven. And it is. But what if it is more than that? What if it is about now and not just someday? Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you know me, you will know my Father also (John 14:5-6 NRSV). I know. This is a funeral text. This is the reminder that there is a place to go when we are done with this world. But still. Take another look. Might the many dwelling places be also right now and right here instead of just when we all get to heaven? "The one who believes in me will also do the works that I do" (14:12).Believing and doing are tasks for this life, aren't they? If we are doing the works that he did, then we are dwelling in his house, right? Now, today, not someday. The invitation is to get on the bus and ride with Christ. To do this, we need to know where the bus does stop . We don't really need to occupy ourselves with where it doesn't stop. Or it ought not be what defines us. Instead, let’s find how to be obedient to Christ's will. Let’s find how to do greater works based on our belief of what is possible, rather than simply being concerned about what is not. “You know the way,” says Jesus. You know the way to live. You know the way to the kin-dom, a place of relationship and belonging. You know the way to the kingdom, a place of reimagining how human community might work, what values we might live by, what priorities we might embrace. You know the way. It seems to me that one of the saddest moments of our lives would be to hear Jesus say, "Have I been with you all this time, and you still don't know me?" Let's get to know him by knowing what he is for and what he is about. Let's find out where the bus does stop. And then get on board. Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Call to Worship Easter people, in the midst of our questions and doubts, Jesus answers: I am the way, the truth, and the life. In the midst of our worry and distress, Jesus assures us: I am the way, the truth, and the life. In the midst of misinformation, confusion, and distrust, Jesus reminds us: I am the way, the truth, and the life. In the midst of dead ends and impossible challenges, Jesus shows us: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Come, let us worship as we learn to follow Christ, our way, our truth, and our life. Come, let us worship! Thanks be to God! Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, October 2025. Prayer for the Day Ever-gracious, Way-Making God, we celebrate the gifts of your Spirit. You have not fed us a diet of shame or shrinking, but with the milk of your truth, you have made us strong and faithful servants of Christ. You call us to take up the mantle of justice and to follow wherever faith leads us. You fill us with strength and hope, and you invite us to share in the cost and joys of discipleship. You promise us splendor and beauty in this life and in the world to come. Meet us here, we pray, that your word will be fulfilled in our hearing and that your Spirit will fill us with courage. Amen. Written by Rev. Elizabeth Dilley on the Worship Ways (United Church of Christ) website at https://www.ucc.org/worship-way/easter_5_may_10/ . Prayer of Confession Merciful God: We claim that you sent Jesus to us to take away the sin of the world and to say that we are part of that sin. Maybe our small errors add up; or maybe there is no degree to sin, that one is as hurtful as another. Help us not to dwell on vocabulary. Help us not to focus on what sin means but to acknowledge that we do things that hurt other people, and the creation, and ourselves, and you. Come into our hearts, then, and give us strength and courage to be less hurtful and more loving. These things we pray in the name of Jesus, who showed us how this is done. Amen. Assurance of Forgiveness Friends, hear the good news: Jesus came not to condemn us, but to love us and save us and show us the way. Know that we are forgiven and be at peace. Alleluia! Amen. Written by Beth Merrill Neel on her blog, “Hold Fast to What Is Good.” Used with permission. Posted at https://holdfasttowhatisgood.com/liturgy/prayer-of-confession/ . Benediction May God bless you as you leave this place to follow the Way, to seek after the Truth, and to rejoice in the Life of the Triune God who draws us together and sends us out to be agents of Resurrection life in a hurting world. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, October 2025.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Way-Making God, your offer to us is not just to believe in heaven, but to live the kingdom life here and now. Through Jesus, you show us the way, the truth, and the life—calling us to deeper trust, wider welcome, and greater works of grace. As we bring our gifts, we step into that life, choosing generosity over fear and hope over judgment. Use these offerings, and use us, to make your dwelling places visible in our community, in our compassion, in our courage. We give, because we’ve heard your voice. In Christ’s name. Amen. (John 14:1-14)

title: Youth Lessons
body: Supplies Needed: Signs for the icebreaker (North, South, East, West) Bible or handouts with John 14:1-4 on them Paper and pens or pencil Note to the Teacher Directions aren’t always as simple as reading a map or a list of instructions on an assignment. Jesus gave directions to the disciples at the Last Supper. The disciples’ hearts were troubled, and they were desperately grasping for reassurance and understanding of what was about to happen. This week, we explore the directions Jesus left his disciples and how they apply to our lives today. Icebreaker: What Which Way!? (10 min.) Supplies: Labels for four corners of the room: North, South, East, West. Students start in the center of the room. Begin the game by calling out a silly challenge that includes an action and the direction to do that action. For example, “Run east and spin three times” or “Run south and freeze facing east!” Do a few practice rounds until students feel comfortable with how the game works. Once everyone seems comfortable with the game, explain that after each direction, the last student to correctly complete the action in the correct direction will call the next challenge. Read Scripture (5 min.) Supplies: Bibles Today, our scripture takes place during Jesus’s big “goodbye” to his disciples, his friends. It wasn’t in front of a big crowd; it was a conversation with friends. Jesus reassures his disciples and ensures they understand the directions for continuing this ministry. Read John 14:1-14 . Discussion (10 min.) What does it mean to teenagers today for your “hearts to be troubled?” Why do you think Thomas asked, “How can we know the way? How is the idea of a “way” different from rules or laws? What do you think Jesus means by “I am the way”? What does it mean to you to “know Jesus” beyond facts? What is a “work of Jesus” that you and your peers can do? What would help you to do this “work of Jesus,” especially when your heart is troubled? What causes hearts to be troubled in your friend groups, schools, and communities? Activity (30 min.) Supplies: Paper and pens or pencils In today’s reading, Jesus says, “Do not let your hearts be troubled.” Sometimes that is easier said than done! It would be helpful to have a toolkit, perhaps a first-aid kit, when our hearts feel troubled. Divide the students into groups of three to five people and invite them to imagine a toolkit they can “build” with five items that will help them when they feel their “hearts are troubled” (such as scripture, music, friends, prayers, etc.). Encourage teams to include, as one of their five items, a prayer they will write together, based on the reading from John 14. If there is time, have students share the toolkits with the whole group! For today’s closing, pray over the students, “May the Spirit remind you that you are not alone; help Jesus’ story stay rooted in you.” Or invite a student to pray the group’s written prayer over the class.

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship — Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, obviously, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes) In pairs or small groups, consider the dynamics behind doubt and certainty. (It’s entirely possible to be certain, and be wrong, you know.) How difficult (or not) is it for you to deal with ambiguity? Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes) Read John 14:1-14 . We tend to think of this passage in the context of funerals, but it really is missional in its intent. Ask participants to outline the steps in this conversation to better see where it leads. (vv. 1, assurance; vv. 2-3, promise of continuing guidance and protection; vv. 6-7, confirmation of God’s intended pathway; vv. 8-11, clarification of Jesus’ testimony and “proofs”; vv. 12-14, marching orders) Think about the process in your congregation for disciple-making. What groups, classes, helps, resources, and mentors are in place to shepherd members through the process of being assured of God, finding a safe place to learn and grow, direction for and assessment of gifts for ministry, and opportunities to use those gifts for the church and community? What role do you play in cultivating ministry, either to use your gifts or to nurture the gifts of others? If the church does not have such opportunities in place, what might you do? The promise of Jesus in verse 12 is extravagant and extraordinary, but it must be possible if he has promised it. What does it mean that we are intended to “do greater works than I (Jesus) do because I (Jesus) go to the Father”? Consider that this is addressed not only to individuals, but to the group of disciples. The next claim is also amazing: “I will do whatever you ask in my name, so that the Father may be glorified” (v 13). Note that this is a qualified statement; twice. What is asked must be in Jesus’ name and must glorify God. What does it mean to ask for something in this way? What sort of requests do you think would be acceptable? Unacceptable? Why? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Magnificent God, maker of extravagant promises and giver of amazing gifts, we thank you for the ways you lead us into your pathways and empower us to use our abilities for your kingdom. Inspire and embolden us for ministry in your name; gladden our spirits as we live out your mission. We pray in Jesus’ name. Amen.

title: Knowing that Voice
body: I don’t like being compared to sheep, which is quite unfortunate, because the Bible compares us to sheep all the time. I don’t like that sheep are dirty and smelly, but more than anything, I don’t like that they aren’t smart. At least, that’s what several camp leaders and preachers have told me over the years. But if sheep aren’t very smart, how do they know their shepherd’s voice? In some ways, that’s the question for all of us this week. We, like sheep, don’t always make smart decisions. We stray; we get trapped in ditches; we bleat and cry, waiting for the Shepherd to rescue us. But do we, like sheep, know our Shepherd’s voice? I have long thought that worship and discernment go hand in hand. We often talk about discernment as if it’s purely an individual skill, something we learn and implement in our own lives, but not something we learn and practice together. But, like it or not, we’re sheep (according to this week’s scripture), and sheep practice discernment together. They know and follow the Shepherd’s voice together. Worship gives us opportunities to listen to, identify, and follow the Shepherd’s voice as a community. As you plan worship, consider how you can help your congregation learn to identify and follow Christ’s voice individually and together. If the Shepherd provides abundant life, what does abundant life look like in your community? Where is it lacking? Is that a place where the Shepherd might be calling you to go? Pray for guidance to notice the paths of abundant life and give your congregation time to listen. Teach them the spiritual practice of being present and invite them to practice it as a response to the sermon. Share a simple song like “We Will Follow/Somlandela” (Worship & Song 3160) and encourage congregation members to sing it throughout the week to draw their attention toward God’s voice. These are practices that our congregants may or may not be familiar with, but that we all need reminders to practice as we grow in the life of faith together. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.

title: Preaching Notes
body: “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.” Great verse, one my very favorites. But what does it mean? Or in this case, how do we get it? What do we need to do to experience this abundant life? We need to learn to listen. Okay, it is never as simple as that. That is only a part of our task. We need to not only listen but to follow. We need to not only listen but to trust. We need to not only listen but to hope. We need to not only listen ... well, you get the idea. But for this week, we need to focus on our need to listen. Following, says Jesus in this passage, is a product of listening. He will lead, he tells us in verse four, but only after we’ve come out at the sound of his voice. He will lead, he tells us, if we choose to follow. And the only way we can follow is if we know that voice, if we can recognize the sound of it. It calls for a certain amount of discernment. There are voices we need to run from—voices that don’t have our welfare and safety in mind, voices that don’t want us to prosper and grow, to know the joys of abundant life. So, how do we know? How do we figure out which voice is his and which voice is the one that wishes us harm? Unfortunately, John doesn’t help us out a whole lot in these verses. In part, it takes a lifetime of study and devotion. John Wesley called this lifetime process sanctification , the process of moving closer to Christ, becoming more like him. There is more involved than we can pull out of John, chapter ten. But there are a couple of hints in these verses. First, the Shepherd knows our name. The call that comes from Christ matches us in the deepest essence of our being. He calls us to be who we are, not who we might think we want to be, or who the world tells us we need to be. Following Christ has a “rightness” about it. It is a response to the longings of our soul. And the more we follow, the more we are truly ourselves. In verse nine, we are told that Christ is the way: “Whoever enters by me will be saved.” But then the text says we will come in and go out and find pasture. Come in and go out. There is a lot of movement in the Christian life. We don’t just sit; we don’t just find a safe corner and remain there. We don’t lounge in place waiting to be fed. We find our sustenance in coming and going, in study and service, in spending time with the word and going out to share it. We are called to be coming and going throughout our lives. If we feel as though we are pulled in too many directions, then we need to come back. Worship with the community of faith, study together the Word or books on Christian living or knowing, find places of fellowship for laughter and joy together. On the other hand, if we feel as though our faith isn’t doing much and is all head knowledge , then we need to go—go and serve, go and help, volunteer in the community, do something with our hands, teach or share, help or heal. There are lots of opportunities for us to be going out in service to the world. The odd thing is that it is both in the coming and in the going we learn to listen. We listen through the study and contemplation of the Word. But we also listen through the voices of need and hope in the people around us. And the more we listen, the more we come to recognize the voice of the Shepherd. A life of no regrets is a life lived in hearing distance of Jesus Christ. Did you hear that voice? Rev. Dr. Derek Weber, Director of Preaching Ministries, served churches in Indiana, Arkansas, and the British Methodist Church. His PhD in preaching and media is from the University of Edinburgh. He has taught preaching in seminary and conference settings for more than twenty years.

title: Liturgical Resources
body: Call to Worship Easter people, we gather to worship and to listen, to learn the sound, the feel, the cadence of the Shepherd’s voice. We come seeking our Shepherd’s voice. We gather to worship and to discern, to learn how to recognize our Shepherd’s voice amidst the chaos and noise of our lives. We come seeking our Shepherd’s voice. We gather to worship and to find shelter, to learn to trust our Shepherd’s voice to guide us to safety and provide for us in all things. We come seeking our Shepherd’s voice. Come, let us worship as we listen for the voice of Jesus who guides us, protects us, provides for us, and draws us together in community. We come to worship as the family of Christ, a flock seeking and following our Shepherd’s voice. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, September 2025. Prayer for the Day Loving Shepherd, you know our names; you care for us. When we face darkness and death, journey beside us. When we hunger for your love, fill us with your presence. When we are fearful, feed us at your table. May we dwell in the house of goodness and mercy all the days of our lives. Amen. Adapted from Mary Petrina Boyd and posted on Ministry Matters, http://www.ministrymatters.com/ . Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2015/04/opening-prayer-psalm-23.html . Prayer of Confession God of wisdom, we confess the foolishness of our ways, and our failure to follow you in your paths of right relationships – with you and with others. We have gone astray; we feel lost. We have upheld our own interests first, to the detriment of others. We have failed to be generous with the poor and abandoned our efforts to bring about justice. We feel the stains of our sins, God; have mercy on us according to your steadfast love. Wash the sinfulness out of us and help us to live more faithfully as your servants. We seek your unfailing Lordship and ask for your guiding hand on our lives. You are the immortal, invisible One; to you be honour and glory forever; amen. Assurance of Pardon Merciful and loving God, we thank you for never losing hope for us. When we are lost, you are there on the lookout for us, bringing us back to you like the good shepherd that you are. Your Word tells us of the joy in heaven that awaits us. May this joy flow into our lives each day, and be faithfully reflected into the world around us. Thanks be to God, our Great Shepherd. Posted on the Presbyterian Church in Canada website, http://presbyterian.ca/worship/ . Re-posted on the re:Worship blog at https://re-worship.blogspot.com/2013/08/confession-lost-and-found.html . Benediction Beloved, may God bless you with open hearts and minds so that together we may pay attention, discern, and follow your Shepherd’s voice, for that is the way that leads to abundant life on earth as it is in heaven. Amen. Written by Dr. Lisa Hancock, Discipleship Ministries, September 2025.

title: Offertory Prayer
body: Faithful Shepherd, who calls us by name, you invite us into a life that is rich in meaning, deep in joy, and bold in compassion. You speak, and we long to follow—although the world is noisy and the path unclear. In this moment of offering, we quiet our hearts to listen again. Receive these gifts as signs of our trust in you. May they be used to bring abundance to others, to feed the hungry, to strengthen the lost, and to proclaim your voice of love. In coming and going, in worship and service, make us more like Christ, in whose name we give and pray. Amen. (John 10:1-10)

title: Youth Lessons
body: Supplies Needed: Bibles (or printed copies of John 10:1-10) Paper Writing Utensils Coloring Supplies Optional: Blindfold/scarf Hymnals Note to the Teacher Students have been hearing for years how important it is to listen, as though listening is a simple task. Sometimes, listening isn’t so easy. This week, we will practice listening and learning which voices to pay attention to. Icebreaker: The Voice (10 min.) One student should be selected to be The Ear. The Ear should leave the meeting space (be mindful of your church’s safety policies for this game). The student doesn’t have to go far. This activity will also work if the student selected as The Ear closes their eyes or puts on a blindfold. The remaining students quietly select a student to be The Voice. When the student who was selected to The Ear returns, that person stands with their back to the group. The Voice will say a simple phrase (for example, “Good Morning”). The Ear can ask The Voice to repeat the phrase up to two more times before guessing who was selected as The Voice. If you want to make this icebreaker more challenging, invite other students to say other simple phrases while The Voice says the selected phrase. Be sure The Ear knows which sentence is the one to listen for. Read Scripture (5 min.) Supplies: Bibles (or printed copies of John 10:1-10) We often hear Jesus referred to as the shepherd. The shepherd guides us, the sheep. As a shepherd, Jesus keeps us safe and helps us be safe. In this week’s passage, instead of a human keeping the livestock safe, a physical barrier, the “sheepfold (similar to a corral) protects the sheep. Let’s dive in to see what Jesus tells us about coming into and going out of the enclosure. Read John 10:1-10 . Discussion (10 min.) What “voices” try to tell you who you are most often? Which of those voices are external and which are internal? What distractions steal your attention the fastest? Which distractions keep your attention and become habits? What helps you know that you can trust what you hear? What are some dangers of never “coming in” (rest/worship) or of never “going out” (service/action)? What practices can you do to make sure that you can hear the voice of God above everything else? Activity: A Shepherd’s Soundtrack ( 30 min.) Supplies: Paper Writing utensils Coloring supplies Optional: Hymnals Divide students into groups of three or four and ask them to create a playlist for the shepherd. First, they create a name for the playlist related to today’s passage. For example, “Known by Name,” “The Gate,” or “The Shepherd.” Encourage students to be creative! Their playlists should include six to eight songs that represent themes from today’s passage. The songs may be songs students know, songs found in the hymnal, or made-up song titles that fit. If there is time, ask students to create the album cover art for their playlists. Closing: To close today’s lesson, invite students to share their playlists and describe why they chose the songs they included. Send students off with a blessing: “May you hear the Shepherd call you by name, feel the Shepherd keep you close, and may you follow the Shepherd with every step.”

title: Small Groups
body: Small Groups Fellowship — Snacks or a Meal (10 minutes with snacks; longer, obviously, if there is a meal). Gathering Time (5-10 minutes). In pairs or small groups, discuss what “abundance” means to you. Is your notion different from anyone else’s? How do you quantify “abundance” in intangible things? Group Dialogue (Approximately 30 minutes). Read John 10:1-10 . The Good Shepherd says that his sheep know his voice. How do you discern the voice of God in the midst of so many competing ideologies, ideas, lies, half-truths, promises, and assurances? What “voice” do you trust the most? The Good Shepherd also says that he leads the sheep to “go in and go out.” To where do you “go in and go out”? Where is the safety of the “sheepfold” or “pasture” for you? How does respite there prepare you for going out? What do you “go out” to do for the Good Shepherd? Jesus said that whoever enters by him would be saved. What are you saved from? What are you saved for? What difference does this make in your life and your community day by day? Following Christ, the Good Shepherd, is an exercise in abundant living. What does this mean to you? If your life feels something other than abundant, what needs to change? How might that happen? What disciplines or spiritual practices will bring you more closely into the “sheepfold”? Is this something you want? How diligently would you be willing to work at it and for it? Prayer (10 minutes). Share prayer requests and respond appropriately. Sending Forth (2 minutes). End with the following prayer, a similar prayer, or the Lord’s Prayer: Loving God of salvation and abundance, we yearn for your clear voice above the din of dissension and chaos. Lead us into the safety of your fold so that we may be empowered and equipped to go out into the world to be your bold and faithful witnesses. Amen.

title: Astounded Us
body: How often are we surprised anymore? I think about this from time to time when I watch how my child reacts to seemingly simple things with so much surprise. I pick up salmon to make for dinner—“Mom, I didn’t know you were getting salmon!” I plan a playdate with a friend—“Mom, I didn’t know we were having a playdate!” I declare that it’s bathtime—“Mom, I didn’t know that it’s bathtime!” (To be honest, that last one is not considered a pleasant surprise, but somehow it still seems to be a surprise every time a bath night rolls around.) As an adult, my world is filled with much more certainty because I’m the one shopping for groceries, planning playdates, and keeping track of the schedule, among other things. And while there are many things in this world I cannot control, I’ve been alive long enough to respond to many things—from weather to politics to the latest celebrity news—with “I’m shocked, but I can’t say I’m surprised.” In today’s scripture, the travelers on the road to Emmaus declare that they were astounded by the news from the women who were the first witnesses to the Resurrection. “Astounded” is like surprise-plus. The Greek word translated as “astounded” is ἐξίστημι, which includes a sense of “to throw out of position; displace.” Here are these disciples who are displaced; they’ve gone off on their own in response to news that is so surprising, so astounding that it has thrown their certainty into chaos. These disciples remind us that Resurrection is unsettling. Now, I know, none of us wants to plan a whole worship service around unsettling our congregation. That is neither helpful nor pastoral. And I don’t recommend planning a big surprise in worship, either. Rather, find ways to wrestle with the “unsettledness” of Resurrection. How do our lives change in light of the Risen Christ? There’s a beautiful hymn, “Christ Is Alive” (United Methodist Hymnal 318), that you might use as an opening hymn to set the scene, to prepare the congregation for reflecting on and answering the question: “What does Resurrection require of us now?” Consider, too, how to lead your congregants in prayer. What are the unsettled places in your community where new life and new possibilities engender both excitement and uncertainty? Name them in prayer. What are the uncomfortable places where God is calling you to seek Resurrection? Confess the challenge of choosing Resurrection over the status quo. What voices astound you with their declarations of good news? Listen to them. Eastertide is a time of joy, joy that sits alongside the astounding, displacing news that Love has conquered death. Invite your congregation to live in the tension between joy and astonishment, because this is how we learn to live as Easter people. Dr. Lisa Hancock, Director of Worship Arts Ministries, served as an organist and music minister in United Methodist congregations in the legacy Northwest Texas and North Texas Annual Conferences. After receiving her Master of Sacred Music and Master of Theological Studies from Perkins School of Theology, she earned her PhD in Religious Studies from Southern Methodist University, where she researched and wrote on the doctrine of Christ, disability, and atonement. Lisa is also the co-lead of Growing in Grace: Accessible Worship for All God’s Children.
